‘Love-boat diplomacy’: Trump envoy’s $450M megayacht tour angers Italians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
19:32:21 UTC
04:32:21 KST

Shortly after arriving in Rome in May last year, Tilman Fertitta, the U.S. ambassador to Italy, spent $2 million of his own money renovating Villa Taverna, the lavish residence where the ambassador stays in the Italian capital. He then spent three weeks commuting to work by helicopter from a massive yacht he owns. More recently, he has effectively moved all of his work to another megayacht, where he is now completing a voyage around Italy.
Fertitta, 69, is clearly not an ordinary ambassador. He is the great-grandson of Sicilian immigrants to Texas and one of the wealthiest people ever to serve as a U.S. ambassador. He owns several hotel and restaurant chains as well as the NBA’s Houston Rockets. His net worth is estimated at $11.2 billion, placing him 312th on the list of the world’s richest people.
In recent months, Fertitta has embarked on an extensive voyage around Italy aboard the 118-meter Boardwalk, a $450 million megayacht, hosting some of the most lavish parties of the Italian summer. In scenes that appear to have been lifted from films about the Gilded Age, government officials and mayors mingled with CEOs and celebrities while enjoying the yacht’s amenities: two helipads, two swimming pools, four hot tubs, a diving room that looks like something out of a James Bond movie, a spa and a gym.
Fertitta is paying for the parties and the voyage himself. The cruise began two and a half months ago and Fertitta describes it as a "diplomatic tour" along Italy’s coastline, saying it is part of celebrations marking 250 years of U.S. independence. It also allows him to avoid the renovations taking place at his official residence in Rome. The Washington Post, which described the voyage as "love-boat diplomacy," reported that the ambassador himself estimated the cruise costs him $1 million a day.
It is not unusual for U.S. ambassadors, particularly in Western Europe, to be political donors who receive appointments from presidents they supported. But such political appointments have generally been made relatively selectively. Under Trump’s second administration, however, 90% of ambassadorial nominees are personal political appointments, a far higher proportion than under previous administrations.
The result is a parade of wealthy people and politically connected figures within the U.S. diplomatic corps, including a new group of billionaire ambassadors: Charles Kushner, father of President Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and ambassador to France; banker Warren Stephens, ambassador to the UK; and hair-care mogul Leandro Rizzuto Jr., the U.S. ambassador to the Organization of American States.
But even among them, Fertitta is in a league of his own.
"You have an ambassador that has cachet, and the Italians like that," he told guests aboard the yacht before a party in Bari that drew local politicians and military officials. "They like that [they’re] important enough to us that you’re going to come into our town, on your big boat, and pay respect to us and have us in your home."
Despite that claim, the ostentatious voyage has drawn considerable criticism in Italy. The backlash was evident when the yacht docked in Venice last month and protesters greeted him with chants including "There is no room for billionaires!" and "Venice is not the United States!"
Angelo Bonelli, an Italian lawmaker and co-chair of the Greens and Left Alliance parliamentary group, also launched a parliamentary inquiry seeking clarification on the security costs of the tour. The security operation includes police officers, helicopters and vessels that Italy is required to provide for the ambassador, at the expense of local taxpayers.
The government in Rome has not disclosed the cost, but Bonelli estimates it at between €3 million and €4 million. In an interview with the Washington Post, he said that even without that expense, the tour was pointless and did not fit Italian norms.
"Such a display of wealth is frankly odious,” he said. “In Europe, or at least here, it doesn’t work."
But Ambassador Fertitta is unfazed by the criticism.
"It doesn't bother me in the least because protesting doesn't bother me," he told CNN.
He argued that his voyage is actually helping Italian security forces maintain their readiness.
"“Remember, those boats are out there doing something and those people are out there doing something, and it’s a great exercise for them," he said. "Because there’s a lot more important people than me that they protect at times, so they’re getting good practice. But it’s been nothing crazy or unusual. …That’s the opposition’s job, to find something wrong with this."
As ambassador, Fertitta’s job was supposed to be relatively straightforward. At the start of his tenure about a year ago, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni was Trump’s strongest ally in Europe. But since then, relations between the two have run aground, partly because Meloni refused to rally behind the U.S. in its war with Iran, and Fertitta has tried to mediate amid their increasingly bitter public dispute.
In an interview with the Post, he said that after the confrontation between Trump and Meloni intensified and the two exchanged harsh words, he warned the Italians that they had no chance of winning such a direct confrontation.
"What I’ve said is, ‘You don’t want to get in a verbal volleyball match with Donald Trump’ because he’s relentless, and he’s going to win," he said. "Donald Trump’s a charming person, and you just have to know … politicians around the world need to know how to handle him."
All of this is taking place as the ambassador continues to conduct his work from his yacht, on a voyage expected to end on September 7. It inevitably raises questions about the intersection of personal wealth and government service, but those are not issues that appear to concern the Trump administration.

04:31:00 KST

U.S. President Donald Trump's approval rating remained at the lowest level of his political career amid growing dissatisfaction over the Iran war and the economic policies, according to a new Reuters/Ipsos poll that concluded on Monday.
Just 33% of Americans approve of the job Trump is doing in the White House, marking the third straight Reuters/Ipsos poll with that share of respondents giving the president a thumbs up.
Trump's political brand looks increasingly like a potential weight on his Republican Party, which will be defending slim congressional majorities in the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
Democrats appear more fired up about the elections, with 46% of self-identified Democrats describing themselves as "very enthusiastic" about voting in November, compared to 31% of Republicans, according to the poll, which surveyed 1,167 U.S. adults nationwide.
Asked which party they would vote for if the congressional elections were held today, 36% of independents in the survey picked Democrats and 22% said Republicans.
Since mid-August, Trump's popularity has held at a level it only briefly touched early in his first presidency, and well below the 47% share of Americans who approved of his performance early in his current term.
His rating is lower than the low point his predecessor, Democrat Joe Biden, had with 35% approval, in October 2024.
Like Biden, Trump has been dogged by widespread discontent over high levels of inflation.
Gasoline prices have surged since Trump ordered the U.S. to start bombing Iran in February, and just 36% of Americans approve of the war, the Reuters/Ipsos poll showed.
The conflict has had long lulls over the period, but in recent days the two sides have traded missile strikes and since the war's outset, Iran has largely blocked a major transit point for the global oil trade.
Some 71% of Americans, including four in 10 Republicans, disapprove of how Trump is handling the cost of living.
For the last month, registered voters in the survey have been saying the Democratic Party has better ideas for the economy than the Republican Party, the first time Democrats have led on the issue in about a decade.
The four-day poll had a margin of error of 3 percentage points in either direction.

Santos 'never intended to manipulate any market'

Kalshi imposed a fine of about $2,600 and three-year suspension on Buckhout.
Efforts to contact Stephen Cloobeck and Ben Midgley, former candidates for governor in California and Maine, respectively, who were also penalized by Kalshi, were unsuccessful.
The boom in election betting is likely to test the ability of prediction markets such as Kalshi to police insider trading, according to experts and data shared with Reuters. Kalshi and rival Polymarket have said that they are equipped to identify and block suspicious activity and protect market integrity.

New pressure on PM to allow telehealth for voluntary assisted dying
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
19:30:16 UTC
04:30:16 KST

South Australian government defies Albanese, urges change to voluntary assisted dying telehealth laws
In short:
South Australia's Labor government has openly defied the prime minister's position on telehealth in voluntary assisted dying (VAD), calling for urgent change to a federal law.
It comes weeks after the ALP national conference endorsed a motion committing Labor to removing telehealth restrictions, despite Anthony Albanese's own personal opposition.
The state government has called on the Commonwealth to amend the definition of "suicide" in the criminal code to exclude VAD care.
South Australia has become the first state to formally urge the Commonwealth to change a federal law preventing doctors from using telehealth in voluntary assisted dying (VAD), openly defying the prime minister.
In a letter to federal Attorney-General Michelle Rowland, senior ministers in the Malinauskas government have "implored" the Commonwealth to "take immediate action", arguing the restrictions disadvantage terminally ill people in regional, rural and remote Australia.
"I doubt that I will be the only health minister advocating for this change," SA Health Minister Blair Boyer told ABC News.
The SA ministers' letter said a provision in the Commonwealth criminal code was preventing doctors from using telehealth for VAD and forcing patients to travel long distances to attend appointments, with some dying before being able to access the care.
The intervention puts the SA government at odds with Anthony Albanese, who has expressed personal opposition to changing the law, concerned about the risk of coercion and elder abuse if telehealth replaced compulsory face-to-face consultations.
The letter comes just weeks after the ALP national conference endorsed a motion, committing Labor to removing telehealth restrictions, despite Ms Rowland — the highest law officer in Australia — voicing strong concerns on the conference floor.
Penned by Mr Boyer and state Attorney-General Kyam Maher, and co-signed by VAD practitioners, clinicians and advocates, the signatories to the letter want the Commonwealth criminal code amended so VAD care is not treated as "suicide" under federal law.
Some states and territories permit limited use of telehealth in VAD, but the federal code overrides those provisions by prohibiting the use of a "carriage service" to counsel or promote suicide.
It means doctors risk $220,000 fines and a criminal record for using phone, email or video to discuss the self-administration of VAD medication.
VAD at a glance
Read more
- Each jurisdiction has its own VAD laws, but all require at least some face-to-face consultations as part of the assessment and approval process.
- There are also safeguards, including restrictions on when doctors can provide information about VAD and making it an offence to induce someone to request or access the care.
- Anthony Albanese has argued safeguards could be weakened if more consultations were conducted via telehealth.
"We suggest a targeted amendment to the definition of 'suicide' under the criminal code such that the definition explicitly excludes conduct authorised under a state or territory VAD law," the letter said.
"We now implore the Federal Government to address this issue and amend the criminal code to better reflect contemporary healthcare practice and to reduce unnecessary disparities between jurisdictions."
The move fits a pattern of the Malinauskas government pursuing its own agenda on contentious national policy debates.
In recent years, South Australia has outlawed political donations, established a royal commission into artificial intelligence and spearheaded the development of a teen social media ban, an initiative followed by the federal government.
Mr Boyer predicted other states would soon join the push to change the criminal code, signalling broader pressure could build.
"This is not an attempt to water down safeguards that were put in place. It is simply an attempt to make good on the commitment that was made," he said.
"This is something that should be available to people regardless of where they live."
The federal government recently blocked debate of a VAD telehealth bill pushed by independent MP Kate Chaney, with Health Minister Mark Butler telling parliament he was "not convinced" telehealth was "well suited to VAD right now."
Doctors divided
Views on telehealth in VAD care are also divided within the medical community.
While the Australian Medical Association (AMA) has backed calls to change the federal law, some doctors remain opposed.
Ballarat geriatrician Mark Yates argued the risks of elder abuse and coercion outweighed the benefits of expanding telehealth access.
Professor Yates said data showed rural, regional and remote Australians were accessing VAD at rates proportional to the population, suggesting there was no widespread access problem, and that individual cases of people missing out highlighted broader failures in regional health services.
"I think [those cases] are an argument for jurisdictions to get their acts together and provide better support and services, whether it's wider-based VAD services or better palliative care,"
Professor Yates said telehealth made it harder to detect coercion or abuse and argued the risk was compounded by the small number of doctors providing VAD.
"When we started the VAD debate, the idea was that it would be your friendly GP who's known you for 30 years who would help you with this. That's clearly not the case. There are one or two practitioners that have [overseen] 300 people with VAD in the short time we've had it.
"To appreciate where coercion or abuse sits without being face to face, I think is incredibly difficult. That is where the risk lies."

Iraq sentences militia member for kidnapping American journalist, in rare move against Iran proxies

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
19:30:08 UTC
04:30:08 KST

Iraq has sentenced a man to fifteen years in prison for kidnapping American journalist Shelly Kittelson in late March, the victim announced on social media on Monday.
Kittelson was kidnapped on March 31, when she was targeted by Iranian-backed militias, and released in early April.
“Iraq's Central Criminal Court has sentenced Amir Rahim Jabar Lazim to 15 years in prison under the Anti-Terrorism Law after convicting him of being one of several armed men who took me hostage in Baghdad on March 31,” read her X/Twitter post.
She added, “I am grateful to the Iraqi judiciary for its attention to my case, as well as to all those who helped get me out alive. And, of course, to those who love Iraq as much as I do and try to build a better future for it. Thank you from the very depths of my being.”
Rudaw media in Iraq added that “an Iraqi court has sentenced a key suspect to 15 years in prison under the country's anti-terrorism law in connection with the abduction of American journalist Shelly Kittleson in Baghdad earlier this year, a case the US linked to the Iran-backed Kata'ib Hezbollah armed group.”
Rare prosecution of Iranian-backed militia member
The development is important because Iraq rarely prosecutes members of the Iranian-backed militias. In the past, members of the militias have sometimes been detained by authorities, but are often released. There is now pressure in Iraq for the government to rein in the militias, after the US encouraged Baghdad to make progress toward disarming the groups.
The militias have been involved in acts of kidnapping and murder for years. In 2020, Dr. Hisham al-Hashimi was assassinated by gunmen outside his home in the Zeyouneh neighborhood of Baghdad. He was a journalist and security expert. Kataib Hezbollah was also behind the kidnapping of Princeton researcher Elizabeth Tsurkov in March 2023. She was released in September 2025.
Rudaw noted that “the Central Criminal Court in Baghdad on Sunday sentenced ‘the convict - Amir Rahim Jabbar Lazem - to fifteen years in prison’ pursuant to Iraq's Anti-Terrorism Law ‘for the crime of kidnapping the complainant - Shelly Renee Kittleson of American nationality - on March 31, 2026, in the al-Saadoun area’ in the Iraqi capital, read a copy of the ruling obtained by Rudaw.”
He has already been detained since April for the kidnapping. Other men were involved in the kidnapping. Video at the time showed other individuals. An eyewitness at the scene at the time told Rudaw that "three people surrounded her [Kittleson] and one of them grabbed her from behind."
Kataib Hezbollah suspected to be behind kidnapping
Kataib Hezbollah, which is believed to have been behind the kidnapping, is one of the most powerful of the Iranian-backed militias in Iraq. It has been sanctioned by the US as a terrorist organization. It is part of the paramilitary Popular Mobilization Forces.
Its former leader Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis was killed in a US drone strike in January 2020. He was driving in a vehicle alongside IRGC Quds Force head Qasem Soleimani, who was the target of the strike and who was also killed. The fact that Muhandis and Soleimani were in the same vehicle illustrates the close ties between the IRGC and Iranian-backed militias.
It does not appear Iraq will hold Kataib Hezbollah responsible for the kidnapping or other crimes. Kataib Hezbollah was also likely behind a drone attack that killed three American service members in Jordan in January 2024. It has also been behind attacks on Saudi Arabia.

Segalovitz joins Ra'am, calls for Jewish-Arab political partnership
'It is impossible to fix the country without partnerships, including political ones,' Segalovitz said during the announcement
United Arab List (Ra'am) Chairman Mansour Abbas announced Yoav Segalovitz as number two on the list during a press conference on Monday.
Segalovitz becomes the first Jewish candidate to appear on an Arab party list.
Segalovitz is a former police commander responsible for the Israel Police's Intelligence and Investigation Division, which is precisely why Abbas has selected him for second place on the list.
"The first thing that every father and mother in Arab society thinks about before they fall asleep: Will my children return home safely?" Abbas said during the announcement. "To create change, you need partnership. Civil partnership. To create change, you need to see the other as a human being, not as an enemy."
Abbas extolled Segalovitz as one of the key contributors to the reduction in crime in the Arab community during the 2021-22 government, saying, "When it comes to crime, an officer who has stood up to criminals his whole life without asking what their religion is. An honest, quiet man who doesn't seek headlines. Yoav Segalovitz."
He then turned to the current government and said "In the last four years, the numbers have only increased. Close to a thousand murdered. It could have been different, and we know it, because we saw it happen."
Abbas explained his decision to select Segalovitz, saying, "I'm not looking for someone like me. I'm looking for someone who knows how to do the job. And the Arab citizen who buried his son doesn't ask what the policeman's religion is."
He then said that crime in the Arab community must concern Jewish citizens because, "The weapon that fires today in Tamra will fire tomorrow in Afula. The organizations that collect protection fees from an Arab grocery store owner also collect from a Jewish garage owner. This is not a problem for the Arabs. This is a problem for the state."
Segalovitz echoed Abbas's words, saying, "It is impossible to fix the country without partnerships, including political ones. I explicitly want to break the paradigm of the existing fault lines and prevailing discourse."
"The common notion that after October 7 it is not possible to have a political partnership with the Arab parties is baseless and false," he said. "We can cooperate politically based on trust, recognizing our differences, and committing to joint action."
"There are past grievances, and there is a bloody history. We cannot change the past. The role of political leadership is to change reality and create a better future."
Segalovitz is the only Jewish politician with a positive rating in the Arab community.
The Likud Party responded to the announcement by claiming that Segalovitz, Abbas, Eisenkot, and Liberman would establish a Palestinian state. "Segalovitz won't hide the fact that Mansour Abbas is not willing to recognize Hamas and Hezbollah as terrorist organizations and is pushing to establish a Palestinian state. Together with Eisenkot and Liberman, they are going to establish a Palestinian state government."

Former French PM Balladur dies at 97

Former French PM Balladur dies at 97
PARIS, Aug 31 - Edouard Balladur, who was France's prime minister from 1993 to 1995, has died at 97, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said on X on Monday.
A leading figure of France's centre-right, Balladur was the architect of a sweeping privatisation drive that saw the sale of some of France's most prominent companies, including banks Société Générale and Paribas — later part of BNP Paribas — as well as broadcaster TF1. He also pushed through a reform of France's politically sensitive pension system in 1993.
"Edouard Balladur is closely associated with fifty years of the history of the Fifth Republic. From his early days working alongside Georges Pompidou to his appointment as Prime Minister, he was a leading figure in our public life," Lecornu said on X.
"Edouard Balladur was a statesman with a reformist spirit and will remain a role model for many men and women in his political family," he added.
A stiff technocrat, Balladur was often portrayed by his critics as aloof and disconnected. Plantu, a press cartoonist, sketched him as an aristocrat wearing a wig and seated in a sedan chair. The satirical weekly Le Canard enchaîné renamed him "His Courteous Smugness".
Balladur served as prime minister under Socialist President Francois Mitterrand. REUTERS

Top US general says no plans to send troops to polls for November elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
19:20:28 UTC
04:20:28 KST

Top US general says no plans to send troops to polls for November elections
Remarks come in response to concerns from Democrats that military could be used to interfere in elections.
The chairman of the United States Joint Chiefs of Staff, the country’s highest ranking military officer, has assured an opposition lawmaker that there are no plans to deploy troops to polling places during elections on November 3.
“The Joint Force has no plans to send Federal military personnel or Federalized members of the National Guard to polling places during the 2026 elections,” General Dan Caine said in the letter obtained on Monday by The Associated Press news agency. “Likewise, the Joint Force has no plans to use such personnel to seize ballots, voting machines, or other election-related material.”
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Trump administration to dismiss Reflecting Pool charges against David Hearn
- list 2 of 3US judge repeats block on Trump’s bid to limit voting by mail
- list 3 of 3Trump threatens to report journalist Kristen Welker to broadcast regulator
Caine’s letter was addressed to Democratic US Senator Elissa Slotkin of Michigan, who recently asked Caine and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to confirm they won’t send troops to the polls. Caine, who advises Hegseth and President Donald Trump on military matters, also wrote: “I have neither received nor anticipate receiving any unlawful order concerning the role of the Joint Force in the upcoming November 2026 midterm elections.”
Anxiety among Democrats that the Trump administration could try to meddle in the midterm elections has grown, particularly after the president deployed federal agents in Democratic-led states over the objections of local leaders. He said they were needed for immigration enforcement and due to crime and protests.
Slotkin told the AP earlier in August that Trump has been laying the groundwork to claim November’s elections will have been stolen. She noted that Trump contemplated using the military to seize voting machines after his loss in 2020 to President Joe Biden and has deployed the National Guard to cities against the wishes of Democratic leaders. He also deployed active-duty Marines to Los Angeles during his immigration crackdown in 2025.
Federal law prohibits the deployment of armed federal forces to election locations unless “necessary to repel armed enemies of the United States”. If any element of the military were to get involved, it would likely be the National Guard under state control.
“The nonpartisan tradition of military service and the constitutional guardrails that prevent our military from becoming a domestic police force for one political party are essential to maintaining our democracy,” Slotkin said in a news release this month announcing her letters to US military officials. “Thus, our nation’s senior-most defense and security leaders are the final failsafe for our democracy.”
White House chief of staff Susie Wiles denied in a Vanity Fair interview last year that Trump would use the military to suppress voting in the midterms.
Sonja Thrasher, Slotkin’s press secretary, said Hegseth has not replied to the letter asking him to confirm troops won’t be deployed to the polls in November.
Slotkin had asked for a response by last Thursday.
In 2020, General Mark Milley, then-chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, responded to a similar letter from Slotkin, then a member of the US House of Representatives.
“I believe deeply in the principle of an apolitical U.S. military,” Milley wrote. “In the event of a dispute over some aspect of the elections, by law U.S. courts and the U.S. Congress are required to resolve any disputes, not the U.S. military.”

Defense lawyers for singer D4vd withdraw from murder case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

19:18:42 UTC
04:18:42 KST

Singer D4vd lost his high-profile private lawyers on Monday at a hearing where he entered a new not guilty plea to charges that he killed, sexually abused and dismembered 14-year-old Celeste Rivas Hernandez.
It is not clear why Blair Berk and her colleagues Marilyn Bednarski and Regina Peter parted ways with the singer, whose legal name is David Anthony Burke. They were replaced by a lawyer from the Los Angeles county public defender’s office.
The defense attorneys said in a statement only that the judge granted their request to withdraw after finding that Burke qualified for a court-appointed lawyer.
“We continue to support David and his defense against these serious charges,” the statement said. The lawyers would not answer specific questions about their departure outside the courtroom.
Burke earned at least $10m through his music from 2023 through 2025, according to testimony from his money handlers at a previous hearing. It is not clear how he financially qualifies for a public defender whose job is to defend clients who lack the money for a lawyer.
Without providing details, the public defender’s office said in an email that it had completed a thorough financial evaluation and found he was eligible.
Deputy public defender Walid Kandeel took over the defense. Judge Charlaine F Olmedo denied his first request as the singer’s lawyer to delay the arraignment. Olmedo demanded a plea on Monday instead, and scheduled a status conference for October. No trial date has been set.
Olmedo ruled after a five-day evidentiary hearing in July that there was enough evidence for Burke to stand trial on charges of murder, continuous lewd and lascivious acts with a child under 14 and unlawful mutilation of human remains.
A second arraignment and plea, like Burke gave on Monday, is standard practice after such a hearing and finding. He is eligible for the death penalty, but the district attorney, Nathan Hochman, said after Monday’s hearing that his office was still deciding whether to pursue it.
Hochman said the new lawyers would make no difference in how his office pursues the case, though the switch may delay the process. He said regardless of the timing, his office was “ready to prove all three charges beyond a reasonable doubt”.
Outgoing attorney Berk has for years been among the go-to lawyers for A-list clients, who have included Leonardo DiCaprio, Jennifer Aniston, Reese Witherspoon, Harvey Weinstein and Ozzy Osbourne.
Kandeel, the new attorney, said in a statement: “We recognize the loss of life underlying the allegations and extend our sympathies to those who are grieving. At the same time, David Burke is entitled to a defense that takes his circumstances seriously and carefully examines the evidence.”
Authorities allege Burke stabbed Celeste to death in April of last year after she threatened to expose sexual abuse that began when she was 13 and crater his rising career just days before his debut album dropped.
“i will end ur career and ur life,” she told him in a text message sent the night before her death.
Prosecutors said the following night Burke sent an Uber for her and stabbed her when she entered his house. They presented evidence that her phone went permanently silent at that moment.
Celeste’s dismembered and decomposing body was found in the trunk of Burke’s Tesla in the Hollywood Hills in September while he was on tour.
Prosecutors argued at the July hearing that the “mountains of evidence” they presented were overwhelming. Burke’s lawyers argued that the evidence of murder was insufficient.

Mohammed Hamood Ali Al Ragawi and Rania Abushamala
31 August 2026•Update: 31 August 2026
All Christian schools in Jerusalem announced Monday evening that they will suspend classes starting Tuesday after Israel failed to renew entry permits for more than 70 teachers and staff, preventing them from reaching their schools.
The new academic year in Israel and Jerusalem is scheduled to begin Tuesday.
In a statement, the Christian schools in Jerusalem said that as they prepared to open for the 2026-2027 academic year, they were surprised by the “failure to renew entry permits for more than 70 teachers and employees from our educational, administrative and support staff, suddenly and without prior warning.”
They said the failure to renew the permits prevented the teachers and employees from reaching their schools and directly affected preparations for the start of the academic year.
The absence of such a large number of staff affects various aspects of school operations, including educational, administrative and health services, as well as cleaning and security and safety measures, the statement said.
The schools said the situation “makes it impossible to ensure a safe and stable start” to the academic year for students.
Following consultations and coordination with relevant parties, parents’ representatives and Jerusalem schools, they decided to suspend classes beginning Tuesday, Sept. 1.
The suspension will continue “until the necessary permits for teachers and employees are reissued and renewed, ensuring that the educational process proceeds safely and properly,” they added.
The schools stressed their commitment to students’ right to education, warning that repeated measures of this kind “undermine the stability of our schools and hinder their ability to fulfill their mission,” while negatively affecting students, their families and educational staff.
They called for the crisis to be resolved as soon as possible and for the permits to be renewed to allow students and staff to return to schools and the academic year to proceed normally.
Separately, Munther Isaac, pastor of the Evangelical Lutheran Christmas Church in the West Bank city of Bethlehem, condemned the Israeli measure.
“Israel’s pressure on the Christian presence in Jerusalem continues,” Isaac said on US social media company X.
“Christian schools in the city are going on strike because Israel refuses to issue permits to their West Bank teachers,” he added.
Since October 2023, Israel has restricted entry permits for Palestinian workers from the occupied West Bank, including teachers, coinciding with the start of the genocidal war in the Gaza Strip.

The two leaders met on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan.
“However, we continue to try to realise the path of agreement and understanding and believe that the continuation of the war is neither in our interest, nor in the interest of the region, nor in the interest of humanity,” Pezeshkian said.

Modi urges diplomacy as tensions rise

The Indian prime minister also called for continued efforts toward lasting peace and stability, while stressing the need to protect freedom of navigation and commerce.
“Civilians and civilian infrastructure, including commercial shipping and seafarers, must not be harmed under any circumstances,” Modi said, according to the statement.
Pezeshkian also called for stronger ties with India, saying Tehran was ready to expand cooperation with New Delhi across multiple sectors.
Strait of Hormuz tensions intensify
The meeting came as tensions around the Strait of Hormuz intensified following a US military attack on Lark Island near the strategic waterway overnight and subsequent Iranian retaliation.
Tehran and Washington have remained locked in a confrontation since the war began with US strikes on Iran in late February.
A framework agreement was reached in June following mediation by Pakistan and Qatar, but tensions later resurfaced over navigation in the strait.
The US subsequently launched a two-week bombing campaign in July and reimposed a naval blockade after disagreements between the two sides deepened.
Monday’s meeting underscored India’s effort to promote diplomacy as tensions threaten a strategically vital waterway linking the Persian Gulf with global energy markets.

Nayan Sethin Washington
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday targeted China’s global trade surplus, raising concerns over “excessive imbalances,” weeks before Chinese President Xi Jinping is expected to arrive in Washington for a bilateral summit with US President Donald Trump.
“We are confronting persistent global imbalances that undermine prosperity,” Bessent said in his opening address at the G20 Finance Ministers’ meeting in Asheville, North Carolina. The United States holds the G20 presidency in 2026, leading a forum of the world’s major advanced and emerging economies.
Without naming China, Bessent said that the grouping’s finance ministers and central bank governors “have broadly concurred that it is in the interests of both surplus and deficit countries to address excessive imbalances”.
“We have seen how distorted policies that privileged countries’ own exports have harmed many of the economies represented here today,” he said, adding that a “durable global economy cannot rest on beggar-thy-neighbour acts that stifle fair market-based competition.”
Washington has made trade imbalances a key theme of the G20 ministerial – part of decades-long complaints about Beijing’s high trade surpluses – as a surge in Chinese exports of major products such as automobiles, solar panels and batteries has raised concerns in many countries over Beijing’s alleged “overcapacity”.

Galliano and the Metropolitan Museum canceled the retrospective exhibition after a negative public reaction

Galliano and the Metropolitan Museum canceled the retrospective exhibition after a negative public reaction
Kyiv • UNN
John Galliano and the Metropolitan Museum canceled the retrospective after outrage over his antisemitic remarks. The exhibition was supposed to\r\nopen in May 2027.
Fashion designer John Galliano and New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art have canceled a retrospective in his honor planned for 2027 following a wave of outrage over plans to commemorate a designer whose career was destroyed by antisemitic remarks, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
"After much consideration and discussions with the Metropolitan Museum and all stakeholders, I have, with great sadness, decided that it is best not to hold the exhibition at this time," Galliano and the museum said in a joint statement, which he also posted on Instagram.
"I continue to take full responsibility for the pain caused by my words in the past, especially the pain I caused to the Jewish and Asian communities, and I continue to deeply regret it," he wrote.
Galliano’s career was destroyed in 2011 after a video emerged online showing him insulting people with antisemitic remarks at a Paris bar. Dior fired Galliano, who was then serving as its chief designer, and a French court later found him guilty of antisemitic behavior and handed him a suspended fine of $8,421. At the trial, he apologized.
Galliano returned to fashion in 2014 as the artistic director of Maison Margiela, where he worked for ten years before leaving the fashion house in 2024.
The cancellation of the exhibition was a blow to Galliano, one of the most influential designers in the fashion world. His planned retrospective at the Metropolitan Museum would have been one of the industry’s most high-profile events since his downfall in 2011.
The eight-month exhibition was due to open at the same time as the 2027 Met Gala, the Costume Institute’s spring exhibition, which traditionally takes place on the first Monday of May. In 2027, that falls on the evening of May 3, the beginning of Yom HaShoah, or Holocaust Remembrance Day.
"I do not want the discussion surrounding me to put the Metropolitan Museum in a difficult position or divert attention from the wonderful work of the Costume Institute. I also acknowledge and respect the fact that an exhibition devoted to my work may be painful for some," Galliano said in the statement.

“More than just wanting to attend, our battalion wanted us to go as well. It was stopped two days before the course, when the guidelines stated ‘men only.’ Only then did they contact us and say we couldn’t come,” said the female reservist whose participation was blocked at the last minute simply because she is a woman.
“There’s no one to talk to, we have no contact with them. It’s infuriating, it’s simply unfair. When it was convenient to call on women during the war, they knew how to call on us. Now it’s no longer convenient for them, and we’ve become unwanted.”
The call-up instructions for the operational driving course for reservists require a medical profile of 82 or higher, Rifleman 03 qualification and both military and civilian driver’s licenses — requirements that female soldiers can certainly meet. Yet alongside these requirements is the stipulation based on gender.
“The capabilities required for the position are no greater than those of any female combat soldier in the field,” said the reservist, who has already served hundreds of days under emergency call-up orders. “My hope is that they will give us the opportunity to take on any position that there is no reason we shouldn’t be able to fill,” she added.
'They thought I was a man'
The ability of women to complete the course and actually perform the job is demonstrated by Sgt. Maj. (res.) Naama Tzadok. After completing her mandatory service as a combat soldier in the  Lions of the Jordan Valley Battalion from 2016 to 2019, she continued serving in the reserves with a regional medical company of a southern Gaza border brigade.
“My training took place when the mixed battalions were still doing their basic and advanced infantry training alongside regular foot infantry. I was at the Nahal training base with a Nahal force for four months of basic and advanced training. I did exactly the same training as they did,” she said.
In February 2025, she completed the course in question alongside 30 male combat soldiers.
“I got there because of a technical error — they thought I was a man. When the battalion commander realized they wanted to prevent me from attending the course, he insisted that I go. He said, ‘There’s no way you’re not taking the course. We don’t care — a woman can do it too.’ When they asked him what I would do in the field, he laughed and said, ‘This girl has been in Gaza more than you can imagine,’” she told ynet.
According to Tzadok, “Obviously, I got some looks, like any new woman who arrives in places like these. But they quickly realized that I was just like any of them. I could get under the Hummer in any situation, get in and drive, and I drove no less well than any man. After I completed the training, I realized that the course had been designated for men only.”
After completing the course, which was shortened from three weeks to two because of the war, she performed the role in the field.
“People made faces, but when you’re wearing a helmet in the field, they don’t distinguish between a man and a woman. I would get calls of ‘Hey, man,’ and I would correct them and say I wasn’t a man. I’d ask what needed to be done and do it.”
'Like any man, I managed to lift the Hummer'
Regarding the IDF’s decision to prevent women from attending the training, Tzadok said: “During the war, they had no problem integrating us. We were all working toward one goal. Now, when the pressure has eased a little, suddenly they say, ‘Oh, a woman.’ Suddenly it’s impossible. When they needed us, I was there to prove myself. But now, when they ‘remembered I was a woman,’ they decided we were only making things more difficult for them, even though that’s simply not the case in the field.”
Regarding the exclusion of women from positions in the IDF, she added: “I’m not saying women should do every job. Physiologically, we are built differently. But there are positions we can do — and this is absolutely one of them. There’s no reason I can’t do it. Like any man, I managed to lift the Hummer. There were moments when I changed a Hummer tire and all the men were looking at me. Coming along and saying a woman can’t do A, B or C is a mistake. Most of the people who say that simply haven’t been in the field or in the military.”
The IDF confirmed that women were integrated into the course during the war, but said it has now decided to return to a men-only format.
An IDF spokesperson said: “The operational driving course was intended for infantry battalions in accordance with the battalion’s structure and organization for combat. During the war, due to operational needs and in accordance with requirements that arose from the field, the training was expanded to additional forces in the IDF. As part of this, in a few isolated cases, female combat soldiers participated in the course according to operational needs and the readiness requirements of the unit. In individual cases in which the training is required, the request will be examined and individual approval will be granted accordingly.”
Regarding the exclusion of women from combat positions, it should be noted that after the IDF halted its previous trial integrating women as infantry combat soldiers specializing in operational driving, it decided to launch a new pilot program this November. However, the military has been dragging its feet on the issue and, two months before the planned launch, the IDF has yet to say whether the pilot will actually go ahead.

Poland sees two fires at defense plants in 24 hours
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
19:00:53 UTC
04:00:53 KST

- Two fires broke out at Polish defense-linked facilities within 24 hours, one destroying a Lublin aviation composites plant and another hitting a drone-component maker in Skarżysko-Kamienna.
- JFG Composites supplies Leonardo's PZL-Świdnik helicopter plant, while WB Electronics produces drone components used by Polish and Ukrainian forces.
A fire destroyed a two-story warehouse building in Lublin, Poland, Sunday afternoon, gutting facilities owned by JFG Composites, a subcontractor to Leonardo’s PZL-Świdnik helicopter plant, according to Polish outlet Defence24.
The fire broke out around 2:00 p.m. local time on Kasprowicza Street and spread through the building’s warehouse and office sections, PAP reported, according to Slawa. The building burned to the ground. Emergency services received the report shortly before 3:00 p.m., and about 60 firefighters responded to the scene. Gray smoke was visible from several kilometers away.
According to the city’s State Fire Service office in Lublin, no injuries were reported, and no residents needed to be evacuated.
JFG Composites specializes in manufacturing composite materials and components for the aviation industry, according to Defence24. The company operates as a subcontractor for Leonardo, the Italian defense conglomerate that owns PZL-Świdnik, a Polish manufacturer of aircraft including the AW149 helicopter.
Polish authorities have not disclosed a cause for the fire or confirmed whether it is being investigated as accidental or deliberate.
The Lublin fire is at least the second incident this week at a European facility tied to defense or aerospace manufacturing. A fire also broke out overnight Sunday at a WB Electronics facility in Skarżysko-Kamienna, Poland, which produces components for drones used by Polish and Ukrainian forces.
That fire started shortly after midnight in the plant’s assembly department, according to Radio Kielce, which cited a spokeswoman for local police. Five fire crews and police responded, the facility was not operating at the time, and no injuries were reported. Police are investigating the possibility of arson after journalist Jakub Wiech reported that surveillance footage showed a masked person entering the site shortly before the blaze began.
Neither Polish fire nor the incident’s proximity to JFG Composites’ aviation supply chain role has been publicly linked by authorities to the WB Electronics fire or to the broader pattern of suspected sabotage incidents The Defence Blog has tracked at European defense manufacturers this year.

What’s next for NASA’s new Roman Space Telescope?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
18:57:21 UTC
03:57:21 KST

NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is already exceeding expectations.
After reaching the launchpad ahead of schedule and on budget, the spy-satellite-sourced, $4-billion project pulled off a flawless launch to space on Sunday morning. At a postlaunch press conference, NASA officials noted that the performance of the rocket that took the telescope to space was so picture-perfect that Roman will likely need fewer trajectory adjustments than planned. That means Roman’s onboard fuel could instead help extend the observatory’s five-year mission to a full decade.
Lofted onboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida, Roman was “exactly where it needed to be,” said Denton Gibson, launch director of NASA’s Launch Services Program, at the press event. “That’s a monumental effort because we know the more accurate the launch vehicle is, the more science we can get.”
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
“A launch is such a transition point,” said Julie McEnery, Roman’s senior project scientist at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC). “It’s a transition because it’s an end point for the engineers, but it’s a starting point for the scientists.”
Roman “will contribute to world-changing science,” said NASA administrator Jared Isaacman. In addition to the agency’s Hubble Space Telescope and James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), “Roman will become a household name alongside those great instruments of discovery.”
Separating from its rocket about 30 minutes after launch, Roman successfully deployed its power-providing solar panels and spacecraft-cooling sunshield and will soon unfurl its high-gain antenna for broadband communications with Earth.
In the coming days, the observatory will perform a midcourse correction burn on its approximately three-month voyage to the second sun-Earth Lagrange point, or L2. There, situated 750,000 miles beyond the moon, Roman will begin its science mission to study dark energy, dark matter and exoplanets.
Along the way, the telescope will power up its two core science payloads: a wide-field infrared camera for panoramic views of the cosmos that will be 100 times wider than Hubble’s and an advanced coronagraph for capturing unprecedented images of exoplanets.
Nicky Fox, associate administrator for NASA’s Science Mission Directorate, summarized the sheer scale of Roman’s expected discoveries at the press conference: “Billions of galaxies will be found, tens of billions of new stars, tens of thousands of new planets, and thousands of supernovae—all wrapped up in one beautiful telescope.”
The observatory should beam back its first images before the winter holidays, said Jackie Townsend, Roman’s project manager at GSFC. And the telescope’s first year of science observations, slated to begin in January 2027, will be action-packed.
One of the mission’s top priorities will be putting the coronagraph through its paces—presumably by taking snapshots of known exoplanetary systems. “Let’s get that technology demonstration nailed so that we can think about what we might want to do next with that instrument,” McEnery said. Observations with Roman’s coronagraph could unveil Jupiter-like planets around nearby stars and will guide the development of NASA’s Habitable Worlds Observatory, which will target smaller, more Earth-like worlds.
Another early focus for the mission will involve using Roman’s wide-field camera to stare at the Milky Way’s star-packed central bulge. Those observations will constitute “a deeper, sharper view of the center of our galaxy” than ever before, McEnery said, and will ultimately deliver most of Roman’s exoplanet discoveries while initially helping mission controllers gauge the telescope’s on-sky performance.
In its first year Roman will also undertake a “pilot survey” of supernovae popping off across the sky and will separately gaze out of the galactic plane to gain a better view of the far-distant cosmos—similar to previous “deep field” images from Hubble, JWST and other telescopes.
“A year from now, we will have found thousands of new exoplanets, [and] we will have used the coronagraph to demonstrate new technologies in space for the first time,” McEnery said. “We will have conducted our pilot survey..., so we will be making new precise measurements of supernovae. Those same observations will allow us to catch the unexpected.... I’m pretty certain we’re going to find something we didn’t expect with that. And I think that that will probably be the most exciting result [of Roman’s first year of science].”
Roman’s most promising aspect, perhaps, is its synergy with Hubble, JWST and other facilities such as the U.S. Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile and the European Space Agency’s Euclid space telescope. Rubin and Euclid are each performing their own panoramic sky surveys, with significant areas of overlap with Roman’s. All three projects will collectively contribute to better measurements of how cosmic structure is changing over time—crucial information for clarifying the nature of dark energy and dark matter in the universe’s evolution.
And although, as a survey-style telescope, Roman boasts a wider, faster view of the sky than either Hubble or JWST, McEnery emphasized that doesn’t make these more focused missions obsolete. “There are things that Hubble [and JWST] can do that aren’t duplicated on any of our other observatories,” she said. “[With Roman] we’re redefining what it means to find a needle in a haystack—and when we find those needles, Hubble and Webb can then follow up, while Roman continues to go off and find new things.”
One of the postlaunch press conference’s most surprising moments came after Isaacman received an unexpected call midway through the briefing from President Donald J. Trump, who praised the mission’s success via speakerphone. It marks a change of heart for the administration, which had repeatedly proposed deep cuts to NASA’s science that included canceling Roman entirely. In the end, the observatory was saved by congressional intervention.
Isaacman shrugged off the shift. “The president of the United States is excited about our next great exploration asset that’s underway. I think that’s a great moment,” he said. “So I’m incredibly grateful for his support.... I do believe we’re entering a new golden age of discovery right now, and I think I’m going to have a lot to thank the president for on that.”

 Isaac ben Solomon Israeli (ca. 855 – 955 CE), not to be confused with Isaac Israeli the Younger (an astronomer of Spain, d. 1322 CE), served as physician to the founder of the Fatimid Dynasty in North Africa and wrote several philosophical and medical treatises in Arabic which were subsequently translated and widely read in Latin and Hebrew. France begins new voluntary national service programme
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
18:55:13 UTC
03:55:13 KST

The government's initial aim is to grow the programme to 10,000 volunteers a year, with a long-term goal of up to 50,000 per year in 2035.
This week, 3,000 young people are starting France's new national service programme, a voluntary military scheme that replaces the country's now-scrapped Universal National Service.
The volunteers have signed up for a 10-month stint, where they will learn discipline, drill, military songs and weapons handling. They will begin their service with five weeks of basic military training before joining a unit in the army, air force or navy.
As well as receiving accommodation, food and clothing, participants will be paid €800 per month.
Members of this first cohort were selected based on their applications and motivation, regardless of whether or not they had a degree. For now, all of the assignments they are given are set to take place in France.
The government's initial aim is to grow the programme to 10,000 volunteers a year, with a long-term goal of up to 50,000 per year in 2035.
For the armed forces, the aim is to build up a pool of potential recruits who could later join the military or the reserves.
It remains unlikely that the system will act as a steppingstone towards compulsory national service, however.
The French armed forces currently have around 200,000 personnel and do not have the capacity to take in an entire age group, which could be around 700,000 people a year.
France's strained public finances make this even less likely - the cost of national service is expected to reach around €1 billion by 2030, based on an annual intake of 10,000 young people.

Rania Abushamala
31 August 2026•Update: 31 August 2026
The Syrian Sovereign Fund and UAE real estate developer Arada signed a deal worth around $7 billion on Monday for a major residential and commercial project in Damascus, Syrian Arab News Agency (SANA) reported.
The "New Damascus" project will cover some 4 million square meters (43 million square feet) and include 11,000 residential units, according to SANA.
It will also include hotels, healthcare and educational facilities, offices, commercial spaces and recreational areas, the agency said.
The deal marks Arada's first project in Syria and was signed in Damascus by Ahmed al-Khushaybi, the company’s CEO; and Mohammed al-Khayyat, CEO of the sovereign fund's real estate development sector.
Mazen al-Salhani, chairman of the Syrian Sovereign Fund, said the agreement also includes plans to provide sustainable residential communities for people living in camps and those whose homes have been destroyed.
He said Syrian government bodies would provide the necessary facilities to help implement the project.
Al-Khushaybi said the developer plans to expand to Syria a housing initiative it has implemented for refugees elsewhere.
The initiative will be carried out in cooperation with the sovereign fund under a program called "City for a City," he said.
Al-Khayyat said the development would be based on the "15-minute city" concept, with essential services and everyday needs available to residents within a short distance.
The project will include hotels with more than 500 rooms, hospitals with capacity for up to 300 beds and educational facilities serving 5,000 students, he said.
Government service centers, offices, commercial areas, green spaces and recreational facilities are also planned as part of the development.

🔴 Former French prime minister Édouard Balladur dies at 97
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
18:47:22 UTC
03:47:22 KST

Former French PM Édouard Balladur, once defeated by ally Jacques Chirac, dies at 97
Édouard Balladur, who served as prime minister of France from 1993 to 1995, died on Monday at the age of 97. He led a "cohabitation" government under Socialist president François Mitterrand before waging a bitter battle for the presidency against his friend Jacques Chirac in 1995 – a race he ultimately lost.
French President Emmanuel Macron has paid tribute to former prime minister Édouard Balladur, describing him on X as a "demanding, measured, and devoted servant" of France, who had "devoted his life to the Fifth Republic".
Balladur, who died on Monday at the age of 97, waged a bitter battle for the presidency against his friend Jacques Chirac that left deep scars in their centre-right party.
Chirac was stung to the quick when Balladur, whom he had groomed as his right-hand man, decided to run against him for president two years later.
Former president Nicolas Sarkozy was among the grandees of the Rally for the Republic, the party of war hero Charles de Gaulle, who ditched Chirac in favour of Balladur – but they backed the wrong horse.
To display this content from X (Twitter), you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
Nicknamed Louis XV for his haughty manner, the patrician Balladur was ill-suited for the cut and thrust of the campaign trail and it was Chirac, the more personable of the two, who won the top job in 1995 by presenting himself as a more compassionate conservative.
For most of the campaign Balladur had been the man to beat, having impressed as an unflappable prime minister wrestling with a huge deficit.
But his pronounced double chin and pompous air made him prime fodder for cartoonists, with Le Monde daily invariably depicting him as an 18th-century monarch in a powdered wig being carried about by porters in a palanquin.
Born in the Turkish city of Smyrna, today called Izmir, on May 2, 1929, into a rich family of Catholic Armenian origin, Balladur's family emigrated to France when he was a boy.
He grew up in Marseille and later moved to Paris, where he attended the prestigious Ecole Nationale d'Administration, a breeding ground for generations of senior French civil servants.
He helped to negotiate the accords that ended the May 1968 student and worker revolt and served as chief of staff to right-wing president Georges Pompidou until the latter's sudden death in 1974 from blood cancer.
Thatcher comparisons
In 1986, he became finance minister under then prime minister Chirac, with responsibility for privatising some of France's biggest state companies.
Balladur cut public spending and slashed the civil service, drawing comparisons with British Conservative leader Margaret Thatcher.
Read moreFormer French PM Edouard Balladur: 'France need not apologise for Rwanda genocide'
In 1993, he became prime minister of a "cohabitation" government, when the president (in this case François Mitterrand, a Socialist) and government (centre-right) are from opposite sides of the political divide.
His calm in the face of record unemployment and a ballooning public deficit made him immensely popular, despite him prescribing a bitter potion of austerity.
Flattered by polls showing strong support for him to run for president when Mitterrand's second term ended in 1995, Balladur threw his hat in the ring.
But after leading the race for months he crashed out in third place the first round of voting behind Socialist candidate Lionel Jospin and Chirac, who triumphed in the run-off.
He remained an MP until 2007.
In 2017, at the age of 88, he was charged with funnelling kickbacks on state arms deals with Pakistan and Saudi Arabia towards his failed presidential campaign.
He was acquitted of the charges but his former defence minister François Leotard was handed a suspended two-year prison term for misuse of assets.
Balladur was married with four sons. His family told AFP that a private Mass will be held for the former premier, without giving further details.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Of his attendance, he said: “In any year, I attend hundreds of external events with business organisations and thinktanks, none of which automatically imply my endorsement.” He also recently spoke at a hard-right Cpac event organised by Truss.
Claire Coutinho
Widely tipped as one of the party’s rising stars, Coutinho made a fierce opponent to Ed Miliband when he was energy secretary and she shadowed his brief. A cabinet minister in Rishi Sunak’s government, she has been shifted to Badenoch’s economic unit and made shadow business secretary. Before parliament she was an investment banker at Merrill Lynch and KPMG, and has recently been holding the Labour government’s feet to the fire over rising energy bills.
Colleagues describe her as forensic, she delights in doing her own research about what she terms “the hidden cost of net zero” and has spoken up in parliament for whistleblowers at the national energy systems operator.
She became the first person to represent a political party at PMQs while pregnant earlier this year. Julia Lopez, the MP for Hornchurch and Upminster, will cover for her until the new year while she is on maternity leave. Coutinho is a keen cook in her spare time and once appeared on Nigella Lawson’s cooking gameshow The Taste.
Tom Tugendhat
Badenoch has made a show of purging the more “woke” MPs from the party, banning those who believe in pursuing net zero from standing at the next election for example, so the choice of the moderate Tugendhat as shadow foreign secretary surprised some.
He replaces Priti Patel, who was sacked from the shadow cabinet. Tugendhat has experience in foreign affairs and previously served in the cabinet as security minister from September 2022 to July 2024. A former British army officer, he served in Afghanistan and Iraq.
A remainer, he has also said he does not support leaving the European convention on human rights, which puts him at loggerheads with Badenoch.
Tugendhat stood as the moderate option in the Tory party leadership contest in 2022, but was beaten by a long way by Truss. He tried and lost again against Badenoch when Sunak stood down in 2024.
He was banned from driving for six months in 2022 for using his mobile phone at the wheel.
Katie Lam
A darling of the Tory right, Lam was only elected in 2024. She has been given the role of shadow housing and communities minister, and is likely to relish being Angela Rayner’s opposite number. She is a former special adviser to Johnson, and she worked on Sunak’s first leadership bid. Outside politics she worked at the PR company Portland Communications and the AI company Faculty.
She has sometimes been tipped as a potential defector to Reform after saying many immigrants should “go home” and supporting the policy of revoking indefinite leave to remain. Her comments on immigration have gone further than official Conservative policy at some points.
Lam has written five musicals, including an adaptation of The Railway Children.
Other changes and those staying on
 Chris Philp remains shadow home secretary. He supported Badenoch’s successful leadership campaign and has held the role since she became party leader.
James Cartlidge stays on as shadow defence secretary, a position he has held since Sunak appointed him to the role in 2024.
Andrew Bowie takes up Coutinho’s previous role as energy secretary.
The shadow health secretary, Stuart Andrew, quit the frontbench to “focus on constituency work”, and Damian Hinds assumes his brief.

Putin Has Spent Years Asking India to Sell Russia More—The Trade Gap Is Still Massive

Putin Has Spent Years Asking India to Sell Russia More—The Trade Gap Is Still Massive
Russia has spent nearly four years urging India to increase exports of food, medicine, machinery and other goods, but the effort has produced little change, leaving the two countries’ nearly $60 billion trade relationship overwhelmingly tilted toward Russian oil sales.
In India’s financial year ending in March 2026, bilateral trade reached $59.9 billion, according to figures cited by Bloomberg on August 31.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Of that amount, roughly $55.4 billion consisted of Indian imports from Russia, overwhelmingly crude oil, while Indian exports to Russia totaled just $4.5 billion.
That means India bought more than 12 times as much from Russia as it sold there.
Russia has repeatedly asked India to help fill that gap with everything from pharmaceuticals and food to industrial machinery, telecommunications equipment and vehicle parts.
Russian leader Vladimir Putin again raised the issue less than a year ago, calling on his government to “take certain steps” to reduce the imbalance in bilateral trade and identify “the most promising areas of cooperation.”
Yet Indian exports to Russia have increased only modestly compared with pre-war levels.
India sold Russia about $3.3 billion worth of goods in the financial year that ended shortly after the February 2022 invasion. The following year, exports actually declined to approximately $3.1 billion.
That happened despite Moscow sending New Delhi a list of roughly 500 urgently needed products in November 2022, including spare parts for cars, aircraft, helicopters and trains.
Indian exports subsequently climbed, but remained between roughly $4.3 billion and $4.9 billion annually.
In the latest financial year, they moved in the opposite direction again, falling 8.2% to $4.5 billion, according to India’s Ministry of Commerce and Industry.
Russia has repeatedly urged Indian businesses to expand its market presence. Moscow renewed that push in December 2025, acting on Putin’s call to address the widening trade imbalance.
Previously, Russia started to buy back the oil it sold to India. Russia’s crude accounted for a record 50.83% of India’s oil imports in July 2026, surpassing half of the country’s purchases for the first time and reaching 2.47 million barrels per day.

Putin’s Sixth Attempt to Sell Xi on the Power of Siberia-2 Mega-Project
Russian leader Vladimir Putin is preparing for his sixth meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping since the launch of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, aiming once again to push for the long-delayed “Power of Siberia-2” gas pipeline, The Moscow Times reported on August 31.
Meeting at the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Bishkek, the Kremlin hopes the proposed 50-billion-cubic-meter pipeline will eventually double Russian gas exports to China. This comes as European markets remain largely closed to state energy giant Gazprom.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russia is also developing a domestic lithium-ion battery industry for its military drones to circumvent Western supply interdictions. A massive surge in chemical and machinery imports from China and South Korea is reportedly allowing Moscow to establish local manufacturing well ahead of schedule, a push further bolstered by its recent capture of a major lithium deposit in Ukraine’s Donetsk region.
Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov confirmed that energy cooperation and bilateral economic ties will feature prominently in talks with Xi and Chinese Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang, The Moscow Times reported. Despite optimistic statements from Moscow following prior bilateral summits, negotiations over the mega-project have remained stalled for over a decade. Beijing has consistently refused to publicly confirm or sign binding documents for the project.
The primary obstacle to securing an agreement remains a sharp dispute over pricing, with Beijing demanding rates close to Russia’s heavily subsidized domestic market at roughly $50 per thousand cubic meters.
Citing industry data and sources familiar with the negotiations, The Moscow Times noted that this requested rate is five times lower than current prices for the existing Power of Siberia-1 pipeline, where China already receives a 39 percent discount compared to other international customers.
During Putin’s previous visit to Beijing, Chinese officials reportedly instructed the Russian delegation to stop raising the pipeline project until Moscow is willing to adjust its financial terms, effectively demanding that Russia subsidize Chinese gas imports, The Moscow Times wrote.
The Kremlin aide indicated the pipeline issue could also be raised at the upcoming Eastern Economic Forum in Vladivostok, where Russian and Chinese business leaders are scheduled to gather for a bilateral energy forum.
In another blow to Russian maritime logistics, China had previously honored Western sanctions by withholding critical marine technology needed for Russia’s Arctic ice-class vessels. Without imported propulsion and steering systems, Russian shipyards are unable to build the specialized fleet required to expand the Northern Sea Route.

‘Let Data Reign’: Trump decries opposition to data centres in US
Despite concerns over their electricity and water consumption, US president calls on communities to embrace data centres.
Despite bipartisan pushback against data centres in the United States, President Donald Trump has urged communities across the country to embrace the tech facilities, promising that they would bring jobs.
Trump said on Monday that China is happy with what he called the “anti-Data Center movement”, suggesting that growing disapproval of the centres in the US would divert businesses to the world’s second largest economy.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Japan’s economy slows, missing growth forecasts
- list 2 of 3US national debt passes record $40 trillion
- list 3 of 3Who are the economic winners and losers of the US-Israel war on Iran?
“The only reason that communities throughout the USA should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backwards and poor,” Trump wrote in a social media post.
“If they want to be successful and rich, with far lower taxes and jobs all over the place, let Data Reign.”
As more data centres open across the country, in part to power the growing use of artificial intelligence, the facilities have been met with scepticism – by both Republican and Democratic voters.
Data centres consume an enormous amount of electricity, raising concerns about the effect on the power grid, including possible outages and increased utility bills.
The Trump administration has backed a voluntary pledge by tech companies to entirely cover the price of their energy consumption. But consumer protection advocates have been calling for strict federal regulations around data centres.
Beyond electricity, environmental activists are ringing the alarm over the enormous amounts of water needed to cool down servers at data centres at a time when parts of the country are experiencing droughts.
Some residents living near data centres have also complained of the constant hum they emit.
A Gallup poll conducted in March suggested that 71 percent of Americans oppose establishing AI data centres in their areas.
The issue has gained steam across the political spectrum to the point where some pro-business Republicans are starting to express reservations about data centres.
For example, Republican US Senate candidate Mike Rogers – whose Democratic opponent in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, is a vocal critic of data centres – recently backed a one-year pause on data centres in the state.
El-Sayed has dismissed Rogers’s proposal and pushed to link the former Republican congressman to Trump’s all-out support for data centres.
The Democratic candidate has called for an indefinite pause on data centres until federal regulations are in place to require the creation of union jobs, ensure that utility bills do not increase, provide investments in the power grid and protect water resources.
After Trump’s post, Vice President JD Vance on Monday appeared to acknowledge some of the concerns around data centres. He said that while they are an “important part of the AI economy”, tech firms should establish power stations to support the facilities.
“If you build a data centre, you should be putting power back into the grid, not taking it out,” Vance said. “If that is happening, I don’t think data centres are that controversial.”

Sony and Warner said in the complaint, filed on Friday, that Anthropic pirated hundreds of song lyrics and sheet music from The Beatles, Taylor Swift, Michael Jackson and hundreds of other artists to train Claude to respond to human prompts.

The lawsuit is the latest in a wave of cases brought against tech companies by copyright owners, including authors, publishers, music labels and news outlets, over the use of their work to train artificial intelligence systems. Universal Music Group sued Anthropic in 2023 and this year over the alleged use of copyrighted song lyrics in AI training in lawsuits that are still ongoing.
Anthropic became the first AI company to settle one of the disputes last year when it paid $1.5bn to resolve a class action from a group of authors.
“Anthropic clearly considers that to be just the cost of doing business given that its entire business model continues to be built on copyright theft,” Sony and Warner said in their complaint. “And $1.5bn is obviously not a large enough settlement to deter infringing conduct by a company that has parlayed such mass infringement into a staggering 2-trillion-dollar valuation.”
“This is the third lawsuit from the same lawyers, recycling allegations from cases already before the courts,” an Anthropic spokesperson said on Monday. Sony and Warner also said Anthropic used their lyrics to teach Claude to “generate vast quantities of purportedly ‘new’ AI-generated song lyrics, which compete with Music Publishers’ legitimate copyrighted works as harmful market substitutes”.
The labels are seeking damages of up to $150,000 for each infringed copyright and a court order barring Anthropic from using their works.

Germany funds 100 Humvee-sized heavy robots for Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
18:39:19 UTC
03:39:19 KST

- Ukraine's National Guard received the first 10 of 100 Protector heavy ground robots contracted with German government funding.
- The Humvee-sized vehicles are used for frontline logistics and casualty evacuation, with a payload capacity of 1,480 kilograms in this configuration.
Ukraine’s National Guard just started fielding a robot roughly the size of a Humvee, built to haul ammunition into combat zones so soldiers don’t have to.
Four units of Ukraine’s National Guard have received the first batch of Protector ground robotic complexes, part of a 100-unit contract funded by the German government, the National Guard said. Manufacturer Ukrainian Armor confirmed on X that the first 10 vehicles have already been produced and delivered.
This isn’t a small scout drone rolling on toy-sized wheels. The Protector is one of Ukraine’s largest unmanned ground vehicles, built on a diesel off-road chassis and weighing up to 4,000 kilograms (8,818 pounds), roughly in the weight class of a Humvee. It measures more than five meters (16.6 feet) long and stands nearly two meters (6.5 feet) wide, powered by a 190-horsepower engine.
Ukrainian Armor lists the payload capacity for the version supplied to the National Guard at 1,480 kilograms (3,263 pounds), one of the highest figures among current robotic logistics platforms, and higher than the 700-kilogram rating listed for earlier Protector configurations sold through Ukraine’s Brave1 Market platform, where the vehicle has been listed at $90,000. The National Guard version can also tow a trailer weighing up to 4 tonnes (4.4 tons), adding even more cargo capacity per trip. Soldiers from a separate Ukrainian brigade using the Protector have reported hauling nearly a metric ton of supplies in a single run, enough to resupply a frontline unit for roughly a week.
“Our logistics UGV has already proven itself well in military units subordinate to the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine,” said Vladyslav Belbas, general director of Ukrainian Armor. “Based on positive feedback from military personnel and understanding the need to protect people at the front, partners have contracted 100 of our complexes for the National Guard of Ukraine. Robotizing logistics allows important tasks to be carried out without unnecessary risk to personnel.”
The Protector’s core job is to keep soldiers away from the most dangerous stretch of road on the battlefield, the final approach into frontline positions. Beyond carrying ammunition, food, fuel and engineering supplies, the vehicle can evacuate wounded soldiers, removing them from combat zones without putting a driver at risk. Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense codified the Protector in June 2025, and the vehicle entered serial production within two months. Depending on the configuration ordered, the platform can also carry electronic warfare equipment, a drone launch catapult, or remote weapon modules, including a version fitted with a 12.7mm Browning M2 machine gun known as the Tavria-12.7.
A Protector is already in frontline use with a separate National Guard artillery brigade and is set to be deployed to the Dobropillia sector, according to the National Guard.
“The complex has already proven itself well in our brigade,” said Sgt. Yevhen Kocherhin of that artillery brigade. “I especially want to note the sensitivity and smoothness of control in conditions far from ideal. The power, speed and payload capacity speak for themselves. For our artillery brigade, one of the key tasks is transporting heavy ammunition, and this is exactly where the Protector can significantly reduce risks to personnel.”
The vehicle’s size hasn’t made it invincible. Protector units operated by other Ukrainian formations, including the 429th Separate Unmanned Systems Brigade “Achilles,” have previously survived FPV drone strikes mid-mission and still completed their deliveries, though other units have been damaged beyond recovery by mines while returning from resupply runs.
