Turkish deep-sea search vessel joins efforts to retrieve 20 still missing after Cyprus ferry disaster
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
18:37:06 UTC
03:37:06 KST

A deep-sea search and rescue vessel is on its way to Cyprus as Turkey joins efforts to retrieve the 20 people still missing after a passenger ferry capsized off the island’s northern coast.
The TCG Isin will join the vast operation to find survivors after the high-speed ferry sank on Sunday barely four nautical miles outside the port town of Kyrenia.
Authorities confirmed late on Monday – the first of three days of national mourning in Turkish-held northern Cyprus – that the tragedy had claimed eight lives, increasing the number of passengers still unaccounted for from 17 to 20.
A total of 241 of the 267 people aboard the Filo Jet, bound for Taşucu on the Turkish mainland when it began to take on water, had been rescued, they said. Almost all were either Turkish or Turkish Cypriot.
International sympathy for the victims was highlighted as the Anglo-Cypriot founder of easyJet, Stelios Haji-Ioannou, offered €260,000 (£223,000) in support for the families of the deceased and missing, in a move hailed by Turkish Cypriot officials.
Visiting Kyrenia’s new port, where relatives gathered for news of loved ones on Monday, Tufan Erhürman, the self-styled state’s president, vowed search efforts would “continue with the same intensity, with no interruption, through the day and night”.
The Isin, capable of searching up to 3,000 metres below the sea surface, was due to arrive on Tuesday, he said, as he comforted the families of those still missing.
The ship is expected to play a vital role in recovering the ferry’s voyage data recorder, or black box, now viewed as key in deciphering the cause of a maritime disaster not seen since the breakaway territory declared independence in 1983.
Turkish Cypriot officials told the Guardian it was likely “all those responsible” would be charged with gross negligence as the seaworthiness of the 26-year-old ferry was also questioned.
The owners and shareholders of the privately owned company operating the passenger vessel have also been ordered to appear in court.
It remained unclear whether those still missing had been trapped on board.
“Nobody is saying it publicly, but the hope of any survivors being found at this point is very slim,” one official confided. “Those who weren’t rescued very likely didn’t find a lifejacket. We believe many were elderly people and mothers with babies and young kids.”
In testimony – and video footage – that emerged on Monday, panic-stricken passengers could be seen desperately looking for lifejackets and screaming before the double-hulled ferry flipped over. One mother, Ayten Biçer, described feeling her 12-year-old daughter slip from her hands and disappear as the ferry capsized and sank in a matter of minutes. “She was saying, ‘Don’t let go.’ And I didn’t let go of my daughter. I swear, I didn’t let her go,” she sobbed. Two of Biçer’s other children are among the 20 still missing.
The captain of the ferry and seven crew members were detained on Monday as judicial authorities launched an inquiry into the tragedy amid claims they had been among the first to abandon ship.
Appearing before a local magistrate, the crew attributed the disaster to the bow of the catamaran-style ferry breaking apart in turbulent seas. But eyewitness accounts contradicted that version of events, with passengers telling officials that appeals to turn back to port had fallen on deaf ears as the ferry began to take on water.
Ünal Üstel, the northern Cyprus prime minister, told reporters the Filo Jet was lying on the seabed at a depth of 514 metres and that he foresaw the Turkish salvage ship “reaching [it] tomorrow afternoon”. Boats, helicopters, aircraft and other search and rescue teams had joined the operation, he said, adding that search efforts were continuing “on a 24-hour basis”.
Cyprus has been divided since 1974 when a coup aimed at union with Greece – engineered by the military junta then in power in Athens – prompted Turkey to invade and seize the island’s northern third. Ever since, as many as 45,000 mainland Turkish troops have been stationed in the north.
In 1983, the territory unilaterally declared independence, but in the absence of a settlement, decades of international isolation have ensued.

Type 23 frigates get £2.3m navigation radar work
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
19:36:41 BST
03:36:41 KST

The Ministry of Defence has awarded a £2.33 million contract to procure and support replacement navigation radars for Royal Navy Type 23 frigates after warning that the existing equipment is unsupported and a failure could prevent a ship from sailing, the UK Defence Journal understands.
The contract details notice, published on 30 August, covers replacement Second Naval Navigation Radar equipment and associated in-service support. The contract was signed on 30 July and runs until July 2031, with options allowing it to continue until July 2033.
Defence Equipment and Support awarded the requirement directly rather than holding a competition, citing technical reasons, urgency and the need to maintain the operational capability, readiness and safety of the Armed Forces.
The MOD’s justification states: “The MRUP team are in an unusual and unplanned position whereby the current SNNR used on Royal Navy Type 23 Frigates is unsupported; as SNNR is a critical system this presents a significant risk to Navigational Safety for the T23 vessels and a risk to the operational capability of these Royal Navy vessels.”
It added: “The failure of a Navigation Radar will result in a high-level Operational Defect (OPDEF) and could prevent the ship sailing. With this in mind timescales to procure a replacement radar are of the upmost importance.”
The requirement forms part of the Maritime Radar Update Programme and is intended to replace the existing Second Naval Navigation Radar while minimising changes to the frigates themselves. According to the procurement notice, the MOD sought equipment with the same properties as the existing radar so that existing shipboard infrastructure could continue to be used. This was intended to avoid additional design work and reduce the time needed to carry out the replacement.
The department stated: “Due to the necessity to replace the radar at the earliest opportunity, the Authority will seek to limit any change on the platform. The Authority’s requirement is therefore for a radar which has identical properties to the current radar so as to enable the existing infrastructure on the platform to be used.”
It continued: “This will remove the time required to undertake design work, and to model interaction with it and other systems. This approach will also ensure that the time required to update the radar on the platform is kept to the bare minimum and that the impact on platform readiness is limited, thereby enabling an update to be done whilst a vessel is operational.”
The MOD concluded that the Hensoldt S Band Turning Unit and Antenna was the only system meeting those requirements.
The contract notice lists Kelvin Hughes Limited as the supplier, while the direct-award justification names Hensoldt UK Limited as the company with which the MOD intended to place the contract. The agreement also contains a series of options for additional work. These include fitting Multi-Display Multi-Function Displays to additional Type 23 frigates, producing technical publications, providing additional operator and maintainer training and carrying out security testing.
Later options cover the possible replacement of existing RT1084 equipment with Hensoldt UK equipment using the SharpEye system, modifications identified through an earlier concept design study, and combinations of those changes. One option specifically covers replacing existing RT1084 equipment with a new Hensoldt UK Multi-Display Multi-Function Display and Mk11 S-Band SharpEye radar.
The initial five-year contract can be extended through two one-year options. The earlier voluntary transparency material associated with the procurement estimated that the wider requirement could be worth up to £3.5 million if options were taken up. The contract includes quarterly performance measures covering helpdesk responsiveness, equipment availability, delivery of reports and contract documents, and responses to technical assistance forms and requests for quotation.

MOSCOW, August 31. /TASS/. Gold miner Polyus' adjusted net profit under International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) fell by 59% year-on-year to $829 million in the first half of 2026, according to a company statement.
In the first half of the year, the company's capital expenditures (capex) increased by 2% to $946 million, driven by capacity expansion works at existing operations and the implementation of new projects.
Revenue for the reporting period grew by 27% year-on-year to $4.7 billion. The dynamic was driven by a higher average realized price of refined gold, which partially offset lower gold sales volumes, Polyus noted.
The company's total cash cost (TCC) in the first half of 2026 jumped 64% year-on-year to $1,069 per ounce. The increase was driven by a higher mineral extraction tax (MET) due to an increase in the average realized price during the reporting period, a stronger ruble, inflation (payroll indexation, tariff hikes), and increased repair expenses.
The company's net debt to adjusted EBITDA ratio stood at 1.1x at the end of 2025.
Polyus ranks second among the world's largest gold mining companies by gold reserves and is one of the top five global gold producers. The company's main production facilities are located in Siberia and the Far East: in the Krasnoyarsk Region, Irkutsk and Magadan Regions, and the Sakha Republic (Yakutia). Polyus' primary shareholder is IJSC Wandle Holdings Limited, which holds a 46.35% stake.

Ukraine Opens 25,000 Schools Under New Wartime Safety Rules as Teachers Get Additional 20% Pay Raise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
18:31:59 UTC
03:31:59 KST

Ukraine will open the doors of 25,000 schools on Tuesday, Sept. 1, with local authorities instructed to avoid mass events in areas at heightened risk of Russian attacks.
In a statement ahead of the new school year, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi presented a detailed report from the Minister of Education and Science covering all matters related to the safety of the educational process, including meal arrangements, shelters, and pay increases for education workers.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Our task is to ensure that, despite the war, children have the opportunity to study safely and receive a quality education,” Koretskyi said.
Shelter access expands
School assemblies and other ceremonial events should be held only where local security conditions permit, taking into account shelter capacity and the ability to reach them quickly during an air raid, Koretskyi said, instructing authorities to make decisions locally, based on the risk of Russian strikes.
More than 82% of children in preschool education and 83% of school students nationwide now have access to shelters, covering over 9,000 preschools and 11,000 general secondary schools.
Meanwhile, Ukraine is building another 131 state-funded shelters, including 18 underground kindergartens.
The projects are expected to raise shelter access to 87% of preschool children and students, with the government aiming to reach 92% by the end of 2027.
“Last year, the figure was 77%. In 2022, it was 10%,” Koretskyi said, adding that the rate is considerably lower at universities and vocational education institutions, remaining at 68%. Out of 1,420 universities and colleges, roughly 965 have shelters.
Trump Envoys May Visit Ukraine as Diplomacy Remains Stalled; Russia Does Not Want Peace, Zelensky Says
Higher education institutions will independently determine the format and schedule of the educational process depending on their particular security situation, shelter capacity and the specifics of their academic programs.
Depending on “the specifics of their academic programs, they may combine in-person, hybrid, and remote learning,” Koretskyi said.
Frontline learning
Education formats are expected to vary depending on local security conditions, particularly in frontline areas.
In Odesa, Chernihiv, Sumy, Mykolaiv, and parts of the Dnipropetrovsk region, schools with basic shelters can provide hybrid learning to around 80% of preschool children and students, Koretskyi said.
In the Zaporizhzhia region, the figure is about 72%. In the Kharkiv region, where security risks remain particularly high, hybrid learning is available only in underground schools and reaches about 30% of students.
The Kharkiv region currently has 17 underground schools, with another seven expected to be completed at the start of the academic year.
Though far from the frontline, Kyiv is frequently targeted by Russian forces, with strikes that particularly target civilian infrastructure, including schools. There, 528 kindergartens and 435 schools have shelters, providing access for 91% of preschool children and students.
“Twenty-three kindergartens and 20 schools do not have their own shelters,” Koretskyi said. “For them, the educational process is organized in rented safe spaces.”
According to the head of the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Military Administration, Oleksandr Hanzha on Aug. 27, a new underground school shelter is being built in the Samar district, designed to accommodate more than 1,000 children.
Textbooks and meals
According to Koretskyi, Russia has deliberately targeted printing houses and textbook warehouses.
“Therefore, if it is impossible to promptly print the required number of textbooks, students must be given access to their electronic versions,” Koretskyi said, adding that “this is a direct task for the Ministry of Education, working together with local authorities in each region.”
Children’s meals also remain a priority, according to Koretskyi. If schools are unable to organize full, warm meals because of security restrictions, they must provide ready-to-eat meals instead.
Since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, the digitalization of education has helped thousands of Ukrainian schoolchildren overcome learning losses.
However, authorities continue to work on ways to bring children back to in-person classes so they do not miss out on direct contact with teachers and classmates, as well as the general school experience.
Teacher salaries rise
Starting Sept. 1, teachers’ salaries will rise by another 20%, following a 30% increase earlier this year.
The increase applies to the base salaries of teaching and academic staff, from which most additional payments and allowances are calculated.
For teachers holding in-person classes in frontline areas, an additional payment of Hr. 2,600 ($58) will be retained.
Koretskyi said Ukraine will also move away from the Unified Tariff Scale – the standardized public-sector pay system – and adopt a model that sets base salaries according to an educator’s position and a benchmark tied to Ukraine’s average wage.

A festival will be held in Dolly Parton’s honor across consecutive weekends in Tennessee and England next year, the late country music legend’s estate announced on Monday.
Dubbed “Dollyfest,” the festival was initially scheduled to take place in Nashville on Parton’s 80th birthday this past January. Parton was set to serve as both the host and a performer at the event, which was also planned to include performances from several other musicians. In a statement on Monday, Danny Nozell, the founder and CEO of CTK Enterprises, said that the festival was “a dream of Dolly’s.” But as Parton was dealing with health issues in recent months, she “had to take a step back” from the event, Nozell said.
In the wake of her death last week, Parton’s estate revealed in a press release on Monday that the festival will now be held in 2027 to honor her legacy.
“What Dolly started, we will ensure is brought to life,” Nozell said. “A lot of people always say, WWDD (What Would Dolly Do?), and, well, at this moment, DOLLYFEST is WDWD (What Dolly Would Do!).”
Read More: Dolly Parton's Life, in Pictures
The festival will take place in both Nashville and London, and “will be the party of a lifetime she wanted to share with the world,” according to the release. Parton’s estate has not yet shared details about the specific dates it will be held or the performers it will feature, but said that more information about the event would be shared at a later date.
“We are not discouraging people from celebrating Dolly in the ways they choose,” Nozell said. “However, as far as a traditional memorial goes, that is not something Dolly wanted. So, instead, it feels more appropriate for us to take a beat, let all the tributes that immediately make sense occur naturally, and then, see through this festival-style concept that was truly dreamed up by Dolly.”
“This is something that is authentic to her, something that feels right to me, and something that artists and fans around the world can participate in, while also giving everyone time to grieve, and giving everyone time to plan,” Nozell said.
Last week, Parton’s publicist told news outlets that the country music icon had died after a “brief battle with cancer.” Parton had been dealing with health issues over the past year, postponing and later canceling several shows. She revealed in October that she was having “a few treatments here and there” at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, and said in May that her immune and digestive systems “got all out of whack” over the past few years and that her doctors were “working real hard on rebuilding and strengthening those.”
Almost immediately after her family announced her death, tributes for Parton began flooding in—from politicians like President Donald Trump to musical artists like Beyoncé.
“You were the barometer. The North Star. Bold and brilliant. Talented and tenacious. You taught so many lessons on how to be uniquely oneself,” Beyoncé said in a statement. “Thank you for your profound impact on the world. You are an angel who has made this world a happier place because of your joyful art. You are truly one of one.”
A private funeral service was held for Parton’s immediate family on Friday, The Associated Press reported.
Parton’s great-niece, Lainey Parton, shared a post on Instagram the following day, in which she wrote a touching tribute to Parton and included photos of them together.
“This is a really hard post for me to make. I wanted to wait until after my granny was laid to rest yesterday before I tried to put any of this into words,” Lainey Parton said in the caption. “From the time I was little, my granny always had a way of making me feel like I was enough. She never made my dreams feel too big or made me feel like I couldn’t do something. She believed in me before I even knew how to believe in myself.”
“It still doesn’t feel real that she’s gone. I’m going to miss her voice, her laugh, her hugs, and just knowing she was there,” she continued. “Thank you to everyone who has reached out, sent messages, flowers to my house, or done any of the little things to show me love. I’ve noticed every single one, and they’ve meant more than you know. I feel incredibly lucky that I got to call her my granny.”
There are no public services planned by Parton’s family and estate, but her family encouraged fans to share tributes online and donate to Parton’s Imagination Library, a program she launched in 1995 that mails books to children for free.

Sweden signs contract for four French-built frigates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
18:24:26 UTC
03:24:26 KST

- Naval Group signed a contract to build four FDI frigates for Sweden's Royal Navy, with first delivery scheduled for 2030.
- The deal follows Sweden's selection of the FDI class less than four months ago and includes technology transfer to Swedish industry.
Naval Group signed a contract in Stockholm on Monday to build four defense and intervention frigates for the Royal Swedish Navy, less than four months after Sweden announced its selection of the French-designed FDI class.
The signing took place in the presence of French President Emmanuel Macron and Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson. Mikael Granholm, Director-General of the Swedish Defence Materiel Administration, signed on behalf of Sweden, while Pierre Éric Pommellet, Chairman and CEO of Naval Group, signed for the company. The deal followed exclusive negotiations between Naval Group and Sweden’s Ministry of Defence, conducted with support from the French government.
“I am delighted to be in Stockholm today to sign the contract for the delivery of four FDI frigates to Sweden, a major milestone in the cooperation between our two countries,” Pommellet said. “It is an honour to put our expertise at the service of the Swedish Royal Navy’s sovereignty and naval superiority, and I would like to thank the Swedish authorities for their trust. Naval Group is already fully involved and committed to the delivery of this major project.”
The FDI is a French-designed frigate already in service with the French and Hellenic navies, with two units delivered to date. Naval Group said the existing production line will allow it to meet Sweden’s requirement for rapid delivery, with the first Swedish frigate scheduled for 2030.
The frigate carries anti-air capabilities built around the ASTER missile system and is designed to operate in demanding maritime environments, including the High North, the Baltic Sea and the North Atlantic. Naval Group said the ships will support Sweden’s role in NATO and inter-allied naval operations.
Swedish Navy chief Rear Adm. Johan Norlén wrote in an opinion piece published the same day that the purchase reflects a changed mission for Sweden’s fleet since joining NATO. He said the Navy’s task has shifted from defending only Swedish territory to maintaining operational control over the Baltic Sea and its approaches, including protecting shipping bound for Finland and the Baltic states.
“Sweden’s Navy must now ensure that important shipping can reach us and our allies, such as Finland and the Baltic states,” Norlén wrote.
Norlén said the frigates’ size allows them to carry the weapons and sensors required for air defense against threats ranging from drones to ballistic missiles, and to remain on station for extended periods beyond the Baltic Sea. He addressed criticism that Sweden should invest solely in uncrewed systems, citing a recent meeting with his Ukrainian naval counterpart.
“Today Ukraine mainly uses drones because they lack other capabilities,” Norlén wrote. “They have achieved success in preventing Russia from using parts of the Black Sea for its purposes, but have greater difficulty ensuring the protection of their own shipping there.”
Naval Group said it will build a long-term industrial partnership with Swedish companies as part of the deal, including the transfer of know-how and technology to several Swedish partners.

US, UN hail Libya electoral deal as step toward national vote
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
18:22:00 UTC
03:22:00 KST

The United States and the United Nations on Monday welcomed an agreement between Libya's rival political camps on key electoral disputes, calling it an important step toward breaking the country's prolonged political deadlock and holding long-delayed national elections.
U.S. Senior Adviser for Arab and African Affairs Massad Boulos described Sunday's signing as an "encouraging step forward" in Libya's political process and praised the parties for reaching common ground on key electoral issues.
Boulos urged Libyan factions to capitalize on the agreement by moving ahead with its implementation and working toward national elections, unified state institutions and greater stability.
U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres also welcomed the draft final agreement, saying it represented significant progress toward ending Libya's lengthy transitional period.
"The agreement marks an important step in advancing Libya towards national elections and ending the transitional period," U.N. spokesperson Stephane Dujarric told reporters.
The agreement was finalized Sunday by Libya's 4+4 Small Dialogue Committee, which brings together representatives from the Tripoli-based Government of National Unity (GNU) and authorities in eastern Libya.
The committee has held U.N.-sponsored negotiations since April as part of efforts to overcome the political impasse, establish conditions for elections and ultimately reunify Libya's divided institutions.
According to the U.N., the deal addresses the first two milestones of its political road map: restructuring the High National Election Commission and resolving disputed legal provisions governing presidential and parliamentary elections.
As part of the restructuring, Dhaou Ibrahim Attia was named chairman of the election commission's board, with Sana al-Lishani appointed deputy chair.
The agreement was signed at the headquarters of the U.N. Support Mission in Libya (UNSMIL) in Tripoli in a ceremony attended by international diplomats and representatives of Libya's legislative bodies.
Guterres urged Libya's political actors and state institutions to implement the agreement in good faith, with the U.N. saying the breakthrough demonstrated that progress remained possible through political dialogue.
Libya has remained politically divided between the GNU, led by Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah in Tripoli and controlling much of western Libya, and an eastern administration headed by Osama Hammad and appointed by the House of Representatives in 2022. The eastern authorities administer much of eastern and southern Libya.
Repeated attempts to hold nationwide elections and unify the country's institutions have stalled amid disputes over electoral laws, candidate eligibility and control of state institutions.

Palestinian farmers rebuild what Israeli settlers destroy in West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
18:17:20 UTC
03:17:20 KST

Palestinian farmers rebuild what Israeli settlers destroy in West Bank
Israeli settler pogroms destroy greenhouses and crops, but Burin’s farmers insist on rebuilding.
Burin, occupied West Bank – Ghassan Najjar’s phone starts ringing the moment the Israeli army rolls into Burin. It happens most days now – the whirring convoy of armoured personnel carriers working its way through the village’s narrow streets as soldiers fan out to shutter shops one by one.
Along with roughly two dozen other farmers, Najjar is a member of Burin’s Land and Farming Cooperative. They know that they don’t have the capability to fight back against Israel’s military might with arms so instead focus on the land and keeping their connection to it.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Why has Greece signed a $3.5bn missile deal with Israel?
- list 2 of 3Who are the economic winners and losers of the US-Israel war on Iran?
- list 3 of 3Xi, Modi and Putin attend SCO summit: What’s on the agenda?
But in addition to the military raids, they also face settler attacks, part of a pogrom against Palestinians that has reached fever pitch across the West Bank. Those settlers live in outposts and settlements built on occupied Palestinian land, which makes them illegal under international law.
On July 13, a settler tried to graze his flock inside one of the cooperative’s five greenhouses. Cooperative members struggled to keep the livestock away until Israeli border police arrived. Najjar recalled challenging the officers over why a settler had been permitted onto land the army itself had designated a closed military zone, from which Israeli citizens are, on paper, also barred.
The settler left angry. In Arabic, he told Najjar: “You’ll see.”
The next night, roughly 10 settlers arrived, gutting all five of the cooperative’s greenhouses, cutting away their plastic sheeting and destroying their irrigation networks.
The damage, by the cooperative’s estimate, ran to roughly 30,000 shekels (about $10,000) in plastic sheeting alone. About 9,000 tomato seedlings worth 8,000 shekels ($2,670) had been bought that same morning for planting. They died within hours because there was nowhere else to put them.
For a cooperative that pools land, labour and produce among about 25 families, the loss reverberated beyond the five greenhouses themselves. “We’re talking about 25 families working inside the cooperative,” Najjar said. “This year is the most difficult year for the cooperative. We’re facing many attacks by the settlers and the army.”
Just weeks later, Burin lost more than 1,500 olive and other trees, according to Najjar. Some were burned by settlers. Others were cut down or uprooted by military bulldozers along a local route accessible to Israelis but not Palestinians.
The wheat harvest fared little better: Of the 10,000sq metres (2.5 acres) the cooperative planted, 7,000sq metres (1.7 acres) were burned before farmers could harvest the crop this summer. These days, most of Burin’s farmland sits in closed military zones – renewed, Najjar said, every month or two. On paper, such orders are issued on security grounds to keep out attacking settlers; in practice, they apply overwhelmingly to the Palestinian landowners the settlers are attacking.
The pattern extends far beyond Burin. The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs recorded 1,418 settler attacks this year resulting in casualties or property damage across the West Bank through July, a rate that is on pace to eclipse 2025’s record high of 1,836 such attacks. Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International and other human rights organisations have accused Israeli authorities of enabling settler attacks and described their cumulative effect on Palestinian communities as contributing to forced displacement.
It is in this context that Najjar and the cooperative’s members have developed what they call the “Tom and Jerry Programme” after the cartoon.
“We go to the land early every morning,” he explained. “When the army comes, we run away. And when the army goes, we come back again.”
“Even if we don’t have planting or harvesting to do on the land, we [go to] drink coffee – to tell the settlers and the army that this is our land and we’re not going to leave it,” he said.
Building towards ‘food sovereignty’
Najjar founded the Land and Farming Cooperative in March 2020, weeks before COVID-19 lockdowns reached the West Bank. It started with five members and now counts about 25, 17 of them women, who farm roughly 25,000sq metres (6 acres) around Burin together.
The idea, he said, was never simply agricultural. “We’re not just a cooperative that plants vegetables and sells them,” Najjar said. “For us, the cooperative straddles the economic and the political because everything is connected.”
He described the cooperative as fighting on three fronts at once: the Israeli occupation, what he calls the “bureaucracy” of the Palestinian Authority and the “umbrella” of capitalism and the NGO funding structures that come, in his telling, with strings attached.
Fifteen percent of everything the cooperative sells goes back into the village, funding children’s and women’s programming. Twenty families it considers most in need once received free vegetables outright. The cooperative has since shifted towards helping those families cultivate small plots of their own under what members call their “don’t give me fish; teach me to fish” programme.
“This is the real food sovereignty,” Najjar said. “People who don’t eat from what they’ve grown will never have real freedom.”
Before joining, new members undergo six months of training covering both the political economy of the occupation and the practicalities of agroecology, including how to treat soil and pest problems without resorting to chemicals. Every two weeks, the cooperative meets to plan their work. At the end of each month, members evaluate what succeeded.
Much of the vision for the cooperative, Najjar said, was drafted while he attended what he calls “the Palestinian school of revolution”: Israeli prison. Two months after the cooperative was founded, Najjar was placed under administrative detention, under which Israeli authorities hold Palestinians without charge or trial and detention orders may be renewable indefinitely. Najjar spent roughly a year in prison, four months of it in isolation.
“In isolation, I thought a lot about the cooperative because, to be honest, it gives you the time to think,” he said. “I wrote all the procedures and the goals for the cooperative – exactly what we needed.” By the time he was released, cooperative members had built two additional greenhouses and brought three more plots of land under cultivation in his absence.
“The cooperative is not for us,” he said. “If Ghassan gets arrested, if Ghassan dies, if Ghassan is travelling, the cooperative doesn’t close. It’s for the farmers, for Burin, for whoever believes in freedom and food sovereignty.”
‘We prefer to die on our land’
By Najjar’s count, the July attack was the seventh time the cooperative has had its greenhouses vandalised or destroyed. Asked what drives members to keep rebuilding structures that may simply be torn down again, he returns, over and over, to dignity.
“This is the work between the evil and the right. You have to decide which side you’re going to be on,” he said. “We decided to be at the front of the struggle because this is our land. We connect our dignity to the land, and I don’t think anyone in this world can live without dignity.”
As closed military zones have become the norm, Burin – sandwiched between the notoriously violent settlements of Yitzhar and Har Brakha and the Givat Ronen outpost – has seen 13 outposts established or expanded in recent months, by Najjar’s count. But as people in the village have shifted from regarding his politics with bemusement to respect, Najjar sees the cooperative’s persistence as proof of a more fundamental victory.
“The real occupation is not when they create the checkpoint and invade the village,” he said. “The real occupation is if they occupy your mind. When you are waking up in the morning and working your land – this is the real freedom.”
For now, that resolve manifests in early morning “Tom and Jerry” trips to their lands and in replacing what was destroyed alongside building a fence organisers hope will at least slow the next attack.
“We prefer to die on our land rather than accept another Nakba,” Najjar said. “We work as a family, we work as comrades and we work for freedom.
“We’re not working just for economic reasons or for ‘peace’,” he added. “F*** ‘peace’. I care about freedom. And when you work the land, you feel you have freedom, even if you are under attack by the settler.”

After an air raid alert or shelling, the school morning should not begin with a test — the Ministry of Education and Science has prepared recommendations for teachers
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
21:13:56 EEST
03:13:56 KST

After an air raid alert or shelling, the school morning should not begin with a test — the Ministry of Education and Science has prepared recommendations for teachers
Kyiv • UNN
After air raid alerts, teachers are advised to begin the day with words of support. Stress can impair children's concentration, memory, and ability to learn.
After a night of air-raid alerts, teachers are advised not to begin the school day with tests and, during lessons, to take into account that stress may make it more difficult for children to concentrate and remember information. The Ministry of Education and Science recalled a practical guide prepared jointly with child and family psychologist Svitlana Roiz on supporting schoolchildren who have experienced trauma as a result of the war, UNN reports.
Details
The guide "Trauma-Sensitive Practices in School" contains recommendations for teachers on how to recognize warning signs in children’s behavior, respond to emotional manifestations, and organize learning so that it remains manageable and psychologically safe.
In particular, if a child starts crying during a lesson, teachers are advised not to draw the unnecessary attention of the entire class to them. Instead, they can conduct a short movement or stabilization exercise for all students, and later speak separately and delicately with the child to determine the reason for their condition.
Educators are also advised to take into account that prolonged stress can affect memory, concentration, and the ability to process large amounts of information.
Therefore, it is recommended that learning material be presented in small portions, activities be changed more frequently, pauses be taken, and lessons begin with familiar or relatively simple tasks.
Special emphasis is placed on learning after difficult nights with air-raid alerts and Russian attacks.
After an alert or shelling, schools are advised to begin the morning with words of support rather than a test or assessment. After experiencing stress, children may display either sluggishness and fatigue or increased activity, irritability, or aggression.
The recommendations note that unusual behavior in a child does not always indicate an unwillingness to learn or a disciplinary violation. For example, constant movement, rocking on a chair, or holding an object in their hands may, in some cases, help a child concentrate.
Practices that are recommended to avoid
Particular attention is drawn to possible triggers that may remind a child of shelling or other traumatic events they have experienced.
In particular, exercises that require closing one’s eyes are not recommended unless necessary. For a child who has experienced trauma, this may be associated with a loss of control over the situation.
Unexpected physical contact should also be avoided. Before hugging a child or taking them by the hand, it is recommended to obtain their consent.
During school celebrations and events, it is not recommended to use firecrackers, party poppers, balloons that may burst suddenly, or other effects involving sharp sounds. If such sounds cannot be avoided, children must be warned in advance.
Videos and educational materials about the war also require caution. Teachers are advised to check in advance whether they contain footage of the dead, blood, explosions, or sirens.
Aggression and bullying
The guide addresses children’s aggressive behavior separately. Teachers are encouraged not to limit themselves to prohibitions or punishments, but to try to understand the reasons for the child’s behavior and help them restore a sense of safety and interaction with those around them. To this end, the guide recommends using joint projects, volunteer activities, theater, music, and other group activities.
The guide also emphasizes that assessment can become an additional source of stress. According to a survey titled "In a Word," conducted with the participation of more than 50,000 children, schoolchildren named grades among the sources of stress, alongside air-raid alerts and explosions.
Context
The practical guide "Trauma-Sensitive Practices in School" was first presented by the Ministry of Education and Science and Svitlana Roiz in November 2024 as part of the All-Ukrainian Mental Health Program "How Are You?".
In August 2025, the recommendations on creating a trauma-sensitive educational environment were supplemented.
In particular, schools were advised to create "quiet corners," reduce visual and auditory noise, use gentler school-bell signals, and ensure that children have access to water and sufficient time to eat.
In July 2026, the Cabinet of Ministers approved the Concept for the Development of Psychological Services in the Education System through 2030. The document provides for the creation of a psychologically safe educational environment, early detection of emotional problems in children, and a multilevel system of psychological assistance in educational institutions.

Breaking Down the Savage Season 1 Finale of Furious
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
18:13:40 UTC
03:13:40 KST

Warning: This post contains spoilers for the finale of Furious.
By the end of the eighth and final episode of the first season of Furious, billionaire Jay Easton (Peter McRobbie) is dead, Catherine (Lola Petticrew) is in prison, and Alice (Emmy Rossum) has secured a full-time position working under Nora (Quincy Tyler Bernstine) in the Bureau's basement-level sex crimes unit. But not all was as simple as it seemed, as creator Elizabeth Meriwether's cat-and-mouse thriller still had a final twist up its sleeve.
Over the course of its first seven episodes, Furious tracked NYPD homicide detective-turned-probationary FBI duty agent Alice's hunt for serial killer Catherine, a sex trafficking survivor targeting wealthy, high-profile men involved in her past abuse. Along the way, we learned Catherine's primary motive was not simply retributive justice, but rather a desire to uncover the truth about the mysterious circumstances surrounding the death of her best friend and first love Isabel (Larissa Campos) at the Easton estate over a decade earlier. With the help of Nora's corrupt boss Ed (Danny McCarthy), Jay covered up Isabel's death to shield his involvement in a prolific child sexual abuse and trafficking ring. Catherine is convinced Jay himself killed Isabel, but due to the severe memory distortion she suffers from as a result of her trauma, she can't fully remember what happened on that fateful night.
After Catherine's fiancé Alden (Steve Way) gave Alice's former partner Danny (Scoot McNairy) a flash drive containing years of incriminating evidence against Jay and his associates, it was revealed there was a folder containing an illicit video of a then-14-year-old Alice being abused by one of the men within Jay's network. Episode 7 then ended with Alice tracking down Catherine and, instead of arresting her, manipulating her into driving out to Jay's Connecticut estate while Alice followed closely behind in order to orchestrate an incident that would allow Alice to search Jay's compound and arrest him without handing over the flash drive.
Who killed Isabel?
Although Episode 7 led us to believe Jay's daughter Emma (Hope Davis) was going to be exposed as the person who had killed Isabel, Furious had a much more tragic reveal on the way. While Emma was anything but innocent considering she spent years procuring underage girls for her father and destroyed evidence of his crimes to protect their family, in the finale, she helped Catherine remember that Catherine herself was the one who ultimately injected Isabel with the drugs that killed her.
On the night Isabel died, both girls had been brought to the Easton house to be abused by Jay and his men. However, Isabel had only recently given birth to her daughter Elena (Chloe Carrillo) and started hemorrhaging and crying out in pain, which led to Jay hitting her. Isabel then asked Catherine to end her life and put her out of her misery, and Catherine complied. In the present timeline, after Catherine finally came to terms with what actually happened, Alice arrests her. While the other cops who had arrived then take over the scene, Alice goes upstairs to find Jay and ends up witnessing him dying of respiratory failure—though we will soon learn that she did more than just witness his demise.
How does the finale end?
Since Emma had destroyed all the evidence at the house and Jay was no longer around to be interrogated, it initially seemed like everyone in Jay's circle was going to get off scot free while only Catherine went to prison, reinforcing the show's overarching message about our flawed justice system. But after weighing the personal cost of exposing her video, Alice decided to hand the flash drive over to Nora so she would at least be able to take Ed down.
While visiting Catherine in prison, Alice learned that Catherine had caught on to the fact that Alice had killed Jay that night by purposefully stepping on his breathing tube to cut off his oxygen supply. Alice also decided to take Nora's advice and watch the video of her abuse in order to face her trauma head on. The finale then ended with Alice using the FBI's search database to look up a list of everyone who had ever downloaded her file, implying Alice may have acquired a taste for the same method of vigilante justice Catherine had been so fond of doling out. And since it was announced on Aug. 27 that Furious has been renewed for a second season, it seems like we're eventually going to get to see Alice attempting to balance her devotion to her role as a FBI agent with her newfound thirst for vengeance against those who wronged her.
We also get a satisfying closing note to Alice and Danny's relationship, as they decompress from the events of the season during a romantic getaway at the beach house he mentioned several episodes back. As to what will happen between them in the future, Rossum tells Entertainment Weekly it's open-ended. "Now all of a sudden, they could be together, but he’s also processing not being really able to hold the totality of who she is and her secrets now that he knows the tape and has seen part of it," she says. "So I think it’s really complicated, and I think getting to watch the human toll on him, the potential partner of somebody that has been a victim of violence and sexual violence is really interesting.”

Eurasian nations gather in Bishkek to forge stronger ties, new alliances
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
18:13:36 UTC
03:13:36 KST

Heads of 21 global and rising powers gather in Bishkek for the SCO summit as wars strain the global order. China and Russia have previously used the SCO to project their influence and their stand against the West, but the middle powers are now there to seek new economic and political momentum.
The annual Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit is gathering a diverse group of world leaders from 21 countries in Kyrgyzstan’s capital Bishkek, as they pursue new alliances, ambitions and opportunities with the rise of regional powers in the rapidly evolving multipolar Eurasia.
The two-day summit kicked off on Monday, focusing on political, economic and security engagements and cooperation, a long-promised development bank, connectivity, energy and trade routes strained by wars and conflicts, and the defining challenges of the Global South.
The SCO’s 10 members — China, India, Pakistan, Russia, Belarus, Iran, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan — speak for more than 40% of the world's population.
The bloc increasingly bills itself as an alternative to a Western-led order, as it is joined by leaders of at least 15 states as “dialogue partners,” spanning Central Asia and the rest of the continent, the South Caucasus, as well as the Middle East, including Turkey, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Vietnam, as well as Uzbekistan, Azerbaijan and Armenia.
The bloc, which marked its 25th anniversary, was formed to address regional security issues after the collapse of the Soviet Union, but over time it has evolved into a powerhouse of multi-layered trade, security and political cooperation.
The theme of the summit, “25 years of the SCO: together for sustainable peace, development and prosperity”, is a message in itself to the world as the 21 leaders convene to formulate answers, build influence — and possibly new alliances to the rapidly changing world.
China’s Xi Jinping, India’s Narendra Modi, Turkey’s Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Russia’s Vladimir Putin, together with other presidents and prime ministers, including Iranian president Masoud Pezeshkian as well as UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, arrived in Bishkek on Monday to hold a series of bilateral meetings and later attending the opening of the World Nomad Games, a traditional Central Asian sports and culture event.
The SCO announced that Russia’s war in Ukraine, the Iran war with its far-reaching global economic consequences, as well as the push of the major and middle powers in the SCO for wider global influence, are among the main topics of this year’s gathering, while the host country Kyrgyzstan is aiming to advance the establishment of a SCO Development Fund and an Investment Fund for major projects.
Developing economic connectivity opportunities, including new energy and transport corridors, is also a key objective as the Iran war reshapes the world’s transit and supply chains.
'Golden period' of ties
Host of the summit Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov welcomed his Chinese counterpart Xi on his arrival in Bishkek, and the two leaders signed a treaty on “eternal good-neighbourliness, friendship and cooperation,” which, the Kyrgyz presidency said in a statement, acts as a comprehensive strategic partnership in the new era.
Xi described the China-Kyrgyzstan ties as a “golden period” of development.
Kyrgyz President Sadyr Japarov also held a flurry of bilateral talks on Monday with UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Mongolian President Ukhnaagiin Khurelsukh, Lao President Thongloun Sisoulith, Togolese President Faure Gnassingbe and Vietnamese Vice President Vo Thi Anh Xuan as well as Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian.
As the US and the EU are actively increasing their presence in Central Asia, China is also pushing for a rapid economic engagement across Central Asia, with major transport and infrastructure projects being developed to connect China and the West through Central Asia, such as the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway, which is expected to shorten transport routes between Asia, the Middle East and southern Europe.
As industrial cooperation and transport connectivity are major priorities for Tashkent, Uzbekistan’s President Shavkat Mirziyoyev arrived in Bishkek to also promote the Trans-Afghan Corridor connecting the rapidly developing infrastructure projects of Central Asia’s countries to Afghanistan and ports on the Indian Ocean.
Azerbaijan’s President Ilham Aliyev and Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan held a new round of peace talks in Bishkek on Monday to discuss the former rivals’ next steps in their historic peace process.
The two leaders also discussed new trade and energy cooperation as well as the key Middle Corridor projects through the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP).
Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev also met his Azerbaijani counterpart to discuss trade and investments through joint regional projects.
Putin also arrived in Bishkek on Monday to make his mark on the regional summit and will meet Xi amid Moscow's faltering economy.
The Russian president is scheduled to meet Erdoğan to discuss Russia’s war in Ukraine and Black Sea security, as well as Iran's Pezeshkian, as Moscow has been a strong supporter of Iran during its military confrontation with the United States and Israel.
Putin is also expected to meet Pashinyan following Moscow’s warnings against Yerevan’s newly announced intention to apply for EU membership.

Burnham to tell Commons more public ownership is only way to grow UK economy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
18:13:31 UTC
03:13:31 KST

Andy Burnham will drive home his pledge to bring more essential services back into public control, telling MPs in the Commons on Tuesday that it will be the only way to improve growth across the country.
Burnham will address the house for the first time in 16 years from the frontbench, and six weeks since he became prime minister, after spending the summer recess announcing a slew of policies that will now be put before MPs.
He will use the statement to put public control of services at the heart of his priorities for the coming months, sources told the Guardian, saying he would make the case that it would unlock investment, jobs and growth.
Burnham will say that the cost of everyday services to family budgets is holding back the economy and promise a plan to regain control of the costs.
A No 10 source said: “Andy is optimistic about our country’s future. He has a clear plan for how we turn things round. He is determined we make this the moment we bring back hope.”
The prime minister will face an early test of his commitment to public control as he mulls legislation to make it easier to bring struggling utilities such as Thames Water under government ownership. The Guardian reported last week Burnham was considering laws to make it easier to put companies into insolvency proceedings and then take control of them afterwards.
He will also face crunch decisions on possible changes to the immigration bill to exempt carers, as well as pressure from MPs to back moves towards electoral reform. A quasi-judicial decision on whether to allow more North Sea drilling is also expected soon: a highly divisive issue within the party.
Burnham will tell MPs that he wants to “bring back hope” in politics and pledge to work constructively with opposition parties.
On Monday, the Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, sacked her shadow chancellor Mel Stride and shadow foreign secretary Priti Patel, promoting Andrew Griffith in Stride’s place in the hope of making further inroads in attacking Burnham’s economic approach. Patel is replaced by Tom Tugendhat.
Burnham will give a scathing analysis of how privatised services have done little for the public, saying that utilities and transport have not been run in the public interest and are neither reliable nor affordable.
He will point to action already being taken to bring more bus routes under public control, including through a partnership between No 10 North and the West Midlands Combined Authority. The Liverpool City Region will start taking control of bus services from next weekend.
Burnham has promised a 10-year project to take public control of utilities which is expected to be a major focus of his next few months in power. Allies have said the prime minister is “completely committed” to putting utilities such as energy and water companies into public control, and is looking at every option.
As well as setting out key priorities for his first months in office, Burnham will face a two-hour grilling from MPs about policies announced over the summer – including a cut to VAT on energy bills, £2 bus fares, the scrapping of digital ID, a major expansion of devolution and a plan for a national care service.
Opposition MPs are expected to ask tough questions on how the pledges will be funded as well as how Burnham expects to fill a £4.7bn gap in the defence investment plan left by his predecessor, Keir Starmer.
On Tuesday, the justice secretary, Alex Norris, will also present the government’s plans to cut the number of prisoners eligible for early release, including the killers of PC Andrew Harper.
Though the decision will see most of those convicted of manslaughter remain in prison to serve longer sentences, it has also raised alarm that the number of prison places may reach crisis point faster.
Later in the week, Burnham will face Badenoch for his first prime minister’s questions and will also need to navigate the growing number of Labour MPs who are heaping pressure on him to toughen up the representation of the people bill which returns to the Commons this week.
Nearly 100 MPs have called on Burnham to back a commission on electoral reform, given the prime minister has previously been a vociferous supporter of changing the voting system. MPs have also been angered by the decision to drop any cap on party donations, after pressure from trade unions, despite the prime minister having previously backed a cap of £500,000.
The Liberal Democrats said on Monday they would put their full backing behind an amendment from the Labour MP Alex Sobel that calls for a commission on electoral reform to be established within 100 days.
The party’s leader, Ed Davey, said it was a chance for Burnham to prove he was different to Starmer. “Reform stand to benefit from our terrible voting system and could manipulate it all the way to No 10,” he said.
Davey added: “Keir Starmer never would have agreed to a national commission. He failed to grasp that it is our role as progressives to fix the broken system the Conservatives created. The only question now is: what kind of politician is Andy Burnham? Is he willing to do the right thing?”
Reform will host its party conference this week in Birmingham, with Farage speaking on Friday.
In the latest poll from More in Common, Labour hold a four-point lead over Reform, with the Tories a point behind. The latest Opinium poll found that Burnham’s net approval rating had increased over the last fortnight by three points.

Ukraine revamps security protocols amid Russian drone strikes aimed at ‘paralysing’ capital

AI generated
KYIV - Kyiv on Aug 31 announced a review of security protocols – especially for public transport – after a dramatic surge in Russian drone attacks it says are aimed at “paralysing” the Ukrainian capital.
After intensifying its missile strikes on Kyiv earlier this summer, Russia has also drastically increased its daily drone attacks.
Since last week, jet-powered drones have been attacking Kyiv and surrounding areas, triggering a dozen air-raid alerts a day and forcing a partial shutdown of economic activity.
The metro no longer crosses the Dnieper River, which divides the capital in two, causing traffic chaos.
Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram he had met with local officials on Aug 31 to discuss changes to security protocols, suggesting one metro line remain open despite strikes.
City hall also announced it was preparing changes for schools, including remote learning, as the school year begins in Ukraine on Sept 1.
Kyiv residents took to social media to question whether it was possible to continue living in the capital, especially with children, with some mulling a move to safer areas.
“The enemy is trying to paralyse economic activity in the capital and major cities,” Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergiy Koretskyi said on Facebook on Aug 29.
“Prolonged air-raid alerts affect not only people’s safety, but also the operation of businesses, logistics, transportation, schools, kindergartens,” he said.
He called for adapting security rules “with the aim of better protecting people and preserving the ability to live in our cities and communities”.
Some in Kyiv – a city of three million people – consider the security protocols ineffective, with experts suggesting a more flexible approach.
“If, because of a single drone somewhere in the region, everything or almost everything in the entire capital stops for about 40 minutes every hour, we’re not going to last long like this,” Mykhailo Zhernakov, head of a legal think-tank, said on Facebook on Aug 27.
Overnight from Aug 28 to 29, a Russian strike on an ammunition depot killed 38 people in the capital’s suburbs.
Another attack killed a two-year-old girl in a Kyiv park in broad daylight on Aug 29. AFP

beads, crystals, and steel visualize cloud formations within exhibition in china
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
18:10:47 UTC
03:10:47 KST

Tia-Thuy Nguyen translates cloud formations into installations
Vietnamese artist Tia-Thuy Nguyen presents Fields of Resonance at Almine Rech Shanghai, her first solo exhibition in China. On view from August 28th to October 31st, 2026, the exhibition brings together nearly twenty paintings, sculptures, and installations produced using oil paint, beads, sequins, thread, quartz, crystal, recycled glass, stone, and stainless steel. The exhibition continues Nguyen’s engagement with clouds, a recurring motif in her work since 2018. Initially associated with memories of her father, a pilot who served during the Vietnam War, clouds later became part of the artist’s visual diary as she traveled between Asia and Europe. Their changing forms provide a way to explore memory, emotion, and the movement of energy through the natural world.
 
 Like a sky breeze / 2026 / quartz, crystal, and stone / 19 × 13 × 23 cm | all images ©Tia-Thuy Nguyen
Cloud forms take shape through embroidery, minerals, and steel
In Fields of Resonance, the cloud moves beyond the painted image and becomes a material structure. Nguyen constructs cloud forms through embroidery, assembles them from mineral fragments, weaves them from stainless steel, and extends them into the gallery space. Across these different approaches, durable materials are used to express movement, impermanence, and transformation. At the center of the exhibition, the monumental mixed-media work Fairer than a Fairy, measuring 200 by 300 centimeters, presents a cloudscape built from oil paint, thousands of beads, and sequins. The dense accumulation of small elements gives the painted surface physical volume, positioning the work between painting and sculpture. Nguyen’s background in fashion and engagement with Vietnamese craft traditions inform the use of embroidery as a structural technique. Each bead receives and reflects light differently, causing the surface to shift as the viewer moves around it. Changes in position reveal variations in density, color, shadow, and depth, preventing the image from settling into a fixed appearance. The repetitive process of stitching and assembling also makes time and manual labor part of the work. The resulting surface combines the precision of craft with the fluid visual qualities of an atmospheric landscape.
Oil painting provides another approach to the exhibition’s central motif. In Passionate in Supernatural, Nguyen uses the density and fluidity of oil paint to evoke the atmosphere following a storm. Turquoise, deep violet, orange, and gold overlap across the canvas, suggesting moisture, changing light, and suspended movement. The painting does not reproduce a specific cloud formation. Instead, the shifting relationship between color and pigment expresses the transition between darkness and light, turbulence and calm. Unlike the structured surfaces of the embroidered works, the oil paintings retain the movement of the medium, leaving their forms open and visually unstable. In Another Day of Sun and Like a Sky Breeze, the artist shifts from painted surfaces to compact sculptural compositions made from quartz, crystal, recycled glass, and stone. Their transparency and reflective qualities allow the surrounding light to become part of the works. 
 
 Enduring Vitality / 2026 / stainless steel / 700 x 150 cm
Completed in 2026, Like a Sky Breeze measures 19 by 13 by 23 centimeters. Quartz and crystal fragments gather over a stone base to form an irregular volume resembling a cloud during condensation. White, pale blue, violet, and golden tones appear across the mineral surfaces as light changes. The sculpture combines the physical weight of stone with the visual lightness of crystal. Its angular surfaces suggest both geological permanence and atmospheric change, reconstructing a transient natural form through materials associated with durability and accumulation. Quartz also carries and refracts light through its structure. Instead of applying brightness to the surface, Nguyen allows the material itself to absorb, redirect, and release light. The appearance of the sculpture consequently changes according to its surroundings and the viewer’s position.
The Pause Between Storms introduces Nguyen’s stainless-steel weaving technique. Fine metal strands are bent, joined, and woven into cloud formations that occupy physical space. The material brings an industrial and structurally resistant quality to a process traditionally associated with softer fibers. Through repetitive weaving, the stainless steel is manipulated into forms that appear lightweight and delicate while retaining the material’s structural properties. From a distance, the restrained gray palette and fine lines recall landscape etchings. At closer range, knots, bends, folds, and joints reveal the physical process behind each work. Nguyen leaves the steel in its original metallic state, allowing light to move directly across the surface. Highlights and shadows shift as viewers change position, producing the visual impression of movement within a physically stable structure.
The works bring together a textile-based method of making and an industrial material. Weaving becomes a sculptural process through which strength and delicacy, permanence and impermanence, are held within the same form. Stainless steel takes on a larger spatial role in Enduring Vitality, a seven-meter-long installation in which branching tree forms extend across the gallery floor and walls. Here, steel replaces the drawn line, moving the image from a flat surface into the architecture. The branches twist, overlap, and separate according to the viewer’s position. Their metallic lines operate simultaneously as drawing, structure, and sculpture, while shadows cast across the surrounding surfaces create an additional layer of lines and forms. The tree introduces a grounded counterpart to the exhibition’s cloud motif. Its roots establish a sense of stability, while its branches extend upward through continuous growth. The two motifs are connected through the circulation of natural energy: water rises, condenses, returns to the earth, and supports new life. The cloud disperses and changes, while the tree remains rooted while continuing to develop.
 
Material contrasts connect painting, sculpture, and installation
The materials throughout Fields of Resonance are selected for their physical and visual properties. Oil paint provides fluidity and depth; beads and sequins introduce texture, reflected light, and volume; thread records repetition and manual labor; quartz and crystal refract light through solid matter; recycled glass introduces fragmentation and transformation; and stainless steel provides strength while functioning as fiber, line, and spatial structure. Nguyen retains the distinct qualities of each material instead of disguising them. Steel does not imitate thread, and crystal does not replicate pigment. Their differences become part of the composition. Soft materials accumulate until they acquire weight, while rigid materials are bent and woven into forms that appear delicate.
This movement between materials parallels Nguyen’s practice across painting, fashion, craft, sculpture, and installation. The boundaries between these disciplines remain open: a bead can function as color, light, texture, and volume; a steel strand can operate as line, structure, and image; a canvas can become a relief; and a drawing can expand into architectural space. Across the exhibition, natural motifs are used as structures through which internal and external states intersect. Clouds, trees, light, and mineral formations connect memory with material processes and the viewer’s physical presence. The title Fields of Resonance refers to this exchange. Memories generate images, light activates materials, movement changes perception, and the viewer’s position establishes new relationships between individual works and the gallery. The exhibition develops through recurring contrasts between light and weight, softness and resistance, stillness and movement, permanence and change. These relationships are expressed through painting, stitching, weaving, joining, bending, and assembly.
Across different scales and materials, Nguyen transforms atmospheric and natural forms into physical structures. Clouds become embroidered surfaces, mineral bodies, and woven metal formations, while trees become steel lines extending through space. Light connects these different materials, continually altering their appearance and relationship to the gallery. Fields of Resonance consequently approaches nature as a changing force that moves between memory, matter, light, and the processes of making.
 Passionate in Supernatural / 2024 / oil on canvas / 160 x 200 cm
 The Pause Between Storms / 2026 / stainless steel / 60 x 240 cm
 Fairer than a Fairy / 2026 / beadwork and sequins on canvas / 200 × 300 cm
 Another Day of Sun / 2026 / Quartz, cullet and beads / 30 x 30 cm

 artist Tia-Thuy Nguyen (center)

Sweden signs deal for four French FDI frigates
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
19:09:32 BST
03:09:32 KST

Sweden has signed a contract with France’s Naval Group for four FDI-based air defence frigates, completing a competition that also included British-Swedish and Spanish proposals, the UK Defence Journal understands.
The Swedish Defence Materiel Administration signed the procurement contract on 31 August during a visit to Stockholm by French President Emmanuel Macron, with the ships to enter Swedish service as the Luleå class.
The first frigate is planned for delivery in 2030, with the remaining three following successively. Sweden had selected Naval Group’s Frégate de Défense et d’Intervention design in May and subsequently entered negotiations with France over the purchase.
The Swedish Government said construction of the vessels and training of Swedish Armed Forces personnel can now begin following signature of the agreement.
Swedish Defence Minister Pål Jonson said: “This is a strategically important investment that strengthens Sweden’s defence capability and security in light of a deteriorated international situation. The four frigates will triple Sweden’s current air defence capability. This is essential to Sweden’s security and NATO’s capability.”
The Luleå-class vessels will be based on Naval Group’s FDI design but configured for Swedish requirements. The Swedish Government has previously confirmed that the ships will incorporate a number of domestically produced systems.
These are expected to include Saab’s RBS 15 anti-ship missile, lightweight torpedo, Giraffe 1X radar and Trackfire remote weapon station, together with 57mm and 40mm naval guns from BAE Systems Bofors.
The ships will also be equipped for area air defence. The Swedish Government said in May that advanced air defence was a central requirement for the programme and that the new frigates would contribute to NATO’s integrated air and missile defence capability.
Naval Group Chairman and Chief Executive Pierre Éric Pommellet said when the design was selected in May: “We are extremely honoured to have been selected by the Swedish Ministry of Defence. We are now eager to engage with the Swedish authorities and partners in the execution of this strategic project.”
He added: “The FDI will provide the Royal Swedish Navy with a latest-generation frigate and extended capabilities in all warfare domains with rapid delivery timeline, to meet the operational needs expressed by the Ministry of Defence.”
Naval Group faced two other proposals during the Swedish evaluation. Babcock, working with Swedish defence company Saab, offered the Arrowhead 120, a smaller derivative of the Arrowhead family that also includes the 140-metre design forming the basis of the Royal Navy’s Type 31 frigates.
The Arrowhead 120 proposed for Sweden is approximately 124 metres long and displaces around 4,650 tonnes. Babcock’s proposed configuration included the Saab 9LV combat management system, Sea Giraffe 4A fixed-face radar, Sea Giraffe 1X, RBS 15 anti-ship missiles, Saab lightweight torpedoes and Bofors guns.
Babcock and Saab had already been working on the Luleå programme before Sweden moved towards purchasing an existing foreign design. Saab had been contracted by the Swedish Defence Materiel Administration to undertake basic design work, with Babcock providing engineering support including structural design and auxiliary systems.
The third contender was Navantia’s ALFA 4000. The Spanish shipbuilder offered a 120-metre, approximately 4,300-tonne frigate and had proposed delivering the first two vessels in 2030 and the remaining pair in 2031.
Navantia’s proposed Swedish configuration also incorporated Swedish equipment, including the RBS 15, Bofors 57mm and 40mm guns and Saab Trackfire weapon stations. The company proposed air-defence, anti-submarine and surface-warfare capabilities alongside a hangar and flight deck suitable for helicopters.
Swedish officials said during the competition that the three proposals were assessed against time, capability and price. The government had also stipulated that the programme should concentrate on a mature vessel already in production in order to reduce delivery times.
The FDI is already in production for France and Greece. Naval Group pointed to the maturity of the production line and existing deliveries when making its Swedish proposal. The Swedish Government initially authorised negotiations with France in May for four ships expected to be delivered between 2030 and 2034. At the time, it said the procurement was the first stage of the process and that an order could be placed once negotiations were complete.
That process concluded with the contract signed on 31 August between the Swedish Defence Materiel Administration and Naval Group. Sweden and France also signed a separate framework agreement covering defence cooperation during Macron’s visit, including operational matters, defence equipment and industrial development.

Author-psychiatrist Augusto Cury gains ground in Brazil presidential race polls
SAO PAULO, Aug 31 - Augusto Cury, a psychiatrist and best-selling author with no previous elected office experience, has emerged as a surprise contender in Brazil's presidential race, unsettling a contest dominated by President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and Senator Flavio Bolsonaro.
Recent television appearances and strong social media reach have lifted Cury's standing in opinion polls ahead of the October vote.
Cury, 67, placed third in first-round voting scenarios released on Monday, garnering 11% (up from 2%) support in a Nexus poll commissioned by lender BTG Pactual and 7.8% (up from 1.6%) in an AtlasIntel/Bloomberg poll.
The results marked a rare shift in a race that has been dominated by the leftist-Lula and the right-wing Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro.
Cury's rise could reshape the dynamics of the campaign in the coming weeks, increasing pressure on the frontrunners to respond to a candidate seeking to appeal to voters dissatisfied with years of polarization.
Cury, who is running on the ticket of the little-known Avante party, has sought to position himself as an alternative to the long-standing political polarization between left and right in the country.
Analysts caution, however, that it is too early to conclude whether his gains will prove durable, as the opposition vote remains fragmented.
The Nexus poll showed Lula leading Bolsonaro by 39% to 33% while AtlasIntel put Lula at 43.4% versus 33.7% for Bolsonaro. If no candidate secures more than 50% of valid votes in the first round, the top two candidates advance to a runoff.
"To threaten Bolsonaro, an alternative conservative candidate would need to rise further in polls and reach roughly 15% around mid-September (with Bolsonaro simultaneously falling to about 25%) to credibly make a case for strategic voting against Lula," Eurasia Group said in a statement.
Cury has avoided identifying with either the political left or right, instead campaigning under the slogan "Centered on what matters."
H
NATIONAL PROFILE
A physician and prolific author focused on psychology and emotional well-being, Cury has built a national profile over decades through books, lectures and media appearances.
Cury says he has sold 42 million books in more than 70 countries and describes himself as the world's most-read psychiatrist. Reuters could not independently verify the claim.
With 10.7 million Instagram followers, he has a social media audience approaching Flavio Bolsonaro's 11.4 million, though still smaller than Lula's 14.9 million.
Born in Brazil's most-populous state, Sao Paulo, Cury portrays himself as a political outsider bringing management experience to government. In addition to his medical and publishing career, he says he is a rural producer and business manager.
"My mind is capitalist, my heart is social," Cury recently told reporters, as he criticized some of Lula's policies. REUTERS
