====================================================================================================

Opposition drone bill is ineffective
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
16:47:06 UTC
01:47:06 KST

The opposition-controlled Legislative Yuan passed an opposition-backed bill that sets aside NT$240 billion (US$7.6 billion) for uncrewed systems over the next six years. At first glance, that looks like a major commitment to Taiwan’s defense and industrial development. However, the headline number does not guarantee the stability that industry needs.
Opposition legislators chose to fund the program through the regular annual budget process. Although the NT$240 billion is earmarked for uncrewed systems, the funding must still return to the Legislative Yuan for approval each year. Unlike a multi-year special budget, it remains subject to annual budget discussions, legislative delays and political disputes. Taiwan saw that risk this year, when the annual budget was not passed until this month.
Industry needs greater certainty. When manufacturers decide whether to build production lines, hire engineers, expand testing capacity or develop domestic supply chains, they need more than a six-year target written into law. They need predictable orders and a credible multi-year procurement pipeline. Annual uncertainty undermines the long-term investment Taiwan needs for rapid industrial expansion.
However, the opposition-backed bill creates an even bigger problem: bureaucratic duplication. The law requires the Executive Yuan to establish a “National Uncrewed Vehicle Industry Development Strategy Special Committee,” which would coordinate, promote and supervise uncrewed-systems policy and review the national industry development plan.
The Executive Yuan already has a coordination mechanism. Vice Premier Cheng Li-chiun (鄭麗君) already leads the “Interagency Task Force on Unmanned Vehicle Industry Development and Management.” Officials from the Ministry of Economic Affairs (MOEA), Ministry of National Defense (MND), Ministry of Transportation, National Science and Technology Council and other agencies use it to coordinate industrial development, defense autonomy, supply chains and regulation.
Individual ministries have clear responsibilities. The MOEA has a dedicated drone-industry development office. The MND has professional planning departments responsible for strategic planning, capability assessment and major defense acquisition.
The Legislative Yuan has the institutions necessary to provide rigorous oversight. Legislators on the Foreign Affairs and National Defense Committee oversee defense procurement, force development, drones and uncrewed maritime systems. Legislators on the Economics Committee scrutinize industrial policy. The legislature can question ministers, demand special reports, review budgets, amend laws and examine procurement programs. That is the proper place for oversight.
The opposition-backed legislation instead requires more than half of the new strategy committee’s members to be experts or academics recommended by party caucuses in the Legislative Yuan. This allows caucus-nominated members to participate directly in an Executive Yuan policy coordination and review mechanism. Legislators should not blur those roles.
Legislators should demand transparency, challenge procurement priorities and hold officials accountable when programs fail. However, party caucuses should not need to place their nominees inside an executive policy-making mechanism to exercise oversight.
Clear responsibility produces stronger accountability — and faster execution.
That matters especially for uncrewed systems, where technology evolves far faster than traditional defense procurement cycles. Requirements can change in months, not years. Taiwan needs a process that shortens the path from battlefield requirements to procurement and production. Every additional layer of review creates another source for delays.
The issue is not whether Taiwan should invest more or exercise stronger oversight. It should do both. The question is whether the institutions we create help Taiwan move faster. We should not create new institutions only to make functioning administrative and legislative oversight mechanisms more complicated.
The executive mechanism should be made to work, while the Legislative Yuan should review its results from the legislature. Taiwan does not lack committees. What it cannot afford to waste is time.
Gahon Chiang is a congressional staff member in the office of Democratic Progressive Party Legislator Chen Kuan-ting focusing on Taiwan’s national security policy. He is a research fellow at the Taiwan Inspiration Association.

====================================================================================================

Donovan’s Deep Dives: 823 and two visions of Taiwan’s sovereignty
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
16:47:05 UTC
01:47:05 KST

Every year on the anniversary of the 1958 Kinmen 823 Artillery Bombardment — a central episode in what has become known as the Second Taiwan Strait Crisis — carefully crafted speeches reveal the underlying ideological divide over sovereignty between the Taiwan-centric, pan-green Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) and the pan-blue Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) stance that Taiwan is ultimately a province of China.
The pan-blue side has the added complication that some are hardcore Republic of China (ROC) nationalists, while others are more accommodating of and willing to work with the People’s Republic of China (PRC) to varying degrees.
Different accounts give varying numbers and duration for the conflict, but there were thousands of casualties on both the ROC and PRC sides and as many as 470,000 artillery shells struck Kinmen during the intensive 44-day bombardment.
Photo: Wu Cheng-ting, Taipei Times
For the US, there were fears of a war with the PRC over Quemoy (as Kinmen was then called), with the potential for it to turn nuclear. The US-ROC mutual defense treaty then in force, however, only explicitly covered Taiwan and Penghu. The US Navy provided escort close to Kinmen and provided advanced weaponry, but did not get directly involved in the fighting.
After seizing several islands the ROC held off the coast of China in the years prior, this was the final battle that held off further PRC seizures and preserved the territorial status quo that remains today
This was a pivotal event for Taiwanese in resisting the PRC, and Quemoy became a household name in American Cold War politics.
On the surface, both DPP and KMT politicians’ speeches share much in common. They praise the brave soldiers’ sacrifice in defending the nation, lay wreathes and talk about unity. It is in the details of their speeches that the differences are revealed.
WILLIAM LAI’S LINES ON SOVEREIGNTY
In the pan-green view, Taiwan is a settler and colonial society in much the same way as North America or Australia, and shares a similar timeline of several hundred years. Different colonial rulers, especially the Japanese, and different influences, including American, have created a society and culture different from China.
DPP politicians have complicated feelings about commemorating 823 for two reasons. First, the battle was one of the main justifications for the continuation of KMT-imposed martial law. The other is that most on the pan-green side only reluctantly accept the ROC name, constitution and symbols as a way to maintain independence while avoiding a war with the PRC. Kinmen and Matsu have been part of Fujian for at least a thousand years, and did not share in the Taiwanese settler or colonial experiences.
However, as president of the ROC, William Lai (賴清德) is obligated to maintain sovereignty over the islands and to support the troops. He used his speech to rally support for the military and expanding their role and budgets, a dig at the KMT-led opposition over recent controversies and disagreements over defense spending.
Like most DPP politicians, Lai views China as essentially foreign, which comes out in statements like: “For 68 years, China’s authoritarian forces have never stopped pursuing their ambitions for external expansion.”
Photo: Ou Su-mei, Taipei Times
The presidential office readout of Lai’s speech said that Taiwan must uphold “the spirit of ‘not surrendering a single inch of Taiwan, Penghu, Kinmen or Matsu.’”
Curiously, it didn’t mention traditional ROC claims in the South China Sea, which suggests that he is not going to fight over real estate there. It moreover seems unlikely that Taiwan is going to fight over other traditional territorial claims, including with the ROC’s 11-dash line that the PRC’s 10-dash (until recently 9-dash) is based on.
CHEN YI-HSIN PARROTS PRC
In response, the KMT issued a press release titled: “KMT Calls for ‘Not Surrendering a Single Inch’ on Aug. 23, Asks William Lai: ‘Why Won’t You Dare Mention Sovereignty Over Scarborough Shoal?’” referring to one of the islands in the South China Sea.
The press release covers a blistering attack by KMT Culture and Communications Committee Chairman Chen Yi-hsin (陳以信) on Lai’s speech. Chen is quoted as saying: “But when the Philippines establishes territorial baselines around Scarborough Shoal (Democracy Reef) in the South China Sea, which is part of our country, and when Japan and the Philippines negotiate over rights and interests in waters east of Taiwan — actions that seriously harm our sovereignty and maritime rights and interests — where is President Lai’s commitment to sovereignty?”
The specific term in the headline and in the quote for Scarborough Shoal is Huangyan Island (黃岩島), which is the official PRC name for it. Did an editor add the official ROC name — Democracy Reef (民主礁) — into the quote?
Since 2012, the shoal has been effectively controlled by the PRC. Scarborough Shoal is only 198km from the Philippines’ Subic Bay harbor and just 345km from the capital, Manila, and is considered a serious threat to their national security.
Chen’s leading use of the PRC-preferred name “Huangyan Island,” rather than Taiwan’s official “Democracy Reef,” strikingly echoes Beijing’s terminology, although he claimed the feature for the ROC rather than the PRC.
CHENG LI-WUN’S POINTED SPEECH
KMT Chair Cheng Li-wun’s (鄭麗文) comments were more sophisticated. She called on Taiwan, Kinmen, Matsu and Penghu to unite under the ROC constitution, reiterated her call for negotiating peace with China and supported a concept popular in some pan-blue circles of using Kinmen as a starting point for peace with China. The theory being that the physical proximity and historical ties with Fujian make it an ideal place to start.
She put the blame on the president entirely for recent constitutional crises, is highly debatable. She also attacked him for having sworn an oath to the ROC constitution, and chastised him: “Don’t say one thing and do another, and don’t try to distort the spirit of the ROC Constitution through the two-state theory.”
In other words, she rejects treating Taiwan and China as two separate countries and instead places both sides within a one-China ROC framework.
LU SHIOW-YEN’S FIERY SPEECH
Taichung Mayor Lu Shiow-yen (盧秀燕) commemorated 823 with a fire-and-brimstone speech that was clearly directed at the pan-blue base. Formerly, when she was a lawmaker, she was deeper blue, but in recent years as mayor has carefully cultivated a more moderate image.
On the softer side of her speech, she spoke about the sacrifices soldiers must make to defend the nation, including by her own father, and her direct experience growing up in a military dependents village.
The rest of the speech was more fiery, and she kept repeating two themes. She said: “Because of their [DPP leaders] ideology, because of their hatred, their goal is to make the Republic of China disappear. Some people are promoting Taiwan independence, putting our country at risk of war and are willing to destroy peace at all costs.”
She added: “We have only one goal: to protect the Republic of China and safeguard peace. We absolutely must win in 2026 and 2028.”
Typically, Lu delivers serious speeches in a calm but resolute tone. This was anything but.
Until recently, she was the frontrunner to be the KMT 2028 presidential candidate, but has been sliding in the polls. She may be pivoting back towards the base to shore up support in the party as she gears up for a run.

Ministry maximizing defense spending
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
16:47:05 UTC
01:47:05 KST

The military is reviewing budget execution trends and postponing non-urgent projects to maximize defense spending, the Ministry of National Defense said yesterday as it submitted its budget for next year and other defense documents to the legislature.
The ministry said China’s “gray zone” harassment of Taiwan has intensified while its military capabilities continue to expand rapidly. The assessment was included in its “Five-Year Force Buildup and Administration Plan Report” (五年兵力整建及施政計畫報告), submitted alongside the defense budget for this year and the “2026 China Military Power Report” (中共軍力報告書).
China continues joint combat-readiness patrols, military exercises and China Coast Guard operations, while using maritime militia forces, legal and psychological warfare, and economic coercion. These activities seek to treat the Taiwan Strait as internal waters and strengthen military deterrence against Taiwan, while improving Beijing’s ability to transition from training to combat, the ministry said.
Photo: Screen grab from the Web site of National Chungshan Institute of Science and Technology
The ministry’s domestic priorities include new rifles, night-vision optics, portable counter-drone systems, wheeled combat vehicles and armored fighting vehicles (AFVs).
The military is upgrading submarines and testing the domestically built Hai Kun (海鯤), while developing rescue and replenishment vessels, drones and uncrewed boats.
It is to procure the Strong Bow (強弓) medium-range anti-tactical ballistic missile system and build a multilayered air-defense network under the “Taiwan Shield” (T-Dome) framework. Other priorities include the Tactical Assault Kit (TAK), upgraded air-combat training systems, digitized command and communications networks, and an islandwide fiber-optic backup network.
US procurement priorities include M109A7 self-propelled howitzers and HIMARS multiple-launch rocket systems. The military will continue acquiring Altius 600M and Switchblade 300 systems, and add Altius 600ISR and 700M attack drones.
The army has budgeted NT$57.07 billion (US$1.8 billion) from next year to 2033 for 178 domestically developed Cheetah (獵豹) AFVs, armed with 105mm cannons. The D3 prototype has passed evaluation, with procurement to begin next year. The vehicles will have a maximum speed of 100kph, a range of 500km and the ability to fire while moving.
The army is also to spend NT$10.7 billion from next year to 2032 on 4,647 light tactical off-road vehicles. Another NT$79.54 billion from next year to 2034 is budgeted to replace aging CM21 armored personnel carriers with 410 wheeled combat and command vehicles.
The navy has budgeted NT$18.28 billion from next year to 2032 for a follow-on oil and ammunition replenishment ship. It operates the Panshih (磐石) and Wuyi (武夷), which entered service in 2015 and 1990 respectively, with the Wuyi nearing the end of its service life.
It will also spend NT$21.16 billion from next year to 2034 on two follow-on rescue vessels, as existing ships are more than 80 years old. Another NT$13.85 billion is budgeted for a submarine rescue vessel as the Hai Kun and subsequent domestically built submarines enter service.
The air force has budgeted NT$36.04 billion this year to 2032 for the Strong Bow medium-range anti-tactical ballistic missile system, previously funded through classified allocations.
The system is designed to intercept tactical ballistic missiles at ranges of up to 1,000km and will be integrated with lower-tier systems to form a multilayered defense network. Delivery is scheduled to begin in 2028, although the number of systems remains classified.
Developed by the National Chungshan Institute of Science and Technology, the Strong Bow is a mobile interceptor designed to work with Patriot and Sky Bow III (天弓三型), military sources said.
The army has budgeted NT$10.73 billion from next year to 2030 for a second phase of night-vision optics procurement, including 41,000 monocular and 10,778 binocular devices.
The procurement follows concerns over shortages after some service members conducting nighttime drills in Taipei were seen without night-vision gear. The army said shortages could affect wartime guard duties.
The army also plans to spend NT$2 billion from next year to 2031 on 129,759 protective masks and 264,278 filters, saying its T3-75 masks, manufactured in 1986, are no longer adequate against chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear threats.
As new equipment enters service, the military will retire equipment that no longer meets operational requirements and adjust force structures and personnel allocations, the ministry said.
Garrison and reserve forces will also be reorganized based on operational scenarios and mobilization requirements.
Drawing lessons from the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, the ministry said it would prioritize new weapons, communications and intelligence resilience, ammunition, mobilization and training readiness.
It said it has reviewed previous budget execution in line with Executive Yuan guidelines and will postpone non-urgent projects to direct funds toward the military’s most pressing needs.

Religion is shown in how one acts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
16:47:04 UTC
01:47:04 KST

Taiwanese entertainer Tsai Yi-chen (蔡頤榛) — known professionally as “Wu Hsiung” (五熊) — was arrested in Japan for allegedly splashing a liquid on a Buddhist artifact displayed in a temple. Tsai failed to set a good example as a Christian.
The Christian Bible says: “Then you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.” However, freedom is not about causing damage as one sees fit.
Confucius said that “I could follow my heart’s desires without overstepping the bonds.” While acting as one wants might seem like freedom, the key actually lies in not breaking the rules. As one accumulates wisdom, their words and actions naturally conform to societal standards. Whether Tsai wants to serve her god, her faith should not serve as an excuse to cross others’ boundaries.
Christianity has a ritual of anointing, lightly applying oil to the body or to objects as a symbol of purification and blessing. However, is the oil essential for the effectiveness in practice? If so, is there still any freedom in this faith, or is it instead trapped by the oil?
The Christian god is supposed to be omnipotent, and yet he chooses not to force people to love him? Jesus did not employ violence or coercion when interacting with people of different religions. If someone’s faith fosters a sense of superiority, they lose the ability to love everyone else. Do some Christians really know what they believe in?
Much of the Bible’s centuries of writings have been interpreted in different ways. An oft-cited passage is: “‘I have the right to do anything,’ you say — but not everything is beneficial; ‘I have the right to do anything’ — but not everything is constructive.” No matter what you believe in, one should have the ability to know what is beneficial or constructive.
If your wisdom is limited, you should first learn not to harm or obstruct others.
Kavir Tseng is a bilingual host, and a graduate of Top Leadership Bible School.

Health ministry expands health subsidy categories
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
16:47:00 UTC
01:47:00 KST

The Ministry of Health and Welfare (MOHW) yesterday announced several health policies that take effect today, including increased subsidies for in vitro fertilization (IVF), inclusion of more therapies under National Health Insurance (NHI) coverage, and expanded eligibility for a children’s dental fluoride treatment subsidy.
The Health Promotion Administration said the subsidies for the second and third courses of IVF treatment for women under 40 years old would be increased from NT$100,000 to NT$150,000 (US$3,158 to US$4,737); and increased from NT$80,000 to NT$130,000 for women aged 40 to 45.
About 20,000 people receive IVF subsidies each year, and about 5,000 people are estimated to be eligible for receiving the increased subsidy each year, it said.
Photo: Lo Pi, Taipei Times
The NHI Administration (NHIA) said it has revised the NHI coverage criteria for lipid-lowering drugs to align with clinical treatment consensus, added two types of therapies for rare diseases and 20 other treatment items under NHI coverage, and adjusted the NHI payment standards for some medical procedures.
Lipid-lowering drugs, including statins, ezetimibe and combination drugs containing both, would be included into NHI coverage, in line with the latest clinical treatment guidelines revised last year, it said.
The initiative aims to allow people with hyperlipidemia to receive timely and appropriate medication, reducing the risk of cardiovascular diseases, the agency said, adding that it is estimated to benefit about 998,000 to 1.11 million patients from the first to fifth year, at an estimated cost of about NT$2.28 billion.
Regarding therapies for rare diseases, drugs containing iptacopan, an oral treatment for adults with paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria (PNH), and drugs containing maralixibat chloride, oral solution and tablets used to treat severe itching (cholestatic pruritus) caused by Alagille syndrome (ALGS) in people aged one year or older, would be included for NHI coverage, it said.
Iptacopan has been included in insurance coverage for adult patients with paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH). As an oral medication, iptacopan offers clinical convenience, providing PNH patients with more treatment options and helping to enhance treatment accessibility and care quality. It could help about 30 people, with a projected pharmaceutical expenditure of about NT$183 million.
In response to clinical demands, 20 medical procedures, including peripheral atherectomies for treating people with peripheral artery disease, have been added to NHI coverage, the NHIA said, adding that about 11,000 people should benefit from the inclusion.
NHI payments to healthcare providers for operating procedures in pediatric and obstetrics departments have been increased, as well as inpatient nursing services, to address the issue of healthcare provider shortages in certain departments, it said.
The MOHW Department of Oral Health said eligibility for children’s dental fluoride treatment subsidy would be expanded “from birth to until Aug. 31 of the year the child enters elementary school.”
Eligible children can receive the subsidy once every six months when they see a registered dentist for the service before entering elementary school, and children with disabilities, from low-income households, who live in remote areas, outlying islands or indigenous communities, or who are younger than 12 years old, can receive the subsidy once every three months, it said.
The expanded eligibility is expected to benefit about 130,000 people per year, the department said.
Tooth decay in primary teeth among five-year-old children has been reduced from 65.4 percent in 2018 to 46.3 percent in 2024, and the average number of decayed, missing and filled teeth among 12-year-old children has dropped from 3.31 in 2000 to 2.01 in 2020, it said.

Nvidia to invest US$3.5 billion in MediaTek
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
16:46:59 UTC
01:46:59 KST

Nvidia Corp is investing US$3.5 billion into MediaTek Inc (聯發科), deepening collaboration with the Taiwanese chip designer at a time when it’s working to persuade more companies to build chips that plug into its dominant data center ecosystem.
Nvidia will buy bonds convertible into MediaTek shares, the companies said in a joint statement yesterday.
The investment broadens a partnership between the two chip designers that will see MediaTek using NVLink Fusion and the newly announced NVHBM technology as part of an Nvidia tech suite to help components communicate more seamlessly in data centers. The Taiwanese company is trying to challenge Broadcom Inc and Marvell Technology Inc by helping owners of data centers create their own components.
Photo: CNA
For Nvidia, the new agreement is the latest effort to ensure the future of artificial intelligence (AI) is built around its hardware platform and standards.
The US chip giant has been building data center interconnect systems like NVLink Fusion and partnering with the likes of MediaTek to ensure it maintains a central role in the entire hardware chain, not just with its class-leading AI accelerators.
The MediaTek agreement follows a similar announcement by Amazon.com Inc, which agreed to deploy an additional 2 million Nvidia components. Critically, Amazon also pledged to use Nvidia’s connection technology with its in-house chips.
Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang (黃仁勳), who was born in Taiwan, is tightening ties with a company working to reduce its reliance on the smartphone market. MediaTek earlier this year secured a partnership with Alphabet Inc’s Google, and is gaining credibility as a design partner to major tech firms that are seeking to build their own AI chips. That momentum has led the chipmaker’s market value to roughly triple in recent months.
The agreements with MediaTek and Amazon give Nvidia the opportunity to retain its central role in the build-out of AI data centers even when companies are deploying chips designed to replace its main offerings. The deal is yet another example of Nvidia’s leadership investing in customers, rivals and other companies involved in the AI industry. Concern about the seemingly circular nature of those investments has percolated in investor circles, though Nvidia has strongly disputed the idea it’s creating false demand.
MediaTek already works with Nvidia on the US chipmaker’s nascent effort to get into the laptop industry. The Taiwanese company is helping with Nvidia’s RTX Spark product for that market.
MediaTek has also signaled that it plans to hire aggressively to better capture business opportunities from the AI boom. Forecasting AI chip revenue of about US$2 billion this year, the company has set the goal of securing as much as 15 percent of an US$80 billion segment of the data center market next year.

State-owned oil supplier CPC Corp., Taiwan, said yesterday that it will keep natural gas prices for domestic and industrial users unchanged in September but will increase them by 5.83 percent for companies that generate electricity.
In a statement, CPC said liquefied natural gas (LNG) prices have been on the rise because of uncertainty over supply amid stalled negotiations between the United States and Iran and a push by European countries to build up LNG inventories before winter.
Although natural gas should increase based on the government’s standardized pricing formula, CPC said it would keep prices for domestic users unchanged in line with government policies to stabilize consumer prices.
Photo courtesy of CPC Corp, Taiwan
For industrial users, CPC said it would absorb the additional costs after taking into account consumer prices, overall economic conditions and the need to ease cost pressures on businesses.
It has absorbed NT$140 billion (US$4.42 billion) in losses on sales to the industrial sector since 2021, it said.
Natural gas prices for the electricity sector, however, will be increased by 5.83 percent to better reflect higher LNG costs, CPC said.
Whether that will translate into higher electricity costs is uncertain, especially given that state-run utility Taiwan Power Co. has also tended to absorb increases in the price of its inputs to keep power costs down for end users.
CPC said it will continue to monitor global LNG prices and review its pricing policy in line with government policy.

Mauled Australian swimmer recalls punching shark
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
16:46:55 UTC
01:46:55 KST

An Australian school teacher mauled by a large shark at a Sydney beach said she fired a “left hook” at the predator before it dragged her underwater.
Leah Stewart, a primary school teacher, was placed in an induced coma and had part of her left arm amputated after the June 13 attack at Sydney’s Coogee Beach.
Stewart decided to go for a late-morning swim in the “crystal clear” sea, unknowingly sharing the water with a shark described by witnesses as a great white measuring up to 4m long.
Photo: Reuters
The teacher said she was finishing her swim and approaching the sand when she heard a girl scream.
“I turned, and there was a huge, huge fin behind her. It was massive, and at first I thought: ‘Oh, it’s a dolphin,’” she told Nine Network television’s 60 Minutes in a program that aired on Sunday.
“I looked at the size of it and I realized, that’s not a dolphin. And so we just start screaming at the top of our lungs, just like ‘shark, shark, shark,’” she said.
She swam a few more strokes, then felt something in the water, and turned around to see it slowly approaching.
“Its face was horrific. I’ll never forget its face, it was huge. And its teeth, and its mouth was massive, and its eyes, it’s just black little beady eyes. We were looking face to face,” Stewart said.
Fearing it would bite her face, she decided she had to punch it.
“I thought, well, which limb am I willing to lose? I’m right-handed, so I decided let’s do a left hook,” she recounted.
“I just kind of throw my left arm, and it just grabs onto my forearm and rips, rips away my skin, my muscle, everything,” she said.
Stewart said she was in shock as she looked down and saw her own injured hand.
“The next moment, I feel it grab onto my left thigh, and it rips me underwater,” she said.
As the shark pulled her down, she took a big breath, thinking to herself that she had to survive for her young daughter, August.
“I twisted myself around, and I just started punching it over and over and over again, just punch, punch, punch, and it was like fighting a dinosaur,” she added.
“It was so big; it was like punching a brick wall. And I think I must have got a really good one in. And so it let me go, and I just kind of popped back up,” she said.
Stewart, in her mid-30s, was helped ashore by Charlie Verco, an elite paddleboarder who happened to be in the water nearby. Medics treated her on the beach before she was taken to hospital.
About 10 days after the attack, doctors reduced her sedation and she emerged from her coma.
Australian scientists believe rising ocean temperatures are shifting sharks’ migratory patterns, which may be contributing to an uptick in attacks.
A 12-year-old boy died after he was bitten by a shark while swimming in Sydney Harbour in January.
Three divers were fatally mauled in separate incidents between May and June — two in Western Australia and the third in Queensland.
There have been nearly 1,300 shark incidents around Australia since 1791, of which more than 260 resulted in death, according to a database of shark encounters with humans.

Integrated systems to lead AI boom: TSMC executive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
16:46:55 UTC
01:46:55 KST

The next phase of artificial intelligence (AI) growth would be driven by the large-scale deployment of integrated computing systems as the industry enters the “true industrialization of AI,” Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電) AI and high-performance computing business development director April Li (李湘) said yesterday.
AI agents are moving into enterprise workflows, while investment in specialized data centers and physical AI is accelerating, Li said in a keynote speech at the Semicon Taiwan IC forum in Taipei.
“In this new era, market leaders will not be the ones who simply make better models, but those who build the most integrated systems,” Li said.
Photo: I-Hwa Cheng, AFP
Rather than relying on advances in individual chips or models alone, future AI infrastructure would increasingly need to integrate computing, memory, interconnects, storage and power management across chips, server racks and entire data centers, she said.
The shift is being driven partly by soaring demand for AI inference — the process of using trained models to respond to requests and perform tasks, Li said.
Global inference token volume has increased about 500-fold from its 2022 level, while more complex reasoning and agentic AI systems consume more tokens than conventional one-shot queries, she said.
“Inference is no longer a low-overhead task,” Li said, adding that it is becoming the dominant driver of system-level expansion as AI agents operate continuously in the background.
The growing workloads are putting pressure on four areas — logic scaling, interconnect efficiency, memory performance, and power delivery and cooling, she said.
Data movement alone can account for up to 60 percent of system activity in typical workloads, leaving accelerators operating at below 40 percent utilization, she added.
Meanwhile, AI packages might contain more than 1 trillion transistors by 2030, making multi-die architecture and heterogeneous integration essential, Li said.
To address those constraints, TSMC is developing technologies covering advanced logic, packaging and optical interconnects, she said.
She highlighted the chipmaker’s 3DFabric platform, which incorporates technologies such as system on integrated chips 3D stacking and chip-on-wafer-on-substrate advanced packaging, as well as its compact universal photonic engine platform for high-speed optical data transmission.
TSMC is also working to improve high-bandwidth memory performance by using advanced logic technology in high-bandwidth memory base dies, Li said.
In a question-and-answer session, Li said TSMC must develop an in-depth understanding of the supply chain “from silicon to the data center to the token” and work with ecosystem partners to validate its technologies as early as possible across that chain.
That reflects how TSMC’s role has expanded beyond manufacturing individual chips, she said.
“Gone are the days when we can just ship wafers across the fence,” Li said.

The town-like complex is unique in design, but not in its placement. Dozens of data centers have been constructed in the southwestern province in the past few years. They are part of a government strategy that has seen much of the digital infrastructure for breakneck artificial intelligence (AI) development across China’s eastern seaboard established in the country’s less populated, rural west. The build-out is ongoing. China

Academic calls for protection amid coral bleaching
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
16:46:54 UTC
01:46:54 KST

Taiwan should tighten regulations on coastal development to boost coral resilience, an academic said yesterday after a report showed that coral bleaching was increasing in the Kuroshio subregion, where Taiwan is located.
Compared with the historical baseline period from 1980 to 2009, global hard coral coverage from 2020 to 204 was down about 9.5 percent, the “Status of Coral Reefs of the World: 2025” report published yesterday by Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network showed.
Global hard coral cover was estimated at about 25.8 percent in 2024, it showed.
Photo: Yang Yuan-ting, Taipei Times
Plunges occurred in 1998, 2010, 2016 and from 2023 to 2024 during four global coral bleaching events, the report said.
Although some coral recovered, global coral coverage decreased again during a heat wave, it said.
The extent of coral decline varies across 10 monitored regions worldwide, the report said, adding the East Asian waters have the largest coral reef area with relatively stable coverage over the past 40 years.
However, the fourth global coral bleaching event, which was announced in 2023, caused an annual 3.2 percentage-point decrease in the waters’ coral coverage, with the median dropping from 32.2 percent to 29 percent, it said.
Academia Sinica Biodiversity Research Center researcher Chen Chao-lun (陳昭倫) said the incorporation of Taiwan’s coral monitoring data in the global report showed that research from academic institutions, compiled with civilians, has the potential of being included in global environmental evaluations.
That helps raise Taiwan’s visibility to the world, he said.
The report’s key takeaway for Taiwan is that East Asia remains a hopeful region, but it is not immune to climate change, Chen said.
A major concern is that the “recovery window” is shrinking, he said.
If it takes a reef takes a decade to recover when another large-scale heat wave is coming within five years, there would not be enough time for corals to grow, reproduce and rebuild their communities, he said.
From 2019 to last year, more than one-quarter of the world’s coral reefs experienced bleaching-level heat stress at least four times, Chen said.
That means a worryingly high coral bleaching frequency of nearly once a year, he added.
Tunghai University life science professor Wen Guo-zhang (溫國彰) said the shortened coral bleaching frequency indicated that another extreme heat event struck before corals could recover or complete species succession.
He called for tightening regulations on coastal development sediment, establishing protected areas, and removing abandoned fishing nets to increase local corals’ resilience.
What is most needed are binding legal penalties and substantive law enforcement, Wen said.

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
16:46:53 UTC

Indonesia yesterday said it was investigating claims that “several” citizens had joined the Russian military and were deployed in the war in Ukraine.
The information, which came from Ukrainian authorities, was being verified with several ministries and government institutions, the Indonesian Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Jakarta said in a statement.
It did not say how many Indonesians were under suspicion.
Photo: AFP
If the information is true, the fighters risk losing their citizenship under a law that requires Indonesians to obtain presidential permission if they want to serve a foreign military.
“If the involvement of Indonesian citizens in the armed forces of a foreign country is verified, it is an individual act and does not represent the policy or position of the Indonesian government,” the ministry said.
Indonesia has not traditionally been a source of mercenaries for Russia or Ukraine, which have both recruited foreign fighters throughout the war.
“Information regarding the identity, citizenship status, recruitment process, and form of involvement of the individuals mentioned still needs to be further confirmed,” the ministry said.
“The Indonesian government will also investigate the possibility of fraud, exploitation, or recruitment through job offers that are not in accordance with the intended purpose,” it said.
Citizens from African countries have reportedly been forcibly conscripted into the Russian army to fight in Ukraine after being lured with promises of jobs abroad.

“Super Garuda Shield,” held annually since 2006, is to run until Friday next week and include more than 4,700 personnel, with 13 other countries taking part, including Japan, South Korea, Australia and Canada.
The exercises are to take place in several regions of Indonesia and include infiltration drills, firing of stinger missiles, jungle training and naval maneuvers.
Photo: AFP
This edition comes after the two countries’ defense ministers signed a major defense cooperation partnership in April, which Jakarta has said would include US support in its military modernization initiatives and training of its troops.
“We are not just meeting for another annual training cycle. We are writing a historic new chapter in our bilateral relationship,” Major General Patrick Ellis, US Army Commanding General of the 4th Infantry Division, said in a speech opening the exercises in Bandung.
Jakarta has long maintained a foreign policy of non-alignment, with Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto vowing to befriend all nations and maintain good ties with the US and China.
Indonesia earlier this month agreed to boost its military ties with Beijing during a visit by China’s foreign and defense ministers.
Super Garuda Shield will also include humanitarian disaster relief efforts. Natural disasters like earthquakes and landslides are common in Indonesia.

Qingqing: Ugh. . . There was another traffic jam near my house this morning. It was so annoying.
Huahua: What happened? What was going on?
Qingqing: Today was the first day of school for elementary and secondary schools. There’s one near my house, so the roads were packed with parents taking their children to school. There were cars and scooters everywhere. It was terrifying.
Huahua: We start work relatively late. How did you end up running into school traffic?
Qingqing: I have a project that I need to finish soon, so I planned to get to the office early and work on it. I didn’t realize that today was the first day of school.
Huahua: Now that school has started, you should plan what time to leave home, so you won’t get caught in the crowds again.
Qingqing: That’s true. When I think about those parents who have to rush to work after dropping their kids off, I realize how hard it is for them, too.
Huahua: You’ll understand when you have children of your own someday.

Ministry escalates anti-fraud efforts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
16:46:50 UTC
01:46:50 KST

The Ministry of Digital Affairs (MODA) yesterday said it is working with Meta, Google, Line and TikTok to counter scams that use artificial intelligence (AI) by using real-time intelligence sharing and countermeasures to stop fraud at the source.
Minister of Digital Affairs Lin Yi-ching (林宜敬) introduced the ministry’s new “using AI to counter AI fraud” initiative at a news conference, highlighting efforts to combat scammers who use AI to generate large volumes of fraudulent information.
Online platforms should not act as mere observers, but should join the government’s anti-fraud efforts, especially as they have access to information that the government does not that can be used to neutralize scams, Lin said.
Photo : CNA
Meta said it has launched a real-time AI scam verification system alongside the Taiwanese fact-checking organization MyGoPen and the Taiwan Digital Security Development Association.
It regularly exchanges intelligence with the government and tracks the networks of accounts that abuse its services, it said.
From March 2024 until the middle of last month, Meta said it removed 10.9 million scam advertisements in Taiwan and disabled more than 40,000 scam advertising accounts.
Google said it uses AI to detect and combat scam organizations.
It provides features such as the AI-powered “Circle to Search” feature, Android scam-call detection and identity verification through selfie videos for Google accounts, it said
Last year, it blocked or removed more than 8.3 billion advertisements worldwide and suspended more than 24.9 million accounts that violated its policies, with AI used to block more than 99 percent of the adverts, it said.
Line said it has implemented industrywide cooperation and automated takedown mechanisms, with warning features for accounts impersonating public figures and suspicious links.
From November 2024 to last month, Line said it took action against 142,006 accounts suspected of scam activity under the Fraud Crime Hazard Prevention Act (詐欺犯罪危害防制條例), with its automated system processing cases in less than one hour.
It worked with the Taiwan Network Information Center and three major telecom providers to take down more than 1,500 phishing domains in 24 hours, it added.
TikTok said it works to reduce people’s exposure to scam content through its user reports, advertising policies and labels for AI-generated content.
The platform removed 45,063 scam adverts and took action against 784 advertisers in the fourth quarter of last year and the first quarter of this year, it said.
Key challenges in tackling digital fraud include scam accounts abusing platform services, an increase in user-generated content involving scams and phishing links that direct people to external sites when clicked, the Administration for Digital Industries (ADI) said.
The ADI vowed to continue to guide platforms in strengthening protection measures, saying it had three targets for improvement this year.
First, it said it would continue using AI detection to expand its database of scam-related keywords, fake event content and related scam indicators to enable blockers for scam adverts and fake accounts.
Second, it would strengthen identity verification mechanisms and management of blacklists for high-risk accounts, expanding efforts to prevent such accounts from re-entering platforms, it said.
Third, the ADI said it would provide users with real-time warnings at high-risk points of contact, such as when receiving private messages, friend requests and suspicious links.
The agency continues to expand its anti-scam database as scam tactics continue to evolve, ADI Director-General Lin Jiunn-shiow (林俊秀) said.
That includes working with cybersecurity software company Trend Micro, TrustTech company Gogolook and the National Police Agency to integrate data and improve the efficacy of AI-powered anti-scam efforts, he said.

Smart blood tube prep tech easing nurses’ workload
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
16:46:46 UTC
01:46:46 KST

Taipei Medical University Hospital (TMUH) yesterday said it is the first hospital in the nation to put a smart specimen tube preparation system into practice, sparing nurses the tube preparation and labeling duties and significantly reducing the time required to collect blood samples from patients.
TMUH began introducing a smart specimen tube preparation system in general wards in line with the government’s Healthy Taiwan Cultivation Plan to invest more in smart technology to optimize clinical workflows, and has extended it to the intensive care unit, emergency department and the hemodialysis section, the hospital said.
The hospital installed 21 sets of the system across 18 nursing units, integrating smart technology into frontline clinical care, it said.
Photo Courtesy of Taipei Medical University Hospital
TMUH nursing department director Lin Shu-Chuan (林淑娟) said blood collection is one of the most common clinical procedures nurses perform.
After getting the order, the workflow usually involves the nurse first verifying the patient’s required test items, determining the testing schedule, selecting the proper type and number of specimen tubes, and manually applying patient barcode labels to the blood collection tubes, she said.
The process is time-consuming and relies on human judgement and precise execution, she said, adding that if the nurse accidentally selected the wrong test tube or labeled it inaccurately, the sample might be rejected and the patient might need to have more blood drawn.
Lin said after the smart specimen tube preparation system was introduced, nurses can just select the doctor’s order on a screen or scan the requisition barcodes and the system automatically determines the appropriate tube types based on the order and applies the required labels on the tubes, sparing nurses manual tube preparation and labeling duties.
After the system was gradually fielded over about three months, the usage rate in the general wards has reached as high as 95.6 percent, preparing up to 24,965 test tubes as of last month, she said.
The hospital said an on-site evaluation of the efficiency of the system found that the average time for preparing three test tubes has been significantly reduced from 1 minute and 23 seconds before the system was introduced to only eight seconds.
For 24,965 test tubes, it means time savings of up to 520.1 hours, or a 90.4 percent efficiency improvement in tube preparation workflows, TMUH said.
Lin said the value of the system goes beyond reducing processing time and easing nurses’ work burden, it enhances accuracy and improves patient safety through standardized procedure and data integration.
TMUH superintendent Shih Chun-ming (施俊明) said promoting smart healthcare is not only about introducing new technology, but ensuring it addresses practical needs and clinical problems, so the hospital has leveraged technology to reduce nurses’ burden of doing repetitive tasks, while improving efficiency by offering more valuable person-centered care.

Backlog of orders growing, Value Valves Co reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
16:46:45 UTC
01:46:45 KST

Value Valves Co (捷流閥業) yesterday said that its backlog of orders is expanding, and current orders from companies in the semiconductor and electronics industries have increased 15 percent year-on-year, as the company benefits from the booming artificial intelligence (AI) supply chain.
The company, based in New Taipei City’s Tucheng District (土城), said it has clear order visibility for about seven months and expects orders from the semiconductor and electronics industries to account for 30 to 40 percent of its total revenue this year.
It said it also has orders from power plants at home and abroad.
Photo courtesy of Value Valves Co
“As capital expenditures on AI-related infrastructure gradually translate into actual demand for industrial valves, the company’s strategic positioning within the booming AI supply chain continues to yield positive results and is expected to become a key engine for future order growth,” Value Valves said in a statement following a business outlook presentation in Taipei.
The company manufactures valves in various specifications at facilities in Taiwan and China, with butterfly valves being its major revenue contributor. Its products are used in the petrochemical, semiconductor and shipbuilding industries.
Cumulative revenue in the first seven months of this year increased 2.55 percent year-on-year to NT$1.37 billion (US$43.3 million), and net profit in the first half of the year grew 51.78 percent from a year earlier to NT$148.98 million, with earnings per share of NT$3.18, company data showed.
Industrial valves are key components responsible for the opening and closing, regulation, isolation, checking and safety control of various fluids and gases, ensuring their precise delivery according to process requirements, Value Valves said.
A large semiconductor plant typically requires about 30,000 to 40,000 valves, each with different functions such as flow control, equipment isolation, system protection and improving operational efficiency, the company said.
If a critical valve malfunctions, it would not only cause local equipment shutdowns, but also affect process continuity, production yield and plant safety, it said.
“What the outside world sees are the rapidly expanding wafer fabs, data centers and advanced packaging lines driven by this AI wave, but what we see is the massive and sophisticated fluid and gas control systems that are hidden behind, supporting the day-and-night operations of factories,” Value Valves said.
In addition to securing business opportunities in this wave of AI infrastructure buildout, the company is also optimistic about orders from the shipbuilding industry amid the global energy transition and expanding demand for liquefied natural gas carriers and dual-fuel vessels, it said.

500 millionth Taipei YouBike renter to get NT$20,000 prize
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
16:46:44 UTC
01:46:44 KST

The person who becomes the 500 millionth renter of Taiwan’s public bicycle-rental system, YouBike, in Taipei in the coming weeks will receive a shopping voucher for NT$20,000 (US$630), the Taipei City Department of Transportation said yesterday.
In a press release on the program’s high number of riders, the department projected that the 500 millionth YouBike renter milestone would be hit around Sept. 14.
The projection is based on the department’s statistics, which show that Taipei’s bike-rental system hit its 100 millionth user mark in April 2018.
Photo: CNA
It then took about three and a half years to hit the 200 millionth mark, before surpassing the 300 millionth milestone approximately two and a half years after that.
With the relaunch of the first-30-minutes-free policy under Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) on Feb. 28, 2024, it then took just 17 months for the system to accumulate another 100 million users to hit 400 million.
The city department said the person identified as the 500 millionth YouBike user to rent a bike from a station in Taipei and return it within the capital will receive NT $20,000 in shopping credits, redeemable for vouchers at any of its commercial partners.
Additionally, the five cyclists who rent a bike in Taipei immediately before and the five who rent one immediately after the 500 millionth user will each receive NT$1,000 in shopping vouchers for use at Taiwan lifestyle and beauty retail chain Poya.
The department added that the 11 winners will be announced on its official website and also the Taipei YouBike Facebook fan page, while the winners themselves will be notified via text messages and phone calls.
According to the department’s statistics, there are 1,794 YouBike stations around Taipei at present, averaging 150-200 meters between each other.
Taipei is home to 27,438 YouBike bicycles, of which 4,350 are electric models that help riders accelerate.
YouBikes in Kaohsiung
Echoing Taipei’s efforts to help the city go green by supporting commuting with YouBikes, the Kaohsiung City Transportation Bureau on Monday also announced that it will be adding 1,200 more bicycles to the city’s YouBike system.
The bureau said it has planned to add 965 bicycles and 235 electric bikes by November this year, bringing the total number of YouBike bicycles in the southern Taiwan port city to 14,306 units, 2,141 of which would be electric.
Since incorporating the YouBike 2.0 system into the city in 2020, Kaohsiung now has 1,500 stations, and its system has accumulated about 91 million users, the bureau said.

The department approved two foreign investments in Taiwan and four overseas investments by Taiwanese companies, totaling NT$12.835 billion and US$358.36 million, respectively, the ministry said in a statement.
Lam Research will invest the equivalent of NT$9.835 billion in Lam Research Taiwan to support research, development and design operations for critical equipment used in advanced semiconductor manufacturing processes, the statement said.
Photo: Taipei Times file

It will invest 15 billion yen (US$94.36 million) in Nuvoton Technology Corp Japan for integrated circuit (IC) product design, development and manufacturing.
In addition, YMA Corp (源川國際) will invest US$60 million in its US subsidiary, YMA (TX) Inc, to manufacture solid-state batteries and drone-related components.
Li Yi International Investment Co (利億國際投資), a subsidiary of Hon Hai Precision Industry Co (鴻海精密), will invest the equivalent of US$57.01 million in Mitsubishi Fuso Bus Manufacturing Co to support bus manufacturing and sales operations.

Gudeng Precision Industrial Co (家登精密), which supplies wafer pods and reticle carriers to the world’s major semiconductor companies, yesterday said that it expects revenue from advanced packaging wafer carriers to grow at a double-digit percentage annually through 2028 as customers ramp up production.
“We believe the revenue contribution from advanced packaging [wafer carriers] will grow gradually,” Gudeng chairman Bill Chiu (邱銘乾) told a media gathering in Taipei. “The company has been focusing on developing high-end wafer carriers over the past 20 years and aims to secure a large customer base around the world.”
Gudeng has expanded its product portfolio to the advanced packaging segment since 2019 to supply circular and square wafer carriers. The company is a key supplier of extreme ultraviolet lithography pods to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電), and counts Intel Corp and major Chinese chipmakers among its customers.
Photo: Lisa Wang, Taipei Times
Chiu did not respond to a question about whether Gudeng has sent its new rectangular wafer carriers to TSMC for certification. TSMC plans to ramp up production of its chip-on-panel-on-substrate packaging in 2028.
The company said that it is positive about the second half of this year and the first quarter of next year thanks to rising customer demand.
“In Taiwan alone, several chip manufacturing facilities are being planned. As long as those fabs are dedicated to nanometer-class chips or advanced packaging, we would have good opportunities,” Chiu said.
Gudeng has started deploying manufacturing facilities in the US in response to customer demand, he said, adding that in the initial stage, the company is installing several automated machines to produce parts for the aerospace segment.
The US production line in Phoenix, Arizona, is to enter production in the next quarter, the company said.
In Japan, Gudeng sees progress in ramping up production of its first production line, Chiu said.
It is scheduled to enter volume production at the end of this year at the earliest, he said.
Gudeng’s biggest presence is in Taiwan, accounting for 52 percent of sales in the first half of this year, followed by China at 29 percent and the US at 17 percent.
Revenue grew 22 percent year-on-year to NT$4.18 billion (US$132 million) in the first half of this year, and net profit surged 206.72 percent to NT$776 million from NT$253 million. That translated into earnings per share of NT$8.09, up from NT$2.64 in the same period last year.

Taiwan-Singapore trade going strong, envoy says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
16:46:39 UTC
01:46:39 KST

Taiwan could remain Singapore’s largest trading partner for a second consecutive year, as bilateral trade reached a record high in the first half of this year, Representative to Singapore Tung Chen-yuan (童振源) said.
Taiwan surpassed China and Malaysia last year to become Singapore’s largest trading partner, with bilateral trade totaling S$170.3 billion (US$133.8 billion), a 46 percent year-on-year increase.
Trade in the first half of this year reached S$152 billion, up 94.1 percent from the same period last year, Tung said in an interview with the Central News Agency.
Photo: CNA
Singapore was also Taiwan’s largest source of foreign investment last year. Approved Singaporean investment in Taiwan reached US$5.34 billion, accounting for 60.1 percent of total foreign investment. Taiwanese investment in Singapore reached US$1.05 billion, making the city-state Taiwan’s third-largest overseas investment destination.
Tung said Taiwan and Singapore have maintained close and diverse ties, with the representative office focusing on strengthening exchanges amid developments in artificial intelligence (AI) and changing geopolitics.
Over the past three years, the office has pursued what Tung calls “total diplomacy,” connecting government agencies, businesses, industry associations, universities, cultural groups and civil society through industry matchmaking, research exchanges and professional networks.
Tung highlighted the Taiwan-Singapore Economic Partnership Agreement, which took effect in 2014 and covers goods, services, investment, government procurement and e-commerce.
In December last year, the two sides also signed a revised agreement on avoiding double taxation and preventing tax evasion. The agreement lowers withholding-tax ceilings and improves tax coordination, reducing uncertainty for cross-border investment.
AI, semiconductors and related components accounted for about 85 percent of Taiwan’s exports to Singapore last year, while related products made up about 80 percent of Singapore’s exports to Taiwan.
On July 29, the representative office helped HannStar Board (樺漢科技) and the Singapore Manufacturing Federation organize a forum on semiconductor and AI applications. Executives from Google, Arm Holdings and Intel attended alongside representatives from Singapore’s semiconductor, AI, smart-technology and venture-capital sectors.
The office also promotes Taiwan through reports, seminars and WhatsApp channels covering agriculture, culture, tourism, healthcare and business opportunities. It has established professional networks for financial officials, academics, technology and biotechnology professionals, and listed-company executives.
Tung said his residence hosts about 300 events annually, attracting roughly 4,000 participants.
He described “total diplomacy” as a cycle in which exchanges create networks, networks build trust, and trust leads to cooperation and new demand, strengthening the Taiwan-Singapore partnership.

The National Cultural Association of Taiwan (NCAT) is planning a two-day “Taiwan Day” cultural event in Poland on Sept. 11 and 12, featuring Taiwanese contemporary dance and folk arts, as well as a bazaar showcasing Taiwanese food and culture.
Events on the first day are being held in Lodz in central Poland, with performances by the Lei Sheng Art Group, a Taiwanese folk arts group, and Taipei Gong Le Xuan, a Taiwanese beiguan music ensemble.
The performances would “transform the Polish streets into a Taiwan temple front,” according to a social media post by the association yesterday.
Photo : CNA
There would be a bazaar with more than 10 vendors showcasing Taiwanese foods and goods, including dumplings, sometimes called a Taiwanese analogue to Polish pierogi. There would also be offerings of bubble tea and Taiwanese tea, the post said.
On Sept. 12, the two groups would be joined by the MeimageDance Troupe, founded by choreographer and National Award for Arts winner Ho Hsiao-mei (何曉玫), for performances in Opole in southwestern Poland, according to the post.
MeimageDance is also to perform in Austria on Sept. 5 and in Hungary on Sept. 18 and 19, the post said.
At a promotional event in Taipei Monday, Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim (蕭美琴), who serves as NCAT vice president, said the cultural tour is aimed at inspiring Europeans to visit Taiwan and experience the country in person.
Taiwan is a resilient and diverse society with a wide range of folk beliefs, contemporary arts and distinctive foods such as bubble tea and xiaolongbao, all of which are part of the everyday experiences and shared memories of the people of Taiwan, Hsiao said.
While Taiwan faces difficulties in its diplomatic relations, its goodwill toward the world has never wavered, Hsiao said, adding that she hoped cultural diplomacy could help deepen the international community’s understanding of Taiwan.

Han Hak-ja, the 83-year-old leader of the Unification Church, was yesterday sentenced to two years in prison for bribing the wife of ousted former South Korean president Yoon Suk-yeol and other corruption charges.
The Seoul Central District Court convicted Han, widow of church founder Sun Myung Moon, of violating the political funds acts, bribery and embezzling church funds, the court’s public affairs office said.
A team of investigators led by special prosecutor Min Joong-ki earlier requested a 13-year prison term for Han. Both Han and Min’s team have one week to appeal.
Photo: Reuters
Han earlier denied the allegations. She is the top leader of the Unification Church, officially called the Family Federation for World Peace and Unification, which her husband founded in 1954.
The Seoul court sentenced a church official to six months in prison and gave two other church officials suspended terms over their involvement in Han’s case.
Last year, Han was arrested and charged with giving then-first lady Kim Keon-hee luxury goods in 2022 when Yoon was in office. She was also charged with giving conservative lawmaker Kweon Seong-dong, a Yoon loyalist, 100 million won (US$73,000) months before Yoon’s inauguration.
In January, Kim received a 20-month prison term at the Seoul Central District Court for receiving gifts including a Graff diamond necklace and a Chanel bag from the Unification Church, which sought political favors in return.
In April, an appeals court increased her sentence to four years in prison by convicting her of additional charges, including receiving another Chanel bag from the church and stock price manipulation.
The presidential couple suffered a dramatic fall from grace after Yoon’s imposition of martial law in late 2024 that led to his impeachment and eventual removal from office.
In February, Yoon was sentenced to life in prison for rebellion in connection with his martial law enforcement.
On Dec. 3, 2024, Yoon abruptly imposed martial law and sent troops and police officers to the National Assembly, saying he aimed to eliminate “anti-state forces” and “shameless North Korea sympathizers.” The martial law lasted six hours as he was forced to lift it after the assembly unanimously voted it down.
Yoon has defended his action, calling it a desperate attempt to draw public support for his fight against the liberal opposition Democratic Party that obstructed his agenda.

Lin is leading a delegation visiting the Pacific island nation to meet with Palauan President Surangel Whipps Jr and attend events held alongside the forum. The delegation arrived on Thursday last week and departs on Thursday.
Lin yesterday wrote on Facebook that he met with Whipps and Palauan Vice President and Minister of Health and Human Services Raynold Oilouch on Sunday.
Screen grab from Minister of Foreign Affair Lin Chia-lung’s Facebook page
Together, they inspected solar power generation and storage systems and launched a Taiwan-Palau hydrogen energy cooperation initiative, he said.
The initiative is expected to assist Palau in meeting its energy independence targets, Lin said.
Installed under the One Stop Shop Building solar project, the solar power generation and storage systems would utilize Palau’s abundant sunlight to generate and store electricity to power government facilities and charge e-buses, he said.
That helps link power generation, energy storage and green transportation, he said.
Four Taiwan-made e-buses were officially handed over to Palau in a ribbon-cutting ceremony held after a music performance and a drone demonstration, he said.
Lin said he and Whipps took a test ride on one of the buses.
The buses would be used to transport national leaders and representatives traveling from across the Pacific to attend the forum, he said.
The buses would remain in service after the forum for locals and travelers, he added.
Lin and Whipps also participated in the opening of a golf-course landscaping demonstration park in Palau.
Lin said he hopes to build on Palau’s unique natural environment to create more opportunities for bilateral cooperation in sustainable tourism.
Whipps yesterday thanked Taiwan for cooperating with the Pacific island nation in fields such as education, healthcare, security, climate action and infrastructure, Lin said.
He cited Whipps as saying that such cooperative projects enhance the nation’s energy independence and environmental protection, creating more growth opportunities for Palauans.
Lin said it is his fifth time visiting the nation, adding that the Taiwan-Palau relationship feels more like family with each visit.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31

01:46:35 KST

One person died and about 15 people are missing or unaccounted for after a major flash flood at the Grand Canyon forced evacuations, pushed large boulders into the Colorado River and knocked out the sole water pipeline that serves tourists and residents, the US National Park Service said on Sunday.
The body of a 46-year-old man was recovered on Sunday evening near Crystal Rapids along the Colorado River, the park service said without providing additional details. Officials from an Arizona coroner’s office were on scene.
The flooding on Saturday in Bright Angel Creek, which flows into the river, led to more than 60 people being airlifted from the depths of the canyon. The park service asked anyone with details about hikers or campers still unaccounted for to get in touch. The Arizona Department of Public Safety was helping with additional evacuations on Sunday.
Photo: AFP / J. Baird / National Park Service
The limited potable water supply because of the damaged pipeline means that starting yesterday, tourists would not be able to stay overnight at lodges and hotels within the park. Year-round residents are being asked to conserve water.
“These measures are crucial for ensuring the safety and sustainability of water resources,” the park said in a statement.
Visiting the Grand Canyon can be particularly dangerous in the summer, because of the risk of flash flooding that accompanies the monsoon or rainy season. Clear days can give way quickly to thunderstorms and downpours.
Photo: AP
Parth Desai was hiking through a narrow passage in Bright Angel Canyon with fellow physicians and a park ranger when heavy rain started falling on Saturday.
“We saw the creek flood, waterfalls coming up out of nowhere, boulders, mud, landslides happening everywhere,” he said.
Later, as they made their way toward Phantom Ranch, a colleague shouted “up, up, up, up,” as a 1m debris wall headed toward them and they ran up into a patch of cacti, he said.
They were rescued by helicopter late on Saturday after making it to the Phantom Ranch area, he said.
Torrents of water wiped out footbridges over the creek and altered the landscape, widening the creek bed and extending an existing river rapid or creating a new one. The flood was a major blow to an enduring effort to modernize the pipeline that serves 6 million visitors a year and about 1,600 residents of Grand Canyon Village.
“Heaven help us if the whole thing down there at the bottom has to be reconstructed,” said Jack Schmidt, director of the Center for Colorado River Studies at Utah State University. “Where are they going to get the money?”
Halting overnight stays at the park because of a lack of water is rare, although the pipeline frequently has failed over the years. A US$208 million rehabilitation of the pipeline and upgrades to the associated water delivery system started in 2023, with the park service calling it a crucial investment to ensure the park can meet the needs of residents and visitors. The project was expected to be completed next year.
Popular tourist spots, including the Bright Angel Campground, the North Kaibab Trail and Phantom Ranch, home to a historic canteen and dormitories, remained closed on Sunday. Lodging is still available just outside the park’s South Rim entrance station in Tusayan.

“For years, critics questioned the reliability of CPO. The doubts are being thoroughly dismantled by real-world data and market validation,” TSMC vice president K.C. Hsu (徐國晉) said at a SEMI forum in Taipei.
The company is on track to enter production of CPO later this year, Hsu said in another forum arranged by Imec in Taipei yesterday, about four months after TSMC announced its progress in CPO development in May.
Photo: Lisa Wang, Taipei Times
Imec is the world’s leading independent research and innovation hub in nanoelectronics and digital technologies.
As server racks and data centers are expanding to handle massive artificial intelligence (AI) workloads, networks are being pushed to their limits, and that has stimulated demand for optics, the “nerve system” of data centers, Hsu said.
Last year, optical transceiver sales recorded a 25 percent growth from the previous year, with high-end products growing the fastest by 60 percent, he said.
The growth of optical transceiver sales is to accelerate this year at an annual rate of 50 percent, driven by increasing AI infrastructure expansion worldwide, Hsu said.
Next year, silicon photonics is to emerge as a dominant sales platform and on track to command more than 50 percent of the market, he said.
In 2028, AI technology upgrades would trigger a “massive new” wave of growth, he said.
To meet that demand, the underlying technology of optical transceivers is undergoing a permanent construction shift, Hsu said.
TSMC would utilize its compact universal photonic engine on a single packaged substrate, a type of CPO technology, and that would offer more than 10 times power efficiency compared with traditional copper wire-based applications, he said.
“The co-packaged optics is being adopted faster than originally expected,” Imec vice president Philippe Absil said. “I’ve seen market reports that were showing very moderate and gradual adoption, moving into 2030 when it could mean something in terms of markets.”
However, another report showed that the CPO would deliver five times the size of the traditional market today, showing that the growth is much higher than expected, he said.

Kumamoto Prefecture Governor Takashi Kimura thanked Taiwanese for donating more than NT$300 million (US$9.47 million) to support communities affected by a magnitude 7.1 earthquake that struck the Japanese prefecture on July 28.
Kimura recorded a video message thanking people in Taiwan for their assistance, saying that Taiwanese organizations quickly launched fundraising and relief efforts after the disaster, while some groups delivered supplies and provided hot meals at evacuation shelters.
The support made local residents feel the warmth and solidarity from Taiwanese during the difficult period, he said.
Screen grab from Facebook
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs began accepting public donations for the Kumamoto earthquake relief on Aug. 1. As of Monday last week, donations from the public had exceeded NT$300 million.
Separately, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co, which operates a plant in Kumamoto’s Kikuyo, donated ￥250 million (US$1.57 million) to support relief and recovery efforts.
The corporate donation is separate from the NT$300 million raised through the government-backed fundraising campaign.
In his video message, Kimura also highlighted the close travel links between Taiwan and Kumamoto.
Direct flights connect Kumamoto with four Taiwanese airports — in Taoyuan, Taichung, Tainan and Kaohsiung, he said, adding that he hoped Taiwanese visitors would return to Kumamoto and help support its recovery through tourism.
The message underscores the longstanding ties between Taiwan and Japan and the role of Taiwanese assistance in supporting Kumamoto’s recovery.
Kimura emphasized that tourism was an important part of the prefecture’s post-disaster recovery.
Kumamoto Prefecture reported that as of Friday 38 people had died and 364 had been injured, while 43,292 homes had sustained damage.
The disaster also disrupted basic infrastructure. At one point, about 108,000 households in the prefecture were without running water.
By Thursday last week, that number had fallen to about 300 as restoration work continued, local media reported.
Transportation services have also begun to recover. The Kyushu Expressway has reopened to traffic, while full operations on the affected sections of the Kyushu Shinkansen high-speed rail are expected to resume on Sept. 18, the reports said.
A month after the earthquake, Kumamoto continues to face reconstruction and relocation challenges.
Local authorities and residents are working to restore damaged infrastructure, provide housing and support evacuees, while rebuilding communities affected by the earthquake.

Taiwan codeveloped satellite wins mission award
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
16:46:34 UTC
01:46:34 KST

The cube satellite developed by the Taiwan Space Agency (TASA) in partnership with ArkEdge Space Inc and the University of Tokyo’s Intelligent Space Systems Laboratory last week won the Small Satellite Mission of the Year Award from the American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics (AIAA).
ONGLAISAT, an acronym for onboard globe-looking and imaging satellite, is a 6U Earth observation satellite measuring 10cm by 20cm by 30cm.
TASA developed the optical remote-sensing payload, while the Japanese side handled the satellite platform, launch arrangements and satellite operations.
Photo: CNA
The mission was to validate technologies related to the design and manufacturing of a new optical payload, as well as image processing.
The satellite was deployed from the International Space Station into low Earth orbit on Dec. 9, 2024. It conducted more than 100 imaging operations over about two months after completing initial operations last year.
The development team presented the technology and the imagery captured by ONGLAISAT at the Small Satellite Conference in the US last week, where the AIAA Small Satellite Technical Committee awarded it the Small Satellite Mission of the Year Award, TASA said.
By integrating a high-precision attitude determination and control system with an advanced optical remote-sensing system, ONGLAISAT successfully captured Earth observation imagery with a ground resolution of 2.44m, TASA said.
Using time-delay integration imaging technology, it achieved a signal-to-noise ratio of more than 100, demonstrating the potential of small, low-cost satellites to perform high-resolution optical Earth observation missions, it added.
The mission was a milestone for the commercialization of global micro-satellite constellations and high-frequency, high-resolution Earth observation, it said.
The mission proved that advanced optical and imaging-control technologies can operate even on 6U cube satellites, whereas such cutting-edge technologies previously would had to be a part of large, high-cost remote-sensing satellites, TASA said.

Chou, who goes by Tzuyu, is the only Taiwanese member of the girl group Twice.

Screen grab from Instagram
She is reportedly planning to pursue a solo career under her parents’ agency, Yu Hai Entertainment, although China has also reportedly offered to help Tzuyu develop her career in China.
Chinese-language media have reported that China’s help would include access to broadcasting, concerts and talent agencies if she publicly endorses Beijing’s “one China” principle and says that “Taiwanese are Chinese.”
For the past decade, China has used threats and incentives to pressure Taiwanese entertainers to endorse its political positions, foundation Secretary-General Luo Wen-jia (羅文嘉) said in an interview with the Liberty Times (the sister paper of the Taipei Times).
Taiwanese artists in the Chinese market can have their work abruptly halted if they do not comply with government demands, while those who cooperate are rewarded with greater market access, Luo said.
However, those who cooperate tend to have career peaks that do not last long, he said, adding that China uses them and then discards them once they no longer have value.
China’s “united front” efforts target not only entertainers, but also politicians, influencers and media commentators, Luo said.
He criticized the legislature’s cutting of media and culture funding from the government budget, saying that lawmakers used to routinely call for more cultural funding and support for artists, regardless of which party was in power.
In a post on the paid fan platform Bubble, Chou asked her fans to wait patiently for news on her career plans and cheer her on rather than worry.
“I know there are all kinds of rumors circulating online, but even so, you’ve been willing to patiently wait for me until I can come back with new work,” she wrote.
