The backlash against screens in schools is escalating
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
14:36:37 UTC
23:36:37 KST

In New York City, teachers have two more weeks to prepare for the start of school—and no access to the educational technology software they typically use to teach. City officials have issued a tech freeze while they deliberate over how artificial intelligence (AI) will be allowed in classrooms, amid public pressure to place a two-year moratorium on the technology.
Across the country, parents, teachers, school districts and state legislatures are currently grappling with similar questions revolving around how much technology should be allowed in the classroom. Just this week, as part of a massive settlement, Meta agreed to institute “school mode” so that kids can’t access Instagram during school hours. Most states now ban student cell phone use in schools, and a broader movement to limit educational screen use is gaining momentum. In March Utah and Alabama became the first states to limit the use of screens in classrooms.
Educational technology companies claim their apps and tools can make learning fun and boost student achievement. Schools also want to prepare students for a future where technology is ubiquitous. But many parents and educators see screens as an expensive distraction providing little additional benefit over analog learning with pencils and paper. And while the financial and educational stakes of these debates are high, the scientific research on the subject is highly nuanced: the effectiveness of these platforms can vary widely, researchers have found. Broadly speaking, digital tools that merely require students to drill new skills don’t promote learning, whereas platforms that are interactive and creatively engaging and provide real-time feedback show benefits.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Tech in schools “is like a lightning rod,” says Christopher Saldaña, a K–12 education policy researcher at the University of Wisconsin–Madison. “In some ways, the backlash is a long time coming because we’ve had all these claims about what education technology can do that haven’t always panned out.”
The educational technology (or “ed tech”) industry generated $48 billion in revenue in 2024 and is projected to grow to $90 billion by 2030. The U.S. has some 13,000 public school districts but no central authority that vets marketing claims and provides guidance on which platforms schools should adopt, Saldaña explains.
Individual districts “don’t have the money to be able to vet any of these claims or verify them themselves,” he adds. “They’re often at the mercy of whatever vendors are telling them.”
Data privacy has also emerged as a key concern among grassroots parent groups advocating for screen-free schools. A Utah State Board of Education investigation surveyed educational software with data privacy agreements and found that 61 percent shared student data with third parties and 36 percent shared data with advertisers.
Under Alabama’s new rules, the state’s Department of Education will be required to institute limits on screen time in early childhood education. Utah’s new law bans screens in classrooms for K–3 students, except for computer science lessons and testing. It also bans sending devices home with K–3 students. The Los Angeles Unified School District, the second largest school district in the country, passed a resolution limiting screen use in classrooms in April.
Still, those rules are the exception. Most school districts are forging ahead with technology in classrooms. In a survey of teachers and school leaders conducted this year by the EdWeek Research Center, 74 percent of respondents said that their schools haven’t reduced their investment in education technology as a result of parent pushback and have no plans to do so in the near future. Teachers reported an overall positive effect of educational technology on students’ engagement in learning and mastery of skills but an overall negative effect on their social-emotional skills, overall well-being and behavior in the classroom.
Though digital learning tools are still widely used, bans on noneducational tech in school are now commonplace. At least 39 states and Washington, D.C., have prohibited cell phone use in public schools. Some of these laws only ban devices in class, while others ban them for the entire school day, including lunch and recess. These measures have become increasingly popular among the general public; a Pew survey conducted this spring found that support has risen across all age groups of U.S. adults since 2024.
Research on the impact of these phone bans is mixed. A study of schools that used lockable phone pouches from the company Yondr found that disciplinary incidents rose and student well-being fell in the first year of the phone ban. But in the ensuing years, disciplinary incident rates reduced and student well-being increased. There was no meaningful effect on test scores or attendance throughout the study period, however.
“Bans are just a starting line. They are never a whole comprehensive solution,” says Larz May, founder of #HalftheStory, a digital wellness nonprofit focused on teens. “What we’ve seen on the ground is that alongside phone bans, there are other cuts and issues that are impacting [kids]”—such as funding cuts to art programs and extracurriculars.
Phone ban policies restrict how teens can interact without providing further resources for connection and flourishing, May says. “What we’re hearing is, ‘You’re taking these things away, but what else do you have to offer?’”
Students’ main concerns around technology in schools now revolve around AI, May says. Research conducted by the College Board in 2025 found that high school students are “on the fence” about the risks and benefits of AI in their schooling, even as 84 percent reported using it to help with schoolwork. The study also found that one in five high schools allow generative AI but have no formal policy on what kind of use is acceptable.
The uncertainty is breeding anxiety among students, May reports. “One kid told me ... that he actually videos himself while he’s doing his homework, just in case he gets accused of using AI,” she says. “Kids are going to extreme measures out of fear.”
Meanwhile, ed tech platforms are integrating AI further into their products, says Silvia Noguerón-Liu, a literacy studies researcher at the University of Colorado Boulder. While she stresses that the educational technology platforms used in classrooms are typically well-vetted by districts, the offerings of ed tech companies are expanding and are often marketed as time-saving measures to teachers.
“The last ed tech conference I attended had the big names [in ed tech], and they all had an AI exploration room that felt a little bit dystopian,” Noguerón-Liu says. “Now where this gets very, very problematic is when you rely on it for content,” she says, because charts, information and lesson plans created with AI can often be inaccurate.
And whether technology in a classroom is helping or hurting depends a lot on the teacher, experts say. Educators need training and resources to use technology effectively, and they don’t always get it. “In my mind, teachers’ knowledge and teachers’ actions,” Noguerón-Liu says, “that’s the most impactful component.”

Visitor numbers at Ukrainian shopping centres have fallen significantly following massive Russian attacks on major retail facilities.
Source: Andrii Lototskyi, CEO of consulting company Retail & Development Advisor (RDA), as reported by LIGA.net
Quote from Lototskyi: "We are seeing a significant drop in footfall. Customers will think twice about whether they really need to go to a shopping centre."
Details: Lototskyi noted that this could result in falling sales and tenants struggling to pay their rent.
As of the end of July, 38 Ukrainian shopping centres with a combined area of 1.4 million sq m had been damaged or destroyed since the start of the full-scale war. Some, such as the Kvadrat shopping centre and Blockbuster Mall in Kyiv, have been damaged more than once.

14:24:07 UTC
23:24:07 KST

Authorities in the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC) have suspended port officials who authorised the departure of a passenger ferry that capsized off the coastal city of Girne, Prime Minister Unal Ustel said, as search teams continued looking for 18 missing people.
Ustel said on Monday that the government had launched a full investigation into the disaster and would not allow any negligence or wrongdoing to be concealed.
“The relevant port officials who authorised the ship's departure have also been suspended from duty, an investigation has been launched against them, and new officials have been appointed in their place,” he said.
A Turkish Navy Underwater Offense (SAT) team dispatched from Türkiye has joined the ongoing search and rescue operation, Ustel said, adding that finding the missing passengers remains the government’s top priority.
14 suspects appear in court
Fourteen people were brought before the Girne District Court on Monday as investigators examined the circumstances surrounding the capsizing.
The suspects include the ferry’s captain, seven crew members, a company employee and two Girne Port officials. Police are also searching for two additional people under a court order.
The captain and crew told the court that the vessel overturned after its bow broke off amid rough waves. They said weather conditions appeared suitable when the ferry departed and that the vessel had valid navigational and administrative certificates.
The court ordered police to examine passenger-recorded videos and investigate the ferry’s previous accident and repair history as part of a technical inquiry.
Nine suspects, including the captain, first officer, a company employee and several crew members, were ordered held for another three days. Five others, including two port officials, were released pending trial.
The next hearing is scheduled for Thursday, when investigators are expected to present additional statements, documents and other evidence.
Search continues after eight deaths
The Filo Jet capsized while attempting to return to Girne Port after taking on water through its bow shortly after departure.
The ferry was carrying 267 people — 259 passengers and eight crew members. Authorities said 241 people were rescued, eight died and 18 remain missing.
Relatives of some passengers gathered outside the court and protested as the suspects were brought before the judge.
Ustel pledged that any negligence, fault or responsibility uncovered by the investigation would be addressed under the law.

JAKARTA, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- The number of high-confidence forest and land fire hotspots in Indonesia has declined nationwide, but the risk remains as authorities continue intensive firefighting and prevention efforts, particularly in Kalimantan and Sumatra, the Ministry of Forestry said Monday.
Data from the ministry's SiPongi monitoring system showed 946 high-confidence hotspots nationwide as of Sunday night, down 629 from the previous day. West Kalimantan recorded the highest number at 455, followed by Central Kalimantan with 308.
Forestry Minister Raja Juli Antoni said the decline did not mean the fire threat was over.
As of Sunday, authorities had recorded 93 fire incidents across 12 provinces, with fires at 33 locations extinguished and firefighting operations continuing at 60 others.
Joint teams have deployed ground crews, water-bombing helicopters, aerial patrols and weather modification operations, supported by 52 helicopters across Kalimantan and Sumatra.
Antoni warned that peatland fires could continue to smolder even after visible flames disappeared, potentially reigniting without repeated cooling and wetting operations. ■

Thailand's economic growth expands in July
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
22:23:12 CST
23:23:12 KST

BANGKOK, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- Thailand's economic growth increased in July on a monthly basis, supported by the global technology and artificial intelligence upswing, easing conflict in the Middle East, and government stimulus measures, the Bank of Thailand said on Monday.
According to the central bank, merchandise exports excluding gold advanced 2.3 percent in July from a month earlier, mainly driven by electronics shipments that also contributed to improved manufacturing production.
However, exports remained heavily reliant on imported inputs, while private investment dipped 0.3 percent month-on-month as machinery and equipment spending cooled after an earlier acceleration, the central bank said in a statement.
Tourism strengthened on higher receipts and a rise in foreign arrivals, especially from long-haul markets, as flight capacity recovered due to easing tensions in the Middle East and seasonal demand during the summer school break, said the central bank's senior director Pranee Sutthasri.
Private consumption rose 1.2 percent compared to the preceding month on stronger spending in services, particularly dining, supported by government measures and domestic tourism during a special long holiday, Pranee told a news conference.
She noted that headline inflation dropped from the prior month as energy costs fell on lower imported oil prices and reduced contributions to the state Oil Fuel Fund, though core inflation edged up slightly owing to cost pass-through in processed food and food ingredients.
Looking ahead, the central bank expects the Thai economy to continue recovering, yet the rebound remains uneven, with key drivers including exports and private investment.
Meanwhile, government measures, reduced inflation, and rising labor income are lifting household consumption as agricultural prices and tourism strengthen, the official added. ■

Finland Cuts Russian War Criminal’s Sentence, Rules Facial Carving Did Not Cause Enough Suffering
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
14:18:41 UTC
23:18:41 KST

- Category
- World
Finland Cuts Russian War Criminal’s Sentence, Rules Facial Carving Did Not Cause Enough Suffering
A Finnish appeals court has reduced the life sentence of Russian militant Voislav Torden, also known as Yan Petrovsky, to 12 years and six months after finding him guilty of three war crimes committed against Ukrainian soldiers in 2014.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The Helsinki Court of Appeal partially overturned an earlier ruling that had sentenced Torden to life imprisonment for four war crimes, Finnish public broadcaster Yle reported on August 31.
One of the charges dismissed on appeal concerned a Rusich symbol carved into the cheek of a Ukrainian soldier with a sharp object. The court found that the wound was superficial, did not bleed, and did not cause sufficiently severe physical or psychological suffering to qualify as a war crime under the charge considered.
Torden served as deputy commander of the Russian paramilitary group Rusich. Much of the case focused on a September 5, 2014 ambush against Ukrainian troops from the Aidar Battalion in the Luhansk region.
Rusich fighters took part in the attack alongside the Batman Battalion and other Russian-backed formations, using a Ukrainian flag during the ambush. Twenty-two Ukrainian soldiers were killed and four were wounded.
According to Yle, the appeals court found that Torden fired a light machine gun at Ukrainian troops and was guilty of a war crime. However, judges said there was insufficient evidence to prove that he or two other Rusich members personally shot wounded Ukrainian soldiers.
The court also ruled that Torden did not bear command responsibility for the shootings, although it found him partially responsible for the deaths and injuries because of his role in the attack.
Other convictions were upheld. The court found that Torden photographed a Rusich commander posing beside the severely burned body of a dead Ukrainian soldier and later distributed the image on social media.
He was also convicted over online statements presenting it as Rusich policy not to take prisoners and to show no mercy.
In setting the 12.5-year sentence, the court considered Torden’s role as Rusich deputy commander, his participation in the deadly ambush, and the use of material from the attack for propaganda. He was also ordered to compensate wounded Ukrainian soldiers and relatives of those killed.
The Helsinki District Court had sentenced Torden to life imprisonment in March 2025. He appealed the verdict, seeking dismissal of the charges or a reduced sentence.
Torden was detained in Finland in 2023. Ukraine later requested his extradition, but Finland’s Supreme Court rejected the request, citing concerns over prison conditions in Ukraine. Rusich has fought alongside Russian forces in Ukraine and has been sanctioned internationally. Torden is also under European Union and US sanctions.
In a separate case, Ukrainian paratrooper Andrii from the 79th Air Assault Brigade told UNITED24 Media that a Russian surgeon burned the words “Glory to Russia” into his stomach with a medical cautery tool while he was held in Russian captivity. Andrii spent more than 14 months in captivity before returning to Ukraine in a May 2025 prisoner exchange.

Two Struck Ships Run Aground in Türkiye After Black Sea Attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31

Two Struck Ships Run Aground in Türkiye After Black Sea Attacks
A Russian-flagged cargo ship that was attacked off the coast of Russia has drifted across the Black Sea and run aground on a beach in Türkiye, Turkish Demirören News Agency (DHA) reported on August 30.
The 108-meter-long vessel, identified as the OMSKIY-107, washed ashore at Alacalı Beach in the Şile district of Istanbul.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The cargo ship was initially targeted near the Russian port of Novorossiysk, a major naval and maritime logistics hub. Following the incident, the crew abandoned the heavily damaged vessel in lifeboats, leaving the uncrewed ship to drift toward the Turkish coastline.
The incident follows a pattern of maritime insecurity near the Russian logistics hub. Recently, the MSC, the world’s largest container shipping company, temporarily suspended all new bookings to and from Novorossiysk after one of its vessels, the MSC ULSAN III, was struck by a drone while approaching the port.
Witnesses on the shore who spotted the approaching vessel immediately contacted local authorities, prompting a rapid response from the Turkish Coast Guard, DHA wrote.
Upon arriving at the scene, emergency teams secured the perimeter around the grounded ship and initiated an investigation into the incident. According to DHA, initial aerial photographs and on-site inspections revealed severe damage to the vessel, with the captain’s bridge appearing entirely charred and burned out.
While footage of the drifting ship was captured by bystanders on their mobile phones, officials have not yet confirmed the exact timing of the initial attack in Russian waters or the current whereabouts of the evacuated crew.
In a separate incident, the Hong Kong-flagged tanker M/T Golden Sapling also washed ashore on the Turkish coast, running aground in Samsun’s Alaçam district after reportedly suffering damage from a drone attack in the Black Sea.
According to the Turkish newspaper Cumhuriyet, the vessel had been drifting unmanned for days due to severe weather after another ship evacuated its 21 crew members and transported them to Russia. The tanker had not transmitted a signal since August 26, prompting immediate investigations by Turkish Coast Guard and Port Authority teams upon its grounding.
The recent maritime strikes are indicative of the disruption facing Russian naval operations across the Black Sea. Several damaged Black Sea Fleet vessels—including a Molniya-class missile boat with its shattered superstructure concealed under camouflage netting and multiple Soviet-era landing ships—are reportedly currently sheltering in the bays of occupied Sevastopol following repeated Ukrainian strikes on Russian naval assets.

"Italy ‘recruits’ Fedorov" — Italy’s top media outlets ran headlines about the former defense minister beginning work for another country
Kyiv • UNN
Mykhailo Fedorov will advise Italy’s defense minister pro bono on drones and air defense. In Ukraine, there are concerns about a leak of military technologies.
Italian media published articles with headlines stating that Italy is “recruiting” former Ukrainian Minister Mykhailo Fedorov. The articles appeared after Fedorov announced that he had become an adviser to Italian Defence Minister Guido Crosetto on defence issues, UNN reports.
According to Italian media reports, Fedorov decided to cooperate with Italy, providing it with his expertise.
“It is no coincidence that the main topics of his meeting with Minister Guido Crosetto were drones, air defence and so-called “unmanned” systems—remotely controlled or autonomous vehicles or devices,” Italy’s leading news agency ANSA writes.
The agency reports that, announcing his new position, Fedorov specified that “Ukraine’s experience could become the foundation for a new European defence model”.
“We must be “able to quickly test and implement new solutions, combining technology with reliable production capabilities. Minister Crosetto expressed his satisfaction: I am glad that Mykhailo Fedorov agreed to offer me his services,” ANSA quotes Italy’s Defence Minister.
Fedorov, for his part, stressed that “Ukraine and our team “have experience that we are ready to share”.
“In this position, I will help Italy implement modern technologies of warfare, strengthen its defence sector and adapt to new global security challenges,” Italy’s national news agency Adnkronos quotes Fedorov as saying.
The influential British publication the Financial Times, for its part, writes that Ukrainian MPs, veterans and civil society leaders, including many who supported Fedorov after his dismissal, were outraged by the news of his trip abroad.
“Many questioned his motives when, on Friday, after a visit to Rome, he announced that he would work as an unpaid adviser to Italy’s defence minister. Oleksii Honcharenko, an opposition MP who chairs the parliamentary investigative committee, wrote that Fedorov’s role in Italy could pose “a threat of leakage of knowledge about our advanced military technologies”, the Financial Times wrote.
As is known, the Law of Ukraine “On State Secrets” establishes a special procedure for transferring classified information to a foreign state or international organisation—on the basis of an international treaty or another state decision provided for by law. Such actions carried out privately are illegal.

Swedish firm tests unique unmanned hydrofoil craft
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
14:13:14 UTC
23:13:14 KST

- Aston Harald Composite completed the first test flight of its unmanned GhostFoiler hydrofoil vessel in Stockholm last week.
- The demonstrator, built on hydrofoil technology developed at KTH Royal Institute of Technology, will next join NATO's REPMUS 2026 exercise in Portugal.
A Swedish composites manufacturer just flew a boat that doesn’t touch the water.
Aston Harald Composite completed the first test flight of an unmanned hydrofoil vessel called GhostFoiler in the waters of Stockholm last week, weaving among ferries and recreational boats in the city’s archipelago. The company said the craft performed well for a first attempt, after resolving grounding and shielding issues that came up during setup.
“The first flight is always special,” the company said. “The test went according to plan, after sorting out the usual grounding and shielding issues, and we were soon flying among ferries and recreational boats in the Stockholm archipelago. It flew well!”
Hydrofoils are not new. Boats mounted on underwater wings have existed for more than a century, using the same lift principle that keeps an airplane in the sky, but applied to water instead of air. What makes GhostFoiler different is that nobody is standing on it. The vessel has to sense the water’s surface, its own height above it, and constantly adjust to stay stable, all without a human balancing on deck the way a foilboard rider would. That’s a substantially harder control problem than keeping a hull floating on the water in the conventional way, and it’s the reason foiling drones have lagged behind ordinary drone boats.
The technology GhostFoiler runs on traces back nearly two decades to a student project at KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm. In 2008, naval architecture professor Jakob Kuttenkeuler led a group of 15 students in building an early electric hydrofoil board called Evolo, widely credited as one of the first electric hydrofoils ever built and an ancestor of the eFoil boards now sold commercially around the world. Kuttenkeuler has continued that research at KTH’s Maritime Robotics group, developing Evolo into an experimental hydrofoiling testbed for autonomous control systems, sensor fusion and navigation. That academic work was spun out commercially under the name EvoloFoil, which built the hydrofoil rig and flight-control system now flying on GhostFoiler.
Aston Harald Composite, a small Swedish composites manufacturer, built the physical vessel itself. The company designed the hull and manufactured its composite structures, including a carbon-fiber catamaran hull, the lightweight, high-strength material more commonly associated with racing sailboats and aircraft than with typical drone boats. Propulsion comes from two 10-kilowatt electric outrunner motors built by another Swedish company, Zparq AB, which Aston Harald described as extraordinarily quiet, a useful trait for a vessel that may eventually be used for reconnaissance or surveillance work.
The demonstrator is now headed to Portugal, where it will operate under the GhostFoiler name as part of Team Sweden at NATO’s REPMUS 2026 exercise. REPMUS, short for Robotic Experimentation and Prototyping using Maritime Uncrewed Systems, is an annual NATO exercise where allied nations bring uncrewed underwater, surface and aerial systems to test them together in realistic maritime scenarios, making it one of the main venues where early-stage technology like GhostFoiler gets evaluated alongside systems from established defense contractors.

An exhibition of Johnny Depp's paintings has opened in Germany
Kyiv • UNN
An exhibition of 60 works by Johnny Depp has opened at Benrath Palace in Düsseldorf. The exhibition will run until September 27; the actor visited it before the concert.
The exhibition entitled "The Art of Johnny Depp" ("Johnny Depp’s Art") is being held at the Baroque Benrath Palace in Düsseldorf and is open until September 27. It features 60 works by the film star, UNN reports, citing DW.
Details
Shortly before the exhibition opened, Johnny Depp performed with the band Hollywood Vampires at a concert near Cologne, but he did not attend the exhibition’s opening. Stefan Schweizer, chairman of the board of the Benrath Palace and Park Foundation, told the newspaper Neue Ruhr Zeitung (NRZ) that the actor had nevertheless visited the museum "before the concert on Friday and viewed the exhibition in a small group."
The museum’s press release states that Johnny Depp began creating art in childhood but for a long time, until 2022, did not show his works to the general public. It also says that among the exhibition’s key works is the series Five, dedicated to the five most psychologically challenging years of Johnny Depp’s life. Another important image in the exhibition is Bunnyman ("Rabbit Man"), a character from a recurring dream that Depp and his son Jack saw independently of each other.
The publication notes that this is not Depp’s first exhibition in Germany. In March 2026, an exhibition of 13 of his paintings and prints was held in the small town of Emmendingen. Some works had sold out several days before the opening, so additional copies had to be commissioned.

Hitting a High Point: The Australia-Indonesia 2+2
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
14:08:00 UTC
23:08:00 KST

Last week, Australia and Indonesia held their tenth 2+2 defense and foreign ministers meeting in Melbourne. The two countries signed the landmark Jakarta Treaty on Common Security in 2024, and although the Indonesian parliament has yet to ratify the treaty, the 2+2 meeting proceeded with the assumption that this is simply the pace of Indonesia’s legislative processes, and that discussions can turn to how best to operationalize their cooperation.
The headline claim is that the relationship between the two countries is now “at a high point.” The Albanese government has made the relationship with Indonesia one of the central pillars of Australia’s foreign policy, understanding how vital friendly, cooperative, relations with its giant near neighbor is to the country’s security. Indonesia, for its part, has recognized it has a capable partner in Canberra that can help advance its own security interests, while maintaining its strategic autonomy.
Although the two countries are seeking to broaden their relationship, at present, defense and security cooperation remain the core elements and these areas were naturally a major focus of the discussions last week.
Given the nature of their geographies, this has developed into a focus on maritime security. At the 2+2 meeting it was announced that Australia will provide aerial drones and training to Indonesia’s Coast Guard. Given that illegal fishing is a central concern throughout Indonesia’s vast waters, and that Chinese often use maritime militia disguised as fishing vessels, greater maritime domain awareness is considered essential for Jakarta.
Alongside this, Australia and Indonesia agreed to increase cooperation on cybercrime, critical infrastructure, and artificial intelligence, building on their existing memorandum of understanding on enhanced cybersecurity and critical technology cooperation. This includes incorporating a defensive cybersecurity component into their bilateral defense exercise, Keris Woomera. Here, cybersecurity is not treated as a separate technical issue, but as a central pillar of military preparedness and national defense.
There is a similar thinking around economic security as inseparable from traditional security. The ministers announced a number of initiatives designed to make their economies more resilient to external shocks and any disruption to supply chains. This included new cooperation to jointly analyze critical supply chain issues and new scholarship courses that will be focused on economic security and resilience – hoping to develop a new cohort of analysts and bureaucrats focused on these issues.
The two countries have already demonstrated how economic interdependence can provide security benefits, with Indonesia working with Australian industry to facilitate a 250,000-tonne agricultural-grade supply of urea due to disruptions from the war in Iran. Alongside this, Australian liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) exports to Indonesia have increased threefold over the past year, again in response to supply chain disruptions in the Middle East.
These practical forms of food and energy security are becoming increasingly intertwined with geopolitics. The two countries therefore have an interest in using the resources of one another to address their vulnerabilities. Given both their proximity to each other, and their current distance from global hotspots, there is an opportunity to build resilience together that can withstand any global shocks.
These shocks include the environment. The 2+2 meeting announced the second phase of KINETIK – the Australia-Indonesia Climate and Sustainable Infrastructure Partnership, which will provide US$430 million over ten years to support sustainable infrastructure and climate investment in Indonesia. Its aim is to mobilize public and private capital into clean energy, water, waste management, and sustainable transport, helping Indonesia build climate-resilient infrastructure and accelerate its energy transition. With the hope of the two countries also developing their green technology capabilities.
The 2+2 meeting also demonstrated considered strategic alignment over the regional order – something that hasn’t always been the case. The two countries reaffirmed their commitment to international law, sovereignty and ASEAN centrality, with both expressing concern about rising tensions in the South China Sea and insisting that the Code of Conduct being developed by ASEAN and China must comply with international law.
The significance of the 2+2 is the growing web of cooperation between Canberra and Jakarta. From defense exercises to maritime surveillance to cybersecurity and economic resilience, there has been a noticeable step up in the relationship. This does not amount to a formal alliance, but more a convergence of interests and a recognition that as neighbors there is a natural interconnectedness. The previous distance in outlook and coordination is starting to be overcome.

What Zheng He’s Changing Role Reveals About China’s Maritime Strategy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
14:08:00 UTC
23:08:00 KST

The Ming Dynasty navigator Zheng He is often closely associated with Xi Jinping’s Belt and Road narrative. But the historical figure has been used as a diplomatic tool for decades, long before Xi launched the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI).
Zheng He entered the diplomatic storytelling of the People’s Republic of China within a decade of its founding. Under Hu Jintao and Wen Jiabao he became part of a broader historical argument about China’s rise, a role that remained prominent during the first years of Xi’s presidency.
Much attention has been paid to why Beijing revived Zheng He. But few have noticed how mentions of Zheng He changed: Since 2018, China’s top leaders have increasingly moved away from using him to argue that a stronger China would not become a conquering power.
As early as the late Qing period, Chinese nationalists recast Zheng He as evidence that China had once possessed global reach. During the Republican era he entered Chinese history textbooks and became a domestic symbol of national capacity. Around the time of the Bandung Conference, Beijing began recoding him for diplomacy. Zheng He was increasingly presented as a powerful but anti-colonial emissary of Afro-Asian friendship, particularly in China’s relations with newly independent African states.
Under Hu Jintao and Wen Jiabao, China’s top leaders systematically invoked Zheng He in diplomatic settings to answer a question at the heart of China’s rise: How would a China that was becoming powerful again use its power? In 2003, while explaining China’s “peaceful rise and development” at Harvard University, Wen described Zheng He as a diplomat who had sought friendly relations with other countries across seven voyages, tying this history directly to the Chinese tradition of loving peace.
In 2005, speaking to the Mexican Senate, Hu again used the Silk Road and Zheng He’s voyages as historical evidence of China’s commitment to peaceful development. In Pretoria in 2007, Hu invoked Zheng He before turning to China’s own experience of colonialism to argue that China would not impose its will on Africa.
The logic of Hu’s argument rested on an asymmetry of power. A fleet incapable of conquest proves nothing by refraining from violence. Only if the fleet is understood to possess the capacity to conquer can its peaceful approach serve as evidence of restraint. To Chinese leaders, Zheng He’s story showed how China would exercise superior power without undertaking conquest. Beijing drew on this argument particularly when it sought to reassure foreign audiences about how China would use its growing power, including in its diplomacy with African, Southeast Asian, and Arab states.
This usage persisted for a while after Xi took office. In 2014, Xi placed Zheng He directly within his argument that the Chinese nation carries “no gene for invading others or seeking hegemony.” At the first Belt and Road Forum in 2017, Xi listed Zheng He alongside Zhang Qian, Du Huan, Marco Polo, and Ibn Battuta as friendly envoys along the Silk Road. As the Maritime Silk Road became central to Xi-era diplomacy, Zheng He remained an obvious historical resource.
The later Premier Li Keqiang was especially consistent in bringing up Zheng He during this period. At the 2015 China-ASEAN Leaders’ Meeting and the East Asia Summit, Li invoked the navigator to argue that the South China Sea had been a sea of peace and freedom of navigation for six centuries. Three years later, at the 2018 East Asia Summit, Li was still using Zheng He in much the same way.
After 2018, however, the pattern of top-level use began to change. The decline was most visible in the field of regional maritime order, where references to Zheng He had once figured prominently. At the 2019 East Asia Summit, Li addressed similar regional issues without invoking Zheng He. By the 2023 Belt and Road Forum, even the language of civilizational exchange and connectivity no longer required name-dropping Zheng He.
One contributing factor may have been the 2016 South China Sea arbitration, which made historical arguments about maritime rights more legally awkward. But the timing does not line up perfectly. Two years after the ruling, Li was still making much the same argument. Instead, the break came in 2019, which means the arbitration alone cannot account for it.
China’s maritime strategy and naval capabilities were themselves changing. In 2012, the 18th Party Congress formally called for China to become a “maritime power.” Three years later, the defense white paper China’s Military Strategy directed the People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) to move from a posture centered on “offshore waters defense” toward a combination of “offshore waters defense” and “open seas protection.”
At celebrations marking the PLAN’s 70th anniversary in Qingdao in 2019, Xi introduced the idea of a “maritime community with a shared future.” He also stressed that China followed a defensive national defense policy and that the navy would safeguard international sea lanes, shoulder international responsibilities, and provide more public goods for maritime security.
The U.S. Department of Defense’s 2025 China Military Power Report describes the PLAN as fielding Asia’s largest force of principal surface combatants, submarines, and amphibious warfare ships. As China built aircraft carriers, sustained far-seas escort missions, established overseas support facilities, and expanded its shipbuilding capacity, Beijing increasingly shifted the basis of its reassurance from historical precedent toward declared policy and contemporary behavior.
The growth of China’s naval capabilities reduced Zheng He’s value as evidence of maritime power. It also changed the analogy itself. In the 2000s, the official narrative constructed by Hu and Wen used Zheng He to show that maritime capability and peaceful intent could coexist. But by the late 2010s, China’s expanding naval power had become an observable reality, increasingly open to judgment through the navy’s actual conduct. The more the Zheng He narrative linked formidable maritime power with voluntary restraint, the more it invited foreign audiences to apply the same standard to China today. The analogy had therefore become more politically demanding.
Zheng He still appears, but mostly in bilateral settings to discuss historical ties with specific countries or communities. In April 2025, Xi’s signed article in the Malaysian press mentioned sites in Malacca associated with Zheng He. On April 21, 2026, during a meeting with Mozambican President Daniel Chapo, Xi noted that Zheng He’s fleet had visited the Mozambican coast more than six centuries earlier. In June of the same year, the Chinese embassy in Tanzania again presented Zheng He’s voyages as a historical symbol of long-standing exchanges between Chinese and Swahili civilizations. Later that month, Jakarta launched a series of cultural exchanges under the banner of “Zheng He’s Voyage: Envoys of Friendship.” In these settings, Zheng He primarily serves as a marker of shared history. In that sense, Beijing is returning Zheng He to the more limited diplomatic role he played in the 1950s and 1960s.
Zheng He’s visibility remains high. Exhibitions in Jakarta and Nairobi marked the 620th anniversary of his voyages; an academy in Angola now bears his name, as do international freight links. But in recent top-level diplomacy, he no longer serves primarily as evidence of China’s national character.
That retreat has also made the difference between Zheng He and another historical icon, Zhang Qian, easier to see. Zhang Qian, the Han Dynasty envoy sent to the Western Regions, has long been regarded as a pioneer of the overland Silk Road. Compared with Zheng He, he represents the active opening of new routes and spaces for exchange. Existing discussions often treat the two as equivalent historical precursors of the Belt and Road. Yet Zhang Qian cannot easily perform Zheng He’s old role of providing reassurance as to China’s peaceful intentions.
The shift has also been uneven across Zheng He’s main diplomatic settings. He appears to have receded more sharply in Africa than in Southeast Asia. In its diplomacy with Africa, Beijing increasingly draws on 20th century anti-colonial solidarity and the Forum on China-Africa Cooperation to narrate historical ties. In Southeast Asia, by contrast, physical sites associated with Zheng He in Malacca, local memories of his voyages, and the Maritime Silk Road continue to sustain a highly localized political afterlife for the navigator.
Another round of China-ASEAN leaders’ meetings and the East Asia Summit will take place this November, while Shenzhen will host the APEC summit in the same month. Whether Zheng He reappears will be worth watching. If Beijing invokes him again, the more revealing question will be what it asks him to prove this time: restraint six centuries ago, or simply a shared local past.

Xi Jinping and Putin met in Kyrgyzstan on the sidelines of the SCO summit
Kyiv • UNN
Putin and Xi Jinping met in Kyrgyzstan ahead of the SCO summit. Moscow seeks to make visa-free travel with China permanent.
Russian dictator Vladimir Putin met with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Bishkek on Monday, where they arrived to participate in the summit of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation. Anadolu Agency reports, UNN writes.
Details
Putin and Xi Jinping arrived in Kyrgyzstan to participate in the SCO summit, the main official events of which will begin on Tuesday. The meeting with the Chinese leader was the first in a series of Putin's bilateral talks with foreign leaders on the sidelines of the summit.
It is noted that Russia is ready to work with China to make the visa-free regime between the two countries permanent.
"We are ready to work together to make the visa-free regime permanent if the Chinese side considers this possible and beneficial," Putin said during a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Bishkek.
Russia introduced a reciprocal visa-free regime for Chinese citizens in December 2025, allowing them to stay in Russia for up to 30 days without a visa until September 14, 2026. China had previously introduced a similar regime for Russian citizens.
The two countries subsequently agreed to extend the visa-free regime for their citizens until the end of 2027.
The dictator of the Russian Federation said that the visa-free regime contributed to an increase in the number of trips between the two countries: tourist trips increased by 43% in the first half of 2026.
Chinese Ambassador to Russia Zhang Hanhui previously reported that the number of Chinese tourists in the Russian Federation increased by nearly 50% in the first quarter of 2026 after the introduction of the visa-free regime.
The drive to make the visa-free regime permanent emerged amid efforts by Moscow and Beijing to deepen people-to-people contacts and economic ties. Tourism is part of broader bilateral cooperation.

Popular sweeteners may leave effects that last for generations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
14:04:01 UTC
23:04:01 KST

Popular sweeteners may leave effects that last for generations
Popular zero-calorie sweeteners changed the gut and metabolism of mice, with some effects unexpectedly echoing into future generations.
- Date:
- August 31, 2026
- Source:
- Frontiers
- Summary:
- Two widely used zero-calorie sweeteners, sucralose and stevia, may have effects that linger far longer than the sweet taste itself. In mice, researchers found that both sweeteners altered the gut microbiome, reduced beneficial compounds produced by gut bacteria, and changed the activity of genes involved in metabolism and inflammation. Some of those changes were also detected in later generations that had never consumed the sweeteners themselves.
- Share:
Choosing the diet version of a favorite soda often means consuming non-nutritive sweeteners. These additives provide sweetness without the calories found in sugar. However, some health organizations have begun raising questions about their possible long-term effects, including whether they may disrupt energy metabolism and eventually contribute to a higher risk of diabetes or cardiovascular disease.
New research in mice adds to those concerns. The study suggests that sucralose and stevia, two widely used sweeteners, can alter the gut microbiome and gene activity in ways that may affect metabolic health. Some of these biological changes were also observed in later generations.
"We found it intriguing that despite the growing consumption of these additives, the prevalence of obesity and metabolic disorders such as insulin resistance has not declined," said Dr. Francisca Concha Celume of the Universidad de Chile, lead author of the article in Frontiers in Nutrition. "This does not mean that sweeteners are responsible for these trends, but it raises the question of whether they influence metabolism in ways we do not yet fully understand."
Testing Sucralose and Stevia Across Generations
Researchers began by dividing 47 male and female mice into three groups. One group received plain water, while the other two received water containing either sucralose or stevia. The doses were designed to resemble amounts that a person might reasonably consume as part of a normal diet.
The mice were then bred for two successive generations. Unlike the original animals, both later generations were given only plain water.
"Animal models allow us to control environmental conditions very precisely and to isolate the effect of a specific factor, such as a dietary compound, while also following several generations within a relatively short time," explained Concha.
Tracking Blood Sugar, Gut Bacteria, and Gene Activity
Researchers tested each generation for oral glucose tolerance, a measure used to evaluate how effectively the body handles glucose and identify signs of insulin resistance, which is an important warning sign for diabetes.
They also collected fecal samples to examine changes in the gut microbiome and measure concentrations of short-chain fatty acids. These compounds are produced by gut bacteria and can influence biological processes related to gene regulation. Changes in their levels could therefore point to epigenetic effects that may be transmitted from parents to offspring.
Scientists think sweeteners may alter short-chain fatty acid production by disrupting normal gut microbiome function. Those disruptions could ultimately influence gene expression.
The team also measured the activity of five genes in the liver and intestines. The genes are involved in inflammation, the integrity of the gut barrier, and metabolism. By examining them, researchers hoped to identify possible epigenetic changes connected with gut function, inflammation, and metabolic health that could help explain some of the suspected negative effects of non-nutritive sweeteners.
Sucralose and Stevia Produced Different Effects
The two sweeteners did not affect the mice in exactly the same way, and their effects also shifted between generations.
Among first-generation offspring, signs of impaired glucose tolerance appeared only in males descended from mice that consumed sucralose. By the second generation, researchers found elevated fasting blood sugar in male descendants of the sucralose group and female descendants of the stevia group.
Mice that consumed either sweetener also developed more diverse fecal microbiomes, but they had lower levels of short-chain fatty acids. That pattern suggests their gut bacteria were producing fewer beneficial metabolites. Reduced short-chain fatty acid concentrations were also found in both subsequent generations.
The effects associated with sucralose were stronger and more persistent. Mice exposed to sucralose showed larger changes in the composition of their fecal microbiomes, including greater numbers of potentially pathogenic bacteria and fewer beneficial species.
Sucralose Changes Persisted Longer
Sucralose also appeared to increase the activity of genes linked to inflammation while reducing the activity of genes associated with metabolism. Those effects were still detectable two generations after the original exposure.
Stevia also altered gene expression, but the changes were weaker and did not persist beyond one generation.
"When we compared generations, these effects were generally strongest in the first generation and tended to decrease in the second generation," said Concha. "Overall, the effects linked to sucralose were more consistent and persistent across generations."
"The changes we observed in glucose tolerance and gene expression could be interpreted as early biological signals related to metabolic or inflammatory processes," said Concha. "For example, the animals did not develop diabetes. Instead, what we observed were subtle changes in how the body regulates glucose and in the activity of genes associated with inflammation and metabolic regulation. It is possible that such changes could increase susceptibility to metabolic disturbances under certain conditions, such as a high-fat diet."
What the Mouse Study Does and Does Not Show
The researchers caution that the findings show associations between sweetener exposure and changes in metabolic health, but they do not prove that the sweeteners directly caused all of the observed effects.
The results also come from mice, meaning the biological response to non-nutritive sweeteners may differ in humans.
"The goal of this research is not to create alarm, but to highlight the need for further investigation," said Concha. "It may be reasonable to consider moderation in the consumption of these additives and to continue studying their long-term biological effects."
Story Source:
Materials provided by Frontiers. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Francisca Concha Celume, Francisco Pérez-Bravo, Fabien Magne, Ricardo Olivares, Martin Gotteland. Artificial and natural non-nutritive sweeteners drive divergent gut and genetic responses across generations. Frontiers in Nutrition, 2026; 13 DOI: 10.3389/fnut.2026.1694149

Oil prices rose by more than 2% after U.S. and Iranian strikes
Kyiv • UNN
Brent and WTI rose by more than 2% after U.S. and Iranian strikes. Tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz declined due to the attacks.
Oil prices rose by more than 2% on Monday after the United States attacked an Iranian island in the Strait of Hormuz and Tehran said it had carried out a retaliatory strike, as the conflict enters its sixth month, UNN writes, citing Reuters.
Details
Brent crude futures rose by $2.35, or 2.67%, to $90.45 a barrel by 13:06 GMT (16:06 Kyiv time), while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude rose by $2.31, or 2.77%, to $85.71. The price of Brent crude had risen earlier that day to $91.52, its highest level since August 25.
On Sunday, U.S. forces struck two launchers on Iran's Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz, the first known U.S. strikes on the country since late July. In response, Iran attacked two U.S. air bases in Jordan, Iranian media reported on Monday, citing the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
Goldman Sachs heightens warning over diesel fuel amid wars31.08.26, 10:00 • 12631 view
"The resumption of military strikes in the Middle East and concerns about further disruptions to oil supplies have driven oil prices higher," said UBS analyst Giovanni Staunovo, adding that markets will focus on whether or not the situation will de-escalate.
U.S. President Donald Trump said on social media on Sunday that Iran's energy hub on Kharg Island had been "blown to smithereens," but there was no evidence of an attack on the island. The post, which included an AI-generated video, provided no additional details. Iran denied any strike on the island and said oil production operations were continuing.
Attempts to reach an agreement to end the conflict remain deadlocked, as mediators seek to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, through which one-fifth of the world's oil supplies passed before the war began in late February.
The market's strong reaction on Monday was partly due to low trading volumes because of a public holiday in Britain, said Saxo Bank analyst Ole Hansen.
Shipping data showed that the number of visible vessels carrying commodities passing through the strait over the weekend fell to five per day, underscoring the caution of operators concerned about attacks on vessels.

British warship makes first visit to Ream Naval Base
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
15:00:37 BST
23:00:37 KST

British patrol ship HMS Tamar has become the first Royal Navy warship to visit Cambodia’s Ream Naval Base, conducting joint training with Cambodian personnel during a week-long visit to the country.
The Royal Navy said the visit was HMS Tamar‘s first to Cambodia and the third call by a British warship to the country in three years, continuing engagement previously undertaken by sister ship HMS Spey.
Tamar spent the week in Sihanoukville, around 130 miles southwest of Phnom Penh, with activities including military training, meetings with Cambodian naval leaders and engagement with local organisations.
The ship was escorted into Ream Naval Base by two Cambodian patrol craft before being met by a guard of honour on the jetty. Commander Tom Lindsey, Commanding Officer of HMS Tamar, subsequently held discussions with Royal Cambodian Navy representatives covering current and potential future cooperation between the two services.
The visit follows a period of renewed Royal Navy engagement with Cambodia after an absence lasting more than six decades. Lindsey said in the Royal Navy release: “My ship’s company pulled out all the stops in welcoming key leaders from Cambodia’s Royal Navy, government officials, local school children and families.”
He added: “In doing so we showcased what Britain can offer and allowed us to message the importance of prosperity in this region to the UK’s own security and prosperity, enabled through maritime trade. Our respect for sovereignty and the rules-based system, which supports peaceful resolution through dialogue, is part of our national character and is a key part of our mission here in the Indo-Pacific.”
Cambodian sailors joined their British counterparts aboard Tamar for medical and damage-control training, including trauma care at sea and procedures for responding to flooding aboard a vessel.
The patrol ship also hosted a reception attended by government officials, military representatives, diplomats, business figures and regional leaders.
Lindsey said: “This visit was a great opportunity for my ship’s company to undertake defence engagement in a manner close to their hearts: through sports, including football and volleyball games alongside the Royal Cambodian Navy, with a celebratory barbecue afterwards, and through community outreach supporting a local children’s charity.”
He described the call at Ream as particularly notable for the ship, adding: “It has been a privilege to bring Tamar to Cambodia for the first time – and for it to be the Royal Navy’s first visit to Ream Naval Base makes it doubly special.”
The Royal Cambodian Navy operates a fleet of around 20 vessels, according to the Royal Navy, consisting mainly of patrol craft and landing vessels alongside the corvette Koh Kong Senchey.
Its roles include coastal security, counter-smuggling, counter-narcotics work, action against people trafficking and piracy, and search and rescue operations supporting fishermen. Members of Tamar‘s ship’s company also visited the M’lop Tapang organisation in Sihanoukville, which provides shelter and other support for children and young people. Sailors carried out maintenance and painting work at the organisation’s facilities.
Leading Medical Assistant Stanex said in the release: “A personal highlight for me was going to the children’s charity centre to paint the recreation area because we got to help those who had nothing and see the joy in the kids’ faces as we worked together to brighten up the area.”
HMS Tamar is one of the Royal Navy’s Batch 2 River-class offshore patrol vessels and has been deployed to the Indo-Pacific alongside HMS Spey on a long-term basis.
The two ships undertake maritime security cooperation, defence engagement, humanitarian assistance and disaster relief activity, and work intended to counter illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing across the region. The Cambodian visit concluded with further engagement between the two navies, including football and volleyball matches followed by a joint barbecue, before Tamar continued its wider Indo-Pacific deployment.

====================================================================================================

Stress hormones drive female-specific brain rewiring following ketamine anesthesia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
14:00:21 UTC
23:00:21 KST

A recent study found that female mice, but not males, experience a surge in a stress hormone during recovery from ketamine anesthesia, prompting immune cells in the brain to reshape neuronal connections. This points to profound sex differences in how the brain regains function after being anesthetized. The findings were published in Science Advances.
Recovery from anesthesia is a complex biological process required to resume normal bodily and brain functions. Ketamine is unique among anesthetics because it targets specific inhibitory systems in the brain. It is normally viewed as a standard anesthetic that causes a temporary and fully reversible loss of consciousness.
Recent observations suggest ketamine can actually reinstate juvenile-like plasticity, or the brain’s ability to rewire and form new connections, and induce mild anxiety in female animals. This aligns with other work showing that biological sex plays a role in anesthesia responses. For instance, a study covered by PsyPost in 2024 indicated that females tend to regain consciousness and cognitive function faster than males following exposure to general anesthetics.
Microglia, the resident immune cells of the brain, are known to interact with neuronal networks and respond to environmental changes, shaping how neurons fire. However, their specific role in anesthesia recovery, particularly regarding potential sex differences, has remained largely unexplored.
The research, led by Alessandro Venturino and Sandra Siegert, a professor at the Institute of Science and Technology Austria, aimed to see if microglia behave differently in male and female brains during anesthesia recovery.
“We were interested to investigate which consequences ketamine anesthesia had on microglia,” said Siegert, who leads the Siegert Group. “Microglia are known to respond to neuronal activity and anesthesia alters the brain activity, which led us to hypothesize that microglia might respond to it.”
To test this, the team administered a single dose of a ketamine-based anesthesia mixture to adult male and female mice. They then examined the primary visual cortex, an area of the brain where ketamine is known to induce structural changes.
Looking at the brain tissue four hours after the injection, the scientists noticed a distinct difference between the sexes. Female mice exhibited increased levels of a protein called CD68 in their microglia, indicating heightened cellular activity. The physical shape of the female microglia also changed, and they formed prolonged contacts with the branching structures of nearby neurons. Male microglia did not show these pronounced changes.
To see if these cellular contacts altered brain function, the team recorded the electrical activity of the neurons in slices of brain tissue. They found that the frequency of spontaneous electrical impulses increased in the female mice, suggesting enhanced neural plasticity and synaptic function. When the researchers chemically depleted the microglia in a separate group of female mice before administering the anesthesia, this boost in electrical activity did not occur. This provides evidence that the immune cells are necessary for the observed neural changes.
The researchers then used genetic sequencing to figure out what was driving this female-specific response. They found that female microglia selectively increased the expression of a gene called Fkbp5. This gene produces a protein involved in the body’s response to stress hormones, particularly corticosterone.
Blood tests confirmed that two hours after the ketamine injection, female mice had corticosterone levels nearly three times higher than their baseline. In contrast, male corticosterone levels remained relatively flat. To test the role of this hormone, the team surgically removed the adrenal glands, which produce corticosterone, in a group of female mice.
Without the adrenal glands, the ketamine-induced changes in microglial activity and neuron interaction vanished. When these mice were given a direct injection of corticosterone, the microglia rapidly resumed their active state and began contacting neurons again. This indicates that the stress hormone directly drives the immune cells to remodel neural connections.
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2026, which detailed how recovering from ketamine anesthesia triggers a female-specific surge in corticosterone that activates microglia to promote new neural connections.
“It was fascinating to see that not the typical suspicious candidates for sex differences, namely the sex hormone estrogen, is the main driver of this effect but that the effect is mediated through the stress-response via the hormone corticosterone,” Siegert said.
A general reader might assume these findings mean human women will experience identical brain remodeling after receiving ketamine. The authors note that the study was conducted in mice, and human biological responses to anesthetics and stress hormones can differ. The experimental design also focused on a single time point of four hours post-anesthesia, meaning the long-term persistence of these new neural connections is currently unknown.
The anesthetic dosage used in the experiment also differs from how the drug is sometimes applied in psychiatry. The researchers gave the animals a dose sufficient to reach a level of anesthesia deep enough to perform surgery without pain or movement. “It’s important to say that we used an anesthetic dosage of ketamine, in combination with other drugs commonly used to ensure surgical plane for animal surgery,” Siegert noted. “How much our results can be translated to dosages commonly used for treating depression requires a follow-up study.”
Despite these caveats, the results highlight how biological sex can fundamentally alter the body’s response to pharmacological treatments. “Medication can have different effects and consequences between sexes,” Siegert explained. “In the case of ketamine, we know surprisingly little about sex-differences, even though it is frequently used. Our data suggests that females are more sensitive to the effects of ketamine.”
Beyond hormones, other factors such as the neurotransmitter noradrenaline appear to fluctuate differently between the sexes during recovery and might interact with the stress response. Future research could explore how different types of anesthetics, which act on different brain receptors, might influence these immune-driven changes.
More broadly, the team hopes to continue unraveling the mysteries of these immune cells and how they interact with glial cells, the supportive, non-neuronal cells that protect and maintain the brain. “Our main research focus is on identifying which role microglia have in the adult healthy brain,” Siegert said. “They are highly active but we still have only a rudimentary understanding of their daily role on how they act on neurons and other glial cells in the brain.”
The study, “Corticosterone-linked microglial activity underpins sexually dimorphic neuroplasticity after ketamine anesthesia,” was authored by Alessandro Venturino, MohammadAmin Alamalhoda, Thomas Negrello, Kelly Jin, Cindy T. J. van Velthoven, Ryan John A. Cubero, Jake Yeung, Peter Koppensteiner, Bosiljka Tasic, and Sandra Siegert.

Elia Zenghelis, Co-Founder of OMA and Architectural Educator, Passes Away at 89
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
14:00:00 UTC
23:00:00 KST

Elia Zenghelis, Greek architect, co-founder of the Office for Metropolitan Architecture (OMA), and one of the most influential architectural educators of the late twentieth century, died on August 30, 2026, at the age of 89. His death marks the passing of a figure whose influence on architectural thought extended far beyond the buildings he designed, shaping the intellectual formation of several generations of architects through decades of teaching across Europe and the United States.
Born in Athens in 1937, Zenghelis studied architecture at the Architectural Association School of Architecture in London, completing his studies in 1961. He joined the practice of Douglas Stephen and Partners, where he worked until 1971, while simultaneously beginning to teach at the AA in 1963. At the school, he became a prominent voice for a more radical, avant-garde architectural discourse, helping to transform the AA into a fertile ground for radical ideas.

Ukraine converts iconic HMMWV into robot vehicle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
13:59:56 UTC
22:59:56 KST

- Drone Fight Group delivered three HMMWVs equipped with its Kaban remote control system to Ukrainian military units.
- Kaban converts existing vehicles into remotely operated platforms controlled via satellite, rather than building a new unmanned vehicle from scratch.
Ukrainian company Drone Fight Group has deployed an HMMWV, known popularly as “Humvee”, converted into a remotely operated vehicle using its Kaban system, delivering three units to Ukrainian military formations, the company said.
The vehicles went to the 3rd Army Corps, the 429th Separate Unmanned Systems Regiment “Achilles” and the 49th Brigade of Ukraine’s Armed Forces. Kaban gives an operator remote control over vehicle movement, lights, infrared illumination, searchlights, two-way audio communication and onboard computer data.
Rather than building a purpose-made unmanned ground vehicle, Kaban is designed to convert existing vehicle platforms already in military service. The company said this approach lets operators upgrade vehicles already in a fleet and configure them for logistics, resupply, evacuation, reconnaissance support and other missions where keeping a driver inside the vehicle creates unnecessary risk.
The system includes a digital map for plotting routes and placing markers, along with manual navigation correction intended to keep the vehicle moving if GPS signals are jammed or spoofed. A predicted trajectory display helps the operator steer and maneuver. If the connection between operator and vehicle is lost, the system stops the vehicle automatically.
Kaban connects over satellite, extending its operating range beyond what short-range radio control typically allows. The company said the control station and vehicle can operate at significantly greater distances depending on network availability and mission conditions, rather than requiring an operator to remain physically close to the vehicle.
“Our goal is not simply to make a vehicle drive remotely,” said David, lead developer of the system. “We are building a system that gives an operator enough information and control to confidently perform real missions from a safer location. That includes vehicle systems, navigation, communications, fail-safe behavior, and the ability to adapt the platform to different operational requirements.”
The system can also be extended with mission-specific equipment, including net launchers and drone launch platforms, according to the company.
Deployment follows four stages: assessing the vehicle platform and mission requirements, installing and configuring the Kaban hardware and controls for that specific vehicle, testing vehicle controls and communications across multiple scenarios, and training operators, with ongoing technical support after deployment.
“There are enormous fleets of conventional vehicles already in service around the world,” said Vladyslav Plaksin, co-founder of the Kaban project and founder of Drone Fight Group. “Kaban is about giving those platforms a new capability. Instead of replacing a vehicle with a purpose-built unmanned system, we can convert an existing platform and remove the driver from missions where having a person inside the vehicle creates unnecessary risk.”

Military source refutes US claim on Iran mining Hormuz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
13:50:14 UTC
22:50:14 KST

According to local Iranian Tasnim News Agency, the military source telling it on Monday, “The claim by the Americans that ‘with last night’s attack, they wanted to prevent Iran from laying mines in the Strait of Hormuz and that they were successful in doing so’ is fantasy and story-making, and last night’s confrontation had nothing to do with mine-laying.”
“On the one hand, the Americans say that they have neutralized all the mines, and on the other hand, they claimed that last night they prevented the laying of new mines. The question now is: Then exactly how are the tankers that violate the rules and hit the mines punished?!” the source added.
The military source stated, “The Americans intended last night to prevent Iran from punishing the vessels that violated the rules, but they failed in this effort as well. The violating vessels were punished, and their bases in the region were also hit by Iranian projectiles.”

The City of Copenhagen is ready to send more displaced Ukrainians to Jutland after five Jutland mayors opposed the government’s bill to halt immigration from 14 Ukrainian regions in Jyllands-Posten.
Andreas Keil, Social Democrats, Mayor of Employment, Integration, and Business, wrote this in a letter to the mayors.
“If you have the opportunity to receive a number of displaced Ukrainians, it will be a great help to Copenhagen,” he wrote in the letter.
He further writes that it will simultaneously be a concrete contribution to the redistribution among municipalities that Minister for Immigration and Integration Morten Bødskov (Social Democrats as well) has previously requested.
“I understand it to mean that the five Jutland municipalities would like more settlement, labor, and have more opportunities to accommodate the newcomers, while we, conversely, in Copenhagen are challenged to find accommodation for more than the 3,800 Ukrainians we already accommodate now,” he stated.
The letter has been sent to the mayors of Hjørring, Lemvig, Vesthimmerland, Skive, and Brønderslev Municipality, respectively.

The City of Copenhagen is ready to send more displaced Ukrainians to Jutland after five Jutland mayors opposed the government’s bill to halt immigration from 14 Ukrainian regions in Jyllands-Posten.
Andreas Keil, Social Democrats, Mayor of Employment, Integration, and Business, wrote this in a letter to the mayors.
“If you have the opportunity to receive a number of displaced Ukrainians, it will be a great help to Copenhagen,” he wrote in the letter.
He further writes that it will simultaneously be a concrete contribution to the redistribution among municipalities that Minister for Immigration and Integration Morten Bødskov (Social Democrats as well) has previously requested.
“I understand it to mean that the five Jutland municipalities would like more settlement, labor, and have more opportunities to accommodate the newcomers, while we, conversely, in Copenhagen are challenged to find accommodation for more than the 3,800 Ukrainians we already accommodate now,” he stated.
The letter has been sent to the mayors of Hjørring, Lemvig, Vesthimmerland, Skive, and Brønderslev Municipality, respectively.

Do not hide in elevators, near gas stations, or in the basements of panel buildings — what not to do during a kamikaze drone attack
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
16:47:13 EEST
22:47:13 KST

Do not hide in elevators, near gas stations, or in the basements of panel buildings — what not to do during a kamikaze drone attack
Kyiv • UNN
The police advise going to a shelter immediately during an air raid alert or following the two-wall rule. Do not hide near gas stations, in elevators, or in basements.
The Patrol Police provided advice on how Ukrainians should act during an attack by kamikaze drones — they should not hide in elevators, near gas stations, or in the basements of panel buildings, reports UNN.
Details
Law enforcement officers reminded the public that the enemy continues to use attack UAVs, so it is important to know what to do in the event of a threat.
Most importantly: upon hearing the air-raid alert, immediately head to a shelter! Choose reliable shelters: specially equipped facilities, underground passages, parking garages, and basement floors. If the shelter is far away, follow the "two-wall" rule
The police also explained what should not be done:
-  do not remain in a vehicle; get out of the car and move away from the road; 
-  do not hide in building entrances, archways, elevators, stairwells, near gas stations or kiosks, or in the basements of panel buildings; 
-  do not approach downed or damaged drones, as they may contain explosives or pose another danger; 
-  do not publish photos or videos of impact sites or UAV flight paths. 
In addition, law enforcement officers urged people to follow safety rules and take care of themselves.
We remind you
As reported by Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat, Russia increased the number of jet-powered drones used in attacks on Ukraine, deploying five times more of them in July than in June.

IMF mission begins negotiations with Ukraine on reforms and the 2027 Budget
Kyiv • UNN
The IMF mission, led by Gavin Gray, is assessing Ukraine’s reforms and the draft 2027 Budget. The negotiations are taking place במסגרת the EFF program.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) mission began talks with the Ukrainian authorities and other stakeholders on Monday, focusing on the economic outlook, reform commitments under the Extended Fund Facility (EFF), and the draft State Budget of Ukraine for 2027, UNN writes, citing Anadolu.
Details
The mission is led by Gavin Gray, the IMF mission chief in Ukraine, according to a statement by the Fund’s representative office in Ukraine.
The discussions will assess Ukraine’s progress in the macroeconomic and structural reforms agreed under the current EFF program, as well as the government’s plans for next year’s budget.
The mission follows the first review of the new four-year EFF program, which gives Ukraine access to approximately $8.1 billion, the statement said.
The IMF Executive Board approved the first review in July, paving the way for the disbursement of approximately $690 million.
The new EFF arrangement, agreed between IMF staff and the Ukrainian authorities at the end of 2025, aims to support macroeconomic stability, debt sustainability, and external viability, as well as advance structural reforms and governance measures.
The talks are taking place as Kyiv prepares its 2027 budget amid continued wartime spending and significant financing needs.
The Ukrainian government seeks to secure continued international financial support while maintaining economic stability and implementing the reforms required under the IMF program.
