====================================================================================================

PM Modi's jackets, Rahul's shirts, Mamata's sarees: How leaders use fashion for political messaging
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
12:40:35 UTC
21:40:35 KST

PM Modi's jackets, Rahul's shirts, Mamata's sarees: How leaders use fashion for political messaging
Aastha Jha / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 31, 2026, 21:56 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
PM Modi during his visit to meet naval personnel aboard INS Vikrant (left); Rahul Gandhi during 'Chhattron ki Goonj' programme (right)
From Indira Gandhi's sarees to Narendra Modi's carefully curated bandhgalas, from Rajiv Gandhi's sneakers and sunglasses to the Thackerays' colour-coded political imagery, what Indian politicians wear has often been more than a question of personal style. Their clothes have helped construct identities, signal ideology, project modernity, invoke tradition and increasingly generate the kind of visual moments that social media loves.So when Rahul Gandhi appeared in a pink shirt and later in a yellow one, the change from his usual white clothing drew attention online. The yellow shirt, along with the line "Smash the patriarchy", became part of the social-media conversation. The interest was less about the shirt itself and more about how unusual it looked compared with his regular public appearance.But this is not the first time that a politician's attire has made more headlines than their speech. Prime Minister Narendra Modi's clothes have often drawn attention, from his signature jackets and bandhgalas to the regional outfits he wears during visits across the country. Over the years, they have become a familiar part of his public image.
As designer Gaurav Jai Gupta puts it, "Fashion can communicate before a politician has spoken a single word. Clothing conveys identity, ideology, relatability, authority and even regional or cultural affiliation almost instantly." Politics, he adds, is fundamentally about perception, and "an outfit can become the visual shorthand for an entire political moment.
Indira Gandhi, elected as Prime Minister on January 14th, 1977, adresses to the crowd in the Rae Bareli Lok Sabha constituency (Credit: Magnum Photos)
PM Modi: How his wardrobe became part of his public image
Prime Minister Narendra Modi has taken political dressing into the era of personal branding.His wardrobe moves easily between traditional Indian clothing and sharply tailored modern silhouettes. The signature kurta, sleeveless jackets and bandhgalas have become instantly recognisable, while his international appearances often combine Indian craftsmanship with global tailoring.Some of the looks have become headline-makers in their own right.His wardrobe has since offered plenty of other visual moments.A burgundy bandhgala during his first overseas trip as prime minister created a polished diplomatic look. A signature khadi kurta during his Bhutan visit emphasised Indian textiles and craftsmanship. In Nepal, saffron attire paired with a rudraksh mala made a strong cultural and religious statement at Pashupatinath Temple.This habit of dressing for the country he's visiting — or the region of India he's in — is itself a strategy, according to Gupta: "I would definitely consider it a form of fashion diplomacy. Clothing can be a very subtle way of acknowledging the culture of the country you are visiting while siultaneously representing your own identity." Retaining elements of one's own traditional identity alongside that, he says, "reinforces national representation."His recent looks have been more state-centric. From sporting the gamcha look in Bihar, to a turban in Punjab, and even the traditional mund in Kerala, Modi has worn his "vocals for locals" tag.
PM Modi in several traditional attires
Pink, yellow, blue – Rahul's pattern?
For years, Rahul Gandhi's public wardrobe has largely stayed within the safe territory of political dressing — white kurta-pajamas, jackets and understated casual wear. It is a familiar uniform in Indian politics, one that keeps the focus on the politician rather than the clothes.But the pink and yellow shirts were different.Bright, instantly noticeable and far removed from the monochrome political wardrobe, they became an unlikely talking point. Gupta explains why a single garment can take on a life entirely of its own online: "The internet loves symbols that are simple, recognisable and easy to reproduce. A yellow shirt is, in itself, just a yellow shirt. But once social media attaches a narrative to it, the garment can acquire an entirely new meaning." The audience, he says, effectively co-authors the outfit's significance — "memes, edits, captions and commentary can transform an ordinary look into a cultural reference point," helped along by the fact that "colour is highly emotional and visually immediate."
Rahul's shade of politics through the years
He did not wear it just anywhere, either. He wore it to the 'Chhatron ki Goonj' programme, where the audience was predominantly Gen Z. But this is not the first time the Leader of Opposition has made news for his fashion. In 2019, Rahul attended a Kerala college event in a t-shirt and jeans, taking a break from his classic white kurta look, with his "You can call me Rahul" reels still going viral.Likewise, it was not a conincidence that he went with a blue t-shirt, when he held up the red book in his hand and said "Save the Constitution", or a black one to protest outside the Parliament.It's a pattern. Every Rahul Gandhi's politics has reflected in his preference for colours.
The Thackerays: When colour carries politics
If PM Modi's wardrobe demonstrates the power of personal branding, the Thackerays show how colour and clothing can become political shorthand.Bal Thackeray initially adopted the shirt-and-trouser look of the urban office worker, appealing to an aspirational Maharashtra audience. Later, as Hindutva became central to his political positioning, orange became a defining element of his public appearance.Fashion designer Nivedita Saboo, who has dressed several politicians, explains why colour carries this kind of political weight in the first place: "Colour communicates emotion before language does. Saffron can evoke spirituality, sacrifice, nationalism and Hindu cultural identity. White can communicate simplicity, peace, authority or the traditional Gandhian vocabulary. Electric or deep blue has powerful associations with social justice, equality and Ambedkarite politics." But, she cautions, "colour is never universal. Its meaning changes with culture, history, political association, fabric, styling and even the person's body language. That's why political dressing is fascinating: you can say something without saying anything."Uddhav Thackeray developed his own visual identity through simple, brightly coloured sadra-pajamas closely associated with Maharashtrian culture.
Uddhav and Raj Thackeray, whose political styles reflect the Thackeray family's use of colour and cultural imagery
Aaditya Thackeray, meanwhile, represents another generational shift, combining traditional Indian clothing with contemporary fashion.Three generations. Three styles. And three different ways of speaking to their audiences without saying a word.
Mamata, Kejriwal and the politics of looking 'aam'
Then there are politicians whose biggest fashion statement is that they appear to have made very little effort at all.Mamata Banerjee's white cotton saree with a blue border and hawai chappals have become almost inseparable from her political identity. Arvind Kejriwal's muffler achieved a similar status.The appeal is simple: don't look like a politician; look like the people who vote for you. As Gupta puts it, "politics is about recognition and relatability, not necessarily luxury." A consistent, uncomplicated look, he says, "can become incredibly powerful because people can immediately identify it" — Mamata Banerjee's saree and Kejriwal's muffler "function almost like logos," communicating accessibility in a way an expensive designer wardrobe rarely can. "In a country like ours, simplicity is more relatable," he says. "In mass politics, that emotional connection can be far more valuable than sartorial sophistication."The repetition is what makes it powerful. Eventually, the garment becomes a logo.See the white-and-blue saree, think Mamata. See the muffler, think Kejriwal. See the kurta and jacket, think Modi.And now, in the age of viral fashion moments, perhaps even a yellow shirt can enter the political visual dictionary.
Arvind Kejriwal’s signature muffler became a recognisable part of his political image
Vijay: Breaking Tamil Nadu's white-shirt, veshti political dress code
When Vijay took oath as Tamil Nadu chief minister, he broke from the traditional white shirt-and-veshti look, arriving instead in a sharply tailored black suit. He has since made black-and-white suits a regular part of his public image.Addressing the attention around his wardrobe, Vijay said, “Many people have been talking about the new suit that I have been wearing recently. Are we not allowed to wear a coat and suit? Is it meant only for people in positions of authority? There is nothing like that.”Explaining his choice, he added, “I am not wearing many colours. It is just black and white, like all our hearts. The choice of these colours is to show that I will remain transparent and simple in everything, just like black and white.”
Tamil Nadu CM Vijay in his iconic black and white suit
Indira Gandhi: The saree that became a power statement
Long before politicians had to worry about going viral, Indira Gandhi had already mastered the art of having a recognisable political look.Her sarees, from Banarasi silk to handlooms and Tanchois, became an important part of her public image. They projected tradition and authority at the same time, allowing her to appear deeply rooted in Indian culture while commanding political spaces at home and abroad.The saree wasn't simply a sartorial choice. The way she wore it, with the pallu covering her head from the loose end of the saree, made it distinct.
Indira Gandhi in one of her signature sarees during a public event
Gupta points to exactly this kind of repetition as the foundation of a political fashion identity: "Consistency is the key to creating a fashion identity. When a politician repeatedly wears a particular silhouette, colour palette, accessory or garment, it becomes part of their visual vocabulary." Indira Gandhi's sarees, he notes, "became inseparable from her public image," much "like branding in fashion or advertising: repetition creates recognition." Eventually, he says, "you don't need to see the entire person; a particular silhouette, colour combination or accessory can be enough to trigger recognition." But he's careful to add a caveat: "successful political style usually feels authentic rather than overly constructed. The strongest personal brands emerge when the clothes reinforce something the politician already represents."For women in politics especially, clothing has always carried an extra layer of scrutiny. Too traditional, and a leader can be boxed into convention. Too Western, and questions about cultural authenticity can follow.Moreover, most female political leaders of the time or the ones who preceeded her wore sarees the same way.Indira's style largely sidestepped that binary. She made traditional Indian clothing look powerful.
Nehru's jacket, Rajiv's sneakers: Political wardrobe evolves
The political fashion story goes back even further.Jawaharlal Nehru's iconic jacket became so closely associated with him that his name effectively became part of the garment's identity. The jacket was a descendant of the northern Indian achkan, a closed-neck, coat-like garment traditionally associated with Indian nobility. It was largely when the style was marketed to Western audiences that it took the "Nehru" name, after the prime minister popularised it through his public appearances. The minimalist look later found fans beyond politics, including the Beatles and Sammy Davis Jr, who reportedly owned more than 200 Nehru jackets.
Jawaharlal Nehru in his signature Nehru jacket, which later became a global fashion symbol
Khadi and handlooms carried an even bigger political history, associated with nationalism, self-reliance and the freedom movement.Then came Rajiv Gandhi.Dark sunglasses, sneakers, sleeveless fleece jackets and khadi kurta-pajamas gave him a distinctly more contemporary appearance. His wardrobe reflected the image he projected politically — younger, modern and more comfortable with the technological future.
Rajiv Gandhi sporting a pair of sneakers
In other parts of the world, political leaders also turned their clothes into signatures. Mao Zedong's four-pocketed tunic, known as the Zhongshan suit and later the Mao suit, became closely associated with communist China and was brought back into fashion during his rule. Usually seen in muted shades of grey, green or blue, the suit became a visual shorthand for Mao and communism before falling out of favour after his death in 1976.
Mao & Castro: The outfit of revolutionaries
In other parts of the world, political leaders also turned their clothes into signatures. Mao Zedong's four-pocketed tunic, known as the Zhongshan suit and later the Mao suit, became closely associated with communist China and was brought back into fashion during his rule. Usually seen in muted shades of grey, green or blue, the suit became a visual shorthand for Mao and communism before falling out of favour after his death in 1976.
Mao Zedong’s uniform-like suit became a visual shorthand for his revolutionary politics
Fidel Castro, meanwhile, swapped the traditional military and political imagery for tracksuits later in life. He was famously photographed wearing a red, white and blue Adidas tracksuit while recovering from surgery in 2006. The look soon became part of his public image, with Castro later wearing sportswear from brands including Fila, Puma and Nike.
Fidel Castro in his guerrilla boots during his early political years (left); Castro in a tracksuit in his later years (right)
What would it take to dress for Gen Z?
If a yellow shirt at a college event can trend for days, the question naturally follows: what does it actually take for a politician's wardrobe to land with a generation raised on Instagram and short-form video?Saboo, who has worked closely with politicians on exactly this brief, is blunt about the trap most of them fall into. "Gen Z has grown up in a visual culture where identity is communicated through what you wear," she says. "But breaking the dress code simply to look young can backfire. Gen Z is extremely good at detecting what feels manufactured. The clothes have to feel like the person, not like a stylist has dressed them to look young." A politician who "wears the traditional kurta beautifully and owns it completely," she argues, can be "far more compelling than somebody wearing sneakers and a T-shirt because someone told them that's what young people like." For her, the real shift isn't from tradition to trend — it's "from dress code to personal code."Asked to imagine one outfit that could say "young India" without a single slogan, she describes something quietly hybrid: a relaxed, engineered jacket in a lightweight Indian textile over a tapered trouser, perhaps a modernised kurta with sharper, almost architectural proportions underneath, finished with one unexpected element — an unusual seam, a technical fabric panel, a monogram, a contemporary sneaker.
The palette, she says, would be "sophisticated rather than loud — ivory, charcoal, deep blue or earthy neutrals with one energetic accent." The test, in her words: "It shouldn't look like 'politician trying to be fake and dress young.' It should look like India's next generation has naturally evolved its own version of Indian clothing."Her advice to politicians boils down to five principles: don't dress younger, dress more authentically; modernise proportions rather than identity; find one recurring signature — a colour, a silhouette, a jacket, a watch — rather than constantly changing the wardrobe; make sure the clothes actually function in a country that "lives fast"; and, above all, stop being afraid of personality. As she puts it, "politics has traditionally rewarded conformity. Gen Z is attracted to people who appear comfortable in their own skin." Fashion, she concludes, "cannot manufacture relatability. It can only amplify it."
Aastha Jha is a writer at The Times of India, covering politics. She also writes on business, global affairs, social issues, with a focus on policy, governance and their impact on everyday lives. Her work brings together reportage and analysis, tracking developments in India and abroad while examining the broader social and economic currents shaping public discourse.

Feature: Iceland referendum highlights domestic challenges, divided views on EU path
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
20:40:22 CST
21:40:22 KST

by Xinhua writers Zhu Haochen, Weng Xinyang and Meng Fanyu
REYKJAVIK, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- At a polling station inside the Kringlan branch of Reykjavik City Library on Saturday, voters streamed in and out as Icelanders cast ballots in a nationwide referendum on whether to restart accession talks with the European Union (EU).
For a country of around 400,000 people in the middle of the North Atlantic, the ballot offered only two choices: "Yes" or "No." A "Yes" vote would authorize the government to reopen membership negotiations with the EU.
Yet conversations with voters across the country suggested that the issues behind the referendum were far from a simple binary choice.
A staff member at the Kringlan polling station told Xinhua that public interest in the referendum had been high.
"Iceland has long faced many problems, particularly in the economic and financial fields, and domestic policies alone are not enough to solve them," he said. "Many people hope that moving closer to the EU could offer Iceland another way forward."
At the same polling station, an elderly voter who had just cast his ballot saw things very differently.
He acknowledged that Iceland faced long-standing challenges but insisted they were for Icelanders themselves to address.
"These are Iceland's own affairs. We should handle our own affairs ourselves," he said, arguing that the country should remain independent and avoid outside interference. "Besides, the EU itself is beset by crises."
The contrast was echoed elsewhere in the capital.
At a polling station in Reykjavik City Hall, three students from the University of Iceland said they had all voted "Yes."
One of them, Frodi Gunnlaugsson, said fluctuations in the Icelandic krona and inflation had caused serious difficulties for both the economy and ordinary households. High housing prices, he said, had also left many young people unable to afford a home and settle down.
He also voiced dissatisfaction with what he described as problems concerning government integrity and governance. For him, closer integration with Europe could offer a way to break out of Iceland's current difficulties.
For other Icelanders, however, some issues should not be placed lightly on the negotiating table.
Fisheries, both an economic pillar and an important part of Iceland's national identity, have long stood at the center of the country's debate over EU membership. Official data show that marine products accounted for nearly 40 percent of Iceland's total goods exports in 2025.
Sveinn Margeirsson, a senior executive at major Icelandic seafood company Brim, told Xinhua that Iceland had spent decades building a fisheries system based on expanded jurisdiction over its surrounding waters, science-based quotas and higher value-added production.
If Iceland were to restart accession talks and eventually join the EU, its fisheries could come under the bloc's Common Fisheries Policy, raising questions over how management powers and fishing quotas would be determined and whether Iceland's existing restrictions on foreign ownership could be maintained.
Margeirsson said keeping control of fisheries resources in Icelandic hands was crucial because it affected the entire chain from harvesting and processing to employment and trade, and ultimately whether the value created by the industry would remain in Iceland.
He said he had voted "No."
Foreign policy and geopolitics also weighed on the debate.
U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly made remarks about taking control of Greenland, another North Atlantic island. U.S. media have also reported that Billy Long, nominated to serve as U.S. ambassador to Iceland, once joked that Iceland could become the "52nd state" of the United States.
Such remarks, together with doubts over U.S. reliability and concerns about NATO's future, have added to the strategic uncertainty facing Iceland, a NATO member with no standing army.
At the vote-counting center in Reykjavik's Laugardalsholl arena on Saturday night, staff member Bjorn Arnar Karason told Xinhua that he had voted "Yes," partly because of what he saw as a more unsettled international environment and U.S. rhetoric over Greenland.
Joining the EU, he said, might offer Iceland an additional layer of security.
"Greenland is our northern neighbor," Karason said. "The U.S. interest in Greenland makes me feel as if there is always a dark cloud hanging over us."
According to Icelandic public broadcaster RUV, more than 220,000 of the country's roughly 270,000 registered voters cast ballots in the referendum.
Preliminary results showed 52.8 percent voting against restarting EU accession talks and 47.2 percent in favor, securing victory for the "No" side.
Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir said at a press conference on Sunday that the government respected the result and would not pursue EU accession negotiations during its current term.
The referendum has settled the immediate question of whether Iceland should return to the negotiating table. The deeper issues it exposed, however, remain.
Rejecting renewed talks does not remove the economic and social pressures that helped bring the EU question back into Icelandic politics. At the same time, geopolitical uncertainty continues to complicate the country's security and strategic choices.
For some Icelanders, deeper European integration offers the prospect of greater economic stability and security. For others, preserving national independence and control over fisheries, agriculture and natural resources remains paramount.
The vote may have closed one path for now, but Iceland still faces a broader challenge: how to strengthen its economy and navigate a changing international environment without giving up the degree of autonomy many Icelanders are determined to preserve. ■

Across China: "Sea daughters" fight plastic pollution with love, business model
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
20:40:09 CST
21:40:09 KST

Environmental volunteers collect marine plastic waste in Zhoushan City, east China's Zhejiang Province, Feb. 3, 2026. (Xinhua)
HANGZHOU, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- As the sea glimmers under the first dawn light, a cluster of women in red vests spread out along the shoreline of Changtu, a small island in east China, harvesting not shells but plastic bottles, discarded foam, and other debris tide‑washed in overnight.
For years, these once stay‑at‑home wives and mothers, now environmental volunteers, have waged a quiet but persistent campaign against marine plastic pollution, driven by love, faith and a sustainable business model.
"We used to think our duty was just waiting at home while men ventured out to the sea," said Hu Songsu, 66, founder of the "Gold and Silver Island Association of Fishermen's Wives," at the town, known for rich in large yellow croaker and hairtail herring, in Zhejiang Province.
In 2017, Hu, together with a group of like‑minded women, launched the association, initially focusing on fishing safety. "When a wife tells her husband 'come home early and stay safe,' the husband listens," Hu explained.
But over time, Hu noticed a troubling change: the sea was becoming choked with trash. Discarded fishing nets tangled propellers, while used dry-cell batteries were dumped into the sea -- a scene unimaginable back in her childhood.
"The sea feeds our families. We can do more," Hu said.
The association quickly rolled out a "Blue Sea Rescue" project. Starting with 19 boats whose captains were respected village leaders, they persuaded fishermen to bring their waste back ashore.
For those who balked at the extra hassle, their wives appealed to their beliefs: "You pray for safe voyages every year. But prayers alone aren't enough. Bringing back waste is your real merit."
Even more compelling was the practical argument: polluted waters mean fewer fish. "How can fish survive in a polluted sea? Where will our livelihoods go?" Hu said.
To boost incentives, the association set up a transfer station where marine waste is sorted and sold to recycling companies.
Part of the profits goes to impoverished fishing families, while the station's managers -- most of them fishermen's wives -- also receive monthly pay of 1,000 yuan (about 147 U.S. dollars) to 1,500 yuan.
Fishermen can redeem recycling points earned from handed‑in waste for rice, cooking oil and other daily necessities, or purchase new batteries at subsidized prices when they return old ones.
Evolving from gentle persuasion into a well‑run operational model, the association has recovered over 350 tonnes of marine debris, including 75,000 used batteries.
In 2025, the association won the national March 8th Red Banner Collective award, one of the highest honors conferred by the All‑China Women's Federation. Their work also contributed to the Blue Circle project, which claimed the United Nations' Champions of the Earth award.
This year, Hu was named one of the country's top 10 ecological and environmental volunteers by the Ministry of Ecology and Environment.
What began as a small circle of fishermen's wives has grown into a group with 235 registered volunteers, now widely known as the "East China Sea Daughters."
Researchers and university students visit the island, some shadowing fishermen and their wives at docks, on boats and at the sorting station. "They come to see how ordinary women are changing the ocean," Hu said.
Hu is never alone. Across China, the spirit of these "sea daughters" resonates with volunteer groups operating in vastly different landscapes.
In south China's Shenzhen, "eco‑sentinels" patrol the city's streets and waterways, addressing environmental complaints before they escalate. In northwest China's Qinghai Province, volunteers on horseback travel to summer pastures to collect plastic waste along the shores of Qinghai Lake.
This August marks China's first ecological and environmental volunteer service month. According to the Ministry of Ecology and Environment, 30 provincial‑level regions have rolled out action plans, mobilizing some 38,000 volunteers for more than 650 activities.
For the fishermen's wives in Changtu, August is also the busiest time of year. They repair fishing gear and stock supplies as the peak fishing season is approaching.
Still, Hu never misses her dawn patrol along the shore.
"For us, a healthy ocean is our real wealth," she said. ■

Marine heatwaves leave coral reefs less time to recover: report
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
20:40:06 CST
21:40:06 KST

SYDNEY, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- The world's coral reefs are losing the time they need to recover between increasingly frequent marine heatwaves and global bleaching events driven by human-induced climate change, a report said on Monday.
The Status of Coral Reefs of the World: 2025, published by the Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network (GCRMN), is the most comprehensive assessment of coral reefs to date, drawing on more than 40 years of global data from 21.1 million observations, 87,299 surveys, representing 36,886 sites across 124 countries, territories and economies, according to a GCRMN statement.
"Climate change is driving more frequent and severe marine heatwaves, but local pressures such as poor water quality, overfishing and coastal development are making reefs even less able to withstand them," said the report's lead author Manuel Gonzalez Rivero from the Australian Institute of Marine Science.
Global hard coral cover declined by about 9.5 percent, from an average of 30.2 percent during 1980-2009 to 27.3 percent in 2020-2024, with climate change-driven heat stress identified as the primary cause.
Four major global bleaching events since 1998 have reduced hard coral cover, with reefs only partially recovering between events.
Major bleaching events previously occurred about once a decade. Since 2010, they have occurred approximately every five to six years. However, many corals need at least five years just to mature and begin reproducing.
"Coral reefs once had decades to recover after major bleaching events. Today, they're lucky to get five or six years," said Gonzalez Rivero.
The report said ambitious reductions in greenhouse gas emissions, combined with effective management of local pressures, offer the strongest pathway to maintain hard coral cover. ■

Feature: Back to school in war zones
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
20:40:03 CST
21:40:03 KST

BEIRUT, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- For 21-year-old university student Reine Nasrallah, the start of a new academic year is marked by concerns about how to reach her university and cover the cost of daily transportation, rather than the usual excitement of reuniting with familiar classmates and professors.
After the Israel-Hezbollah war forced her family to flee their home in the southern Lebanese city of Nabatieh, Nasrallah transferred to the Lebanese University's Hadath campus near Beirut, while she and her mother moved into a rented home in the Chouf District.
"The war turned my life upside down," Nasrallah told Xinhua. "We left our home in a hurry after it was destroyed. We could not even take our clothes or belongings with us."
Life in displacement is difficult. The family now pays about 500 U.S. dollars a month to rent the apartment in Chouf, while Nasrallah spends about 20 dollars a day commuting to and from the university, according to her mother, Rana.
"Some days, we simply can't afford the cost of getting to university," Nasrallah said.
For Nasrallah, an even greater challenge has been keeping up with her studies amid the conflict. She said the disruption has prevented her from meeting academic requirements on schedule. She has also developed vision problems, frequent headaches and dizziness.
"My mother had to sell a piece of her jewelry to cover my medical treatment and some of my education expenses," Nasrallah said.
Nasrallah's experience reflects the hardships faced by many students from war zones in Lebanon, as they prepare to start another academic year amid continued uncertainty.
A nationwide assessment conducted by Lebanon's Ministry of Education and Higher Education in June found that 340 public, private, and technical and vocational schools had been damaged during the war, including 17 that were completely destroyed.
The damage affected several governorates, including Nabatieh and South Lebanon. The UN Children's Fund warned in July that at least 100,000 children could be left without a classroom when the new school year begins unless urgent repairs are carried out before September.
Even for students who are able to return to campus, the challenges of learning do not go away. With Israel still carrying out occasional strikes in southern Lebanon, the sounds of explosions and drones continue to weigh heavily on the students, creating an atmosphere of fear and anxiety that can disrupt learning.
"Studying while hearing the sounds of drones, airstrikes, and artillery shelling, and after losing relatives and loved ones, makes it difficult for students to concentrate," Hassan Jaber, a professor from Lebanese University, told Xinhua.
Such conditions, he added, directly affect academic performance and increase the pressures students face both inside and outside the classroom.
Psychologist Amani Hamdan said the effects could linger long after the conflict ends.
"The living, economic, and security conditions experienced by students have created high levels of anxiety and stress," Hamdan told Xinhua, adding that many have lost the sense of stability needed to concentrate and learn.
Displacement, the loss of homes, financial pressure, and fear of renewed strikes can affect students' mental health, she said.
Hamdan called for psychological support and counseling in schools, as well as academic accommodations for affected students, including greater flexibility in examinations when necessary.
With the new academic year approaching, Rana has once again parted with a pair of earrings she treasured for years to help pay her daughter Nasrallah's tuition. Life goes on, but the end of the war remains a distant prospect.
"I don't know how much longer I can hold on," she murmured. ■

====================================================================================================

After 25 Years, the Shanghai Cooperation Organization Faces an Uncertain Future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
12:40:00 UTC
21:40:00 KST

The Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Summit, taking place on August 31 and September 1, will be another opportunity for China and Russia to try to promote an alternative to Western-led international institutions. But the organization, now in its 25th year, faces internal rivalries and tensions that are becoming ever more difficult to sweep under the rug.
The SCO appears to be high on geopolitical symbolism and low on genuine relevance, at least on the political and security front. Despite its Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure (RATS) and the Peace Mission military exercises between SCO member countries, the organization’s security agenda has been weak, with very little to show in terms of actual results. It is not a security treaty, and it has had little effect in diluting the political and military tension between its major players.
One such point of tension is the Sino-Indian conflict. This is a long-running contest that predates the SCO by decades and periodically erupts into clashes at their disputed border. The most recent one took place in 2020 and was unusually violent, causing the first casualties resulting from such clashes in decades and throwing the relationship into a freezer. Talks this month have made some progress, but the fundamentals of the border conflict are likely to remain unresolved. The two sides have discussed ways to improve understanding of the border demarcation in appropriate areas. In an effort to manage border issues, two new additional military hotlines were agreed upon to connect India’s Eastern Army Command and Central Army Command with their Chinese counterparts. While these institutionalized communication channels are useful to avoid incidents along parts of border, an absence of mechanisms is not necessarily the problem. These may be useful, though in previous crises, such mechanisms were not.
A larger problem is that China’s growth and power have created new security complications for countries such as India, which is carefully managing its engagements with the SCO as a fine diplomatic balancing act between Washington on one side and Beijing and Moscow on the other. While its relationship with Washington has come under stress, New Delhi understands the limits of alternative options. Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s engagements with the SCO, the Quad, and other minilateral groupings are a demonstration of what India calls its multidirectional foreign policy. A good example of this emerged from the 2025 SCO Summit in Tianjin, where a photo op between Modi, China’s Xi Jinping, and Russia’s Vladimir Putin gave India an opportunity to show that it had options. However, the fact that China continues to be India’s most important national security threat will limit the utility of these partnerships. The SCO cannot resolve these problems.
Still, in 25 years, the SCO has evolved from having a narrow Central Asia border security focus to become a wider regional institution. Beijing and Moscow’s use of the SCO to speak the language of multipolarity has found certain appeal among Global South countries seeking alternatives to Western-led architectures. But this message is clouded as the two repeatedly violate the U.N. Charter by taking unilateral actions against their neighbors, exhibiting little respect for international law. Many in the Global South may ignore such violations, but the hypocrisy tends to accumulate and undermine the legitimacy of such messaging. Moreover, countries such as India don’t want the SCO to become such an anti-Western grouping.
One area where the SCO is progressing is in intra-group trade, though it’s unclear if the organization itself was responsible for this. This is also primarily driven by China-Russia and China-India bilateral trade. By some estimates, intra-SCO trade in 2024 was worth $725 billion , up from $463 billion in 2021. The initiative to establish an SCO Development Bank, which the members agreed to in principle at the 2025 Summit, would further strengthen Beijing’s efforts to shape a new economic architecture, potentially as “China’s answer to Western financial hegemony.” China has been pushing this since 2010 with the goal of expanding the global footprint of the Chinese yuan and emerging as an alternative to Western-led post-Bretton Wood institutions.
But even here, there are problems. The SCO Bank initiative itself is not without its frictions and fears. Russia is a reluctant supporter because of Moscow’s fear of Chinese economic dominance in Central Asia, traditionally Russia’s backyard. India has also remained skeptical of the bank because it would enhance China’s regional dominance. In fact, this has been an issue since the SCO began. While China wanted it to be a regional economic grouping, Russia made every effort to shape it as a security bloc precisely due to a fear of Chinese dominance. Furthermore, India works closely with Western financial institutions and is against the idea of making the SCO into an anti-Western bloc driven by China and Russia.
The SCO faces an uncertain future. Its key members fear each other at least as much as they need each other, and the reasons they need each other are themselves varied. There is no acknowledged leader to the group either, despite China’s material dominance. This isn’t a solid foundation for any ambitious structure, but it may survive because none of the major partners can afford to abandon it.
This article was originally published in ASPI’s The Strategist.

====================================================================================================

Fossil feet may be misleading scientists about human evolution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
12:38:26 UTC
21:38:26 KST

Fossil feet may be misleading scientists about human evolution
Surprisingly agile monkeys are forcing scientists to rethink how the ancient ancestor of humans and chimpanzees may have climbed through the trees.
- Date:
- August 31, 2026
- Source:
- Ohio State University
- Summary:
- Wild monkeys in West Africa can climb vertical tree trunks using foot flexibility scientists did not realize they possessed. The discovery challenges a key assumption about what the last common ancestor of humans and chimpanzees looked like and how it moved.
- Share:
New research suggests that whatever scientists ultimately discover about the last common ancestor of humans and chimpanzees, one characteristic may be difficult to dispute: it was probably capable of climbing trees.
Humans and chimpanzees went their separate evolutionary ways between 6 and 7 million years ago, when they diverged from the last common ancestor (LCA) they once shared. Reconstructing that ancestor has become an important part of understanding human evolution, including the emergence of walking on two legs.
One major question concerns where and how the LCA moved through forests. Did it spend much of its time among high horizontal branches, climb vertically from the ground, or combine both behaviors?
Rethinking What Feet Reveal About Climbing
Chimpanzees are highly capable tree trunk climbers, aided by ankles that can flex much farther than human ankles. Monkeys, by contrast, have often been viewed as relying more heavily on their arms to move through trees. That distinction has influenced ideas about whether the human-chimpanzee ancestor should have possessed feet more like those of modern apes or monkeys.
New video evidence from West Africa is challenging that assumption.
Researchers from The Ohio State University studied wild sooty mangabey monkeys, whose feet do not have the same highly flexible ankles found in chimpanzees. Detailed observations and measurements showed that the monkeys can nevertheless bend parts of their feet enough to climb narrow vertical tree trunks while seeking food, hiding or finding places to sleep.
"People are making behavioral inferences from fossils, and some say a monkey can't vertically climb as well as an ape can," said first study author Luke Fannin, assistant professor of anthropology at Ohio State. "We're saying there's a functional equivalence here. So you can't rule out vertical climbing just because something doesn't have a chimpanzee-like foot."
The research appears this week in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.
A New Clue to Human Evolution
Determining what the LCA looked like and how it moved could help researchers understand the evolutionary steps that eventually produced habitual bipedalism, a form of movement practiced regularly only by humans.
Humans are apes, but the new findings suggest that an ancestor with feet resembling those of monkeys might still have been capable of climbing in ways comparable to modern apes.
"Part of paleoanthropology is understanding how our evolution happened, and it's often through the hallmark of how we move because modern humans move quite differently than our cousins, the chimpanzees, do, and they're the living primate we're most closely related to," Fannin said. "And we're trying to understand why that is."
Fannin collected video of wild mangabeys at the Taï Forest Monkey Project field station in Ivory Coast. The project is co-directed by W. Scott McGraw, professor and chair of anthropology at Ohio State and senior author of the study.
"The great thing about having the video is that it allows us to capture exactly what the monkey is doing in a high-resolution manner. So we can actually say how the joint is loaded. Before, we had hunches, but in this way, it's far more precise," McGraw said.
Monkeys Show Unexpected Foot Flexibility
During a tree climb, a chimpanzee ankle can flex upward by about 45 degrees. Most human ankles, in comparison, can flex by roughly 20 degrees.
The mangabeys achieved something surprisingly similar through a different part of the foot. Fannin measured as much as 46 degrees of flexion in the animals' midfoot while they climbed vertically.
That finding complicates competing ideas about how the LCA traveled through forest environments. Some theories have suggested that an ape-like foot was necessary for effective vertical climbing, while others allow for an ancestor with a more monkey-like foot.
"What's neat about this paper is it adds clarity, but it also makes the broader picture more fuzzy," McGraw said. "Because this notion that you have to have a foot like an advanced ape to vertically climb, which is a difficult task, is not true. You've got a bunch of monkeys that aren't extinct - and which can be filmed - that are very competent at performing a biomechanically challenging behavior right now in a forest in West Africa.
"The videos that Luke made in Taï are particularly important because they provide some of the first kinematic documentation of a locomotor behavior in a monkey that has largely been unrecognized or underappreciated."
Humans Still Carry a Connection to Trees
Vertical climbing is not limited to nonhuman primates. Some modern hunter-gatherers and human foragers are also highly capable climbers. In humans, however, that ability is thought to depend more heavily on flexible ligaments, tendons, and muscles than on the structure of the foot bones.
Fannin and McGraw also point out that although walking on two feet is one of the defining characteristics of modern humans, climbing remains part of human behavior. Our tendency to ascend and reach higher places may reflect a deep ancestral relationship with trees that extends beyond anatomy alone.
"Arboreality is fundamental to understanding primates - including ourselves - because it has shaped our body to a large degree: hands and feet, wrists and ankles, nails instead of claws, etc.," McGraw said.
Added Fannin, "Regardless of where you're starting from, which we don't know yet, vertical climbing is universal, and the anatomy is going to perform that behavior. So I think that to get at the question of a monkey-like or ape-like last common ancestor, we need more fossils."
The research was supported by Dartmouth College, the Explorer's Club, the U.S. National Science Foundation, the Emory National Primate Research Center, the Primate Society of Great Britain and a Schmidt Sciences Postdoctoral Fellowship.
Former Ohio State undergraduate Carmen Pape was also a co-author.

Russia Says Its Secret Laser Has Downed Hundreds of Ukrainian Drones—No One Has Verified It
Unknown

Russia Says Its Secret Laser Has Downed Hundreds of Ukrainian Drones—No One Has Verified It
Footage circulating across Russian pro-military channels appears to show a Russian laser weapon engaging aerial drones, with military bloggers claiming several of the systems are already protecting strategic facilities in southwestern Russia, Defence Blog reported on August 31.
The claims have not been independently verified, and neither Russia’s Defense Ministry nor another government agency has publicly confirmed the system’s reported combat record.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
One Russian military blogger described the footage as an “exclusive” and claimed the laser systems had already destroyed several hundred Ukrainian drones.
“Only we have sensational footage of the destruction of Ukrainian drones in the sky by a combat Russian laser complex,” the blogger wrote. “Several of these laser installations now cover our strategic facilities in the southwest of the country.”
Based on the available footage, the weapon appears to be built around a containerized platform combining a directed-energy laser, targeting and guidance equipment, and a separate command post from which an operator controls the system.
The complex also appears to include its own detection equipment for locating and tracking aerial threats, reportedly combining radar and optical sensors.
Russian sources have not publicly disclosed the system’s official designation, power output, effective engagement range or manufacturer.
The blogger also claimed developers are already working on a second-generation version intended to engage substantially faster targets, potentially including tactical aircraft and cruise missiles.
That capability has not been independently demonstrated.
“I am not inclined to overestimate this innovative type of weapon based on ‘new physical principles,’ but combined with traditional air defense systems, a combat laser will definitely be useful for protecting the country from air raids,” the blogger wrote.
“It is also gratifying that we not only have such combat ‘purple beams,’ but they have also proven their effectiveness. Now these ‘Jedi swords’ need to be developed and constantly improved. Such is the path.”
Directed-energy weapons have attracted growing interest from militaries around the world as a potential lower-cost answer to increasingly large drone attacks.
Unlike conventional air defense systems, which expend missiles or ammunition with every engagement, a laser can theoretically continue firing as long as sufficient electrical power and cooling are available.
That makes the technology particularly attractive for countering relatively inexpensive drones, where using costly surface-to-air missiles can quickly become economically unsustainable.
But laser weapons also face significant practical limitations.
Heavy rain, fog, dust, smoke and other atmospheric conditions can weaken or scatter a laser beam, reducing its effectiveness. Longer engagement distances also increase the impact of atmospheric interference.
Sustained firing creates another challenge because high-powered lasers generate substantial heat, requiring sophisticated cooling and power-management systems.
Earlier, Russia’s top business lobby appealed directly to Russian leader Vladimir Putin for heavy weaponry, electronic warfare systems, and dedicated military reservists to protect private industrial facilities.

Ukraine Turns Kinburn Spit Into a Trap for 2,500 Russian Troops

Ukraine Turns Kinburn Spit Into a Trap for 2,500 Russian Troops
Ukrainian forces have largely isolated Russian troops on the temporarily occupied Kinburn Spit, disrupting supply routes and destroying the artillery previously deployed there, Ukrainian military personnel told Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty’s Crimea.Realities project on August 31.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Around 2,500 Russian troops remain on the Kinburn Peninsula, according to the Ukrainian servicemen interviewed by Crimea.Realities. Drone strikes and remote mining have reportedly restricted deliveries of ammunition, fuel, and food, while much of the Russian force has shifted farther east beyond the village of Heroiske.
A Ukrainian reconnaissance commander with the call sign “Yava” said Russian logistics previously ran from the direction of Zaliznyi Port toward Heroiske before supplies were moved deeper onto the peninsula.
“They are screaming in intercepted communications that they cannot organize logistics, that they do not want to go there because it means death,” Yava told Crimea.Realities. “The spit has become a trap for them,” he added.
Ukrainian troops said Russian forces had previously operated artillery, self-propelled guns, and other equipment directly from the Kinburn Spit, but systematic strikes have eliminated most of that capability.
According to Yava, Russian forces can now reach coastal areas of Ukraine’s Mykolaiv region only with longer-range artillery positioned in the temporarily occupied part of Kherson region.
Ukrainian units have also remotely mined roads used for Russian rotations and supply runs, targeting cars, motorcycles, and quad bikes carrying personnel and equipment.
The operation is complicated by the continued presence of civilians. Ukrainian servicemen told Crimea.Realities that Russian troops sometimes wear civilian clothing and operate from residential buildings, requiring Ukrainian forces to confirm targets before striking.
The Kinburn Peninsula lies between the Black Sea and the Dnipro-Buh estuary, directly opposite the Ukrainian-controlled city of Ochakiv. Russian forces have occupied the area since 2022, placing them close to Ukraine’s Mykolaiv region and the Odesa-Mykolaiv transport corridor.
In November 2025, Ukrainian Navy spokesperson Dmytro Pletenchuk said the protected coastal ecosystem had been “practically destroyed” by fighting, fires, pollution, and the construction of military infrastructure.

Masked Intruder Seen at Polish Drone Plant Supplying Ukraine Before Fire Breaks Out
A fire broke out overnight at a WB Electronics facility in Skarżysko-Kamienna, Poland, which produces components for unmanned systems used by the Polish and Ukrainian militaries, with authorities investigating possible arson after surveillance footage reportedly showed a masked person entering the site.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Onet on August 31, the fire started at around 12:23 a.m. on August 31 in a production building at the facility. Shortly afterward, a security operator alerted police after an intrusion sensor was triggered on the premises.
Surveillance cameras recorded an unidentified person wearing a balaclava entering the WB Electronics site by crossing the perimeter fence, Onet reported. A backpack and a sweatshirt were later found near the facility.
Police officers, a search dog team, and a drone equipped with thermal imaging technology were deployed to the area. Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW) and Military Counterintelligence Service were also notified and became involved in the response.
Authorities have not determined the cause of the fire and are considering arson among the possible scenarios. “We are treating this matter extremely seriously,” a spokesperson for Poland’s intelligence services coordinator said, according to Onet.
Five firefighting crews responded to the incident and extinguished the blaze. The facility was not operating when the fire began, and no injuries were reported. The affected site produces pump systems used in unmanned aerial vehicles and unmanned ground platforms.
WB Electronics is the core company of WB Group, Poland’s largest privately owned defense group. The company develops and manufactures several unmanned systems, including the FlyEye and FT-5 reconnaissance drones as well as the Warmate and Gladius strike systems.
WB Group systems have been supplied to both Poland and Ukraine, with FlyEye reconnaissance drones and Warmate loitering munitions among the company’s platforms used by Ukrainian forces.
Poland has been strengthening its defenses amid concerns over potential Russian provocations. On August 17, Polish Deputy Defense Minister Cezary Tomczyk said Warsaw was preparing for the possibility of war and warned that a large-scale Kremlin provocation could occur “within a few months.”

Japan’s Record 2027 Defense Budget Request Is Only the Opening Bid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
12:32:00 UTC
21:32:00 KST

Japan’s Ministry of Defense on August 31 submitted a record fiscal year 2027 budget request of roughly 8.9 trillion yen ($55.5 billion). But the headline figure tells only part of the story.
At a media briefing three days before the announcement, Defense Ministry officials said around 160 entries in the request were marked as “item requests” (jiko yokyu), for which no specific funding amount has yet been assigned. The reason is that Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae’s government plans to revise Japan’s three key security documents – the National Security Strategy, National Defense Strategy, and Defense Buildup Program – by the end of 2026. Even procurement quantities for some major equipment could change as part of that review.
The 8.9 trillion yen figure should therefore be seen less as a final price tag than as an opening bid. The budget request will be sent to the Finance Ministry for consideration before a decision is made in late December. The fiscal 2027 budget is set to mark a 15th consecutive annual increase and a 13th consecutive record high, with the final figure widely expected to exceed 10 trillion yen for the first time.
Fiscal year (FY) 2027 is the final year of Japan’s current five-year Defense Buildup Program, which set total defense spending at roughly 43 trillion yen from FY2023 through 2027. But ministry officials said the security environment has changed with greater speed and complexity than anticipated when the current documents were drafted. The request is therefore not simply about completing the existing buildup. It is a bridge to the next phase of Japan’s defense transformation.
The ministry organized the request around three main pillars and nine priority areas. The first, adapting to “new ways of warfare,” covers AI, unmanned systems, stand-off capabilities, integrated air and missile defense, space, and cyber. The second focuses on sustained response capabilities, including Pacific and sea-lane defense, while the third centers on the foundations of defense, including the defense industrial and technological base and personnel.
Artificial intelligence and unmanned systems are central to that transformation. The ministry plans an AI-based decision-support system for the Self-Defense Forces’ (SDF) Joint Operations Command, together with a next-generation AI platform and secure cloud infrastructure. The request also includes UAVs for intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance, and targeting, attack UAVs, small unmanned ground vehicles, and research into a stand-off missile launch module for unmanned underwater vehicles.
Another major investment is Japan’s next-generation fighter, which is being jointly developed with the United Kingdom and Italy under the Global Combat Air Program (GCAP). The ministry’s Acquisition, Technology, and Logistics Agency (ATLA) requested 234 billion yen ($1.5 billion), plus an item request, to push ahead with the fighter program. The funding will support Japan’s contribution to the GCAP International Government Organization (GIGO), joint design work, and the maturation of technologies Japan is developing independently.
ATLA also requested 9.7 billion yen ($61 million), plus an item request, to accelerate research and development of collaborative unmanned aircraft equipped with deception and electronic warfare capabilities and capable of autonomous decision-making while operating alongside the next-generation fighter.
The emphasis on cost and quantity is particularly evident in Japan’s expanding stand-off capabilities. Alongside sophisticated domestically developed missiles, the ministry plans to develop lower-cost stand-off missiles at home while acquiring foreign-made weapons to obtain the capability more quickly. Officials cited U.S. defense company Anduril Industries’ Barracuda as one system under consideration for a concept involving lower-cost stand-off weapons released from transport aircraft.
In effect, the concept amounts to a high-low mix. Lower-cost weapons could complement more sophisticated missiles, allowing Japan to field greater numbers of weapons, while transport aircraft would diversify its launch platforms.
The ministry also plans to begin development of an underwater-launched hypersonic guided missile, exploiting the greater survivability of underwater platforms.
A similar cost-exchange problem is shaping Japan’s defenses. The ministry plans to develop a Ground Self-Defense Force Close-Range Air Defense System, or CRADS, combining guided missiles, an autocannon, and lasers to counter various airborne threats, including low-cost drones that can be fielded in large numbers. Japan is separately pursuing high-power microwave technology against UAVs and expanding the use of decoys.
The underlying lesson is that quantity matters again. Japan is moving toward a mix of high-end and lower-cost systems on both sides of the offense-defense equation.
Staying power runs through the request as well. With Russia’s invasion of Ukraine now in its fifth year, the ministry argues that the ability to sustain a prolonged conflict is itself important for deterrence. The request places greater emphasis on ammunition and guided missiles, fuel, food, transportation, and logistics, while also studying the introduction of transport vessels equipped with autonomous navigation technologies.
Against the backdrop of increased Chinese carrier operations in the Pacific and flights by Chinese and Russian bombers, Japan is also placing new emphasis on Pacific sea-lane defense. The ministry requested 292.2 billion yen ($1.8 billion), plus an item request, to acquire 17 MQ-9B SeaGuardian UAVs. The request also includes further modifications to the Izumo-class destroyers, surveillance facilities on Kitadaito Island in Okinawa Prefecture, and a study of cargo-handling facilities on Iwo To to improve maritime transport.
The ministry sums up its approach to the defense industrial base with a striking phrase: “production capacity itself is deterrence.” The government plans to strengthen domestic production and technology, promote equipment transfers and innovation, and establish a new government-backed organization to reinforce the defense industrial base.
The challenge is financial as much as technological. Officials said the request was calculated at 149 yen to the dollar, compared with the 108 yen benchmark used when the current five-year buildup plan was drawn up in 2022. They acknowledged that the weaker yen has raised the cost of imported equipment and foreign-made components, eroding Japan’s purchasing power.
Taken together, the FY2027 request points toward an SDF that will be more unmanned, more networked, more reliant on stand-off weapons, better prepared for mass attacks, and more closely supported by Japan’s industrial base. But with around 160 entries still unpriced – including programs central to Japan’s future defense posture – the biggest question remains unanswered: How much will this transformation actually cost?

Freed Hongkonger sent back to jail as storm delays deportation from Philippines
Lawyer says Tang Lung-wai’s return to maximum-security prison constitutes ‘illegal detention’ after severe weather halts deportation
A Hong Kong man has been returned to a Philippine prison in what his legal team condemned as “illegal detention”, after severe weather halted his deportation following his release.
Tang Lung-wai’s Philippine lawyer, Blessie Rose Carpena, told the South China Morning Post that prison authorities escorted Tang to the Bureau of Immigration last Friday.
However, because government offices were suspended due to a passing typhoon, he was returned to the maximum-security New Bilibid Prison in Muntinlupa.
“[The Bureau of Immigration’s] delay of his release can constitute illegal detention,” Carpena said, describing Tang as “frustrated and devastated.”
Tang was arrested in the Philippines in July 2000 for possessing methamphetamine, also known as ice, and sentenced to 40 years in prison in 2011. He has maintained his innocence and fought the conviction for more than two decades.
In late July, a Manila court ruled that Tang’s sentence was fully served after factoring in good conduct time allowances, ordering his immediate release and deportation.

Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan hold first Mecca Defense Agreement meeting as more countries eye joining pact
Unknown

- Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan hold first Mecca Defense Agreement meeting as more countries eye joining pact
Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan hold first Mecca Defense Agreement meeting as more countries eye joining pact
Pakistan's Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said over the weekend in the UK that six to seven Muslim-majority countries have expressed interest in joining the pact
Top officials from Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan gathered in Istanbul on Monday for the inaugural meeting of the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, signed August 7. Ahead of the meeting, Pakistan said several countries have already shown interest in joining the defense pact.
Pakistan's Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said over the weekend in the UK that six to seven Muslim-majority countries have expressed interest in joining the pact, without naming them, adding that officials are working on a framework to make accession easier. Bangladesh has been the latest country to signal openness to joining. At the same time, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan said earlier this month the pact could expand to include other regional states, like Egypt.
The pact stipulates that an armed attack against any of the three countries will be regarded as an attack against all, similar to NATO's Article 5 collective defense clause.
Following the meeting, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan described the Mecca Defense Agreement as complementary to NATO rather than a rival framework. "The Mecca Alliance is a historic step based on the principle of defense and complementing NATO," Fidan said. "We have taken practical steps to build a practical security structure in the region, and we are working on a roadmap for other countries to join the alliance."
Fidan also directed sharp criticism at Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, accusing him of prolonging regional conflict. "This criminal, Netanyahu, who takes pleasure in shedding Palestinian blood and Muslim blood, must now be stopped," Fidan said, adding that Netanyahu's approach was causing "immense harm to Israel, to Palestine, and to the entire region."
The Turkish Foreign Minister also said Netanyahu's statements made clear he opposes the establishment of a Palestinian state and does not intend to relinquish "ongoing occupations in countries across the region," calling it evidence Netanyahu wants a "genocidal and occupying approach" to continue. "This is no longer a threat only to us; it is a major threat to the entire region and to the international community," Fidan said, calling on "the international system" to confront what he described as the threat posed by Netanyahu.
Suggested articles
The agreement brings together three Sunni Muslim US allies concerned by the ongoing Iran war and the broader regional conflict, which has included Iranian missile fire on Gulf oil exporters. Six months into the war, negotiations remain at an impasse, and the Trump administration has escalated financial pressure on Tehran through what it has called an "economic D-Day."
Turkey, which fields NATO's second-largest military, has said the pact with nuclear-armed Pakistan and top oil exporter Saudi Arabia is open to further expansion and is not intended to replace existing alliances. President Trump praised the agreement, calling it a bold first step that allows nations to defend themselves.

Rehabilitation and support for a child in the first years of life: what services can be received free of charge
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
15:26:23 EEST
21:26:23 KST

Rehabilitation and support for a child in the first years of life: what services can be received free of charge
Kyiv • UNN
Prematurely born and ill infants can receive rehabilitation free of charge under the Medical Guarantees Programme. Services are available until the age of three with a referral.
For children born prematurely, as well as children with congenital conditions, the state has provided the opportunity to receive free rehabilitation tailored to individual needs, UNN writes.
Rehabilitation for young patients is paid for by the state under the Medical Guarantees Programme. Rehabilitation care may be provided on an outpatient or inpatient basis and/or at the child’s place of residence. Services can be received regardless of the child’s place of registration or residence, the National Health Service of Ukraine explains.
According to the NHSU, in 2026, under the package "Medical rehabilitation of infants born prematurely and/or ill during the first three years of life," 13.39 thousand patients across Ukraine received medical care.
What the infant rehabilitation package provides for
Care begins with an initial examination and consultations with specialists from a multidisciplinary rehabilitation team. According to the NHSU, a comprehensive functional assessment is carried out using international standardised scales, tests and questionnaires; the child’s development is assessed and, where necessary, screening is conducted to identify signs of autism spectrum disorders.
Based on the assessment results, an individual rehabilitation plan is developed, defining goals for the child and the family. The team subsequently regularly assesses progress and, in accordance with changes in the child’s functional status, adjusts the plan and determines the further rehabilitation pathway.
The package includes the necessary laboratory and instrumental examinations, in accordance with medical needs and sectoral standards. The child may also receive consultations with doctors of other specialties, depending on their condition and diagnosis; pain assessment and timely pain relief when indicated; as well as assessment of nutritional status and its correction in case of disorders.
Rehabilitation also includes support for parents
Services are provided by specialists from a multidisciplinary rehabilitation team. Depending on the child’s needs, the care team may include doctors of physical and rehabilitation medicine, paediatricians, paediatric neurologists, physical therapists, occupational therapists, psychologists, speech and language therapists, nurses and other specialists.
An important part of the care is working with the family. Parents are provided with information about the specifics of caring for the child, the child’s development, preventing possible complications and following the rehabilitation team’s recommendations. Psychological support for parents is also provided.
If necessary, specialists select and adjust assistive rehabilitation devices and teach the family how to use them in the child’s natural environment. If the child requires specialised medical care at another facility, the team arranges the appropriate referral.
How to receive care
The basis for receiving services under this package is a referral from a primary care doctor selected under a declaration, a referral from the attending physician, or a transfer from another healthcare facility.
Services under the package are free of charge for the patient, provided they are received at a facility that has the relevant contract with the NHSU.
For example, as UNN reported, such services are provided at the Kyiv Perinatal Centre. Since 2020, specialised early-intervention spaces have operated at this facility, where infants receive qualified care from the first days of life. Follow-up monitoring and medical rehabilitation for infants are also provided there. As the Kyiv Perinatal Centre told UNN, during the past year alone, 279 infants successfully completed individual rehabilitation programmes.

Nearly all Wang Fuk Court owners accept buy-out, leaving 17 holdouts as offer ends
17 of 1,984 Wang Fuk Court owners fail to accept offer as deadline ends, facing compulsory acquisition at lower compensation levels
More than 99 per cent of homeowners at Hong Kong’s fire-ravaged Wang Fuk Court have accepted a government buy-out of their flats, leaving just 17 households facing potential compulsory acquisition after the scheme closed on Monday.
By the cut‑off time at 5pm on Monday, 1,967 or 99.1 per cent of the estate’s 1,984 flat owners had returned acceptance letters. The remaining 17 may face compulsory acquisition at lower compensation levels in the future.
Among those who accepted, 1,559, or 78.6 per cent, have signed formal sale and purchase agreements with the government.
“The government will continue to follow up on the procedures for acquiring the remaining titles at full speed to take forward the title acquisition exercise” it said on Monday.
The HK$6.8 billion (US$867.24 million) scheme was announced in February after a fire tore through seven blocks of the Tai Po estate last November, killing 168 people and displacing about 5,000 residents in Hong Kong’s deadliest blaze in more than seven decades.
In June, the government extended the buy-back offer to Wang Chi House, the only block spared by the fire, adding another HK$1 billion to the scheme’s cost. Officials have ruled out on‑site redevelopment.
Under the scheme, the government is acquiring flats at HK$8,000 or HK$10,500 per square foot, depending on whether the owner has paid the land premium.

Geotechnical and structural engineers were scheduled to inspect the slope Monday. Chen said students could temporarily attend classes elsewhere if officials could not confirm the area was safe.
Chen made the comments during his final policy report and questioning session as Kaohsiung mayor. He thanked residents and city councilors for supporting the city government’s work over the past six years.

New U.S. Air Force Combat Rescue heli squadron activated
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
13:00:51 BST
21:00:51 KST

The United States Air Force has activated a new helicopter squadron at Joint Base Andrews for the first time in 60 years, beginning a transition that will introduce the HH-60W Jolly Green II alongside the base’s long-serving UH-1N Huey fleet.
The 5th Helicopter Squadron was formally activated on 27 August and will operate alongside the existing 1st Helicopter Squadron as the US Air Force brings the HH-60W into service for round-the-clock operations in the National Capital Region.
Until the activation, the 1st Helicopter Squadron had been the Air Force’s only rotary-wing unit in the National Capital Region for six decades.
Lieutenant Colonel Jonathan Bonilla, who became the first commander of the 5th Helicopter Squadron, said in the US Air Force release: “The vision is very straightforward. We aim to rapidly and safely integrate the HH-60W into the missions here in the National Capital Region and establish a premier rotary-wing organization that supports our nation’s most critical missions, without any pause in operations.”
During the next several years, the new squadron will train aircrew and maintainers, establish operational and maintenance procedures and begin receiving HH-60W aircraft. The 1st Helicopter Squadron will continue operating the UH-1N throughout the transition, maintaining the immediate-response mission and supporting daily operations while the new unit builds towards full operational capacity. The U.S. Air Force expects the 5th Helicopter Squadron to reach full operational capacity in 2030. Once the new squadron is able to carry out the mission fully with the HH-60W, the 1st Helicopter Squadron will begin its own transition from the UH-1N to the newer aircraft.
The HH-60W is intended to provide greater speed, range and carrying capacity than the UH-1N, according to the Air Force. The service also points to updated navigation, secure communications, weather equipment, sensors and survivability systems among the capabilities incorporated into the aircraft.
Colonel Kevin Geoffroy, commander of the 316th Operations Group and an HH-60W pilot, said: “The Huey has been part of this mission and this community for generations. Today, we are standing up the 5th Helicopter Squadron — a unit that inherits a proud, storied legacy. We will honor that legacy by delivering excellence as we modernize our fleet at Joint Base Andrews for the future.”
The 1st Helicopter Squadron has supported immediate-response contingency operations in the National Capital Region since 1969 and has flown the UH-1N since 1971. Three of the Hueys currently serving with the unit also flew during the Vietnam War, according to the Air Force. The squadron’s duties include maintaining a continuous response capability for national security requirements while conducting training to keep crews ready for contingency operations.
Lieutenant Colonel Zachary Minner, commander of the 1st Helicopter Squadron, said in the release: “Our 24/7 mission continues while we prepare the next generation of Airmen and aircraft to continue the legacy of excellence. The incredible professionals of the 1st Helicopter Squadron are ready to respond whenever the National Capital Region needs us.”
The HH-60W was developed as the US Air Force’s new combat rescue helicopter and is based on the Sikorsky H-60 family. At Andrews, the aircraft will be used for the National Capital Region mission rather than being limited to its combat rescue role. The Air Force said the type can also support civil search and rescue, medical evacuation, disaster response, humanitarian assistance and rescue command-and-control missions.
The new squadron takes its lineage and heraldry from the 5th Emergency Rescue Squadron, which operated between 1944 and 1956. That unit’s history included early helicopter operations. In 1946, Lieutenant Wilton Bowman flew a YR-5 past Andrews while travelling to a nearby air show, an aircraft that Airmen at the time reportedly described as a “whirling oddity”.
The 5th Helicopter Squadron will now spend the period to 2030 building its personnel, maintenance structure and HH-60W fleet while the 1st Helicopter Squadron continues the existing UH-1N mission in parallel.
