Researchers identify a simple way to soften deep political divides
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
12:00:17 UTC
21:00:17 KST

Consuming news from political or religious groups outside of one’s own circle may help soften exaggerated beliefs about how much those groups dislike you. New research provides evidence that watching or reading outgroup media is linked to feeling a greater sense of connection to those individuals, which in turn is associated with assuming they view your group more favorably. The findings were published in Political Psychology.
People often possess exaggerated meta-perceptions, which are beliefs about how another group views their own group. Specifically, individuals tend to overestimate how much the opposing side dislikes them, known as meta-prejudice, and how much the other side views them as unevolved or uncivilized, known as meta-dehumanization. For example, a 2021 study covered by PsyPost indicated that both Democrats and Republicans drastically overestimate the extent to which the opposing political party dehumanizes and holds prejudice against them.
These exaggerated assumptions can fuel real-world hostility. A 2019 set of experiments and surveys found that when people overestimate outgroup negativity, they are more likely to believe the opposing side is motivated by purposeful obstructionism. Correcting these false impressions is an important step in reducing political and social animosity.
“This project stemmed from a recent study which found that Americans have substantially exaggerated perceptions of what the other political group thinks about them,” said Muhammad Ehab Rasul, a research fellow at the Centre for Trusted Internet and Community at the National University of Singapore. “One aspect that really drove us to explore this topic was to understand what is driving these erroneous meta-perceptions, and if there is a way to create more positive meta-perceptions.”
News media consumption plays a major role in shaping these impressions. The researchers wanted to know if traditional news sources could act as a form of mediated contact, helping people form one-sided feelings of familiarity and intimacy with the opposing group, a concept known as a political parasocial relationship. They suspected that these media-driven connections might help correct harsh meta-perceptions, though they noted that outgroup exposure does not always have a positive effect. In fact, a 2018 field experiment found that paying people to follow opposing political views on social media actually increased their political polarization.
“Today, partisan sorting is becoming increasingly common, meaning that people do not have as much direct interaction with those with opposing views than in previous decades,” said Samantha Moore-Berg, an assistant professor of psychology at the University of Utah. “Yet one way that partisans increasingly can access the other side’s perspectives is through the media.”
The research, led by Rasul and Moore-Berg, examined this dynamic across three studies in the United States and Israel. In the first study, the team surveyed 2,707 American adults, measuring how often participants consumed liberal and conservative news media. The researchers asked the participants to guess how warmly the opposing political party felt about them and how evolved the other party considered them to be.
The authors found that consuming news from the opposing political side was generally associated with reduced negative assumptions. For Republicans, watching or reading more liberal news was linked to lower meta-prejudice and lower meta-dehumanization. For Democrats, higher exposure to conservative news was associated with lower meta-prejudice. Interestingly, when Republicans consumed more conservative news, they tended to report higher meta-dehumanization, suggesting that sticking entirely to ingroup media might worsen some negative assumptions.
“Contrary to initial predictions, we found that exposure to outgroup partisan news is associated with more positive meta-perceptions,” Moore-Berg told PsyPost. “Initially, we expected the opposite pattern, as the media often focuses on negative portrayals of outgroup members.”
At the same time, viewing one’s own party’s news did not universally deepen hostility. “One thing that was interesting is that we did not find significant associations between ingroup news media consumption and meta-perceptions,” Rasul noted. “It is expected that this type of exposure should result in more extreme attitudes and meta-perceptions. However, we do not observe these effects in our findings.”
The scientists then tested whether this pattern would hold in a society where the two groups have a vast power imbalance and different levels of media access. The second study involved 969 Jewish adults in Israel, split between secular and ultra-Orthodox individuals. Participants reported their exposure to mainstream secular news and to specific ultra-Orthodox news outlets.
The team’s diverse background proved essential for this phase of the research. “Our researcher composition played a significant role in access to hard-to-reach study populations, such as the ultra-Orthodox participant group in Study 2, and helped us think about the role of the media in intergroup relations,” Moore-Berg said.
Exposure to ultra-Orthodox news was associated with lower meta-prejudice and lower meta-dehumanization for both secular and ultra-Orthodox participants. The relationship between secular news and meta-perceptions was not statistically significant for either group. The researchers suggest that because secular media is the mainstream default, extra exposure to it does little to change the entrenched views of ultra-Orthodox individuals, who often feel stigmatized by those outlets.
“The finding that outgroup news media is associated with lower meta-perceptions of prejudice and dehumanization is stronger and more stable for groups with equal status and power,” Rasul explained. “Our findings suggest that the link between outgroup news media exposure and meta-perceptions of prejudice and dehumanization is stronger and consistent among Democrats and Republicans, but inconsistent among secular and ultra-Orthodox Jews.”
In a final study of 761 American adults, the researchers explored the psychological mechanism behind these media effects. Alongside measuring news habits and meta-perceptions, they asked participants how much they felt a sense of belonging or connection when watching members of the opposing political party on the news.
As in the first study, Democrats who consumed more conservative news reported lower meta-prejudice. More importantly, the data indicated that exposure to outgroup news was linked to a stronger political parasocial relationship. This heightened sense of imagined connection with the opposing group was, in turn, associated with less extreme assumptions about how much the outgroup disliked or dehumanized them.
“The key takeaway from our findings is that consuming the ‘other’ side’s media can be a way to lower the misperceptions we hold about other groups,” Rasul said. “This may occur as we realize that the other side’s perceptions about us are not as extreme as we may believe.”
Moore-Berg pointed out that this benefit extends beyond a single context. “Our results showed that increased exposure to outgroup media was associated with more positive meta-perceptions for both partisans in the U.S. and religious groups in Israel,” she said. “Media may be a cross-group solution to reducing negative meta-perceptions.”
The cross-sectional nature of the data means the authors cannot confirm that watching outgroup news directly causes people to soften their assumptions. It is entirely possible that individuals who already assume the best about their political opponents are simply more willing to tune into outgroup media channels. Tracking news habits over a long period or assigning participants to watch specific networks would help clarify the exact direction of this relationship.
“These associations could be due to selection effects—partisans who are initially more willing to watch outgroup media might have more positive meta-perceptions to start—or could be due to media exposure,” Moore-Berg explained.
The reliance on self-reported media consumption also presents a challenge, as people do not always accurately remember or admit how much partisan news they watch. Additionally, the specific political climate during each survey might have influenced the responses. The first study took place early in the COVID-19 pandemic, a time of unique media habits and shared external threats, which might explain why its results differed slightly from the third study conducted a few years later.
The researchers also noted that their measures did not capture the nuance of what participants were watching. “We only examined general media exposure rather than the specific content within the media that participants consumed,” Moore-Berg added.
Looking ahead, the team hopes to pinpoint the mechanisms driving these results and explore alternative platforms. “It could be that exposure to outgroup views via TikTok, for instance, may affect meta-perceptions differently than say exposure to CNBC or Fox News,” Moore-Berg said.
Rasul hopes these insights can eventually inform broadcasting practices to lower intergroup hostility. “One of the key implications of our study is that media outlets should aim to portray more moderate views of individuals with different religious and political backgrounds and avoid airing extreme opinions,” he concluded.
The study, “The role of partisan news and political parasocial relationships in shaping meta-perceptions: Cross-national evidence,” was authored by Muhammad Ehab Rasul, Boaz Hameiri, Gila Hacohen, Nechumi Malovicki-Yaffe, and Samantha L. Moore-Berg.

Beijing has hit out at Tokyo’s moves to arm submarine drones with long-range missiles and test hypersonic weapons in Australia
China’s defence ministry spokesman Zhang Xiaogang highlighted the two initiatives on Thursday, saying Japan had “openly expanded its military arsenal”.
Zhang said the “dangerous” moves had a “striking resemblance” to Japan’s pre-World War II militarisation, though he did not explain why these particular weapon programmes could pose challenges for the PLA.

SC agrees to hear Centre's plea
NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Monday agreed to hear on Tuesday a plea filed by the Centre seeking to quash FIRs registered against students who participated in protests over the NEET examination paper leak.A bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana took note of Solicitor General Tushar Mehta’s submission seeking an urgent hearing. As the bench was about to rise after the day’s proceedings, Mehta said, “We want to move an IA (interlocutory application). It’s regarding that protest for quashing of FIRs... We are invoking Article 142 (of the Constitution).”
The bench observed that if the parties were reconciling the matter, it had no objection and agreed to list it for hearing on Tuesday.SC had earlier allowed withdrawal of eligible FIRsThe Supreme Court had earlier directed that state governments were at liberty to withdraw FIRs registered against protesters involved in the nationwide demonstrations over the NEET paper leak. The court, however, clarified that those accused of grave and heinous offences would not be covered by such relief.
The latest development comes as the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has called for a protest march in Delhi on September 5, accusing the Centre of failing to honour assurances made on July 25 that had led the group to withdraw its 36-day agitation over examination irregularities.
According to the CJP, the march will be led by families of students who died by suicide following the cancellation of the NEET exam and subsequent re-test, as well as those who were allegedly subjected to police excesses during the July agitation.

Donbasification: How Russia Manufactured an Identity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

I come from Sloviansk, in Ukraine’s Donetsk region.
For anyone who has followed Russia’s war against Ukraine since 2014, the name will probably be familiar. Sloviansk was where armed men led by Russian citizen and former FSB officer Igor Girkin seized government buildings in April 2014, and where one of the first major battles of Russia’s war in eastern Ukraine unfolded.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
And yet, more than twelve years later, I still regularly encounter versions of the same story: “that something happened in Donbas in 2014 because the people there were fundamentally different from the rest of Ukraine; that Ukraine somehow fractured naturally between a Russian-speaking East and a Ukrainian-speaking West; that an internal conflict erupted and Russia subsequently became involved.”
For somebody from the region, it is difficult to overstate how profoundly misleading that narrative is.
I also had an unusual vantage point from which to watch the mythology behind it develop. While I grew up in the Donetsk region, part of my family comes from the Lviv region, and I spent considerable parts of my childhood travelling between the two. East and West. The two “Ukraines” we were repeatedly told existed.
I saw differences, of course. Ukraine is a large country. Its regions have different histories, accents, traditions, economic structures and experiences of the Soviet period – all of that is normal. But I also saw something else: how genuine regional differences could be exaggerated, manipulated and eventually transformed into supposed incompatibilities.
Poland Joins US Drone-Warfare Drills Built on Ukraine’s Battlefield Lessons
For decades, Ukrainians were encouraged to see one another through caricatures. The West was supposedly nationalist, hostile to Russian speakers and alien to people in the East. The East was supposedly Russian, Soviet, culturally separate and suspicious of Ukrainian nationalism. Language became political identity. Geography became loyalty. Political campaigns exploited those divisions, while Russian television, culture, information operations and political influence continually reinforced them.
Eventually, the mythology became so familiar that people outside Ukraine – and sometimes Ukrainians themselves – began treating it as an organic description of the country.
My dear friend Vlad Vernygora, an international relations and political science scholar who now serves as an officer in Ukraine’s National Guard, has given this phenomenon a particularly useful name: Donbasification.
Vlad is also a New Zealander. He studied at the University of Canterbury before building an academic career in Europe, teaching international relations and political science and researching, among other things, contemporary political empires and their strategic narratives. After Russia launched its full-scale invasion, he returned to Ukraine and joined the National Guard. Today, he serves as an officer in the 1st Corps Azov.
In a piece published by Estonia’s Delfi under the striking headline “A warning to Estonia: You too can be turned into a Donbas – so learn from us,” Vlad describes Donbasification as something much more sophisticated than separatism. It is the deliberate construction of an enemy-made regional identity inside another country: taking real regional characteristics, layering mythology, propaganda and historical distortion over them, exaggerating genuine differences, suppressing inconvenient history, and eventually presenting the resulting artificial identity as evidence that the territory never properly belonged within the nation at all – and using that manufactured division against the state itself.
It is a phenomenon I recognise intimately, both as a Ukrainian from the Donetsk region and as someone who spent much of my childhood moving between Ukraine’s East and West. And it is worth examining in full, because Donbasification helps explain not only what Russia did to my home region, but something much larger: how an imperial power can manufacture the very division it later claims merely to have discovered.
First, what exactly is Donbas?
Even the word itself carries part of the story. Donbas derives from the Donets Basin – originally an economic and geographical description of the enormous coal and industrial basin that developed across parts of eastern Ukraine and western Russia.
It was not an ethnic territory, nor a nation within a nation. It did not even correspond precisely to an administrative region.
What we commonly call the Ukrainian Donbas broadly encompasses Donetsk and Luhansk regions, but the economic basin historically extended beyond them into parts of Kharkiv and Dnipropetrovsk regions and across today’s international border into Russia.
Soviet atlases treated Donbas as an economic region: coal, steel, factories, mines. A resource basin, not a separate homeland.
That distinction matters enormously, because one of Russia’s greatest propaganda achievements was transforming an imprecise term of economic geography into something that sounded almost ethnic, a cultural identity if you will.
Eventually we began hearing about the supposed people of Donbas as though they constituted a separate people with a political destiny fundamentally different from that of other Ukrainians. This is the heart of what Vlad calls Donbasification.
The myth grew through propaganda, Russian popular culture and disinformation, continually reinforcing the idea that Ukraine’s East was fundamentally different from the West and laying the ground for a supposed internal conflict. The most dangerous invention was the idea of a separate people of Donbas – a pseudo-identity that could eventually be used to justify separation and territorial expansion.
Once that proposition becomes accepted, the next steps become much easier. If the people are different, perhaps they require autonomy. If they require autonomy, perhaps Kyiv is oppressing them. If Kyiv is oppressing them, perhaps resistance is inevitable. And if resistance is inevitable, perhaps Moscow is not invading at all, perhaps it is simply helping.
That is how an imperial project is gradually rewritten as an internal dispute.
Before Donbasification came Russification
None of this began in 2014. Donetsk and Luhansk suffered terribly under Soviet rule, including through the Holodomor and Stalinist purges. Communities were destroyed, populations changed. Workers were brought from Russia and elsewhere in the Soviet Union to supply the enormous industrial machine being built around the mines and factories.
And forced Russification followed.
This happened throughout Ukraine, but its depth in the industrial East was particularly profound. A whole region was taught to forget its own voice. Russian language became dominant in urban public life, administration, higher education, professional advancement and media. Ukrainian schools disappeared or were converted to Russian-language instruction. Ukrainian was increasingly pushed into the private sphere and associated with villages, while Russian carried status, opportunity and power. Speaking Ukrainian could mean losing a career. Street names, newspapers, institutions – everything reinforced Moscow’s dominance.
That distinction is essential because language would later be used as supposed evidence of national identity.
Millions of Ukrainians were Russified and then their Russification was presented back to them as proof that they were Russian. It is an extraordinary circular argument.
First an empire suppresses your language. Then it points to the prevalence of its own language as evidence that the land belongs to it.
The demographic consequences of Soviet terror and industrial migration reinforced the process. Soviet symbols dominated public space. Russian television and publishing dominated cultural consumption. Generations grew up inside an information environment in which Moscow remained the cultural center of gravity even after Moscow ceased formally to govern Ukraine.
But none of this transformed Donetsk or Luhansk into Russia. We have an unusually clear historical test of that proposition.
On Dec. 1, 1991, Ukrainians were asked directly whether they supported an independent Ukraine. Every administrative region of the country voted yes.
Nationally, support exceeded 90%. In Donetsk region, 83.9% voted for Ukrainian independence. In Luhansk region, 83.86% did the same. Crimea and Sevastopol returned majorities for Ukrainian independence too.
That referendum is extraordinarily inconvenient for the mythology subsequently built around Ukraine’s East. When people there were actually asked which country they wanted to belong to, the answer was Ukraine.
Manufacturing East against West
But independence did not end Russian influence. Ukraine emerged from the Soviet Union politically and institutionally weak, with elites shaped by the system they had inherited. Russian economic leverage remained enormous. So did Russian media penetration, cultural influence and political networks.
The Soviet architecture was not dismantled overnight. Russian-language television remained everywhere. Soviet monuments and street names remained. Russian cultural products saturated the information space.
And alongside them came something more corrosive: the constant political construction of an East-West divide.
This part of Donbasification is particularly personal for me because I knew both sides of the country that were supposedly incapable of understanding one another.
I knew Donetsk region and I knew Lviv region. Growing up, I watched narratives about each being fed to the other.
People in the East were repeatedly warned about dangerous western Ukrainian nationalists who supposedly hated Russian speakers. People in the West were presented with an East supposedly incapable of imagining itself outside Russia’s cultural orbit.
Real political disagreements existed, so did regional differences. But those differences were repeatedly inflated into questions of identity and belonging. The trick was subtle.
You do not necessarily have to persuade somebody that they are Russian. You only have to persuade people that they are not quite like other Ukrainians: that Kyiv does not understand them, that another part of their country despises them, that their language and way of life are somehow under threat, that their history is separate, and ultimately that perhaps they are being governed by somebody else’s state. Repeat that story often enough and for long enough, reinforce it through politics, media and culture, and gradually what were once ordinary regional differences can be turned into a fault line – one that, when the moment comes, can be deliberately exploited.
The ground was prepared before the soldiers arrived
Under Viktor Yanukovych – himself from Donetsk – corruption and Russian penetration of the Ukrainian state deepened dramatically, reaching extraordinarily high levels inside Ukraine’s political, security and defence institutions, while Moscow continued applying economic and political pressure.
The narrative was that Donbas was strong, different, and that it would not be dictated to by Kyiv, while Russian television, popular culture and news reinforced the information environment in which these ideas circulated and became increasingly normalized. Then came 2014. In Crimea, Russian soldiers appeared without insignia while Moscow initially denied what it was doing, and in eastern Ukraine, Russia similarly sought to present its aggression as something indigenous – a local uprising rather than an operation directed and supported by Moscow. Sloviansk became one of the places where that fiction was born, which for me makes this far more than an abstract historical argument: it is my hometown.
Russia would spend years describing the war that followed as a rebellion of Donbas against Ukraine. The mythology created before the war now became the explanation for the war.
Russia did not simply exploit an existing separatist identity; it manufactured it.
Continued in Part 2: “The Roots That Survived”

‘Every step towards disarmament matters,’ nuclear testing survivors warn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

‘Every step towards disarmament matters,’ nuclear testing survivors warn
He was born without arms, a legacy of four decades of nuclear explosions at the Semipalatinsk test site in his native Kazakhstan.
Artist and anti-nuclear activist Karipbek Kuyukov walked through the halls of UN Headquarters in New York on Monday alongside diplomats, scientists and survivors, carrying a message he has spent his life delivering: no one should ever again suffer what his generation endured.
Mr. Kuyukov, who paints holding the brush with his lips and toes, was among the participants of a symbolic walk ahead of the General Assembly’s high-level meeting on the occasion of the International Day against Nuclear Tests, marked annually on 29 August.
The short procession, part of the #StepUp4Disarmament campaign, ended in front of a large photograph on display in the General Assembly building, depicting people demanding the closure of the Semipalatinsk site.
“I would like to tell our story, the story of Kazakhstan,” Mr. Kuyukov told UN News.
456 nuclear tests
Between 1949 and 1989, the Semipalatinsk site saw 456 nuclear tests. Hundreds of thousands of people living nearby were exposed to elevated levels of radiation, with consequences carried within families across generations.
“My parents were living witnesses of those tests, and as a result, I was born without arms,” Mr. Kuyukov said.
He was 20 years old when Kazakh poet Olzhas Suleimenov launched the Nevada-Semipalatinsk anti-nuclear movement.
‘Entire nation rose up’
“The entire nation rose up against this monster, against the Semipalatinsk polygon,” he recalled.
The movement reached far beyond Kazakhstan.
Mr. Kuyukov remembered standing at a protest alongside a chief of the Shoshone people, whose lands lay near the United States test site in Nevada, and joining peaceful rallies at the gates of Semipalatinsk with activists from French Polynesia, where France conducted tests at Mururoa Atoll, and from Japan.
Shuttered for good
On 29 August 1991, the Semipalatinsk site was shut down, a date the General Assembly later proclaimed, at Kazakhstan’s initiative, as the International Day against Nuclear Tests. This year marks 35 years since the closure.
“I can say with pride that my country, Kazakhstan, began its path to sovereignty precisely with that peaceful decision,” Mr. Kuyukov said. “I believe this is a great honour for us and can serve as a worthy example for other countries.”
Every step counts
Addressing participants of the walk, UN High Representative for Disarmament Affairs Izumi Nakamitsu said the silence that fell upon Semipalatinsk 35 years ago “did not happen by chance”.
“It was achieved through the determination of people, communities and leaders who rejected nuclear testing,” she said.
Kazakhstan’s Permanent Representative to the UN Kairat Umarov described the walk as “a very simple but very powerful way to remind us that every step towards disarmament matters”.
This year also marks the 30th anniversary of the opening for signature of the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty (CTBT). Robert Floyd, Executive Secretary of the CTBT Organization, told the young people taking part in the walk that disarmament is “a journey that works across generations”.
“The day will come when your generation will lead, will make the decisions, will be in the boardrooms, will be in the assembly halls,” he said. “And we will be cheering on your great steps forward.”
No one immune
Speaking later in the General Assembly, Ms. Nakamitsu warned that concerns about a possible resumption of nuclear explosive testing have re-emerged amid deep geopolitical tension.
She recalled the Secretary-General’s message: “the world must never witness another nuclear explosion.”
The President of the General Assembly, Annalena Baerbock, stressed that the consequences of nuclear explosions know no borders.
“In an interconnected world such as ours, there is no truly ‘remote region’ immune from the effects or dangers of nuclear testing,” she said.
Five generations of cancer
Among the speakers was Tina Cordova, a fourth-generation survivor of the 1945 Trinity test in New Mexico, who also joined the morning’s symbolic walk.
“We were the first people exposed to radiation anyplace in the world as ash fell from the sky in the days after the bomb,” she told the Assembly, describing five generations of cancer in her family. “We were never warned before or after of the danger, so we lived our lives off the land as we always did.”
She closed with an appeal to the delegates, saying that “after 81 years, it is time we set our families, our children and grandchildren free from nuclear threat.”
Message to the young
For Mr. Kuyukov, the fight is now about those who come next. Seeing young people join movements against nuclear weapons always reminds him that “in war, it is innocent children who suffer first.”
“The future is in their hands,” he said. “They, too, must secure a safe world for the next generation. We have experience and we can share it because we know how this is done.”
Asked what he would say to world leaders at a time when, in his words, the situation in the world has become dangerously tense, the artist called for reconciliation.
“To reach a new world – one of kindness, mercy and compassion – we need to let go of old grievances and past mistakes and leave them in history,” he stressed. “Now, we can only move forward together, showing the way to the new generation.”

‘Slavery is not a thing of the past’: UN supports call for reparations
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
12:00:00 UTC

‘Slavery is not a thing of the past’: UN supports call for reparations
Slavery is not just a thing of the past. Its effects continue to be felt in systemic inequality and racism. This was reiterated on Monday by the UN Committee against Racial Discrimination (CERD) as the world marks the International Day of People of African Descent.
The committee is calling on States to implement comprehensive restorative justice, combining compensation, restitution, rehabilitation and structural reforms.
The passage of time cannot serve as a pretext for States to refuse to recognise these historical injustices or to adopt “appropriate measures of restorative justice and accountability for these crimes”, according to the committee.
Comprising18 independent human rights experts elected for four-year terms, the committee’s main task is to examine the periodic reports submitted by member countries on the measures taken to combat racism and discrimination.
It also advocates for comprehensive and far-reaching remedial measures, both financial, non-financial and structural, including restitution, compensation, rehabilitation, satisfaction and guarantees of non-recurrence.
National plans and deadlines
“The elimination of racial discrimination cannot be effective, complete or sustainable without a full commitment to review and redress the ongoing harms and consequences of the trafficking of enslaved Africans and racialised slavery,” the experts said in a statement.
To ensure the effectiveness of reparations, they advocate the implementation of national action plans with specific deadlines, developed in consultation with people of African descent and the committees in charge of reparations.
The committee also called on States to repeal or revise laws and policies that perpetuate racism or discrimination or that obstruct restorative justice. It demanded transformations of laws, policies, and institutions that continue to perpetuate racial inequalities.
“Acknowledgments and apologies should be accompanied by concrete measures and should not replace other appropriate forms of redress,” the experts argued.
Private actors face responsibilities
CERD also examined the responsibility of private and other non-State actors, including religious organizations, universities, businesses, banks, insurers and other financial institutions that participated in, facilitated or profited from the trafficking of enslaved Africans.
The committee also called on States to ensure that these actors contribute effectively to restorative justice, in particular by recognising their historical role, opening relevant archives and contributing to reparation measures “in a manner proportionate to their involvement and the benefits they have derived from it”.
The committee stressed that these responsibilities remain relevant: the harms linked to the trafficking of enslaved Africans and racialised slavery persist in the form of “systemic racial discrimination and structural inequalities”.
Committee members specifically pointed to racialised violence, stereotypes and structural barriers that fuel disparities in education, health, economic mobility and environmental security.
These legacies of slavery have been “reinforced by policies perpetuating anti-Black racism”.

A strike by airport workers in Kenya caused flight delays for thousands of passengers
Kyiv • UNN
A strike by workers at Jomo Kenyatta International Airport delayed and canceled flights. Union negotiations with the authorities over the demands are ongoing.
The strike by workers at Kenya’s main international airport (a country in East Africa) continued for a second day, causing flight delays on Monday and affecting thousands of passengers. Union representatives said that negotiations with the authorities over the workers’ demands were ongoing. Reuters reports, UNN writes.
Details
The strike at Jomo Kenyatta International Airport was caused by a number of unresolved issues, including the failure to conclude a collective agreement with the Kenya Civil Aviation Authority, as well as a lack of cooperation from the Kenya Airports Authority and Jambojet, a subsidiary of Kenya Airways.
On Sunday, the Kenya Airports Authority said that some flights were delayed, without specifying the reasons. On Monday, it did not respond to a Reuters request for comment. The Kenya Civil Aviation Authority and Jambojet also did not respond to inquiries.
Rwanda’s national carrier, RwandAir, said on the social media platform X on Sunday that it had canceled two flights due, it said, to air traffic control problems at Nairobi airport.
Passengers told Reuters that they had waited for hours at the airport for information about their flights.
"When I arrived, the flight had been moved to 1:00 a.m. So the delay was an hour and a half, and then it was moved again—to 4:30 a.m. At around three o’clock, I went to check in. I was told that the flight had been canceled," said Rabbi Mendel Goldman, who was traveling to a wedding in Florida.
"The earliest flight they can offer us is only tomorrow evening, so we will have to wait," Goldman said on Monday. "We’ll try to make use of this time somehow, but for now I’ve already been here at the airport for 12 hours."
KAWU Secretary General Moss Ndiema said that the union and government representatives had met on Sunday to resolve the issues, but no agreement was reached.
"We agreed to continue negotiations tomorrow, from 11 a.m. In the meantime, the strike is continuing," he said on KTN television on Sunday.

Italy's population to shrink by 4 million by 2050, stats agency says
Unknown

Italy's population to shrink by 4 million by 2050, stats agency says
ROME, Aug 31 - Italy's population will shrink by almost 4 million by 2050, undermining the sustainability of its economy and welfare system as the proportion of elderly people increases, national statistics bureau ISTAT warned on Monday.
In new demographic projections extending to 2080, ISTAT said Italy's resident population would fall to 55 million in 2050 from 58.9 million at the start of 2025, before dropping to 45.8 million by 2080.
Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said when she took office in 2022 that boosting the birth rate would be a government priority, but her efforts have produced scant results.
Births have declined steadily since 2008 and fell last year to around 355,000, the lowest number since Italy's unification in 1861, while deaths have risen as the population ages.
ISTAT said annual births would now remain broadly stable until 2030, before falling to 335,000 by 2050.
Deaths were projected to rise from about 652,000 last year to a peak of 869,000 in 2058 as Italy's large post-war baby boom generation reaches old age.
The share of Italians aged 65 or over is expected to jump to 34.5% in 2050 from 24.7% in 2025, while the proportion of people of working age, defined as 15 to 64 years old, will fall to 55.3% from 63.4%.
A shrinking pool of workers and a surging number of pensioners will pose "new challenges to the economic system and welfare," ISTAT noted.
The demographic decline will be uneven across the country. Poorer southern Italy was forecast to suffer the steepest losses, with its population falling from 19.7 million in 2025 to 16.7 million in 2050, while central and northern regions will see a more modest decline. REUTERS

MEA said that the Indus Water Treaty will remain in abeyance
NEW DELHI: Ministry of external affairs on Monday categorically rejected a ruling by World Bank-constituted Court of Arbitration on Indus Water Treaty, terming it an "illegally constituted" organisation.In a statement, MEA said that New Delhi's decision to put the water treaty with Pakistan in abeyance "will remain in force.""This so-called Court was constituted by the World Bank in patent breach of the terms of the Treaty and India categorically rejects its so-called award, just as it has firmly rejected all prior pronouncements by this illegally constituted body," the ministry said."India has never recognised the existence in law of this illegally-constituted and so-called Court of Arbitration, and has consistently maintained that the very establishment of this alleged arbitral body constitutes a grave violation of the Indus Waters Treaty. Accordingly, India has never appeared before this body and has refused to take any cognisance of its earlier pronouncements," it added.
Also read: 'India could use water as weapon': Pakistan minister as Indus Waters Treaty remains in abeyanceThe ministry also said that the Court of Arbitration has no "jurisdiction whatsoever to pronounce on India’s sovereign decisions.""Its pronouncements, now or in the future, will have no effect on India’s actions in connection with the projects being undertaken by India," MEA said.
This comes hours after the Court of Arbitration said that the grounds on which India decided to put the Indus Water Treaty in abeyance did not “justify suspension or termination.”
“Accordingly, the Indus Waters Treaty remains fully in force, and India must observe its obligations under the Treaty,” the court saidNew Delhi put the agreement in abeyance following the Pahalgam terror attack in April last year.Since then, Pakistani leaders have repeatedly called water their “red line” and threatened India over the move, describing it as an “act of war.”

Russia used five times as many jet-powered drones in July as in June
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
14:49:00 EEST
20:49:00 KST

Russia used five times as many jet-powered drones in July as in June
A Ukrainian military official has said Russia used five times as many jet-powered drones to attack Ukraine in July as it did in June, following a change in its drone attack tactics and increased use of jet-powered UAVs, which are more difficult for the Ukrainian Air Force to shoot down.
Source: Yurii Ihnat, spokesperson for the Ukrainian Air Force, in an interview on the national joint 24/7 newscast
Quote: "The enemy has changed the weapons it uses more than its tactics. In other words, it has significantly increased the number of jet-powered [drones – ed.] specifically. This happened... in July. The enemy used five times as many jet-powered UAVs in July as in June. That was the month when the number of these UAVs, along with Banderol missile drones, began to increase significantly."
Details: Ihnat reported that Russia had launched more than 1,500 UAVs on Ukraine over the past four days. Of these, 800 – more than half – were jet-powered.
Ihnat said the Russians have resorted to using jet-powered drones as Ukraine's defence forces were successfully shooting down and jamming large numbers of conventional petrol-powered Shaheds.
"Of course, they did not start using jet-powered UAVs just recently, but they have now increased their use, realising that they cannot be shot down using the conventional methods we already employ against ordinary UAVs," the spokesperson said.
He added that Ukraine's interception rate for jet-powered UAVs is currently lower than for conventional drones, 88-90% of which are shot down.
Ihnat explained that the successful interception of jet-powered drones requires the use of ground-based air defence systems, aviation systems and platforms, fighter jets equipped with air-to-air missiles, and other weapons.

Russia Drops FAB-500 Bomb on Sloviansk, Destroying Part of Apartment Building, Injuring 4
Russian forces struck an apartment building in Sloviansk, Donetsk region, with a FAB-500 aerial bomb early on August 31, injuring four people and damaging dozens of residential buildings, local authorities reported.
Sloviansk Mayor Vadym Liakh said the Russian airstrike hit the city at around 4:20 a.m., with the impact recorded in the central part of Sloviansk.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The strike destroyed an entire section of a multi-story apartment building from the first through the fifth floor, as well as a private house. At least 32 other apartment buildings, a hotel, a kindergarten, and a vehicle were also damaged, according to the mayor.
The Donetsk Regional Prosecutor’s Office said four residents between the ages of 61 and 66 were injured while inside their homes.
The victims sustained blast-related injuries, bruises, and lacerations and are receiving medical treatment, prosecutors said.
Law enforcement authorities reported that the strike damaged a total of 34 apartment and private residential buildings, as well as six vehicles.
The attack on Sloviansk came amid further Russian strikes elsewhere in Ukraine. In the Bucha district of Kyiv region, at least 38 people were killed and another 20 injured after Russian forces struck an enterprise, triggering a subsequent detonation.
Emergency medical teams provided assistance to all those affected, with seven of the injured requiring hospitalization.

Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Guo Jiakun’s Regular Press Conference on August 31, 2026
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
19:45:01 CST
20:45:01 KST

At the invitation of the government of the Russian Federation, from September 2 to 4, Member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee and Vice Premier of the State Council Ding Xuexiang will travel to Russia to attend the 11th Eastern Economic Forum and hold the 13th meeting of the China-Russia Investment Cooperation Committee, the 23rd meeting of the China-Russia Energy Cooperation Committee, and the 8th China-Russia Energy Business Forum.
Xinhua News Agency: With rescue efforts still underway following the mudslide in Gyirong, could you please provide further details on the progress of rescue work related to foreign countries?
Guo Jiakun: The devastating mudslide, triggered by a sudden glacial collapse in Nepal’s border area, has caused massive casualties and left many unaccounted for in both China and Nepal. While urgently carrying out rescue and relief efforts at home, China also immediately reached out to Nepal to support its emergency response and disaster relief. President Xi Jinping sent a condolence message to Nepali President Ram Chandra Poudel. Premier Li Qiang also expressed condolences to the Nepali side. The meeting of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee called for emergency assistance to the affected areas in Nepal and international cooperation in rescue and relief.
On August 29, Foreign Minister Wang Yi spoke with Nepal’s Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal over the phone. He noted that China and Nepal are a community linked by mountains and rivers and a shared future. In the face of the disaster, the two countries should stand firmly together, join hands to overcome the difficulties, and demonstrate the traditional friendship through concrete actions. The Chinese government has provided Nepal with emergency cash assistance and humanitarian aid. The first batch of 50 tons of relief supplies has already arrived in Kathmandu. Two rescue teams composed of Chinese tunnel rescue experts have rushed to the disaster-stricken areas in Nepal. We have also shared with the Nepali side important information such as images, satellite, and hydrological data of the disaster-affected areas, including early-warning information on an upstream barrier lake. China is actively assisting stranded Nepali citizens in returning to Nepal as soon as possible. As of noon yesterday, all Chinese nationals in Nepal’s disaster-hit areas, with whom contact has been reestablished, have been safely relocated.
At present, China is making every effort to search for and rescue those unaccounted for both within the country and abroad. At the same time, we maintain close communication with foreign embassies in China to jointly identify missing foreign nationals and properly handle follow-up matters.
China News Service: To follow up on your announcement about Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang’s trip to Russia to attend the 11th Eastern Economic Forum and hold the 13th meeting of the China-Russia Investment Cooperation Committee, the 23rd meeting of the China-Russia Energy Cooperation Committee, and the 8th China-Russia Energy Business Forum, could you share with us the background, program and China’s expectation of the visit?
Guo Jiakun: Themed on “The Far East: Development for the Benefit of People,” the 11th Eastern Economic Forum will be held in Vladivostok, Russia from September 1 to 4. Vice Premier Ding Xuexiang will attend the plenary session of the forum, co-chair the institutionalized meetings of China-Russia Investment Cooperation Committee and China-Russia Energy Cooperation Committee, as well as China-Russia Energy Business Forum with Russian leaders, and hold meetings with them.
This year marks the 30th anniversary of the China-Russia strategic partnership of coordination, and the 25th anniversary of the signing of the China-Russia Treaty of Good-Neighborliness and Friendly Cooperation. China will take this opportunity to implement the important common understandings of the two heads of state, make greater progress in developing the China-Russia comprehensive strategic partnership of coordination for the new era, and bring benefits to the two peoples. China also looks forward to working with various parties to step up communication, enhance mutual trust, stick to openness and cooperation, and share the opportunities of development, so as to make greater contribution to promoting regional revitalization and development as well as the common welfare of the people of all countries.
CGTN: His Majesty King Harald V of Norway passed away. I wonder if China has any comment?
Guo Jiakun: King Harald V was highly esteemed and deeply loved by the Norwegian people. He was committed to promoting China-Norway friendship, paid multiple visits to China and made significant contributions to bilateral exchange and cooperation. China mourns his passing and extends sincere condolences to the royal family, government and people of Norway.
Bloomberg: Some Indian TV channels have blamed China for the floods and mudslide disaster. They say China is going ahead with major construction projects in hydropower and infrastructure. Would the ministry like to comment on this?
Guo Jiakun: We noted that experts and official institutions of China and Nepal have made some assessment on the cause of the disaster. According to their analysis, the mudslide was triggered by a collapse of a high-altitude glacier in Nepal. In the face of tragic disasters, we reject malicious speculation that has no factual basis.
Sky News: It appears that China has censored and taken down some of the more dramatic videos of that terrible flood smashing into Gyirong Port. Can I ask why China has done that? There have been some suggestions that the numbers of missing and dead are being understated. Can I ask what China’s response is to those accusations?
Guo Jiakun: Intensive search, rescue and relief operations are still underway in an orderly manner in the disaster-hit areas. China has been open, transparent and timely in information release. Smear and disinformation is most unwelcome at a time of disaster response.
Shenzhen TV: It is reported that the Third APEC Senior Officials’ Meeting concluded in Dalian on August 28. Could you brief us on the meeting and its main outcomes?
Guo Jiakun: From August 17 to 28, the Third Senior Officials’ Meeting of APEC China and related meetings were held in Dalian. Deputy Foreign Minister Ma Zhaoxu attended the meeting and delivered remarks.
This was the largest Senior Officials’ Meeting held during the APEC China Year in terms of both attendance and number of events. During the meeting, APEC committees and working groups held nearly 130 meetings and events, covering areas such as trade, transportation, food, customs, science and technology, energy, health, disaster reduction, and anti-corruption. More than 3,000 representatives from APEC member economies, the APEC Secretariat, and APEC observers attended the meetings.
Participants held in-depth discussions under the theme of APEC China Year and “Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together” and around the three priority areas of “Openness, Innovation, and Cooperation”, and focused on comparing notes on the outcomes for the APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting to be held in Shenzhen this November.
Under the “Openness” priority, China hosted a policy dialogue on connectivity, laying the groundwork for developing an upgraded APEC Connectivity Blueprint.
Under the “Innovation” priority, China hosted a policy dialogue on the digital economy and artificial intelligence as drivers of economic growth. Participants held in-depth discussions on leveraging AI to promote economic growth, improve people’s well-being, and bridge the digital divide, continuing the positive momentum generated by APEC Digital Week held in Chengdu in July.
Under the “Cooperation” priority, China keeps advancing result‑oriented cooperation covering such areas as anti‑corruption, customs, food security, fisheries and maritime affairs, public health and energy. Major deliverables have been secured on themes such as improving integrity for prosperity and customs cooperation to bolster trade security and facilitation.
The final Senior Officials’ Meeting of the APEC China Year will be held in Shenzhen on the eve of the APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting this November. We welcome reporters to continue following and covering events under the APEC China Year.
Reuters: More than 900 people are believed to be stuck inside blocked hydropower project tunnels in Nepal after the flood last week. Were there any Chinese nationals working at these projects and has the government or the ministry identified if any of those Chinese nationals are trapped in the tunnels?
Guo Jiakun: Nearly 100 Chinese nationals are among those missing in Nepal. The Nepali side has been trying every possible means to search for and rescue those missing or trapped. Tunnel experts from China have arrived in the affected area in Nepal to assist in rescue efforts.
Phoenix TV: Japan’s Self-Defense Forces (SDF) in a statement on August 28 said that they had dismissed SDF officer Kodai Murata. The SDF said it is extremely regrettable that one of its members committed such an act, and it will take thorough measures to have its personnel strictly follow laws and regulations. What is China’s comment? Does this address China’s concerns?
Guo Jiakun: It is shockingly malignant for a sitting Japanese SDF officer to break into the Chinese embassy carrying a knife and threaten the Chinese side with violence. This incident seriously violates the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, gravely threatens the safety and security of Chinese diplomatic personnel and premises, and exposes deep-seated problems in Japan, including the rampant spread of right-wing impact and lack of supervision and discipline in the SDF. We noted that Japanese public prosecutors have indicted the person concerned. We urge the Japanese side to earnestly fulfill its duty, bring the perpetrator to account, conduct a thorough investigation and correct the wrongdoings. This is also what the international community hopes to see.
Bloomberg: U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the world cannot have a US$1.2 trillion trade surplus with China and he said the G20 countries should reexamine their terms of trade with the country. Would the Foreign Ministry like to comment?
Guo Jiakun: China‑U.S. economic and trade ties are mutually beneficial in nature. China never seeks trade surplus. We oppose unilateral tariff measures in all forms. Committed to high‑standard opening up, China, with its vast market, offers new opportunities to all, including the United States. Both sides need to act on the important common understandings reached between the two presidents, resolve outstanding issues through consultation on the basis of equality, mutual respect and mutual benefit, and strive to maintain the hard‑won positive momentum in bilateral trade.

China unveils measures to expand, upgrade consumer goods consumption
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
19:43:44 CST
20:43:44 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- China has unveiled measures to expand and upgrade consumer goods consumption, aiming to bring total retail sales of consumer goods to around 60 trillion yuan (about 8.85 trillion U.S. dollars) by 2030, according to an implementation guideline made public on Monday.
The guideline, jointly issued by seven government departments, including the Ministry of Commerce and the National Development and Reform Commission, calls for fostering 10-trillion-yuan markets in areas such as green, smart and health consumption by 2030.
Retail sales of trillion-yuan product categories, including automobiles, home appliances, communications equipment, textiles and clothing, are also expected to continue growing, with these markets remaining among the world's largest.
The guideline outlines four major tasks to promote goods consumption, namely promoting the consumption of durable goods, improving the quality of everyday consumer goods, supporting consumption of specialty products and fostering demand for upgraded products.
It further specifies measures that include expanding automobile consumption across the entire industrial chain, promoting smart home applications, supporting consumption of products for elderly people and children, and boosting consumption of green, smart and health products. ■

China's space-based computing cloud starts regular in-orbit services
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
19:43:12 CST
20:43:12 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- A China-built space computing cloud has recently started offering regular in-orbit experimental services, according to its developer.
Led by Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications (BUPT), the orbital computing power facility automates end-to-end operations across satellite platforms, space servers, ground stations and data centers, giving worldwide users a full life-cycle service from task submission, deployment, execution, monitoring to results delivery.
Space computing refers to an emerging computing paradigm that deploys data processing, storage, intelligent analysis and decision-making capabilities on orbital platforms, such as satellites and space stations.
The Chinese computing cloud platform operates on the Tiansuan Constellation, launched by BUPT in 2021. As the world's first space computing constellation, it has deployed 16 low-Earth-orbit satellites and seven ground stations, supported more than 60 institutions in orbital tests and drawn researchers from more than 50 countries and regions to its ecosystem.
It offers several key technological capabilities, such as building reusable platform-based services, supporting long-term reliable operation of onboard software, and laying a foundation for real-time in-orbit processing of space data and autonomous satellite decision-making.
Since entering service, the platform has supported multiple tasks, including in-orbit big-data computing and 6G communications. More than 100 users have accessed the energy-efficient service, the university said on Sunday.
Compared with ground-based data centers, the advantages of space computing cloud lie in real-time responsiveness and global coverage.
Traditional data centers are constrained by high energy consumption, limited land resources, high cooling costs, and limited coverage, which can hardly meet future demands for ultra-large-scale, green, and globally covered computing power, while space-based computing offers a zero-carbon, sustainable, and widely accessible alternative, said Yu Guobin, deputy director of the commercial space department of the State Administration of Science, Technology and Industry for National Defense, at 2026 Space Computing Industry Conference held in Beijing in April.
The official noted that the space-based computing technology can offer real-time and intelligent services to emergency response, marine observation, aviation and shipping, and polar expeditions.
According to the BUPT, the platform's value lies in helping the space information industry move from hardware delivery to persistent service delivery, cultivating new industrial growth areas in satellite internet, 6G, commercial space and emergency communications. Some of these fields are among the key emerging industries that China aims to foster over the next five years. ■

Chinese-built expressway opens to boost Serbia's economic development: Serbian president

This photo taken on Aug. 30, 2026 shows a view of the Chinese-built Danube Corridor expressway in Pozarevac, Serbia. The Chinese-built Danube Corridor expressway will boost Serbia's economic development, Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic said Sunday at the expressway's opening ceremony. The expressway officially opened to traffic on Monday.(Photo by Wang Wei/Xinhua)
POZAREVAC, Serbia, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- The Chinese-built Danube Corridor expressway will boost Serbia's economic development, Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic said Sunday at the expressway's opening ceremony.
Vucic, along with First Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Sinisa Mali, Minister of Construction, Transport and Infrastructure Aleksandra Sofronijevic, and Zhang Zhe, charge d'affaires of the Chinese Embassy in Serbia, attended the event.
After traveling along the Danube Corridor expressway on Sunday, Vucic spoke highly of its significance for Serbia's development, saying that the project will play an important role in advancing Serbia's national interests, boosting domestic tourism and driving economic growth in the country's eastern region.
The expressway would officially open to traffic on Monday, announced Vucic.
Zhang said he believed that the completion of the Danube Corridor would attract an increasing number of tourists to the scenic eastern part of Serbia.
"This also confirms what we often say -- roads connect not only cities with cities, but also the friendship of peoples and opportunities for future development," Zhang said.
According to Shandong Hi-Speed Group, the project's contractor, the Danube Corridor expressway is an important branch of the E75 motorway in Europe and another flagship project of China-Serbia cooperation.
The 68-km expressway has four lanes in both directions and a designed speed of 100 km per hour.
Construction took five years, during which Vucic visited the site seven times and hailed the project as "the road to the future." ■

The water level of the Rhine has risen in Germany, but shipping remains restricted
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
14:41:16 EEST
20:41:16 KST

The water level of the Rhine has risen in Germany, but shipping remains restricted
Kyiv • UNN
The level of the Rhine near Kaub rose to 72 cm after the rains, but about 1.5 meters is needed for vessels to be fully loaded. By the end of the week, the water level may fall again.
The water level in the Rhine River in Germany has risen sharply after recent rains, but shipping is still difficult. Vessels can already carry more cargo, but the water level still does not allow them to operate at full capacity. Reuters reports, UNN writes.
Details
According to the WSV, on Monday the water level at the gauge station in Kaub, near Koblenz, was about 72 cm, compared with 60 cm on Friday. In mid-August, the level fell below 10 cm — significantly lower than the previous record low of 25 cm recorded in 2018.
For reference
WSV is Germany’s Federal Waterways and Shipping Administration.
Additional information
Despite the improvement, vessels continue to operate with reduced loads. For fully loaded shipping, the water level in Kaub needs to be around 1.5 metres.
Cargo has to be distributed among several vessels, increasing costs for industry. A significant share of freight transport has also been redirected to road and rail.
Rain is forecast this week, but any improvement will depend on how much precipitation actually falls
The WSV forecasts that the water level in the river may fall again toward the end of this week, although it is expected to remain significantly higher than at the beginning of August.
This summer, Germany and other European countries experienced a series of heatwaves and a lack of precipitation, which led to falling water levels on waterways such as the Rhine — an important route for transporting grain, minerals, coal and petroleum products.

Families of those missing after Nepal floods struggle to cling to hope
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
11:39:10 UTC
20:39:10 KST

Nepal flood rescue recovery efforts keep hope alive for desperate families as 4,200 people remain missing
Kathmandu, Nepal — Five days after a rocky mountainside and the glacier it supported collapsed near Nepal's border with Tibet, unleashing torrents of flash floodwater, mud and debris on the valleys below that swept away everything in their path, rescuers were still searching Monday for reasons to hope.
Over the weekend, a 6-year-old girl was miraculously pulled from the mud-covered rubble, fueling hope that more of the 4,200 people still listed as missing in the wake of the disaster could be found alive.
Nepal's national disaster agency said Monday that at least 903 people had been killed, and the fear is that the toll will spiral as recovery efforts continue along the scars carved into the landscape by the raging floods.
But the danger hasn't passed. The sacred Trishuli River was surging again Monday, this time from heavy monsoon rains that have spurred search and rescue teams to try and move even faster to find anyone still alive in the ruins.
Samarth Srivastav was among the thousands of people desperately hoping a loved one might still emerge from the layers of thick mud and rubble in the Himalayan valleys.
"We're just trying to hope for good news now," Samarth told CBS News from Atlanta.
His father Vivek was on the Nepal-Tibet border when the disaster struck last week.
Samarth said his father joked with him on their last phone call about how steep the river valley walls around him were, saying, "You know, if I fall down there, like, I'll get swept away."
Just hours after the call, a tsunami of glacial ice, water and mud swept away Tibet's immigration checkpoint on the border, and Vivek hasn't been heard from since.
"Initially after hearing about it, you know, it was kind of like, okay, you know, maybe by the end of the day, you know? Might hear something back. And then the next day came and we didn't hear anything all day. And then more and more," he said. "As the number of missing people on record started to increase and, like, the severity of the situation actually started to hit, you know — we're seeing all these videos pop up on social media of people recording the disaster and everything that actually happened — I think that's when we actually started to get worried and realize that something might actually be wrong. This is actually a really bad situation."
Since then, Samarth said it has been nothing but "increasing anxiety" for his family.
"We still have the hope that he's probably okay — he's able to come back, he's probably doing fine out there," he said. "But, it's the fact we don't know anything yet, is just so scary to us."
The torrents of floodwater and everything they picked up and carried with them pushed as far as 150 miles away, into neighboring India.
At Nepal's biggest hospital, in the capital Kathmandu, an outside wall has been all but covered in posters bearing the photos of bodies recovered from the calamity. Another wall, on a smaller street nearby, was starting to fill up Monday.
They are walls of the unknown dead — photos of some of the people still likely listed as missing.
Many of the images are deeply disturbing, but desperate family members have no choice but to step up to pore over the grim images, pleading for any information about missing loved ones.
In Georgia, Samarth said he was trying to keep calm, despite a lack of any information from officials in Nepal, or at home in the U.S.
"Honestly, I haven't really heard as much from the U.S. government," he said. "There's not really much else we can do except just, like, sit and pray."
Other American families with loved ones missing told CBS News over the weekend that they want more help from U.S. authorities, as well as the Chinese and Nepalese governments.
One Virginia family told CBS News on Monday they had experienced a rollercoaster of emotions as conflicting information about survivors comes out, and while some members had lost hope that a husband and wife last thought to have been in Tibet could still be found alive, others were determined to wait for confirmation.
So far, Chinese authorities have not confirmed whether any foreign tourists survived the disaster in Tibet.

Hong Kong’s flagship technology hub at the border received a better-than-expected six bids from conglomerates and hi-tech firms for its inaugural land tender by the deadline on Monday, with industry leaders describing the project as a springboard for mainland Chinese firms going global.

It added that the site sale used a weighted “two-envelope” scoring system, allocating 70 per cent to technical proposals and 30 per cent to financial offers.

Hongkonger jailed 3½ years for molesting girlfriend’s daughter, filming assaults
Defendant, 47, jailed after police found nude photo of 11-year-old girl in his wallet during response to family quarrel
A moving services manager has been sentenced to 3½ years in prison for molesting his girlfriend’s 11-year-old daughter at home and filming and photographing the assaults, with a Hong Kong judge imposing a heavier penalty to reflect the impact on the vulnerable child.
Deputy District Judge Ivy Chui Yee-mei said on Monday that a deterrent sentence was necessary for the 47-year-old defendant, whose offence was “far worse” than most indecent assault cases because he possessed 233 videos and photos taken during the attacks between August 2023 and March 2024.
Citing a psychologist’s report, Chui noted that the defendant was not a paedophile but had shown a sexual interest in his then-girlfriend’s daughter.
The defendant told the psychologist he had been under the influence of alcohol and had mistaken the girl for his girlfriend.
He pleaded guilty to 18 charges: seven counts of indecent assault and 11 counts of possession of child pornography.
He admitted using his phone to take photos and a home security camera to record videos during the assaults. A nude picture of the girl was found in his wallet when he was arrested.
The judge said that as the defendant was seen as a stepfather to the girl, the case involved a serious breach of trust.
