“What’s Wrong With That Company?” Lavrov Defends Russia’s Alliance With Iran and North Korea
Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov defended Moscow’s close ties with Iran and North Korea after being asked how the two countries had effectively become Russia’s main allies.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
During an interview with Russian broadcaster RBC on August 28, the interviewer said Russia now had “two allies—North Korea and Iran” and asked how Moscow had ended up “in such company.” The Russian Foreign Ministry later published a transcript of the exchange.
“What’s wrong with that company?” Lavrov replied. The interviewer then noted that Iran and North Korea had previously been widely regarded as pariah states and had now become Russia’s principal partners.
“They were considered pariahs by those who imagined themselves the winners of the Cold War and proclaimed the ‘end of history’ forever,” Lavrov said.
Russia has significantly expanded political and military cooperation with both countries during its war against Ukraine. North Korea has supplied Moscow with weapons and personnel, while Iran has become a key partner in Russia’s drone and defense cooperation.
Lavrov did not challenge the interviewer’s characterization of Iran and North Korea as Russia’s two main allies, instead arguing that Moscow saw no problem in its increasingly close relationship with either country.
The remarks come days after Russian State Duma Deputy Speaker Pyotr Tolstoy called for strikes on Ukrainian cities aimed at demoralizing civilians. Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry said the comments amounted to public calls for war crimes and argued they warranted scrutiny by the International Criminal Court.

Ukraine Details Russia’s 3M22 Zircon Missile and Identifies 70 Companies Behind It
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
09:58:22 UTC
18:58:22 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Details Russia’s 3M22 Zircon Missile and Identifies 70 Companies Behind It
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR) has released new details on Russia’s 3M22 Zircon missile, including its guidance system, propulsion, and the network of 70 enterprises involved in its production.
According to the statement of August 30, the intelligence agency published the information through its War&Sanctions portal as part of an ongoing effort to document Russia’s ballistic missile capabilities.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Zircon was originally developed as an anti-ship weapon for deployment aboard Russian nuclear-powered submarines and Project 22350 frigates equipped with 3S14 universal vertical launch systems, HUR reported.
However, Russia’s difficulties operating its fleet in the Black Sea during the war against Ukraine prompted it to adapt the 3M22 for launches from land-based Bastion-M missile systems, the agency said.
HUR added that the Zircon carries a warhead weighing approximately 120 kilograms, which it described as unusually small given that the 3M22 is the most expensive missile among Russia’s strike weapons. For comparison, the agency said Russia’s smaller Banderoľ cruise missile carries a 150-kilogram warhead.
The missile uses a two-stage propulsion sequence after launch. Once the 3M22 leaves its launch container aboard a vessel or from a coastal missile system, a booster motor accelerates it to the altitude and speed required to activate its main propulsion system. The booster then separates and the main sustainer motor takes over. According to HUR, both use solid propellant.
During the initial phase of flight, orientation and stabilization thrusters located on a protective fairing position the missile on course toward its designated target. The fairing subsequently separates from the missile.
Russia has claimed that the Zircon can reach speeds of up to Mach 9 during certain phases of flight. HUR, however, said the highest speed recorded to date does not exceed Mach 6.8 and is not maintained throughout the entire flight.
The 3M22 uses a combined guidance system, relying on inertial navigation during the midcourse phase before switching to an active radar seeker during the terminal stage, according to the agency. Its onboard digital computing system is the Baget-83, which HUR said is also commonly used in other Russian ballistic missiles.
The missile’s tail section contains electrohydraulic steering actuators and aerodynamic control surfaces that serve as its primary means of maneuvering. The control surfaces remain folded while the missile is inside its launch container and deploy after launch. HUR said the entire tail section of the Zircon is made of titanium.
Alongside the technical assessment, Ukrainian intelligence identified 70 Russian enterprises involved in the Zircon production chain. The companies are responsible for manufacturing the missile’s major systems and components, including its body, engines, and solid rocket propellant.
HUR also published information on officials and employees of key enterprises involved in the program, as well as foreign-made technological equipment used by the manufacturers.
The Zircon disclosure follows a similar HUR investigation into Russia’s Iskander-M ballistic missile program. Ukrainian intelligence previously released details on 35 companies linked to the production of Iskander-M missiles, shedding light on the industrial and supply networks supporting Moscow’s ballistic weapons production.

Israel and Greece sign $3.5 billion deal to build “Achilles’ Shield,” a multilayered air-defense network
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
09:58:05 UTC
18:58:05 KST

- i24NEWS
- Israel
- Diplomacy & defense
- Israel and Greece sign 10-billion-shekel deal for multilayered air-defense shield
Israel and Greece sign 10-billion-shekel deal for multilayered air-defense shield
The program will include the transfer of technology and expertise to Greek companies, supporting local production and maintenance capabilities
Israel and Greece expanded their security partnership on Monday by signing a major air-defense agreement valued at approximately $3.5 billion, or more than 10 billion shekels.
Known in Greece as “Achilles’ Shield,” the program will create a multilayered defense network built largely around Israeli technology. It is designed to protect Greece against a range of threats, including ballistic missiles, drones and aircraft.
The agreement was signed in Tel Aviv by Israeli Defense Ministry Director General Maj. Gen. (res.) Amir Baram and Greek defense procurement chief Yannis Boras. Senior government officials and executives from Israel’s leading defense companies attended the ceremony.
The planned network will incorporate several Israeli systems, including Rafael’s David’s Sling and Spyder platforms and Israel Aerospace Industries’ BARAK MX. Elta Systems, an IAI subsidiary, will provide multimission MMR radars.
A new national command-and-control platform will connect the various components, allowing Greek forces to manage the country’s air defenses through a unified system.
The broader deal includes a separate $30 million contract for Rafael’s Drone Dome counter-drone systems, which will be used to defend strategic sites.
Israel and Greece also intend to deepen cooperation between their defense industries. The program will include the transfer of technology and expertise to Greek companies, supporting local production and maintenance capabilities.
Described as one of the largest military procurement agreements in Greek history, Achilles’ Shield reflects the countries’ growing strategic relationship in the Eastern Mediterranean.
The deal also comes amid continuing tensions between Greece and Turkey, as Athens moves to accelerate the modernization of its air and missile defenses.

The City of Copenhagen is ready to send more displaced Ukrainians to Jutland after five Jutland mayors opposed the government’s bill to halt immigration from 14 Ukrainian regions in Jyllands-Posten.
Andreas Keil, Social Democrats, Mayor of Employment, Integration, and Business, wrote this in a letter to the mayors.
“If you have the opportunity to receive a number of displaced Ukrainians, it will be a great help to Copenhagen,” he wrote in the letter.
He further writes that it will simultaneously be a concrete contribution to the redistribution among municipalities that Minister for Immigration and Integration Morten Bødskov (Social Democrats as well) has previously requested.
“I understand it to mean that the five Jutland municipalities would like more settlement, labor, and have more opportunities to accommodate the newcomers, while we, conversely, in Copenhagen are challenged to find accommodation for more than the 3,800 Ukrainians we already accommodate now,” he stated.
The letter has been sent to the mayors of Hjørring, Lemvig, Vesthimmerland, Skive, and Brønderslev Municipality, respectively.

Parents at Tel Aviv school strike over migrant children's admission
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
09:46:20 UTC
18:46:20 KST

The parents’ committee at the new Ronit Elkabetz secondary school in southern Tel Aviv, Israel, announced that it would shut down classes on Tuesday over the admission of migrant children to the school.
In a letter to the Tel Aviv municipality, the parents accused the city of having "failed" to uphold the admissions policy agreed upon with them, which they claimed had resulted in "unequal treatment of children from the Kfar Shalem neighbourhood."
The parents said they would continue the strike until their demands were addressed, Israeli newspaper Haaretz reported on Sunday.
The municipality rejected the parents’ claims, saying migrant children would comprise less than 10 percent of the school’s student body.
In a letter to the municipality last month, parents alleged that migrant children had been admitted without meeting the same requirements as other applicants, according to the report.
"Only after registration ended did it become clear that students from families of asylum seekers, refugees and migrant workers had also been placed at the school – material information that was not disclosed to parents in advance, thereby denying them the opportunity to make an informed decision," they wrote.
This "could directly harm the future of our children and of the institution as a whole," the parents committee said.
The municipality rejected the allegations, saying the migrant students had not been admitted to or placed in the school’s arts programmes.
"Therefore, the claim that these students were placed in a specialised track without meeting its admissions requirements is incorrect," it stated.
The dispute comes weeks after Israel’s Supreme Court ruled that the concentration of migrant children in two south Tel Aviv schools constituted racial segregation and ordered authorities to integrate them into other schools.
The case also follows years of controversy over the segregation of non-Israeli children in Tel Aviv's education system.
The municipality has previously faced legal challenges over schools attended almost exclusively by children of asylum seekers and migrant workers, with petitioners arguing that the city must integrate them with Israeli students under the principle of equality.
The Tel Aviv municipality said in response that every child in the city is entitled to compulsory education "regardless of religion, race or sex."

Israel, Greece sign $3.5 billion air defense deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
09:46:17 UTC
18:46:17 KST

- Israel and Greece signed a €3 billion defense export deal called "Achilles Shield" for a multi-layered Israeli-built air defense array.
- The deal includes David's Sling, SPYDER, BARAK MX, MMR radars, a new command system, and a separate €26 million Drone Dome contract.
Israel and Greece signed a defense export agreement worth approximately €3 billion ($3.5 billion) Monday, under which Israel will build Greece a multi-layered air defense array combining several Israeli-made systems, according to a statement from Israel’s Ministry of Defense.
The deal, known in Greece as “Achilles Shield,” is the largest defense export agreement in the history of Israel-Greece relations and one of the largest in Israel’s history, according to the ministry. Israel’s Ministry of Defense Director General, Maj. Gen. (Res.) Amir Baram, signed the agreement with his Greek counterpart, Ioannis Bouras, at a ceremony at the ministry’s headquarters.
The array includes the David’s Sling missile defense system, developed by Israel’s Missile Defense Organization with Rafael as prime developer, along with Rafael’s SPYDER air defense system. It also includes the BARAK MX system, built by Israel Aerospace Industries, and MMR multi-mission radars for air surveillance, manufactured by ELTA Systems, an IAI subsidiary. Rafael will separately develop a new national command and control system intended to integrate the full range of air defense capabilities under the program.
A supplementary contract worth €26 million ($30 million) was signed alongside the main deal for Rafael’s Drone Dome systems, intended to defend strategic sites in Greece against drones.
Greece is the second European country to acquire the David’s Sling system, according to Rafael Chairman Yuval Steinitz. The ministry described the program as the first time it will supply a country with a complete air defense array covering threats ranging from ballistic missiles to hostile drones.
“My visit to Greece a few months ago, as the guest of Greek Defense Minister Dendias, was another expression of the depth of the strategic relationship between Israel and Greece and of our shared determination to keep strengthening it,” said Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz.
“The ‘Achilles Shield’ deal is a strategic milestone in Israel’s defense relationship with Greece, reflecting the deep trust our partners around the world place in Israel’s technological edge and the proven track record of our defense systems in the field,” said Baram.
IAI Chairman Boaz Levy referenced the company’s systems performing during recent fighting against Iran and its proxies.
“IAI’s operational air defense systems proved their capabilities in the recent fighting against Iran and its proxies, successfully intercepting a range of threats, chief among them exo-atmospheric ballistic missiles,” Levy said.
The agreement includes a broader industrial cooperation component. Israel’s Ministry of Defense said it will expand defense industrial cooperation with Greece, including the transfer of knowledge and technology to Greek industry, as part of ongoing government-to-government dialogue between the two countries’ defense ministries.
The Israeli ministry has operated under what it described as an emergency production framework since the outbreak of the war in Gaza, combining output for the Israel Defense Forces with continued exports to partner countries. The ministry attributed part of Greece’s decision to Israeli systems’ battlefield performance during that conflict and the broader regional fighting involving Iran.

In Kyiv, various possible formats for organizing the educational process have been developed. Schools plan to begin the first week of the academic year in a blended in-person and remote format

"The city has identified various options — from holding classes in shelters for younger schoolchildren to blended or remote learning. The possibility of operating in a second shift is also being considered," the Kyiv City State Administration stated.

First exam reforms, now 'school thik karo' campaign: How CJP is changing the discourse of politics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
09:36:24 UTC
18:36:24 KST

First exam reforms, now 'school thik karo' campaign: How CJP is changing the discourse of politics
Kunal Varma / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 31, 2026, 18:48 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
NEW DELHI: From colleges to schools. From Gen Z to Gen Alpha. From Jantar Mantar to cities and villages in states. The students’ protest has continued; only the stage has shifted. The Cockroach Janata Party’s (CJP) “School Thik Karo” campaign has put the spotlight on the sorry condition of government schools in many states. Gen Z showed the way from Jantar Mantar when they forced the NDA government to make Dharmendra Pradhan resign over NEET paper leaks. Gen Alpha took the cue and brought the protests to villages and towns across states, demanding better school infrastructure and government accountability.The CJP campaign asking for school audits in villages got a huge response. The pictures and videos of schools uploaded on CJP’s X timeline exposed the sorry state of government schools across states. This was followed by ground inspections by CJP teams, which led to confrontation and a strong pushback by some state governments.Two days after the CJP launched its campaign and announced that schools in Rajasthan would be on its radar, the state education department issued new guidelines regulating the entry of outsiders, including media personnel, into government schools.
Under the directives, photography, videography, interviews, audio recording and live streaming involving students or school activities on campus needed prior permission from the school principal or head of the institution.
The Rajasthan order went on to threaten action under applicable laws in case of any breach.So, when a CJP team went to inspect a government school on August 21, it was attacked and forcibly pushed back, allegedly by the locals. Videos of the incident showed a large number of people engaging in a heated exchange with the CJP team, pushing and shoving its members as they tried to enter the village. Some clips also showed stone-pelting and smashed windows of cars. Locals said the village did not need outside political groups to intervene in the school’s affairs.
This perhaps became the July 20 Jantar Mantar moment (when Delhi Police used force to stop Gen Z protesters from their Sansad march) of the CJP school campaign as the violent confrontation propelled the issue to the national centre stage.
School students protest in UP
Meanwhile in Uttar Pradesh, Gen Alpha students of a government school staged a protest twice, in a span of four days. over shortage of subject teachers. They briefly blocked traffic also. Students of a government school in Kannauj boycotted classes and held protests against the principal for alleged caste discrimination and ordering the felling of trees inside the school campus. The students of PM Shri Composite School in Gugarapur surrounded the vehicle of the in-charge principal at the school gate as he was leaving and raised slogans against him.Protests also happened in Fatehpur, Hamirpur against lack of facilities in schools. In Hamirpur, 'Gen Alpha' children laid siege to the collectorate to demand the construction of a paved road to their school.In Unnao, hundreds of students of a government-run residential school staged a protest over alleged poor-quality food, inadequate drinking water, shortage of teachers and the behaviour of the principal, briefly disrupting traffic at a city crossing.
'Ministers’ dogs got better facilities than students'
In Maharashtra, CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke conducted a social audit of government-run and municipal schools in Latur district. He led a team at a Zilla Parishad school at Ujani village in Latur's Ausa tehsil.After his audit, Dipke said schools in the state were in a pitiable condition, and even "ministers’ dogs got better facilities" than students. He sought the resignation of Maharashtra school education minister Dada Bhuse. Later, Maharashtra police registered a case against the CJP convenor and others for allegedly entering a government school without permission, disrupting official work and threatening teachers.
The state governments cited rules to browbeat the CJP teams away from its schools. But at the same time, they were forced to act to nullify the impact of the CJP campaign. So, while some states announced new measures to improve the condition of schools, others increased the pace of work already underway to ensure that results were seen on the ground quickly.
CJP claims credit
The CJP was quick to claim credit for govt actions and basked in glory.“The impact we’ve been able to make with such a small team in such a short span of time is just unreal. Multiple state governments have had to bow down. Authorities had to listen to Gen Z and Gen Alpha kids and give them their due,” it said in a post on X.
“But this does not end here. We need to keep going until even the remotest regions of the nation, even the most deprived communities, have access to the highest standard of educational facilities. They may use force, they may file cases, they may do whatever they can to crush this, but we will remain committed to the same demand,” the post read.
Political parties take a cue from CJP
While it can be debated whether or not the CJP campaign forced the governments into action, what can be said with certainty is that the CJP has managed to do what many political parties could not - inspire the youth to come to the streets and seek accountability from power.The two CJP campaigns also point to an interesting shift - which should be a learning lesson, especially for parties in the opposition space. We have seen the opposition parties raise the pitch against government on issues like caste and religion as these have greater potential for voter mobilisation. Rarely do we see campaigns by the opposition parties centred around health or education reforms. But that seems to have changed.
Youth outreach
The Congress has taken a cue and is trying to stay focused on students’ connect and raise issues that concern the youth. In Rajasthan, the state Congress unit is also on the streets to highlight gaps in state government school infrastructure.And it’s not just the opposition that is course-correcting; the ruling BJP has also drawn a roadmap to engage with the youth and understand their concerns. In the middle of the Gen Z protest, Prime Minister Narendra Modi debuted on Instagram and tried to communicate directly with the youth who were on the streets. The BJP has in fact formed a dedicated team to spearhead its Gen Z outreach. The team includes BJP chief Nitin Nabin, national general secretaries Smriti Irani and Vinod Tawde, Gujarat minister Harsh Sanghavi, Chhattisgarh minister OP Choudhary, along with several other leaders.
Clearly, the CJP has managed to change the political discourse and has put the focus on the youth as potential game-changers in electoral politics. As we gear up for the next rounds of assembly elections in the run-up to the 2029 Lok Sabha challenge, we may see youth outreach taking centre stage like never before.

As China-US space race heats up, Shanghai unveils space-computing hub
Songjiang is already a vital link in China’s satellite supply chain as home to SpaceSail, the low-Earth-orbit challenger to SpaceX’s Starlink
The dedicated centre in the city’s southwestern Songjiang district, unveiled at the forum on Sunday, brought together aerospace developers, semiconductor makers, artificial intelligence specialists, cloud vendors, as well as researchers and investors to advance in-orbit data processing, local news outlet Shanghai Observer reported.
Space computing enables satellites to analyse data in orbit, reducing the need to transmit raw files back to ground stations and speeding up real-time intelligence. More ambitious long-term plans envision orbital data centres powered by solar energy to ease pressure on land-based power grids.
Having launched over 200 satellites to date, SpaceSail aims to deploy a 15,000-satellite mega-constellation by the end of 2030. By comparison, Starlink has placed over 11,000 satellites in orbit to date, serving customers across more than 150 countries and territories.
Songjiang is also home to satellite manufacturers including Gesi Aerospace and Xuntian Qianhe, as well as the Shanghai Aerospace Precision Machinery Research Institute.

Spain signs K9 howitzer export contract with Hanwha
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
09:30:01 UTC
18:30:01 KST

- Hanwha Aerospace signed an export contract with Spain's Indra Sistemas for K9 self-propelled howitzers on August 31, marking the system's first Western European sale.
- Spain becomes the 11th country to operate the K9, joining Poland, Romania, Turkey, Finland, Estonia, Norway, Australia, India, Egypt and South Korea.
South Korea’s Hanwha Aerospace signed a contract to export K9 self-propelled howitzers to Spain, bringing the number of countries operating the K9 to 11 worldwide.
The contract was signed with Indra Sistemas, Spain’s state-linked defense electronics company, according to a regulatory filing Hanwha disclosed August 31. Hanwha did not disclose the contract’s value, unit count or delivery schedule, citing confidentiality provisions.
Under the payment terms, Hanwha will receive an initial payment equal to 20 percent of the contract value immediately after signing, followed by an additional 5 percent by the end of the year. The remaining payment schedule was not disclosed.
The contract follows a binding memorandum of understanding Indra and Hanwha signed in March, under which the two companies agreed to jointly develop a new family of tracked artillery vehicles for the Spanish Armed Forces based on the K9 platform. That earlier agreement outlined a program covering 128 tracked artillery vehicles, 120 ammunition resupply vehicles, 21 recovery vehicles and 11 command-and-control vehicles, tied to a Spanish artillery modernization effort with a budget reported at €4.55 billion ($5.3 billion).
Under the arrangement, Indra will manufacture the vehicle hulls in Spain and retain design authority over them, while integrating its own mission systems, battlefield management software and communications equipment. Hanwha’s K9 platform will provide the base for the vehicles’ long-range indirect fire capability.
Spain’s approach differs from how South Korea has typically structured K9 export deals. According to earlier reporting, Spain sought a deeper form of technology transfer than Hanwha has granted previous customers, including design authority held by a Spanish contractor rather than Hanwha itself, along with rights to export the resulting system to third countries. Analysts have said the structure of the Spanish deal could serve as a template for how Hanwha negotiates future K9 sales in Europe, including potential follow-on deals with Poland and Romania.
The K9 is a 155mm tracked self-propelled howitzer with a combat weight of 46.3 tonnes (51 tons), a top road speed of 67 km/h (42 mph) and an operational range of 360 kilometers (224 miles). The system has become South Korea’s most successful defense export, helping make the country the second-largest arms supplier to European NATO members behind the United States.
Ten countries currently operate the K9: Australia, India, Egypt, Norway, Poland, South Korea, Romania, Turkey, Finland and Estonia. Romania signed a $940 million contract for the system in 2023. South Korean media reported last year that Vietnam had separately agreed to acquire 20 K9 units, though that deal was not among the 11 countries Hanwha counted in Monday’s disclosure.
Hanwha has not disclosed a delivery timeline for the K9 systems covered under the Spanish contract, the specific number of vehicles included, or whether the export approval process in South Korea, a required step before the technology transfer can proceed, has been completed.

Huang Kuo-chang wins damages over reports alleging he recruited hackers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
09:27:27 UTC
18:27:27 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — TPP Chair Huang Kuo-chang (黃國昌) won a defamation lawsuit Monday against Mirror Media over reports accusing him of organizing an army of internet trolls and selling sensitive information obtained through hackers.
During an investigation into the hacking of Radio Taiwan International’s website, Mirror Media interviewed suspect and engineer Wu Cheng-hsun (吳政勳) and published a series of reports alleging that Huang maintained an army of hackers. Huang subsequently sued the publication, seeking NT$5 million (US$157,703) in damages, the removal of related materials, and publication of the ruling on Mirror Media’s website for 30 days, per UDN.
Citing Mirror Media’s reporting, DPP lawmaker Lin Chu-yin (林楚茵) suggested in October 2025 that Huang was at the helm of an army of hackers, adding that the DPP legislative caucus had reported the allegations to the Control Yuan. DPP lawmaker Wu Szu-yao (吳思瑤) lamented that there were no mechanisms to punish at-large legislators for misconduct.
The court ruled Monday that Mirror Media and the journalists responsible for the reports must pay NT$360,000 and NT$180,000, respectively, while NT$60,000 must be paid to Huang’s then-assistant, Cheng Kai-yeh (鄭凱燁), per Tai Sounds. The court also ordered Mirror Media to remove the related materials from its website and publish the verdict for 30 days.
Mirror Media said in a statement that it had repeatedly verified the information Wu provided before publishing the reports. It argued that because a news organization does not operate like a judicial fact-finding body, it should not be required to prove with absolute certainty that the claims in a report are true.
Mirror Media said in a follow-up statement that it would appeal the ruling, citing the need to uphold press freedom.
During court proceedings, Wu changed his account, claiming that he had told reporters what they wanted to hear so Mirror Media would report his allegations concerning RTI, per ETtoday. He testified that, as far as he knew, Huang did not maintain hackers to steal sensitive information or obtain personal information by hacking household registration agencies.
Wu also said Huang had not recruited hackers in the name of exposing corruption and that Wu himself was not a hacker. In its defense, Mirror Media said it had conducted due diligence in verifying Wu’s information, pointing to a recording of his interview as evidence, per ETtoday.
Commenting on the ruling, Huang said the damage had already been done, per Newtalk. He said Taiwan’s media environment must improve or democracy could suffer.
Huang has also prevailed in lawsuits brought by Mirror Media over his description of the outlet as “gutter press” and other criticisms, per Liberty Times.
In one such case, the court ruled that, given the controversy surrounding Mirror Media’s reporting on the corruption case involving TPP founder Ko Wen-je (柯文哲), Huang’s comments, though unpleasant, were protected speech.

18:27:16 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Kaohsiung will step up efforts to control its invasive green iguana population in September by offering NT$300 (US$9.46) vouchers for each qualifying adult iguana removed by trained and certified members of the public.
The Kaohsiung City Government Agriculture Bureau said the new strategy will shift the focus from maximizing the number of iguanas removed to targeting mature animals capable of reproduction, per CNA. The city will prioritize iguanas with a snout-to-vent length of at least 30 centimeters.
The bureau said it is prioritizing mature iguanas to make better use of limited manpower rather than spending resources primarily on juveniles, which have a relatively low chance of surviving to adulthood. Juvenile green iguanas face threats from predators, food availability, and environmental conditions, and their first-year survival rate is less than 5%.
Green iguanas enter their breeding season from about October through February. During this time, males develop orange-red coloration and display more pronounced territorial and courtship behavior.
These changes during mating season can provide clues for identifying adult iguanas and breeding hotspots. Females reach sexual maturity at about 2 to 3 years old and can lay up to 70 to 80 eggs in a clutch, according to the Kaohsiung Museum.
Kaohsiung had removed 27,654 green iguanas as of Aug. 25, with Niaosong District accounting for the largest number at 9,661. Daliao District followed with 4,145, while Linyuan District recorded 3,644, per the Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency.
The Agriculture Bureau said it has conducted five training sessions for members of the public, with 626 people completing the training and obtaining capture identification certificates. Other southern Taiwan counties and cities will adopt a similar voucher system targeting adult green iguanas to strengthen regional control efforts, the bureau said.
The Forestry and Nature Conservation Agency said local governments removed about 260,000 green iguanas nationwide last year, a record and roughly three times the 2024 total. Pingtung County recorded the most removals, with 130,288, followed by Kaohsiung with 62,608.
Green iguanas have also been reported as far north as Miaoli and Hsinchu. The agency has been working with local governments to strengthen patrols and prevent their further spread. Native to tropical regions of Central and South America, green iguanas can grow to between 1.8 and 2 meters long, with the tail accounting for about two-thirds of their total length.

NASA’s Roman Space Telescope launches to reveal the Universe’s darkest secrets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
09:23:21 UTC
18:23:21 KST

NASA’s Roman Space Telescope launches to reveal the Universe’s darkest secrets
NASA’s newly launched Roman Space Telescope is heading a million miles from Earth to map the universe at extraordinary speed and uncover some of its deepest mysteries.
- Date:
- August 31, 2026
- Source:
- NASA
- Summary:
- NASA’s Roman Space Telescope has launched on a million mile journey to L2, where it will scan huge portions of the cosmos for clues about dark matter, dark energy, and distant worlds. With survey speeds roughly 1,000 times faster than Hubble and a torrent of 1.4 terabytes of data per day, Roman could uncover cosmic surprises astronomers have never seen before.
- Share:
NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope has begun a three-month journey covering roughly one million miles as it travels toward its final orbit. The observatory lifted off at 7:26 a.m. EDT Sunday aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket from Launch Complex 39A at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida.
Once operational, Roman will combine sharp infrared vision with an unusually wide view of the sky. That combination will allow astronomers to examine enormous regions of space while also looking far back into cosmic history. Among its primary goals are studying dark matter, dark energy, and worlds outside of our solar system, known as exoplanets. Its sweeping observations are also expected to support many discoveries beyond those central objectives.
"Roman is exactly the kind of success story we want to see across NASA," said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. "Delivered ahead of schedule and on budget, this mission reflects more than a decade of dedication from the NASA workforce and our industry partners. Now, Roman will give us a new atlas of the universe, push the boundaries of discovery, and demonstrate what is possible when America's space program pairs bold ambition with disciplined execution."
Roman Begins Its Journey Into Deep Space
Controllers at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, started receiving telemetry from Roman just seven minutes after launch. Falcon Heavy operated as planned and separated from the observatory 31 minutes after liftoff. After detaching from the rocket's center core, the two boosters returned safely to the launch site, where they can be refurbished.
"Roman will be a discovery machine that will bring us closer than ever before to answering humanity's most profound questions about our cosmic history," said Nicky Fox, associate administrator for the Science Mission Directorate at NASA Headquarters in Washington. "With its large field of view and fast survey speeds, Roman will usher us into a new era of discovery and make the invisible visible, setting the foundation for humanity's search for life beyond our solar system."
During the first part of the mission, Roman communicates with controllers using the Near Space Network, a system of ground stations and relay satellites that handles tracking, telemetry, and commands. Roughly 70 minutes after launch, communications shift to NASA's Deep Space Network, which will help guide the observatory toward the second Sun-Earth Lagrange point, or L2, about one million miles from Earth.
L2 is a region where the gravitational influences of the Sun and Earth allow spacecraft to maintain a relatively stable position with limited fuel use. Roman will first communicate through the Canberra Deep Space Communication Complex in Australia. Approximately six hours later, communications will transfer to the Madrid Deep Space Communication Complex in Spain and then to the Goldstone Deep Space Communication Complex in California. Together, these facilities will help maintain continuous contact with the spacecraft during its journey.
Key Systems Deploy After Launch
One hour and 23 minutes after launch, the Roman team confirmed that the observatory's solar panels and lower instrument sun shade had deployed successfully.
Over the next several days, Roman's high-gain antenna and visor-like deployable aperture cover will also deploy. Mission controllers will carry out the first of two course corrections, and Roman's Coronagraph Instrument will be switched on.
The Coronagraph Instrument will demonstrate technology that could eventually be used by future missions such as NASA's Habitable Worlds Observatory concept to directly photograph planets resembling Earth. Directly imaging such planets is extraordinarily difficult because a host star can be billions of times brighter than the planet orbiting it. A coronagraph helps by blocking much of the star's light so that nearby planets become easier to detect. Roman will move that technology forward by capturing images of planets similar in size to Jupiter.
A 300 Megapixel View of the Cosmos
A few weeks into the journey, Roman's main scientific instrument, the Wide Field Instrument, will be activated.
The instrument is a 300 megapixel infrared camera equipped with 18 4K detectors, each roughly the size of a saltine cracker. Those detectors will gather photons from distant astronomical objects and turn them into detailed panoramas of the cosmos.
Roman was designed to remain optically stable while rapidly moving from one observation to another. That means it can cover huge portions of the sky without lengthy pauses between observations. NASA says the telescope is designed to survey the universe about 1,000 times faster than the Hubble Space Telescope.
This speed is one of Roman's defining advantages. Hubble can capture extremely detailed images of relatively small areas of the sky, while Roman is designed to combine similarly sharp views with a much larger field of view. That should allow astronomers to study enormous numbers of galaxies, stars, and planets in a fraction of the time previously required.
First Roman Images Expected in Early 2027
For the remainder of its three-month commissioning period, scientists and engineers will carefully test and calibrate Roman's instruments. These procedures are designed to make sure the observatory is operating precisely before its full science program begins.
NASA expects to release Roman's first images in early 2027.
Once science operations are underway, Roman will transmit about 1.4 terabytes of data to Earth every day. That is the highest daily data rate yet for a NASA astrophysics mission. The enormous volume of information will require more than traditional analysis alone.
Machine learning, artificial intelligence, and citizen scientists will help researchers search through Roman's observations and identify potentially important discoveries. Astronomers can then investigate the most promising findings in greater detail.
"We've never been able to view the universe with eyes like Roman's before," said Julie McEnery, Roman's senior project scientist at NASA Goddard. "There's no telling what more we'll know and have seen by this time next year."
A Major New NASA Astrophysics Mission
Roman is the fourth primary NASA mission to launch aboard a Falcon Heavy rocket. Earlier this year, NASA's Launch Services Program worked with SpaceX to move the launch date forward after the telescope was completed earlier than expected.
NASA Goddard manages the Roman mission, with participation from the agency's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California; Caltech/IPAC in Pasadena, California; the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore; and scientists from a range of research institutions.
The mission's main industrial partners are BAE Systems Inc., L3Harris Technologies, and Teledyne Scientific & Imaging. International contributions also come from ESA, JAXA, the French space agency CNES (Centre National d'Études Spatiales), and the Max Planck Institute for Astronomy in Germany.

AI models pose new risks to global financial stability, Bank of England chief warns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
09:23:13 UTC
18:23:13 KST

Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey has warned that increasingly capable artificial intelligence (AI) models could pose new risks to the global financial system, particularly by increasing the scale and speed of cyber threats, The Guardian reported on Monday.
Bailey, who chairs the Financial Stability Board (FSB), raised the concerns in a letter to G20 finance ministers and central bank governors ahead of their meeting in North Carolina, US.
He said “frontier” AI models, the most advanced systems at the leading edge of AI development, were demonstrating increasingly sophisticated autonomy and threat capabilities.
Bailey warned that cyber disruption involving such systems could have broader consequences because global financial markets and services are highly interconnected.
He also said many countries did not yet have protocols for managing the development, release and deployment of advanced AI models.
“Frontier AI may have the ability materially to alter the speed, scale and economics of cyber-risk, which could undermine market confidence system-wide, especially due to highly concentrated third-party service providers,” Bailey said.
Bailey called for “appropriate steps to support safe and responsible model release and deployment on a global basis”.
Other financial vulnerabilities
The governor also highlighted other vulnerabilities in financial markets, including increased leverage in bond and equity markets and high valuations in concentrated markets.
He said some of those valuations were partly driven by investor optimism over AI.
“I remain concerned therefore that a large shock or combination of shocks could concurrently trigger multiple vulnerabilities,” Bailey said.
Bailey has served as governor of the Bank of England since March 2020 and was appointed chair of the FSB last year.
The FSB coordinates the work of national financial authorities and international standard-setting bodies on policies aimed at maintaining global financial stability.

Russia details roles for its two-seat Su-57D fighter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
09:18:50 UTC
18:18:50 KST

- Rostec says the two-seat Su-57D will train pilots in specialized flight regimes and serve as an airborne control platform for uncrewed aircraft.
- Some analysts believe the program was built partly to support export contracts, with India cited as a country interested in a two-seat variant.
Russia’s state defense conglomerate Rostec disclosed new details this week on the two-seat Su-57D fighter, a designation in which the “D” likely stands for “Demonstrator,” saying the aircraft is intended for two main roles: training pilots on flight regimes that cannot be replicated on ground simulators, and serving as an airborne control platform for uncrewed aircraft.
The two-seat prototype, which first flew in May, is currently undergoing flight testing. Rostec described the aircraft’s second role as central to what it called sixth-generation technology, since the rear cockpit allows the fighter to function as an airborne command post for drone operations.
“This is important for controlling highly intelligent systems such as the Okhotnik, as well as swarm and group systems, when the attention of the main pilot and crew is focused on carrying out the primary combat mission,” said Mikhail Strelets, director of the Sukhoi Design Bureau, part of Russia’s United Aircraft Corporation, speaking on the program “Military Acceptance.”
Rostec said the two-seat variant will also serve as a testbed for combat artificial intelligence systems currently under development by specialists at United Aircraft Corporation.
The aircraft flying today was not built from scratch. Aviation researcher Andreas Rupprecht identified the prototype by its bort number, 055 Blue, matching the fifth Su-57 flight-test prototype, T-50-5, which suffered a severe engine fire on the runway at Zhukovsky in 2014, reportedly witnessed by an Indian delegation. The airframe was rebuilt as T-50-5R and has now been reconfigured with a second cockpit rather than replaced with new-build hardware.
Some Western defense analysts and outlets, including The Defence Blog, have described the two-seat program’s public framing as only part of the picture. Analysts have suggested the aircraft was built in connection with a series of potential export contracts, intended to demonstrate the program’s readiness to prospective foreign buyers rather than to meet a purely domestic training requirement. India has been named as a country with particular interest in a two-seat configuration, drawing on its operational experience flying the two-seat Su-30MKI.
Russia and India signed a contract in 2010 for preliminary design work on the Fifth Generation Fighter Aircraft, a joint program based on the T-50 prototype that specifically required a two-seat variant. India withdrew from that program in 2018 following disputes over cost, workshare and the aircraft’s stealth performance. Russia has continued pitching a two-seat Su-57 to India in 2026, presenting the offer at the Wings India exhibition in Hyderabad, including proposed technology transfer and integration of Indian-origin weapons such as BrahMos and Astra missiles, according to Indian defense reporting. India has not indicated whether it will accept.
The two-seat prototype’s tail carries a logo depicting both the Su-57 silhouette and the S-70 Okhotnik stealth drone, a visual pairing that matches Rostec’s stated goal of using the aircraft to coordinate crewed and uncrewed formations.
Rostec has not disclosed a production timeline, a finalized designation for the aircraft, referred to variously as Su-57D or Su-57UB in Russian reporting, or a target date for integrating the combat AI systems it says the program will help develop.

What to watch at SCO summit as Eurasian bloc marks 25th anniversary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
09:16:18 UTC
18:16:18 KST

Some of Eurasia's most powerful leaders are meeting for a two-day event in the Kyrgyzstan capital Bishkek, bringing together a mix of bilateral ties, longstanding rivalries and regional conflicts.
Chinese President Xi Jinping, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Russian President Vladimir Putin will be among those attending the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Heads of State summit, which marks the group's 25th anniversary.
The gathering comes amid a tentative thaw in China-India relations following years of border tensions, as India and Pakistan navigate the aftermath of their brief conflict last year.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian will also attend as Tehran faces ongoing confrontation with Washington and growing US economic pressure, while conflicts and instability stretching from the Middle East and Ukraine to Afghanistan are expected to feature in discussions.
The meeting comes as SCO members seek to capitalise on shifting global economic and geopolitical dynamics by strengthening trade, transport links and economic cooperation across Eurasia.
SCO as united front against West
The SCO has historically focused on economic issues, but Putin and Xi have also used the summit to promote their vision of a multipolar world and to present a united front against the West.
The SCO’s founding declaration says the group is “not an alliance directed against other states”.
However, at last year’s gathering, Putin accused Western countries of provoking the Ukraine war, while Xi denounced “acts of intimidation”, referring to US-Chinese tensions.
The meeting comes after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Sunday that he would encourage G20 members to re-examine terms of trade with China, denouncing Beijing’s $1.2 trillion global trade surplus as unsustainable.
Diplomacy to watch in Bishkek
One of the most closely watched encounters will be between Xi and Modi as Asia's two most populous countries seek to build on a tentative thaw after years of tensions over their disputed Himalayan border.
Senior Chinese and Indian officials held another round of boundary talks in Beijing on August 25, agreeing to continue efforts toward a settlement and maintain stability along the frontier.
Relations deteriorated sharply after deadly border clashes in 2020, making the leaders' interactions in Bishkek an opportunity to gauge how far the recent improvement in ties has progressed.
The interaction between Xi and Putin will also offer a window into the increasingly close relationship between China and Russia and how the two powers coordinate within the SCO.
The gathering will also put the leaders of India and Pakistan in the same room just more than a year after the two nuclear-armed neighbours fought a brief conflict.
Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif is slated to attend, bringing him together with Modi as tensions persist between the two countries, primarily over Kashmir.
Another leader to watch will be Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, who is scheduled to meet Putin on the sidelines of the summit, according to Iran's official IRNA news agency.
His visit comes as the US threatens increased secondary sanctions against countries and entities that continue doing business with Tehran.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan will address the summit session to be held in an expanded format and hold bilateral meetings with participating leaders on Tuesday.
What’s on the official agenda?
According to the SCO Secretariat, leaders are expected to discuss major regional and international security challenges, including wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, the situation in Afghanistan and India's relations with China and Pakistan.
The Eurasian organisation has taken a more visible collective position in 2026 on Iran and the broader Middle East, including Israel’s war on Gaza, calling for restraint, dialogue and political and diplomatic solutions.
At a July meeting, SCO foreign ministers expressed particular concern over developments in the Middle East and around Iran, reiterating that international conflicts should be settled through political and diplomatic means in accordance with international law and the UN Charter.
Afghanistan remains a longstanding regional priority, particularly because of concerns over terrorism, drug trafficking and cross-border security.
Ukraine is also expected to feature in discussions, though there has been no indication that the war will be a separate focus of the summit.
Counterterrorism remains a core area of cooperation through the SCO's Regional Anti-Terrorist Structure, based in Tashkent. The summit is expected to approve its plans for the coming year, including possible joint exercises.
Economic connectivity will be another major focus, with transport infrastructure and a proposed SCO Development Bank among the projects under discussion.
One major transport project involving SCO members is the 7,200-kilometre International North-South Transport Corridor, which links St. Petersburg with Mumbai through Iran and ports on the Gulf. The future of this corridor amid the ongoing US-Israeli war on Iran is also likely to be discussed among the leaders in Bishkek.
The organisation also agreed in 2025 to establish a network of Silk Road Stations to support international freight traffic across Eurasia.
Members are meanwhile continuing talks on establishing an SCO Development Bank. A fourth round of consultations was held in Shenzhen in June, though its structure and operating arrangements remain under negotiation.
What is the SCO?
The SCO traces its roots to the "Shanghai Five," established in 1996 by China, Russia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan to reduce military tensions and address border disputes following the breakup of the Soviet Union.
Uzbekistan joined when the SCO was formally established in 2001, and the grouping remained largely centred on China, Russia and Central Asia for much of its early history.
Its international profile grew significantly with its expansion in 2017, when India and Pakistan became full members, followed by Iran in 2023 and Belarus in 2024.
For Iran, membership marked a major diplomatic opening after years of geopolitical isolation, while Belarus's accession reflected its broader pivot toward non-Western partners.
Today, the Eurasian organisation has 10 members: Russia, China, India, Pakistan, Iran, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Uzbekistan and Belarus.
Turkmenistan is the only Central Asian country outside the SCO, reflecting its longstanding policy of permanent neutrality. Afghanistan and Mongolia have observer status, while dialogue partners include Türkiye, Azerbaijan and Saudi Arabia.
Together, SCO members have a population of around 3.4 billion, span a vast stretch of Eurasia and account for around 25 percent of global GDP.
Unlike NATO, the SCO is not a military alliance, nor is it an economic union like the EU. Instead, its consensus-based structure provides a forum for security cooperation, economic ties and diplomacy among countries that do not necessarily share the same interests.
Latest SCO Summit aims
The summit is expected to produce a Bishkek Declaration marking the SCO's 25th anniversary, alongside documents on the organisation's development and regional and international issues.
It will also mark the end of Kyrgyzstan's chairmanship and the handover to Pakistan, which is set to lead the organisation for the next year and host the 2027 leaders' summit.
The SCO lacks the binding commitments of a military alliance or economic union, but its scale has made it an increasingly significant forum for dialogue across Eurasia.
The summit underscores how an organisation founded to resolve border disputes has grown into a major multilateral grouping.
Its next challenge will be turning that scale into influence while maintaining consensus among an increasingly diverse membership.

Traber, 75, has been a leading business figure for decades in St Petersburg, where he has held extensive investments in ports and logistics. He was detained in June in connection with the fatal shooting of a businessman and politician, Alexander Petrov, in 2020, Russian media reported at the time.
State-run new agencies TASS and RIA reported on Monday that all charges against Traber had been dropped and the investigation into him closed. He had already been released from pre-trial detention on health grounds, TASS said.
There was no official confirmation of the reports.
Traber first came to prominence in the 1990s, following the collapse of the Soviet Union, when he acquired control of St Petersburg's sea port and oil terminal at a time when President Vladimir Putin was a deputy mayor in the city's administration.
The Kremlin has previously denied any friendship or business connections between Traber and Putin. REUTERS

Five people complained to the Ministry of Health about the private Odrex clinic

Five citizens filed complaints with the Ministry of Health about the activities of the private Odrex clinic over the past four years. In response to these complaints, the regulator conducted unscheduled inspections of legal entities associated with the brand, and one of them had its license to practice medicine fully revoked.
Over the past four years, five citizens have contacted the Ministry of Health with complaints regarding the activities of the private Odrex clinic. At the same time, the activities of legal entities associated with the brand became the subject of unscheduled inspections by the Ministry of Health over issues concerning the quality of medical care. And after the latest appeal — a complaint from the widow of deceased patient Ihor Melai — the Ministry instructed the Odesa Regional Military Administration to conduct a clinical-expert assessment of his treatment at the "Medical House "Odrex," reports UNN.
The UNN editorial team contacted the Ministry of Health with a request after the widow of deceased Odrex patient Ihor Melai filed a complaint regarding the circumstances of her husband's treatment.
In response to the editorial team's inquiry, the Ministry of Health reported that the appeals to the Ministry concerning Odrex's activities were not isolated.
"According to the EDMS data, during the specified period, 5 citizens contacted the Ministry of Health regarding the activities of the Odrex clinic," the Ministry's response states.
Claims regarding the quality of treatment at Odrex, which in recent years have been publicly voiced by relatives of deceased patients and former patients, are not limited to the media space — appeals concerning the clinic's activities were also submitted directly to the relevant state authority.
Odrex, criminal cases and patient deaths
The name of the Odrex clinic often appears in high-profile stories connected with patient deaths and their families' claims regarding the quality of treatment.
In particular, a court hearing in a criminal case concerning the clinic's doctors Vitalii Rusakov and Maryna Bielotserkovska is ongoing in Odesa in the case involving the death of businessman Adnan Kivan. The medical professionals are accused of improper performance of their professional duties.
According to the investigation, after surgery at the Odrex clinic, businessman Adnan Kivan may not have been prescribed the necessary antibacterial therapy, and the postoperative complications may not have been properly addressed. A forensic medical examination indicates that this could have led to the development of sepsis and the patient's death. The accused do not admit guilt.
The court has now moved on to examining the evidence: medical documentation, expert conclusions, clinical protocols and other case materials. The next hearing is scheduled for September 3, 2026.

Former Rusich commander's sentence for war crimes against Ukraine reduced in Finland
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

Former Rusich commander's sentence for war crimes against Ukraine reduced in Finland
The Helsinki Court of Appeal has reduced the sentence of former Rusich Group commander Voislav Torden (Yan Petrovsky) from life imprisonment to 12 years and six months after finding him guilty of three war crimes against Ukraine instead of four.
Source: European Pravda, citing Finnish public broadcaster Yle
Details: The Helsinki Court of Appeal announced its ruling on the appeal against the original sentence handed down to Yan Petrovsky, a former commander of the Rusich Group who used the alias Voislav Torden, for war crimes committed against Ukraine in 2014.
Petrovsky was found guilty of three war crimes and sentenced to 12 years and six months in prison.
In the original ruling in March 2025, the Helsinki District Court sentenced him to life imprisonment after finding him guilty of four war crimes. He subsequently appealed, seeking either the dismissal of the charges or a reduced sentence.
The Court of Appeal ruled that the evidence did not establish beyond reasonable doubt that Petrovsky had personally shot wounded Ukrainian soldiers or that he could be considered primarily responsible for doing so. Meanwhile, the court found that he bore at least partial responsibility as a participant in the events.
The Court of Appeal also ruled that carving the symbol of the Rusich Group into the cheek of a Ukrainian soldier did not constitute a war crime. The court concluded that the available evidence indicated that the injury was superficial and did not meet the threshold for causing severe physical or mental suffering, which would have constituted a war crime.
Petrovsky was detained while attempting to enter Finland in 2023. A court refused to extradite him to Ukraine, citing poor conditions in Ukrainian prisons.

Türkiye’s trade with Turkic states rises 6.6% to $10.1B in first seven months of 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
09:08:58 UTC
18:08:58 KST

Türkiye’s trade with fellow members of the Organization of Turkic States (OTS) has risen 6.6 percent year-on-year to $10.1 billion in the first seven months of 2026, according to the Turkish Trade Ministry.
The ministry said on Monday that trade between Türkiye and other OTS members had expanded nearly twentyfold since 2002, rising from $871 million to $16.9 billion by the end of 2025.
Kazakhstan was Türkiye’s largest trading partner among OTS members last year, with bilateral trade totalling $7.8 billion.
It was followed by Azerbaijan with $4.3 billion, Uzbekistan with $3.1 billion and Kyrgyzstan with $1.6 billion.
Trade with observer countries also grows
Türkiye’s trade with OTS observer countries — Turkmenistan, Hungary and the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus — increased 6.8 percent in 2025 to $10 billion.
In January-July 2026, trade with the observer countries rose 5.1 percent from the same period a year earlier to $6.1 billion.
Annualised trade with OTS members and observer countries consequently reached $27.8 billion as of July, according to the ministry.
The OTS was established in 2009 and adopted its current name at the Istanbul Summit in 2021. Türkiye, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan are members, while Turkmenistan, Hungary and the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus have observer status.
Global production shifts to the east
The ministry said the eastward shift in the centre of global production and trade over the past quarter-century had increased the strategic importance of the Turkic region within international trade and logistics networks.
It added that opportunities offered by the Trans-Caspian East-West-Middle Corridor, commonly known as the Middle Corridor, held significant potential for deeper economic integration across the Turkic world.
The ministry said Türkiye would continue efforts to strengthen economic and commercial integration within the OTS and make effective use of the Middle Corridor’s strategic advantages.
It said these efforts would help further reinforce the Turkic world’s position in global trade.

NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court on Monday declined to intervene against Cockroach Janata Party's protest march on September 5, saying that maintenance of law and order was primarily the responsibility of the government and police.A bench of Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and Justices Joymala Bagchi and V Mohana said that there is no reason to presume that the proposed demonstration would insult in any untoward incident."We will at least, as of now, presume everybody will behave in a peaceful manner. Right now there is no compelling circumstance to assume that any untoward thing will happen," the CJI observed.The bench issued notice to the Centre and Delhi Police and posted the next hearing for September 10, along with other matters concerning the student protests.This comes after a plea was filed by retired Delhi Police officer Rajendra Singh, seeking directions to ensure that large-scale demonstrations and protest marches in sensitive areas of the national capital are held only after obtaining requisite police permissions.The counsel, appearing for Singh, urged the apex court to hear the matter on September 3, citing the proposed march and the upcoming BRICS Summit in Delhi on September 12-13.
The counsel referred to the violence during the July 20 Sansad March announced by the CJP and cautioned that another incident could occur, even if not directly attributable to the organisers.The CJI, however, said the court could not proceed on the assumption that something untoward would happen and reiterated that the police authorities were competent to deal with any law-and-order situation.
"Before us, there is no identified group. You please impress upon the Union or NCT Delhi. It's for them to maintain law and order. They should act as per law," the CJI said."They are expected to maintain law and order, and the enforcing agency has the responsibility to maintain law and order... We are expecting them to act within that framework. From both sides, we are expecting that they will respect, they will conduct themselves, and they will follow the law of the land...," he added.The CJP has announced the September 5 march in Delhi, alleging that the Centre failed to honour its commitment to withdraw cases against students who participated in the July protests over the alleged examination paper leak

Nepal flood death toll reaches 919 as thousands remain missing
Forecasters have warned that additional rain is expected in the badly affected Gyirong region
Nearly a week after a sudden and devastating flood struck Nepal and neighboring areas, authorities continue to uncover the scale of the disaster.
Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority said Monday that 919 people had been confirmed dead, while approximately 4,700 remained missing on both sides of the border. The missing reportedly include nearly 600 foreign nationals, among them one Israeli citizen.
Search-and-rescue operations are continuing as emergency teams contend with unstable terrain and the threat of further flooding.
Chinese authorities have identified eight potential danger zones, with officials describing a crater created by the initial glacier collapse as the most serious threat to a newly formed lake.
Forecasters have warned that additional rain is expected in the badly affected Gyirong region. The downpours could further damage the limited access routes into the disaster zone, while temperatures are forecast to fall to around 7 degrees Celsius (44 Fahrenheit), complicating rescue efforts.
Moderate to heavy rain is also possible across southeastern Tibet, raising concerns that the water level in the newly formed lake could rise further.
Authorities in Beijing have repeatedly suspended rescue operations because of fears that increasing water levels and unstable conditions could trigger another disaster.

BEIJING, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- China will explore the use of artificial intelligence (AI) to advance special education, and promote the integration of AI technology into all aspects of teaching and learning, according to an action plan jointly issued by seven government departments.
The plan for special education development and improvement, released by the Ministry of Education and six other departments, outlines measures to promote high-quality, integrated development of special education and further improve the special education system during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030).
The plan proposes new models of human-machine collaboration, including intelligent learning companions and AI-assisted teachers, and explores AI applications aimed at providing classroom assistance for students with disabilities, as well as home-based teaching for those with severe disabilities.
It also calls for greater use of AI, big data, virtual reality and other new technologies in special education, while encouraging efforts to improve digital infrastructure in special education schools and expand special education resources on the national smart education platform.
The action plan makes the digitalization of special education a key driver of its development over the next five years, said an official with the Ministry of Education.
He noted that advances in information technology have created new opportunities for the sector in recent years. A special education section has been launched on the national smart education platform, while local authorities have also explored ways to use digital technologies to support individualized education.
However, digitalization in China's special education sector remains at an early stage, with shortages of resources and insufficient application still posing challenges, the official said.
China has stepped up efforts to promote the high-quality development of special education over the past decade. By 2025, the country had 2,464 special education schools, 927,000 special education students and 85,100 full-time special education teachers, representing increases of 33 percent, 145 percent and 95 percent, respectively, from 2012, official data showed.
The enrollment rate of school-age children with disabilities in compulsory education had reached 97 percent in 2025, with the plan aiming to keep it above 97 percent through 2030.
The plan also calls for further improvements to support mechanisms for special education, enhanced digital and intelligent capabilities, and the establishment of a high-quality, integrated and inclusive special education system by 2030. ■

Ukraine’s Intel Unpacks Russia’s Hypersonic ‘Zircon’ Missile – Small Warhead and Foreign Tech
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
09:07:24 UTC
18:07:24 KST

Ukraine’s military intelligence agency has exposed new details about Russia’s 3M22 Zircon missile, including its design, warhead, guidance systems, and the companies producing it – along with foreign equipment used in its manufacturing.
The Defense Intelligence Directorate (HUR) said the Zircon was originally developed as an anti-ship weapon for Russia’s nuclear-powered submarines and Project 22350 frigates equipped with 3S14 launch systems.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
But Russia’s Black Sea Fleet has struggled to operate safely during the war, forcing Moscow to adapt the missile for launch from Bastion-M coastal missile systems, according to HUR.
Despite being one of Russia’s most expensive strike weapons, the Zircon carries a relatively small warhead of about 120 kilograms (264 pounds), HUR said. That is lighter than the roughly 150-kilogram (331 pounds) warhead carried by Russia’s smaller Banderol cruise missile.
What’s inside the Zircon?
The missile uses a two-stage propulsion system. A solid-fuel booster first accelerates it to the altitude and speed needed to activate its main solid-fuel engine.
Guidance and stabilization systems initially steer the missile toward its target. During the cruise phase, the Zircon uses an inertial navigation system before switching to an active radar seeker during the final stage of flight.
The missile also carries Russia’s Baget-83 digital onboard computing system, according to HUR.
Kyiv Endures Unprecedented 5-Day Drone Blitz as Russia Alters Tactics
Its rear section features electro-hydraulic control systems and folding aerodynamic fins. The entire tail section is reportedly made from titanium.
Russia has claimed the Zircon can reach Mach 9, but HUR said the highest recorded speed is around Mach 6.8 and that the missile cannot sustain that speed throughout its flight.
The disclosure comes as Russia continues expanding its use of ballistic weapons against Ukraine.
HUR also pointed to Russia’s reported use of an upgraded ballistic missile dubbed the Iskander-1000, which reportedly has a larger engine and launch system allowing it to strike targets at greater distances.
At the same time, Ukraine is facing growing pressure on its air-defense stockpiles. Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat has warned of shortages of missiles for Patriot and other air-defense systems, including those deployed on ground and aircraft platforms.

TOKYO, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- A total of 4,923 food and beverage items in Japan are expected to see price hikes in September, more than triple the tally a year earlier and the largest monthly total in over three years, a survey by a research company showed Monday.
The spike stems partly from surging crude oil and naphtha prices tied to the Middle East conflict, which in turn pushed up the cost of packaging materials, according to Teikoku Databank.
Rising personnel and logistics expenses, along with costlier imports due to the yen's depreciation, also prompted companies to raise prices, the survey covering 195 major food manufacturers found.
The figure compares with 1,467 items a year earlier and marks the highest monthly total since April 2023, when food prices in Japan began climbing amid rising inflation.
By category, seasoning products accounted for the largest share, with 1,959 items set for price hikes in September, followed by processed food at 1,848 items.
For the whole of 2026, the number of food and beverage items with price increases is projected to exceed last year's total of 20,609, with more than 3,000 additional items expected to become more expensive in October, the company said. ■

JAKARTA, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- Mount Sinabung in Indonesia's North Sumatra province erupted Monday morning, sending volcanic ash over the nearby city of Berastagi, a local monitoring official said.
Armen Putra, head of the Sinabung Volcano Observation Post, said a thick, dark ash column rose about 3,500 meters above the summit and drifted east and southeast.

Mount Sinabung remains at Level II, or Alert status. Activities are prohibited within a three-kilometer radius of the summit and within 4.5 kilometers in the southeast sector. Residents near rivers originating from the volcano have also been warned of potential lahar flows. ■

China Focus: Modern tech helps prevent geological risks in China's Three Gorges region
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
17:07:12 CST
18:07:12 KST

This photo taken on Aug. 20, 2026 shows a drone collecting image data of a collapsed area in Zigui County of Yichang, central China's Hubei Province. (Xinhua/Zhang Yang)
WUHAN, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- Integrated modern technology is helping geologists "tame" the treacherous rock formations of the mountainous Three Gorges Reservoir region, bolstering efforts to prevent and mitigate geological disasters.
Thanks to years of efforts in field investigation and technological exploration, the Wuhan Center of China Geological Survey has established interrelated means to fend off geological disasters in this region, according to Li Ming, a senior engineer at the center.
These technological means include a multi-dimensional rock monitoring system, an integrated information platform for geological hazard prevention and control, as well as a series of ecological restoration techniques for dangerous rock masses.
The Three Gorges project is a vast multi-functional water-control system on the Yangtze River, China's longest waterway.
The Three Gorges Reservoir region is characterized by steep mountains, precipitous slopes, and complex rock formations, making it one of the areas in China most prone to geological disasters. So far, more than 3,000 potential hazard sites have been identified.
To cope with the potential hazards, the center has established an information platform for geological hazard prevention and control, integrating multi-source data including geological base maps, disaster registries and monitoring and early-warning information, Li said.
He noted that one deep rock crevice in Zigui County, central China's Hubei Province, extends more than 110 meters deep. Over 50 crevices cut through the mountain massif, forming an unstable rock body with a total volume exceeding 3 million cubic meters.
The engineer further explained that the upper section of the dangerous rocks consists of hard rock, while its lower section comprises relatively soft coal-bearing strata. The unstable rock body sits right next to the main navigation channel of the Yangtze River.
"Should it collapse and plunge into the river, the surge wave generated instantaneously would pose a severe threat to the safety of passing vessels," Li said, adding this dangerous rock mass is currently stable thanks to multiple engineering measures.
Various devices installed on the cliff face are providing round-the-clock precise monitoring of subtle deformations in the rock mass, summarizing data once every hour and uploading it in real time for monitoring and early warning, Li said.
To address the challenge of dangerous rock masses in the reservoir area, the center has developed a specialized technology by fixing such rock masses with lightweight anchor cable and explored an ecological restoration technique for rock crevices using microorganisms combined with fiber filling, according to Dai Zhenwei, who takes charge of the center's geological disaster monitoring and early warning.
The technological explorations are similar to putting a "safety belt" on the unstable rocks. They provide a new approach to solving the challenge of poor durability of traditional protective structures in water-rich environments, Dai said.
In the meantime, drones and diverse satellite monitoring devices have been put into service to conduct the round-the-clock monitoring works to assess the stability conditions affected by the fluctuations in reservoir water levels, according to Huang Jue, a senior engineer at the Wuhan center.
Huang explained that traditional manual inspections normally take a long period of time and costs are high. The drones can fly close to steep cliffs, dangerous rocks and other areas that are difficult for people to reach.
"Moreover, drones can take off immediately when traffic is disrupted after disasters occur and provide first-hand information for rescue decision-making in a timely manner," he added. ■

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
One of the primary targets was the DRL-27 module of the RSP-27 system at the Millerovo airfield.
