homo faber 2026 brings 500 craft artists to venice in es devlin’s ‘island of light’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
07:45:15 UTC
16:45:15 KST

es devlin turns homo faber 2026 into ‘an island of light’ in venice
Homo Faber returns to Venice from September 1st–30th, 2026, with its fourth edition, titled An Island of Light. Taking place across Fondazione Giorgio Cini on San Giorgio Maggiore, the biennial brings together more than 500 artisans from over 70 countries. Es Devlin, serving as artistic director, develops the exhibition as a sequence of immersive installations that respond directly to the island, its architecture, gardens, and relationship with the surrounding lagoon. Across 15 installations, light becomes a recurring material. Water reflects the Palladian architecture, mirrors alter the scale of objects and spaces, and projections, movement, and sound introduce another layer to the experience of craft.
The title An Island of Light begins with Devlin’s own experience of arriving in Venice and seeing San Giorgio from above. ‘When I look at an aerial view of this place, if I’m lucky enough to have a clear day when I’m landing, I can see this island like an object, like a jewel, like a fragile egg, like something I might pick up and hold very carefully so I don’t break it.’ she shares during the opening of Homo Faber 2026, where designboom was present. ‘And yet, when I’m on the island, I have a very different sensation. I feel held by the stone, by the architecture, by the garden, by the cypresses. They call this island the lungs of Venice. I want you to hold the taste of the word ”light” and the word ”island” while you walk through the trees and through the architecture.’
The opening follows our earlier conversation with Alberto Cavalli, executive director of the Michelangelo Foundation, who spoke with us ahead of this year’s biennial about Homo Faber’s wider effort to bring the handmade object and the people behind it back into focus. An Island of Light now gives that idea a physical form, using Devlin’s installations to move attention beyond the finished object and toward the materials, tools, hands, and knowledge involved in its making.
A Great Turning | all images by Giulio Ghirardi © Michelangelo Foundation, unless stated otherwise
from the artisan’s studio to an index of hands
The exhibition opens with A Language of Hands, an installation conceived as an artisan’s studio. Es Devlin introduces the visitor to the atmosphere of making. Multimedia projections and sound evoke a workshop after its inhabitants have left, placing the emphasis on the people and gestures behind the work. ‘The first thing you encounter is a studio, an atelier, and I hope you will feel like you’ve walked in just as 500 artisans have finished their work for the day. As any of you who have spent time in an artisan studio or an artist’s studio know, I’ve never seen anyone not smile when they walk into mine. I think you feel vividly happy when you’re surrounded by the quality of time passing when people are making things,’ the British artist and designer notes. ‘One thing this exhibition is inviting us to remember is that consciousness in humans is important. I read recently that if we understood the body better, there wouldn’t be a word for a mind. We are conscious from the soles of our feet, we make decisions with the hair on the back of our necks, and we think with the tips of our fingers. When you enter the first room, I hope you’ll have a feeling of an environment of people who do just that,’ she adds.
This focus on the body runs through the exhibition design. In most cases, craft is encountered through its finished form, as a glass vessel, a textile, a piece of furniture, or an object placed on a plinth. In An Island of Light, the route begins with the conditions of making. The hand, the workshop, the passing of time, and the physical knowledge involved in working with a material become part of the exhibition.
The following rooms continue this shift in perspective. An Index of Artisans presents black-and-white portraits of the makers participating in Homo Faber, bringing the people behind the objects into view. In An Alphabet of Objects, more than one hundred works are transformed into projected silhouettes. A large moving cylindrical structure casts their forms across the space, creating a changing visual language of shadows. Devlin moves between the maker and the object, between physical material and projected image, repeatedly changing the scale and conditions through which craft is seen.
a large kinetic mirror responds to changing daylight | image © designboom
using water, wood, and light as exhibition materials
The exhibition then extends into the gardens and historic spaces of the Fondazione Giorgio Cini, where A Library of Lungs introduces curved wooden structures inspired by Devlin’s paper sculptures. Installed in relation to the gardens of San Giorgio, the work refers to the description of the island as one of the ‘lungs of Venice.’
Water becomes the central element of A Full Moon Rising, installed in the former Piscina Gandini. A semicircular structure holding moon jars and vessels rises from the pool, while light and reflections move across the water. The installation brings together the history of containers made to hold and transport water with water itself, turning the former swimming pool into a part of the display.
In A Rooted Ascent, a multi-level cork structure organizes works made from wood alongside objects produced through the weaving of natural materials. The installation is accompanied by makers working live in the space, bringing process into direct contact with the finished pieces.
A Full Moon Rising | image by Sophia Bennett © Michelangelo Foundation
devlin works with the architecture of san giorgio maggiore
The historic architecture of Fondazione Giorgio Cini becomes increasingly present as the exhibition develops.
In An Infinite Birdsong, shaped and backlit mirrors create a nocturnal Venetian environment. Handmade birds and insects emerge from the windows of the room, while jewelry inspired by similar forms is displayed at the center. Porcelain, metal, glass, and paper appear alongside reflections and shadows, creating a space where the objects and the architecture are visually intertwined.
One of Devlin’s most direct interventions is A Great Turning, installed in the Palladian cloister. A long pool of water reflects the arches of the portico and a large kinetic mirror responds to changing daylight. The installation works with the existing geometry of the cloister, using reflection to alter the visitor’s perception of its symmetry and depth.
In the Ambulatory of the Palladian Refectory, A Luminous Ark introduces illuminated paper sculptures of Venetian wildlife. Designed by Devlin and made by Chinese paper artist Wen Qiuwen, the suspended birds appear throughout the space like lanterns.
a semicircular structure holding moon jars and vessels rises from the pool | image © designboom
from white light to a rainbow of forms
Inside the Palladian Refectory, Devlin develops two contrasting installations around light and color. The first one, dubbed A Feast of Light, gathers white objects made from porcelain, glass, textiles, paper, and other materials around a large illuminated table. A vertical beam of light moves through the monumental room, while the reflective surface of the table amplifies the monochrome arrangement. White objects that might otherwise appear visually similar reveal different degrees of opacity, texture, reflection, and translucency.
The following installation, A Rainbow of Forms, takes the opposite approach. Color becomes the central element. Objects made from materials including plastic, enamel, resin, and glass are arranged on reflective shelves and rotating structures beneath a mirrored ceiling. The space produces a kaleidoscopic environment in which objects, colors, and reflections continually multiply.
Before the route reaches the Borges Labyrinth, Twenty Silent Songs occupies the Cypress Cloister. The installation consists of 20 rectangular panels framing circular works inspired by the sound waves of 20 imaginary bells. Each work is interpreted by a different artisan or atelier from five continents. The project draws on the history of the cloister as a place of study and prayer and on the bells of the Basilica di San Giorgio, translating an imagined acoustic experience into form.
light and reflections move across the water | image © designboom
ALBERTO CAVALLI ON CREATIVITY, COMMUNITY, AND THE JOY OF MAKING
The fourth edition of Homo Faber brings together more than 700 objects by more than 500 artisans from 70 countries. For Alberto Cavalli, Executive Director of the Michelangelo Foundation, the numbers only tell part of the story. Organizing the biennial, he says, is challenging ‘creatively, humanly, financially,’ but this difficulty is also connected to the ethos of the artisans whose work the event celebrates. ‘The work that slips out easily from your fingers is not worth pursuing,’ Cavalli says. ‘The fruits that you can pick up on low-hanging branches are maybe not the most interesting ones.’ For him, the effort involved in building Homo Faber reflects the wider idea behind homo faber, the human being capable of shaping the world around them through talent, vision, and creativity. ‘Now more than ever, proclaiming the importance of homo faber matters and makes a difference,’ he adds.
Behind the scale of An Island of Light, Cavalli identifies a set of values that shape the Michelangelo Foundation’s wider vision. The first concerns human creativity, individuality, and freedom of expression. Speaking about younger generations and the increasing influence of digital systems, Cavalli jokes that while Grace Jones once sang Slave to the Rhythm, today’s generation risks becoming ‘a slave to the algorithm.’ His concern is mainly about the pressure to conform to systems that increasingly shape how people see themselves and present their ideas. In contrast, he sees making as a space in which individual experience and creativity can take a more direct form. Working with one’s hands, materials, and personal knowledge allows makers to develop and communicate a vision that is not reduced to a predetermined image. The second value is community. Cavalli points to a contradiction in contemporary life, mentioning that digital technologies have made constant communication possible, yet isolation continues to grow. ‘The more you feel alone and left to your own devices, the more you feel weak,’ he highlights. At Homo Faber, the ambition is to create a community in which makers, students, collaborators, and visitors can come together and ‘feel accompanied, heard, seen, embraced, appreciated.’ The final value is joy. For Cavalli, the artisans gathered in Venice demonstrate a form of satisfaction that comes directly from making and transforming the world around them. ‘The artisans are here to teach us the joy that comes from making, from shaping the world according to your vision, according to your hopes, dreams and expectations,’ he comments.
A Rainbow of Forms
a movement beyond objects
The mayor of Venice, Simone Venturini, describes the event as something larger than an exhibition. ‘Homo Faber is not an exhibition, it’s a movement, and right now we need to push for a movement in favor of beauty, harmony and authenticity, in a world that is very material but also troubled. Beauty, authenticity, craftsmanship, heritage can heal the wounds of a very troubled world, and we can do it here, in a neutral space, in an old monastery, in the most important city for art, culture, intercultural value, and dialogue,’ he shares. ‘I think that’s not just about Homo Faber, or only about a product or craftsmanship. It’s about soul and humanity. This is not an exhibition about things, goods, or objects; it’s a movement about humanity, and about soul.’
Devlin’s direction gives this idea a physical form. An Island of Light organizes 700 works through a series of changing environments. Objects appear alongside the materials, tools, gestures, and processes connected to their making, while the architecture of San Giorgio Maggiore becomes part of the experience. Light moves through the exhibition in different ways. It reflects off water in the former swimming pool, enters the Palladian cloisters, catches mirrored surfaces, and transforms objects into silhouettes and shadows. Color and material also shape the route, moving visitors between different atmospheres and spaces. The exhibition design places the objects within a wider context without taking attention away from the makers themselves. Throughout the 15 installations, Devlin returns to the relationship between the finished work and the hand, the material, the workshop, and the accumulated knowledge behind each practice.

Families of Army's 82nd Airborne told Mideast deployments will last into 2027
Family members of U.S. soldiers in one Army division who were deployed to the Middle East earlier this year have been told the deployments will last into 2027, according to a letter obtained by CBS News that was confirmed by two U.S. officials.
The Sunday-dated letter from the leaders of the Army's 82nd Airborne Division based at Fort Bragg, North Carolina, said that the deployments are expected to last a total of up to 12 months.
"We do not share that lightly, and we understand that a longer tour weighs heavily on every household, including our own," division leaders Maj. Gen. Brandon Tegtmeier and Command Sgt. Maj. James Bradshaw said in the letter.
2 women in Iran sentenced to death over protests, rights groups say
Iranian courts have issued death sentences for two women charged over anti-government protests in January, rights groups said Monday, as Tehran ramps up executions of people arrested in the demonstrations.
The two women were sentenced in separate cases but both were related to incidents in the central city of Isfahan, which was a hub of the nationwide protest activity that peaked on the nights of Jan. 8 and 9.
Against the backdrop of the war, Iran has already executed 29 men on charges related to the demonstrations, according to the Norway-based nongovernmental organization Iran Human Rights.
So far, no woman has been executed over the unrest, although Iran has hanged at least 16 women this year on other charges, according to Iran Human Rights.
Taraneh Rahimi, 20, was sentenced to death along with nine men over incidents during the protests in a square in Isfahan that saw two people killed, including a member of the security forces, the Norway-based Hengaw group and U.S.-based Human Rights Activists News Agency said Monday.
Other defendants in the case were given sentences of up to 36 years in prison, including Taraneh's sister Romina, they added.
"Defendants' lawyers did not have access to a substantial portion of the case file and objected that they had not been given sufficient time to review the documents and evidence," Human Rights Activists News Agency said.
In the other case, Leila Abolhasani, a 43-year-old mother of two teenagers, was convicted by a court in Isfahan of setting fire to a store during the protests, the Dadban legal affairs monitor and Human Rights Activists News Agency said.
Her relatives have denied the accusation, saying she was only present at the scene and was filming the burning store, the groups said.
Will Trump's Venezuela oil deal ease U.S. gas prices?
President Trump on Friday said a U.S. deal with Venezuela to tap its oil reserves "will substantially lower Gas Prices for all Americans, long into the future." With the average U.S. gas price still above $4 a gallon nationwide, American consumers may be wondering if help is on the way.
Don't hold your breath, energy experts said.
Trump to meet with oil refiners, distributors Tuesday
President Trump is expected to meet with a group of oil refiners and distributors Tuesday as gas prices remain above $4 a gallon.
A White House official told CBS News the meeting will include a mix of small, medium and large refiners and distributors as well as Interior Secretary Doug Burgum and Energy Secretary Chris Wright.
"The President will meet with industry leaders to collaborate on the best ways to increase refining capacity, further unleash American energy dominance across the entire supply chain, and bring down prices for the American people." White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said in a statement.
The meeting comes after the U.S. struck a deal with Venezuela last week for control of about 65 billion barrels of oil, but experts told CBS News the deal isn't likely to bring down gas prices anytime soon.
According to AAA, a gallon of regular gas in the U.S. cost an average of $4.08 as of Monday.
Bessent says economic pressure campaign aims to drive Iran to negotiating table
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the Trump administration's new economic pressure campaign aims to drive Iran back to the negotiating table.
"The goal here is to create the conditions that they will want to come to the table," Bessent told CNBC on the sidelines of a meeting in North Carolina with finance ministers from the 20 largest economies in the world. "And the president's been very clear: They have to give up their nuclear program, they have to turn over the highly enriched uranium, and they have to stop their support of proxies, and the strait has to be open."
When he was told that increased economic hardship on people in Iran might not influence the regime, Bessent said, "My experience with people like this, the main thing they care about is their head staying attached to their neck."
Vance says Trump was sending Iran a message with AI video of Kharg Island attack

You guys are behaving like a terrorist country. You've got to stop or there are going to be some consequences.'"
Mr. Trump shared the video on Sunday - a clip from the viewpoint of a helicopter as huge explosions around what looks like oil infrastructure are seen in the background. His only message with the video was: "Kharg Island being blown to smithereens!!!"
Qatar condemns Iran's attacks on Jordan, UAE as "blatant violation" of their sovereignty
The government of Qatar issued a statement Monday condemning "renewed attacks by the Islamic Republic of Iran targeting" Jordan with missiles and the United Arab Emirates with a drone.
Qatar's foreign ministry called the Iranian attacks — which officials in Jordan and the UAE said were all intercepted — "a blatant violation of the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the two states, and a flagrant breach of international law, the Charter of the United Nations, and the principles of good neighborliness."
Iran said it had targeted U.S. forces in the two Middle Eastern states in response to the first American attacks in weeks, which came Sunday as U.S. Central Command said Iranian rocket launchers and sea mines were destroyed in strikes on Larak Island in the Strait of Hormuz.

Fox News says Trump vowed "a response" to latest Iranian attacks on Gulf States: "Going to hit them hard"

"There will be a response," Mr. Trump said, according to Yingst.

CENTCOM dismisses Iran's claim to hit tanker with mines in Strait of Hormuz as false, "attempt to intimidate" shippers
The U.S. military's Central Command dismissed on Monday a claim by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps to have struck a supertanker in the Strait of Hormuz with sea mines, calling it "yet another IRGC attempt to intimidate regional commercial shipping through disinformation."
The IRGC claimed overnight to have forced an unidentified tanker to turn around after trying to transit the strait without permission from Iranian authorities.
"This is FALSE," CENTCOM said in a brief statement shared on social media. "No ships have hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz."
The Iranian claim was never corroborated by the U.K. navy's Maritime Operations center, which monitors such attacks and is usually among the first reliable resources to report such attacks on ships. The most recent incident involving a commercial ship in the region reported by the UKMTO was a tanker "struck by an unknown projectile whilst transiting inbound in the Strait of Hormuz" on Saturday.
While the Trump administration insists a southern route, close to Oman's coastline, is safe and open for ships to transit the vital waterway, Tehran refuses to recognize the shipping lane and demands that all commercial vessels coordinate with Iranian authorities to use a northern passage, close to its own shores.
Despite U.S. assurances and American military escorts for some vessels, the number of daily transits of the strait remains at less than half the typical number that would have been seen before the war began.
The resumption of strikes by the U.S. and Iran over the weekend sent global oil prices rising again, meanwhile, with a barrel of international benchmark Brent crude selling for over $91 on Monday, up more than 3% compared to the previous day.

Russia has subjected Kyiv and the surrounding region to five straight days of relentless drone attacks, unleashing hundreds of drones and increasingly deploying faster, jet-powered variants that are putting Ukraine’s air defenses under growing pressure.
The barrage has killed at least 38 people in Kyiv and the Kyiv region and repeatedly disrupted life across the capital, with prolonged air-raid alerts forcing residents into shelters and businesses, transport services and other civilian infrastructure to shut down.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
38 killed in arms depot blast
The deadliest incident occurred late Friday, Aug. 28, in Myla, west of Kyiv, where a Russian strike hit a Ukrainian military depot storing ammunition, drones and explosives.
The strike triggered a massive explosion and fire, followed by secondary detonations that sent flames and debris across the surrounding area.
The death toll has risen to 38, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Sunday. Another 20 people were injured and four remained missing.
Emergency crews extinguished most of the fires, while bomb-disposal teams were clearing unexploded ordnance and other dangerous debris from the site.
Zelensky said the area had been significantly contaminated by the blast and announced that Ukrainian prosecutors had opened a criminal negligence investigation.
The incident has also triggered anger over the continued storage of large quantities of ammunition and explosives near residential areas.
Can Ukraine Set a New Standard in International Law?
It was the second major incident involving a munitions depot near Kyiv in less than two months.
On July 6, a Russian Iskander ballistic missile struck an ammunition warehouse operated by a defense-industry company in Vyshneve, west of Kyiv, triggering hours of secondary detonations that killed nine people and damaged hundreds of homes.
Ukrainian investigators later found that ammunition had been stored near residential buildings in violation of safety requirements, leading to criminal proceedings and the detention of two company executives.
Children among those killed
On Aug. 29, a two-year-old girl was killed by debris from a downed Russian drone in Kyiv’s Obolonskyi District. Eight people were injured in drone attacks across the capital that day.
A 14-year-old girl was also killed in a separate Russian drone strike in Kyiv region’s Boryspil District.
Russia unleashes faster drones
The attacks have also highlighted a shift in Russia’s aerial tactics.
Moscow has increasingly combined traditional Shahed-type drones with jet-powered variants capable of flying at much higher speeds, as well as Gerbera attack drones and Parodiya decoys designed to overwhelm Ukrainian air defenses.
Ukrainian military experts say Russia is rushing some of the new drones directly from production lines into combat.
Their higher speeds make them harder targets for Ukraine’s traditional mobile fire groups, increasing pressure on air-defense systems and combat aviation.
Overnight into Aug. 31, Ukrainian forces said they intercepted 96 of 121 Russian drones launched against Ukraine.
But the sheer volume and frequency of the attacks are creating another challenge: keeping Kyiv under repeated alerts for hours at a time.
Daylight attacks paralyze Kyiv
Russia has also shifted toward rolling daytime drone waves, extending the disruption beyond the traditional overnight attack window.
On Monday morning, Kyiv entered its fifth consecutive day of being under a drone blitz as another Russian drone wave approached the capital.
Falling drone debris sparked a major fire at an ATB supermarket warehouse in Kyiv’s Desnianskyi District.
Other strikes and debris impacts were reported across the city.
In Obolon, a drone hit a 12-story residential building, setting the second to the fifth floor ablaze. In Holosiivskyi District, debris severely damaged the façade of a two-story café. Drone fragments also struck residential areas and non-residential infrastructure in Pecherskyi and Shevchenkivskyi districts.
The repeated attacks are increasingly disrupting Kyiv’s economy and daily routines, affecting public transport, businesses, deliveries and other services.
Ukraine scrambles for new interceptors
The escalating drone campaign is also accelerating Ukraine’s push for cheaper ways to defend the capital.
The military is rushing the testing and deployment of domestic interceptor drones designed to hunt down and destroy Russia’s increasingly fast unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs).
The approach could help Ukraine conserve expensive surface-to-air missiles while countering Moscow’s growing drone production and increasingly sophisticated attack tactics.

Meloni's big reforms flounder but security bills flourish in Italy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
07:40:37 UTC
16:40:37 KST

Meloni's big reforms flounder but security bills flourish in Italy
ROME, Aug 31 - Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's government took office in October 2022 and will become the longest-serving administration in the history of the Italian Republic on September 4.
Here are some of the main legislative efforts undertaken by her coalition, which have achieved varied results.
JUDICIAL REFORM
One of its flagship initiatives sought to revamp Italy's fiercely independent judiciary. Because this involved a change to the constitution, it went to a referendum, which the government lost decisively in March.
PREMIERSHIP
The government said it would introduce the direct election of the prime minister by voters. Meloni called this the "mother of all reforms", however it has not progressed after initial approval in the Senate in June 2024. Critics said it could trigger political chaos and undermine the role of the president. The reform will not be enacted before the next elections.
DIFFERENTIATED AUTONOMY
The law grants greater powers to the regions and has been aggressively promoted by the far-right coalition League party. The legislation was approved in 2024, but the Constitutional Court subsequently struck down key parts of it. The legislation is now in limbo, but the League has said the problems will be resolved before the next election.
IMMIGRATION
The government tightened asylum and anti-smuggling rules, struck migration agreements with North African states and expanded repatriations. However, its flagship scheme, building two detention centres in Albania, was delayed by legal challenges and is now operating mainly as a repatriation facility for migrants already transferred from Italy, not as the offshore asylum-processing system originally promoted by Meloni.
SECURITY AND LAW AND ORDER
Meloni's government has been particularly active on security, repeatedly responding to high-profile incidents with tougher laws and penalties. Measures have included new offences targeting illegal raves, stricter anti-smuggling rules after a migrant shipwreck, tougher penalties for wildfire arson, youth crime and a sweeping 2025 security decree covering protests, prison riots, squatting and other public-order offences.
TAX AND WELFARE
Meloni has pursued a targeted tax-cutting agenda: reducing income tax bands to three from four and pushing measures to benefit the self-employed. However, Italy's total tax burden has barely changed over the past four years, with some tax cuts counterbalanced by tighter limits on deductions for higher-income taxpayers. The government abolished a "Citizens' Income" welfare scheme, replacing it with more restrictive benefits and stricter work requirements. Figures show it also reduced tax evasion by promoting the use of digital payments. REUTERS

Irish warships open fire with main guns
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
08:40:18 BST
16:40:18 KST

Irish Naval Service patrol ships LÉ Samuel Beckett and LÉ George Bernard Shaw have taken part in a Ship Training Period involving live-fire gunnery, manoeuvring, maritime interdiction and replenishment-at-sea training, according to the Irish Naval Service.
Footage released by the service shows one of the vessels conducting a gun exercise at sea, with its main naval gun firing during the training period. The Naval Service described the activity as a demanding package intended to exercise several of the core skills required during operations.
The training included Gun Exercises, known as GUNEX, alongside manoeuvring exercises, Maritime Interdiction Operations and Replenishment at Sea training. Together, those activities cover weapons employment, ship handling, interception procedures and the ability of vessels to operate in close coordination while underway.
The Naval Service said: “This week the Naval Service conducted a Ship Training Period (STP). This was a demanding period of training which involved Gun Exercises (GUNEX), Manoeuvring Exercises, Maritime Interdiction (MIO) and Replenishment at Sea training (RAS).”
LÉ Samuel Beckett and LÉ George Bernard Shaw are both Samuel Beckett-class offshore patrol vessels.
The class is fitted with a 76mm main gun mounted forward, providing a substantially heavier weapon than the smaller-calibre systems carried elsewhere on the ships. Gunnery training allows crews to practise the procedures surrounding weapon operation, fire control and safe engagement while maintaining proficiency with the ship’s principal armament. Maritime Interdiction Operations exercise a different part of a ship’s crew. Such training can involve identifying and approaching vessels of interest, establishing communications, controlling their movement and preparing boarding teams for inspection or enforcement activity.
For a navy whose routine work includes monitoring maritime activity across Ireland’s extensive area of responsibility, those procedures form part of the practical skills required for patrol and security operations. Replenishment at Sea training is intended to develop the close-quarters ship handling and coordination required when vessels transfer stores or other supplies while remaining underway. Even when no material is physically transferred, crews can practise the approach, station keeping, communications and safety procedures involved.
Manoeuvring exercises similarly allow bridge teams to work through coordinated changes of course, formation movements and close navigation with other vessels. Such activity is particularly important when several ships are operating together or when conducting interception and boarding tasks.
LÉ Samuel Beckett was the first ship of the class to enter Irish service, while LÉ George Bernard Shaw is the fourth and final vessel of the design. The ships were built as larger and more capable replacements for older Irish patrol vessels, with an emphasis on endurance and operations in the North Atlantic environment.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwanese suppliers of chemical materials reported higher July revenue as shipments to electronics and semiconductor sectors continued to grow.
Eternal Materials reported July revenue of NT$4.1 billion (US$129.2 million), up 23.86% from the same period a year earlier. Everlight posted revenue of NT$781 million, an annual increase of 25.71%, according to CMoney and UDN Money.
Eternal Materials said orders from the printed circuit board, advanced substrate, and semiconductor industries have strengthened. Its electronic materials portfolio includes dry-film photoresists, silicon microspheres, and materials used in advanced chip packaging, according to CTEE.
Eternal Materials' precision equipment business is also gaining momentum, with several projects undergoing final testing and customer approval. The segment is expected to contribute more to revenue in the second half of the year.
The company expects revenue to increase month over month in the third quarter.
Everlight said its electronic chemicals business is expected to benefit from stronger international contract manufacturing activity. The company is expanding production of photoresists for international customers, with a particular focus on materials used in back-end semiconductor packaging.
A new production line will focus on materials for advanced packaging, with the products currently undergoing customer verification. Photosensitive polyimide (PSPI), another material used in semiconductor packaging, remains at the sample-submission stage.
As electronic chemicals become a larger part of their businesses, the two companies are becoming more closely tied to developments in semiconductor manufacturing, advanced packaging, and high-end materials. Growth will depend not only on traditional product cycles but also on how quickly new technologies are adopted, according to CMoney.
The shift toward higher-value products could support profitability if new offerings complete customer qualification and move into volume production. However, the companies also face risks from customer qualification timelines, the timing of mass production, and changing technical requirements.

New stability record for Italy's Meloni may prove fleeting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
07:36:04 UTC
16:36:04 KST

New stability record for Italy's Meloni may prove fleeting
ROME, Aug 31 - In a country famed for political instability, Giorgia Meloni is poised to lead Italy's longest-lasting government since World War Two, overtaking a record of 1,412 consecutive days set by Silvio Berlusconi in 2005.
Meloni, who has tempered her populist instincts with pragmatism since taking power in October 2022, plans a rally on Friday, September 4 to celebrate the milestone, framing the durability of her coalition as one of its crowning achievements.
After cycling through 68 governments in 80 years, Italy has proved much steadier during a period of global conflict than France, which has had five prime ministers since the autumn of 2022, while Britain has got through four.
But just as Italy has shaken off its reputation for volatility, opinion polls suggest that the 2027 parliamentary elections could usher in a more fragmented and potentially less stable political landscape.
"There is a genuine risk that we could return to the worst kind of a splintered parliament next time around," said Roberto D'Alimonte, a professor of Italian politics at Rome's Luiss university.
While Berlusconi's single-term record is about to be eclipsed, he will remain the longest-serving Italian prime minister overall, with a tenure of about nine years over four terms between 1994 and 2011.
BUDGET DISCIPLINE
Worried about the prospect of renewed political turbulence, coalition allies are quick to tout the dividends of four years of uninterrupted rule.
Deputy Foreign Minister Edmondo Cirielli, of Meloni's Brothers of Italy party, said the government had kept deficits and debt under control, while adding 1.2 million workers to the jobs market, pushing unemployment to under 6%.
"The record figures on employment and unemployment are indisputable," he told Reuters.
Analysts broadly agree that Meloni's strongest achievement has been restoring confidence in Italy's shaky public finances, blighted by a hefty debt mountain.
Lorenzo Codogno, a former chief economist at the Treasury and now head of LC Macro Advisors, said the cabinet had convinced investors it was committed to budget discipline and had curtailed costly policies of past administrations, notably the "Superbonus" home renovation scheme.
"In terms of fiscal responsibility, I think the government has done a decent job. In terms of promoting growth and reforming the economy, not much has been done," he said.
Little effort was made to shake up an inefficient public administration, the health service and education system, while all the government's institutional reforms, including handing more powers to the prime minister, have floundered.
"Part of the reason Meloni has been able to stay in power for four years is that she did not try to change much or upset voters," said Lorenzo Pregliasco, head of YouTrend pollster.
"This is perhaps the most sobering lesson we can draw from this period."
LOSING TRUMP
While ducking ambitious change, Meloni focused on law and order, boosting police powers and cracking down on irregular immigration — a key electoral pledge — cutting the number of new arrivals to 66,316 last year from 157,651 in 2023.
"There has been the paradigm shift imposed by Giorgia Meloni in the management of illegal immigration," Francesco Filini, the head of Brothers of Italy's policy programme, told Reuters, saying much of Europe was now looking to emulate her.
Although she has forged good relations with many European leaders, Meloni's standing abroad has been bruised by the collapse of her once-close ties with Donald Trump after the U.S. president accused her in April of lacking courage and letting the United States down in its war with Iran.
The diplomatic setback, which destroyed any pretence that Meloni could serve as a bridge between Europe and Washington, came within weeks of a stinging domestic defeat, when Italians rejected her flagship judicial reform in a referendum.
The loss punctured the aura of invincibility that had surrounded Meloni's coalition, and while her party remains the most popular in Italy, the standing of her main allies — most notably the far-right League — has dropped steadily.
With time running out, the government has embarked on one last-gasp legislative push, seeking to redraw the electoral law by introducing a system that would give a majority bonus to any bloc winning more than 42% of the vote.
Critics say the change is designed to strengthen the conservative bloc's chances of staying in power. Meloni says it is aimed at providing renewed stability, whoever wins.
NEW PARTY DISRUPTS OUTLOOK
However, the political landscape has changed since the law was devised, thanks to the emergence of a new far-right party led by an ex-general, Roberto Vannacci, who has tapped into anxieties over immigration, security and cultural change with language that is markedly blunter than Meloni's.
A poll published by BiDiMedia on August 26 put the coalition partners on just 38.5%, while the broad centre-left camp, which is deeply divided over foreign policy and prone to relentless infighting, is hovering close to the vital 42% threshold.
Support for Vannacci has surged to 8%, suggesting he could win it for Meloni, if she agreed to bring him into her alliance.
That would be a risky move which might alienate moderate voters and alarm EU allies concerned by Vannacci's extremism. Alternatively, she could hope for an inconclusive vote and seek a post-election pact with Vannacci to give her a working majority.
Either way, the path to another stable government appears narrower than before. The opposition is disunited, while Vannacci's rise risks turning a previously disciplined conservative alliance into a more fractious bloc.
"The markets have liked stability and got used to it, but this is Italy, it won't last for ever," said Codogno. REUTERS

Italy's revolving-door governments — the numbers behind the instability
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
07:35:51 UTC
16:35:51 KST

Italy's revolving-door governments — the numbers behind the instability
ROME, Aug 31 - Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni is due to set a record as leading Italy's longest-serving administration on September 4. Yet the country's revolving-door cabinets have often masked a more stable political system than first meets the eye.
Below are some facts and figures about Italy's post-war governments:
HOW MANY GOVERNMENTS AND PRIME MINISTERS?
Meloni's administration is Italy's 68th government since 1946, led by the country's 31st prime minister of the republican era. Unlike in some countries, a new government is said to have been created after a major cabinet reshuffle, even if the prime minister remains the same.
AVERAGE LIFESPAN
Across the 80 years from the formation of Alcide De Gasperi's government in July 1946 to Meloni's record in 2026, the average cabinet has lasted roughly 14 months. The figure varies according to methodology: calculating only the period from a government's swearing-in to its resignation produces a shorter average, because outgoing cabinets often remain in office in a caretaker capacity.
THE SHORTEST AND THE LONGEST
The briefest tenure was Amintore Fanfani's first government, which lasted 22 days in 1954. Before Meloni, only four administrations lasted more than 1,000 days: Silvio Berlusconi's 2nd government (1,412 days, from 2001 to 2005), Berlusconi's 4th government (1,287 days, 2008 to 2011), Bettino Craxi (1,093 days, 1983 to 1986) and Matteo Renzi (1,024 days, 2014 to 2016). Altogether, Berlusconi served about nine years over four terms.
WHY SO MANY SHORT-LIVED GOVERNMENTS?
Italy's post-war system combined proportional representation, which encouraged a fragmented party landscape, with coalition governments vulnerable to disputes. The constitution also requires a government to retain the confidence of both the lower house and the Senate — two houses with equal powers, giving small coalition partners considerable leverage.
However, the turnover did not always mean a wholesale change of political direction. During much of the post-war era, the Christian Democrats remained at the centre of power, while prime ministers and coalition formulas revolved around them.
Despite frequent changes of government, nine of Italy's 18 post-war legislatures ran broadly to the end of their normal five-year term, while five lasted for four years.
ELECTORAL LAWS: A FREQUENTLY CHANGING RULEBOOK
Italy has deployed three different electoral systems in general elections in the past 22 years, with Meloni promising to introduce a fourth ahead of the 2027 vote, saying it will bring greater stability. REUTERS

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taipei prosecutors indicted two police officers Monday for allegedly accepting more than NT$7 million (US$221,000) in bribes and leaking confidential records linked to 901 phone numbers to members of a criminal group.
CNA reported that the Taipei District Prosecutors Office indicted a detective surnamed Liu (劉) and a police officer surnamed Cheng (鄭) on bribery and other charges. Three alleged members of the criminal group implicated in the scheme are being investigated separately.
Prosecutors said Cheng was introduced in 2018 to a money lender surnamed Chang (張), who asked him to obtain phone records. Cheng allegedly charged NT$8,000 per phone number and asked Liu to access the records because he was not authorized to do so himself.
Liu allegedly obtained records linked to 518 phone numbers and passed them to Cheng, who then provided them to Chang's group. Prosecutors said Chang paid NT$4.14 million in bribes, with Cheng receiving NT$1.55 million and Liu NT$2.59 million.
Prosecutors said another money lender surnamed Chen (陳) later asked Cheng to obtain more records. Liu allegedly used the login credentials of three colleagues to access records linked to another 383 phone numbers, per TVBS News.
Cheng allegedly received NT$1.15 million from the second arrangement, while Liu received NT$1.92 million. Prosecutors said the two officers leaked confidential records linked to 901 phone numbers in total.
The three people implicated in the scheme were linked to a criminal group led by 88 Club operator Kuo Che-min (郭哲敏). The Taiwan High Court sentenced Kuo in May to nine years and eight months in prison for gambling, money laundering, and other offenses. The case is under appeal.
Prosecutors accused Liu and Cheng of accepting bribes in exchange for violating their official duties, leaking confidential information, forging documents, and violating personal data protection laws. Liu has been suspended from duty, while Cheng retired in May.

Ukraine Has 4 Drone Killers for Jet-Powered Shaheds—Now It Wants Thousands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
07:31:36 UTC
16:31:36 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Has 4 Drone Killers for Jet-Powered Shaheds—Now It Wants Thousands
Ukraine has already field-tested four interceptor drone designs capable of taking down Russia’s new jet-powered Shahed-type drones and is now racing to refine the systems and manufacture them by the thousands, Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara said.
Khmara disclosed the development during a meeting attended by a UNITED24 Media correspondent, outlining Ukraine’s efforts to find a scalable response to faster jet-powered drones increasingly appearing in Russian attacks.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“We continue searching for ways to counter jet-powered drones. There are already four potential interceptors capable of shooting down jet-powered Shaheds. They have already undergone field testing,” Khmara said.
“The task is to bring these solutions to the required level as quickly as possible and scale production to thousands of units.”
The announcement comes as Russia increases the number and variety of aerial weapons used against Ukraine, making inexpensive drone interception one of Kyiv’s most urgent air defense priorities.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia launched nearly 2,000 strike drones against Ukraine in the past week alone, alongside more than 1,600 guided aerial bombs and 31 missiles.
“In total, this week alone, the Russians have launched nearly 2,000 strike drones, more than 1,600 aerial bombs, and 31 missiles of various types, including North Korean ballistic missiles, against our people. Strikes on frontline and border communities are virtually constant—Nikopol, Kramatorsk, Kherson, and communities in the Kharkiv, Zaporizhzhia, Dnipro, Donetsk, and Sumy regions,” Zelenskyy wrote.
Jet-powered Shahed-type drones present an additional challenge because their significantly higher speed reduces the time available for defenders to detect, pursue and destroy them compared with conventional propeller-driven variants.
Ukraine has increasingly turned to interceptor drones as a lower-cost layer of air defense against Russian UAVs. Rather than expend expensive surface-to-air missiles against comparatively cheap incoming drones, specialized interceptors can pursue and destroy them at a fraction of the cost.
The appearance of jet-powered variants, however, raises the performance requirements considerably, forcing Ukrainian developers to produce interceptors capable of reaching substantially higher speeds while retaining the guidance and maneuverability needed to catch an aerial target.
Earlier reports indicated that a Russian jet-powered drone flew approximately 960 kilometers from its launch point on August 28, setting a reported new range record for this type of UAV.

Feature: How World Heritage bid breathes new life into a Chinese village
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
15:31:07 CST
16:31:07 KST

NANCHANG, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- On a sultry afternoon, an elderly man sat on the doorstep of his home in Dongbu Village, a riverside settlement about 40 kilometers from Jingdezhen, idly fanning himself in the shade when a visiting official stopped to ask him a question.
"Do you know what big thing your village is doing these days?"
Without a word, he turned the fan in his hand. Printed across its face was a single line: "Supporting the World Heritage bid."
"That's it," he said, "We're applying for World Heritage status."
Everyone laughed. For Han Xiaoshan, deputy director of the World Heritage application office in Fuliang County, where the village sits, the moment was proof that years of knocking on doors had finally sunk in.
"It showed our work hadn't been for nothing," she said. "People here know now that this is everyone's business, not just ours."
It had taken years to get there -- years of persuading villagers to look again at the street, houses and riverfront they had grown up with, and to see not just a familiar home, but a piece of porcelain history worth preserving.
On July 25, the Jingdezhen Handicraft Porcelain Industry Sites were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List, becoming China's 61st World Heritage site. Dongbu was among the newly listed heritage components.
For centuries, kaolin, or China clay, and other porcelain-making materials were brought down from the surrounding hills to Dongbu and shipped along the Donghe River to Jingdezhen's kilns. Goods purchased in the porcelain-making city traveled back along the same route.
With an ancient trade route also running through the village, Dongbu became a busy hub for trade and transshipment by land and water. Its old wharf, commercial street and waterways still trace the transport network that once helped supply Jingdezhen's porcelain industry.
For generations of villagers, however, those remains were simply part of everyday life.
Wu Jinghua, a former village official who has lived in Dongbu for more than 70 years, remembers efforts to protect the old street and wharf beginning around 2000. Systematic restoration gathered pace from 2015 as the World Heritage application moved forward.
Dongbu was traditionally an agricultural village. Tourism developed gradually, but few visitors came at first.
As heritage protection intensified, it began to affect residents more directly. Concrete covering the old stone street had to be removed, old houses faced restrictions on rebuilding and renovation, and makeshift structures and accumulated clutter had to be cleared.
For some villagers, the changes initially meant inconvenience rather than opportunity.
"At first, many villagers did not understand," Wu said. "Old houses were too dilapidated to be worth preserving."
For Han, who joined the application effort in 2022, changing that perception became part of the work.
She and her colleagues went door to door, explaining Dongbu's history and why the old streets and wharf outside villagers' homes mattered beyond the village itself.
Gradually, resistance eased. As the village became cleaner and its historic buildings were repaired, Han said, residents developed a stronger sense of belonging and pride.
The restoration itself followed a principle of "minimum intervention."
Traditional materials and techniques were used to repair old buildings, the wharf and the stone-paved street, with colors and textures kept as close as possible to the originals.
When workers moved utility lines underground, they marked each stone slab before lifting it. Once the work was complete, workers returned the slabs one by one to their original positions. Modern shop windows were replaced with wooden latticework to better match the historic streetscape.
At the same time, the village upgraded water and drainage systems and improved other basic infrastructure.
The changes also created new opportunities for residents.
More than 80 villagers found work during the restoration projects. Others opened homestays, restaurants and teahouses or began selling local produce to visitors.
Under a large banyan tree by the Donghe River, one elderly resident now sells mung bean soup and rice jelly, often going through two buckets a day.
Dongbu has also begun hosting study tours and cultural tourism programs centered on its role in Jingdezhen's porcelain history.
The village now receives at least 190,000 visitors a year, according to Wu. More visitors mean more customers for local food, accommodation and produce, giving villagers additional ways to earn a living beyond farming.
But another change is harder to measure.
The old houses that some villagers once saw mainly as dilapidated structures have increasingly become a source of pride. A history long taken for granted has become more closely tied to how residents see their home.
"This village isn't just our own place anymore," Wu said. "It now has international influence."
For Dongbu, World Heritage status has changed not only how its old street and wharf are protected, but also how residents understand their value.
"We all have the same hope now: to protect our ancient street and wharf well, so that our culture can be passed down for generations," said Wu. ■

Feature: Fresh banana exports to China lift incomes in NW Cambodia's border province
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
15:30:58 CST
16:30:58 KST

Workers wash fresh bananas at the packing factory of a Chinese-invested banana farm in Oddar Meanchey province, Cambodia on Aug. 30, 2026. (Photo by Van Pov/Xinhua)
ODDAR MEANCHEY, Cambodia, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- Lak Sineth, a 29-year-old single mother in Cambodia's northwestern Oddar Meanchey province, has seen her livelihood transformed since she began working at a local banana plantation in 2022.
The plantation, operated by Longfruiter Anlong Veng Oddar Meanchey Agriculture Park Co., Ltd., is close to the border with Thailand. The company currently cultivates the yellow Cavendish banana variety across roughly 530 hectares in the Anlong Veng district, providing steady employment for more than 800 residents.
Now a banana packing team leader, Sineth recalls starting with next to nothing. Her steady income has since allowed her to secure a baseline of financial stability and invest in her future.
"After coming to work at this banana plantation, I could afford my own land and other valuable possessions," Sineth told Xinhua on Sunday. "My life has been much better than before."
Cheat Chumpou, a 24-year-old banana washer, shared a similar perspective. Ever since she joined the factory, her financial situation has improved significantly thanks to the stable wages and supportive environment.
Before securing this job, Chumpou lived with her parents, who are farmers. She recalled that their livelihood was incredibly difficult, and they frequently lived hand-to-mouth.
"I want to thank the Chinese investors for investing in Cambodia," she said. "It has created many jobs and made life much better for Cambodian people."
Oeun Samkeary, the factory's 30-year-old production manager, noted that this yellow banana is a unique variety in Cambodia, standing out for its superior quality and taste compared to local options.
Samkeary added that the company's export volumes to China have grown steadily. Shipments rose from 24,000 tonnes in 2024 to more than 34,000 tonnes in 2025. So far in 2026, the company has already exported 22,000 tonnes to the Chinese market.
"Looking ahead for the rest of 2026, I think exports will keep rising due to growing demand and our newly expanded cultivation area in Cambodia," he said. "The cultivation of this yellow banana and its direct export to China have generated income for local people through job creation."
Cambodia's yellow banana exports have maintained vigorous momentum since 2019, when China first permitted direct shipments from the country.
Thong Mengdavid, deputy director of the China-ASEAN Studies Center at the Cambodia University of Technology and Science, said that China serves as the primary growth engine for Cambodia's commercial banana industry, absorbing roughly 95 percent of the country's total fresh yellow banana exports.
"Access to China's massive consumer base has transformed local banana farming into a modern, export-driven agribusiness," he told Xinhua. "This generates stable year-round employment, facilitates technology transfers, and upgrades infrastructure for thousands of rural farming communities."
Yellow bananas are among five Cambodian fresh fruits that currently enjoy direct access to the Chinese market, alongside mangoes, Pailin longans, coconuts, and durians. ■
Workers wash fresh bananas at the packing factory of a Chinese-invested banana farm in Oddar Meanchey province, Cambodia on Aug. 30, 2026. (Photo by Van Pov/Xinhua)

The City as a System of Health: Breaking Feedback Loops in Planning
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
07:30:00 UTC
16:30:00 KST

The spatial consequences of urban form are revealed when health outcomes are mapped over neighborhoods. Neighborhoods that support walking, daily errands, social interaction, and access to essential services create opportunities to incorporate physical activity into routine tasks. Places that are organized around long distances and automobile travel suppress this opportunity. Physical activity and the motivation to incorporate it into daily life are shaped by the distance to a grocery store, the safety of a pedestrian crossing, the frequency of public transportation, the width of a sidewalk, and the quantity of services within walking distance.
For decades, conversations about rising obesity and metabolic health have concentrated on individual behavior. People are encouraged to exercise more, eat better, and make healthier choices. Good urban design practices challenge the environment that makes these practical and accessible. Consider a neighborhood where the nearest grocery store is several miles away, the streets are wide with high travel speeds, sidewalks are intermittent, and services between are dispersed. Driving is the rational response for this specific task of reaching the grocery store. Walking requires additional time, exposure to traffic and unsafe sidewalk conditions, or routes that don't offer safety or shade. Repeated across millions of daily trips, these ordinary choices influence how people move through their environments.

Russian forces have ramped up the number of missile strikes on Ukrainian cities as Kyiv faces a shortage of air defense equipment.

'Winter is coming'
Ukrainian officials, drone executives and national security experts have previously warned that the country could face another extremely difficult winter, amid fears of another sustained barrage of military attacks on its power grid during freezing temperatures.

Speaking to CNBC earlier this month, Iryna Terekh, CEO of Ukrainian drone maker Fire Point, said Kyiv needs to be realistic about the threat it faces, particularly given the country's acute shortage of air defense systems.
"Winter is coming, obviously, and the last winter was very hard for Ukraine and for big cities in general. This one would be no easier — and probably even harder," Terekh said.

Kerala minister Bindu Krishna hits out at Sunni cleric over remarks on women’s public life.
Kerala labour minister Bindu Krishna on Monday criticised prominent Sunni cleric and Grand Mufti of India Kanthapuram Aboobacker Musliyar over his remarks advocating restrictions on women's participation in public life, saying such statements push women "centuries back".Krishna said the Constitution guarantees equal rights to men and women and rejected calls to restrict women's movement outside their homes."Constitution of India assures equal rights to women and men, irrespective of sex. The people have the right to live a free and liberal life. And also, these types of statements push women centuries back. So, we can't accept such statements. Our women are free to move. They are best rulers. Our girls are always coming through this society, and we can't accept such statements," Krishna told ANI.The minister was responding to remarks made by Aboobacker Musliyar at the Hubbul Rasul Conference in Kochi, where he defended directives issued by the Kanthapuram faction of Samastha Kerala Jamiyyathul Ulama to local Mahalls regarding women's participation in religious events.The controversy follows a circular issued by the organisation directing Madrasas not to allow women to be present among unrelated men at religious programmes.
The directives also advised against featuring young women on public stages or allowing them to participate in road processions alongside unrelated men.Defending the restrictions, Aboobacker said, "Women should remain confined within their homes. They should not enter the public sphere. The Holy Quran says so."
He defended the purdah system, saying it was intended to protect women's dignity. He also argued that allowing women unrestricted access to public spaces could cause "great destruction".Aboobacker said the restrictions were intended to honour and protect women rather than diminish their status.He further argued that Islam had granted women property and inheritance rights centuries ago to improve their status without requiring them to leave their domestic roles.The cleric also said he was not concerned by opposition from political leaders or others and maintained that no one could silence him or force him to alter Islamic doctrines.

Ukraine's Defence Intelligence reveals inner workings of Russian Zircon ballistic missile
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
10:22:00 EEST
16:22:00 KST

Ukraine's Defence Intelligence reveals inner workings of Russian Zircon ballistic missile
Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) has released an interactive 3D model and information on the components of the 3M22 Zircon ballistic missile system.
Source: War & Sanctions portal
Quote: "The Zircon was designed to strike a range of naval targets (hence the letter M [standing for "morskiy" (naval)] in the missile's name) and to be launched from Russian nuclear-powered submarines and Project 22350 frigates equipped with 3S14 universal vertical launch systems. During the Russia-Ukraine war, facing significant problems in deploying its fleet in the Black Sea, the enemy was forced to adapt 3M22 missiles for launch from Bastion-M coastal defence missile systems."
Details: According to the Ukrainian intelligence agency, the 3M22 has a warhead weighing about 120 kg. DIU described this as an extremely low figure for the most expensive missile among all of Russia's strike weapons. By comparison, it noted that the small Banderol cruise missile carries a 150 kg warhead.
"After the missile leaves the launch container aboard a ship or coastal missile system, the booster motor ignites, allowing the missile to reach the altitude and speed required to start the sustainer motor. After the booster separates, the main sustainer motor starts. Both motors – the booster and the sustainer – use solid propellant," DIU said.
The agency noted that the missile is initially aligned with the course towards its target by the orientation and stabilisation system thrusters located on a protective fairing, which is subsequently jettisoned.
Russia claims that the missile can reach speeds of Mach 9 during certain stages of flight. However, DIU said the maximum recorded speed of the 3M22 missile does not exceed Mach 6.8 and is not maintained throughout the entire flight.
"The 3M22 has a combined guidance system – inertial guidance during the cruise phase and an active radar homing seeker during the terminal phase. The missile is equipped with the Baget-83 onboard digital computing system, which is typical of all Russian ballistic missiles," Ukrainian intelligence said.
The missile's tail section contains electrohydraulic steering actuators and aerodynamic control surfaces, which serve as its primary flight-control surfaces. The control surfaces are folded during transport and deploy after the missile leaves its launch container. The entire tail section of the 3M22 missile is made of titanium.
In addition to information on the missile's design and components, DIU released data on 70 companies involved in producing 3M22 Zircon ballistic missiles, their main systems and assemblies, airframes, engines and solid rocket propellant. It also published information on executives and employees of key companies involved in its production, as well as foreign technological equipment used by these companies.

The altered version claimed Li had demonstrated exceptional academic performance and remarkable dedication to her studies.

Israel signs $4.43 billion air defence deal with Greece
- Greece will sign a €3 billion (S$4.43 billion) deal with Israel on Aug 31 for a multi-layer air defence system including missile and radar technology.
- The defence programme, named "Achilles Shield," aims to enhance Greece's airspace protection with anti-ballistic, anti-aircraft, and anti-drone capabilities by 2036.
- Greece spends about 3.5 per cent of its GDP on defence, collaborating closely with Israel and also plans to buy F-35 jets and frigates from other allies.
AI generated
JERUSALEM/ATHENS – Israel and Greece signed a €3 billion (S$4.43 billion) defence deal on Aug 31 under which Israel will build a multi-layered air defence system for Greece as Athens pushes ahead with a broader military modernisation programme.
Israel’s defence ministry said it was Israel’s largest-ever defence export deal with Greece and one of the biggest in the country’s history. The agreement confirmed an earlier Reuters report.
Amir Baram, director-general of Israel’s defence ministry, said the so-called Achilles Shield deal reflected “Israel’s technological edge and the proven track record of our defence systems in the field”.
Under the deal, Israel will supply Greece with the David’s Sling and SPYDER systems produced by Rafael Advanced Defense Systems and the BARAK MX system made by Israel Aerospace Industries, as well as MMR multi-mission radars for air surveillance, manufactured by IAI unit ELTA Systems.
David’s Sling was used by Israel to intercept Iranian missiles during the war with Iran in 2026. Greece becomes the second customer for the system after Finland.
Greece spends nearly 3.5 per cent of its gross domestic product on defence, a higher proportion than many NATO allies due to its long-standing dispute with neighbouring Turkey.
Athens plans to spend about €28 billion by 2036 to build the Achilles Shield multi-layer anti-ballistic, anti-aircraft and anti-drone system, and to buy up to 40 F-35 fighter jets from the US and frigates from France and Italy.
Under the deal on Aug 31, Greece will receive a new national command-and-control system, developed by Rafael, to integrate the country’s air-defence capabilities.
A supplementary €26 million agreement will see Israel supply Greece with Rafael’s Drone Dome systems to protect strategic sites against drones and reinforce existing defences.
Israel will also expand defence-industrial cooperation with Greece, including transfers of technology and expertise to local industry. REUTERS

"KhimProm" organized a network of call centers in Ukraine to recruit drug dealers in Kazakhstan – seven members detained
Details
Under the procedural guidance of prosecutors from the Prosecutor General’s Office, it was reportedly established that "the criminal organization ‘KhimProm’ was operating, whose members, according to the investigation, created a network of call centers in Ukraine to recruit individuals for the illegal sale of narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances in Kazakhstan."
"At the beginning of 2024, one of the organizers of ‘KhimProm,’ who is wanted internationally, decided to continue his illegal activities and created a new stable hierarchical criminal association. He involved another person in its joint leadership. They formed separate structural units, appointed their heads, and distributed roles among the members," the statement said.
According to the Prosecutor General’s Office, "one of ‘KhimProm’s’ areas of activity was operating a network of call centers." The heads of the structural units organized and coordinated the work of their subordinates, assigned tasks, and monitored their fulfillment. Senior operators and operators were recruited to work at the call centers, the agency added.
According to the investigation, "the operators established contact with individuals in Kazakhstan and persuaded them to participate in the illegal sale of drugs and psychotropic substances." For purposes of concealment, the members reportedly used aliases and code names, hiding their personal data.
"As part of the special operation, law enforcement officers conducted searches and a set of investigative actions. As a result, seven members of the criminal organization were detained," the PGO stated.
They were reportedly notified of suspicion of participation in a criminal organization, as well as of organizing the illegal sale of narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances committed by a criminal organization (Part 2 of Article 255, Part 3 of Article 27, Part 4 of Article 28, Part 3 of Article 307 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine).
The organizer of the criminal organization and his accomplice were also notified of suspicion. They are hiding outside Ukraine. Their actions have been classified under Part 1 of Article 255, Part 3 of Article 27, Part 4 of Article 28, and Part 3 of Article 307 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine.
The issue of selecting preventive measures for those detained is currently being decided.

Hong Kong students, at-risk residents can get flu jabs 1 week early this year
Centre for Health Protection says the government’s seasonal influenza vaccination programmes for 2026-27 will begin on September 17
Hong Kong school students and other at-risk residents can receive influenza vaccines one week earlier this year, after the government diversified its procurement efforts and streamlined administrative measures.
Authorities also said on Monday they aimed to boost the injection rate among people aged 65 or above and children aged six months to two years, adding that they would rely on reminders from doctors during medical encounters as a prioritised measure.
Dr Edwin Tsui Lok-kin, controller of the Centre for Health Protection, said the government’s seasonal influenza vaccination programmes for 2026-27 would begin on September 17, one week earlier than those in the previous year.
“Influenza is still active in August despite it having slightly subsided from the peak, and as students gather after school starts, transmission will be quicker,” Tsui said.
“We expect there will be some transmissions and outbreaks in schools after the new academic year starts, and therefore, we advise [students] to receive jabs as early as available.”
The programmes include the Vaccination Subsidy Scheme (VSS), which offers subsidised doses to vulnerable groups such as children, residents aged 50 or above, pregnant women and adults with chronic diseases.

A small piece of architecture that connects local building traditions with collective use
name: backdirwas_5 designer: Studio Carraldo author site:Studio Carraldo
The oven stands on a solid concrete base cast using formwork made from round timber logs sourced from the surrounding forests. This construction refers to the traditional log building techniques found in the nearby farmhouses, translating their character into a contemporary architectural language. The oven’s combustion chamber is formed as a dome of refractory firebricks. The dome stores the heat generated during firing and reflects it back into the interior of the oven, allowing the heat to be retained and used efficiently. The structure is enclosed by a sculptural stainless steel body. At the front, the body continues the width of the concrete base, while its sides taper upwards. A horizontal drip edge forms the upper termination of the oven. The wooden shingles widely used throughout the Alpine region are reinterpreted as large stainless steel panels. Connected through an interlocking system, the individual elements come together to form a precisely assembled outer shell. A small piece of architecture that connects local building traditions with collective use. By: Studio Carraldo | @studio.carraldo Design Team: Valentin Fick, Franka Ruhnau, David Zauels Photographer: Studio Carraldo Edits: Jonas Zauels | @blackbvrds

Malaysia’s air quality turns hazardous as Indonesian wildfires burn

Malaysia’s air quality turns hazardous as Indonesian wildfires burn
Pollution index hits 476 near the border, forcing school closures and triggering emergency cloud-seeding plans in Sarawak
3-MIN READ3-MIN
 Listen
Air pollution in Malaysia’s Bornean state of Sarawak has surged into hazardous territory, with the air pollutant index (API) topping 400 in the worst-hit district, as forest fires raging in Indonesia continue to send thick smoke drifting across the border.
Serian in Sarawak, closest to the frontier with Indonesia’s West Kalimantan province, recorded the highest reading of 476 as of Monday morning.
Kuching, Samarahan and Sri Aman all logged readings above 300 as of 10am, according to Malaysia’s Environment Department.
The API scale classifies anything above 300 as hazardous; readings of 201-300 are “very unhealthy”, 101-200 “unhealthy”, 51-100 “moderate” and 0-50 “good”.
Malaysia has activated its National Open Burning Action Plan and National Haze Action Plan in response, mobilising government agencies to tackle both the fires and the health risks posed by the smoke.

One Dead, 15 People Unaccounted For After Flash Flooding at the Grand Canyon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
07:05:30 UTC
16:05:30 KST

Two people have died and more than a dozen others are missing or unaccounted for after a flash flood ripped through the Grand Canyon over the weekend, according to park service officials.
The National Park Service (NPS) wrote in a social media post on Monday that two bodies have been recovered, with search and rescue efforts ongoing. The NPS earlier shared late Sunday night that rescuers had found the body of a 46-year-old man near Crystal Rapids along the Colorado River. It has not provided any further information about the deceased.
Read More: Nepal Flash Flooding Leaves Hundreds Dead
In a separate statement on Sunday, the agency asked the public for information on 15 individuals who may be missing or remain unaccounted for. As of Sunday morning, 62 people had been evacuated from Phantom Ranch and the lower North Kaibab Trail, and more were expected to be evacuated in nearby areas, NPS officials added.
NPS asked those who know of hikers or backpackers in the inner canyon along the Bright Angel Creek corridor on Saturday, “as well as anyone who had a campground reservation in the affected corridor,” to provide information.
The continuing search may be impacted by rain and thunderstorms that have been forecasted in the area, the agency warned on Monday.
How the Grand Canyon flash flooding unfolded
The flash-flood event occurred in Bright Angel Canyon and the Phantom Ranch area on Saturday afternoon at around 2:30 p.m. Arizona is currently in the throes of the monsoon season, and storms poured over the Grand Canyon from early Saturday morning and returned in the evening.
Nearly all footbridges over Bright Angel Creek were destroyed in the floods, the Park Service said, preventing hikers from crossing. NPS is continuing to assess the extent of the damage. Parts of the canyon—Phantom Ranch, Bright Angel Campground, the Phantom Ranch Canteen and cabins, and the entire North Kaibab Trail from the North Kaibab Trailhead to Phantom Ranch—were closed until further notice.
The Transcanyon Waterline, a 12.5-mile pipeline in the Grand Canyon that carries water for drinking and fire suppression has also been damaged. With that pipeline out of action, the park has a limited water supply and has resorted to conservation measures.
The National Park Service warns of ongoing risk
Other restrictions have been imposed following the floods. By Monday, all concessions inside the park will end overnight accommodations. Only dry camping—camping without utility hookups to water or sewage—will be allowed on the South Rim, and fires on the South Rim and inner canyon areas will be prohibited.
NPS also warned that flash floods may recur and cause debris flow, as thunderstorms and heavy rainfall are anticipated until Monday.
The National Weather Service in Flagstaff, Ariz. has issued a flash flood watch, urging caution in flood-prone areas like creeks, slot canyons, and low water crossings, among others.

Goldman Sachs heightens warning over diesel fuel amid wars
Kyiv • UNN
Goldman Sachs warned of a global shortage of refining capacity due to wars and strikes on refineries. The forecast for diesel fuel margins has been raised to $63 in the U.S. and $49 in the EU.
Goldman Sachs Group Inc. issued a sterner warning about constraints in the global oil-refining market caused by wars in the Middle East and russia’s war against Ukraine, with the bank more than doubling its forecasts for diesel-production profits, UNN writes, citing Bloomberg.
An escalation in strikes on refineries in the Middle East and russia has further constrained already strained global refining capacity, pushing refining margins to new highs. Diesel fuel remains at the epicenter of the surge
Refinery outages are 60% above seasonal norms, while product inventories are falling despite some weakening in demand, they said. The profit from producing a barrel of diesel fuel relative to Brent next year will average $63 in the United States and $49 in the European Union, compared with previous forecasts of $27 and $19.
The world is facing a global fuel crisis, with prices for products including gasoline far outpacing the rise in oil prices. The situation could worsen after russia extended its ban on diesel-fuel exports through September, while demand is increasing in Brazil, the world’s second-largest importer. Meanwhile, the approach of winter in the Northern Hemisphere is expected to boost demand for heating fuel.
In the Middle East, although oil exports from the Persian Gulf have likely recovered to 70–80% of prewar levels, product shipments remain at only 40%, Goldman analysts said in an Aug. 28 note. "A full recovery in demand requires global geopolitical de-escalation," they added.
In futures markets, the price of Brent crude has risen nearly 50% this year and was last trading at around $91 a barrel amid a new flare-up in the Middle East. Meanwhile, futures for European gasoil have more than doubled.
Goldman Sachs has frequently highlighted strains in commodity markets in recent months, saying in March that the war between Iran and the United States was expected to have a much greater impact on fuel than on oil. Earlier this month, the company again emphasized the impact of Ukrainian strikes on Russia’s energy infrastructure, the publication writes.
Shell Plc Chief Executive Officer Wael Sawan said last week that the commodities market is tightening because of a "triple threat" posed by strikes on Russian refineries and risks to shipping in the Persian Gulf and the Red Sea. Meanwhile, TotalEnergies SE’s Patrick Pouyanné said that although some oil cargoes were passing through the Strait of Hormuz, no refined products were being shipped out.
