BEIJING, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- The purchasing managers' index (PMI) for China's non-manufacturing sector came in at 49 in August, unchanged from the level in July, official data showed on Monday.
The sub-index for business activity in the service sector stood at 49.3 in August, also flat from the previous month, according to the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS).
As an indicator of macroeconomic trends, a PMI reading above 50 indicates expansion while a reading below 50 signals contraction.
By sector, the business activity indices for postal services, telecommunications, broadcasting, television and satellite transmission services, as well as internet, software and information technology services all remained above 55, indicating robust growth in business volume.
The business expectation index for the service sector stood at 55.5 in August, indicating a strong outlook for positive market developments.
The sub-index for business activity in the construction sector dropped 0.1 percentage points to 46.9 this month, the data revealed. NBS chief statistician Huo Lihui said construction activity slowed in some regions due to extreme weather, including heavy rains and typhoons.
The business expectation index for the construction sector remained flat at 51.8.
Monday's data also showed that the PMI for China's manufacturing sector stood at 49.8 in August, up 0.6 percentage points from July. The composite PMI output index rose from 49.3 to 49.5. ■

Seoul district offers foreigners multilingual help to navigate South Korean rental market
The foreign population in Gangbuk has nearly doubled over the past decade to roughly 7,000 residents
To help bridge this informational divide and protect vulnerable foreign renters, Gangbuk, a northern administrative district in Seoul, is expanding a comprehensive municipal programme designed to safeguard foreign residents throughout the housing lease process.
Under the enhanced initiative, foreign tenants visiting local neighbourhood centres to register their move-in address or file for an official “fixed date” status (hwakjeong ilja) will receive automated administrative guidance stamped directly onto their documentation in nine languages. The legal stamp – covering English, Chinese, Vietnamese, Mongolian, Tagalog, Uzbek, Japanese, Taiwanese and Thai – outlines essential protections under the Housing Lease Protection Act.
In the South Korean rental market, obtaining an official fixed date is a critical statutory step that grants tenants legal priority to reclaim key security deposits should a landlord face foreclosure or property auction.
Alongside the multilingual stamps, district offices are distributing QR code stickers linking directly to My Seoul, a dedicated mobile application operated by the Seoul Metropolitan Government. By scanning the code, foreign residents can easily install the application to access multi-language housing guidelines, municipal safety updates and multicultural social services.

Ukraine's long-range strikes bring war to Russian territory, undermine Kremlin narratives – expert
Can Kasapoglu, a senior fellow and defense analyst at Hudson Institute, said this in an interview with Ukrinform.
"Ukraine's burgeoning long-range strike regime should not be understood solely as missile and drone warfare; it is also psychological warfare," Kasapoglu said.
The expert noted that Russia's closed information system and disproportionate combat recruitment from peripheral regions insulate the regime's metropolitan social base from an imperial occupation brutalizing Ukrainian civilians.
"The average Russian does not begin each morning reading the Washington Post. Striking military, logistical, and energy targets while generating a gasoline crisis brings the war home and punctures the Kremlin's narrative of normality," Kasapoglu said.
At the same time, he said, Russia's vast territory creates an additional challenge for its air defenses, as it forces Moscow to spread its defensive resources across a large area.
The expert stressed that the effectiveness of this campaign also depends on combining it with sanctions and sustained Western support for Ukraine. However, he said, drones and missiles alone cannot force Russia to make strategic concessions.
"Russia retains greater capacity to strike strategic targets in Ukraine than Ukraine possesses against the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation," the expert said.
He added that Iran and North Korea have significantly strengthened this Russian advantage through their assistance. In addition, Russia is exploiting Ukraine's shortage of ballistic missile interceptors – a NATO-wide inventory problem that grants Russia leverage and enables sustained ballistic missile salvos.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Mainland Affairs Council on Sunday urged citizens considered high-risk to assess the necessity of traveling to China after a social-media user reported that his son was questioned for about six hours after arriving in Shanghai because he had previously worked for Amnesty International.
The user, whose Threads account is identified as vincentchou08, said his son arrived in Shanghai on Saturday afternoon for a business trip and was stopped at immigration before being taken to a private room for questioning. According to the post, three plainclothes officers questioned the man extensively about his previous work with the human rights organization, per CNA.
The officers allegedly asked about his responsibilities; whether he had worked on reports or human rights advocacy involving China, Hong Kong, Xinjiang, or Tibet; the organization's sources of funding; and his contacts with Taiwanese and international politicians and human rights activists.

He also said his trip was for personal reasons and had no political purpose. The post said the man ultimately decided not to enter China and returned to Taiwan later that evening.
The account holder questioned how Chinese authorities had learned about his son's previous employment, suggesting that Chinese intelligence agencies may have compiled lists of employees, interns, and volunteers associated with international human rights organizations and major Taiwanese NGOs. The claim about such intelligence lists could not be independently verified.
The father said he was relieved that his son did not "become another Lee Ming-che (李明哲)," referring to the Taiwanese pro-democracy activist who was detained by Chinese authorities in March 2017 and later sentenced to five years in prison for subversion of state power. Lee was released in April 2022 after completing his sentence and returned to Taiwan the following day.
MAC said Sunday that the individual involved had not reported the incident to the government but that the account was consistent with other cases previously handled by the council. The council encouraged Taiwanese to share their experiences of difficulties encountered while traveling in China, saying such accounts help raise public awareness of potential risks, per CNA.
The council said China has shown intolerance toward criticism involving democracy and pluralism and has been hostile toward personnel from overseas NGOs working on issues including human rights, environmental protection, oversight of public power, labor rights, and gender diversity.
It also warned that people who were politically active in Taiwan earlier in their lives but later moved into nonpolitical fields could still face scrutiny or punishment by Chinese authorities.
The council said China's new “Revision of Exit and Entry Administration” is scheduled to take effect Sept. 15, significantly increasing personal safety risks for Taiwanese traveling to China. The council has urged Taiwanese to register their trips through its online registration system for citizens visiting China, which allows the government to contact travelers and provide emergency assistance.

Sri Lanka’s New Anti-Terrorism Legislation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
03:09:00 UTC
12:09:00 KST

Sri Lanka’s Cabinet has approved a bill to replace the Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA) of 1979. The official Cabinet decision calls the replacement the “Safeguarding the State from Terrorism” Bill, while the government’s December 2025 consultation draft uses the term “Protection of the State from Terrorism.”
The National People’s Power (NPP) government has not given any reason yet for the change of name of the proposed legislation. It will be published in the Gazette and then presented to Parliament.
The Cabinet-approved text has not yet been made public. The only version that can presently be examined is the 2025 December draft, but it is unlikely that the bill will be significantly different from the draft, given the extensive consultations that followed the December draft.
The 2025 December draft is an improvement over the PTA of 1979. It attempts to define terrorism and related preparatory offenses more narrowly than the PTA did. It also contains safeguards that were absent or weaker under the PTA. For example, the draft recognizes access to counsel, requires notification of detention, provides for magistrates and the Human Rights Commission to visit detention facilities, and requires a detainee held under a detention order to be produced before a magistrate every 14 days. It restricts the use of statements made in custody — an important departure from the PTA’s admission of confessions made to senior police officers. A February 2026 assessment by United Nations experts acknowledged these improvements.
However, the December 2025 draft does not curb the exceptional executive power that critics of the PTA want. Under the December draft, the defense secretary can still renew two-month detention orders for a year. When a detention order is produced, the magistrate is expected to approve it, rather than decide independently whether the evidence justifies continued custody. The president may proscribe organizations and impose curfews, while the armed forces and Coast Guard receive powers normally associated with the police.
The government has not explained why it chose “Safeguarding the State from Terrorism,” as a title for the proposed law. But a law framed around safeguarding “the state” probably looks at protecting aspects such as sovereignty, territorial integrity, government institutions, and public order.
Sri Lanka has legitimate security interests and needs counterterror laws. It fought the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) for decades. At one point, the LTTE controlled about one-third of Sri Lanka’s territory. More recently, the 2019 Easter Sunday attackers targeted civilians and hotels, killing 269 people. But the attack also challenged the state’s capacity to detect and deter transnational ideological threats.
The December draft brings all these interests together. Some of its provisions criminalize the collection or supply of broadly defined “confidential information” that may affect national security and defense. Executive proscription, curfew, and the power the police still wields reinforce the state-security character of the law.
Cabinet spokesman Nalinda Jayatissa said the bill would cover terrorism “including organized crimes.” If that formulation appears in the final text, Parliament should ask whether the law is defining a distinct offense or simply extending counterterrorism powers to difficult forms of ordinary crime.
Sri Lanka nevertheless needs a preventive counterterrorism capacity. The Penal Code can punish crime like murder after the act. But terrorist attacks must be interrupted earlier. The state must act when would-be perpetrators are financing an operation, acquiring weapons, training recruits, selecting targets, or coordinating across borders.
These needs have grown more complex since 1979, when Sri Lanka enacted its first anti-terrorism law amid the looming threat posed by the LTTE. For example, the internet allows small groups to access information and technical knowledge from like-minded individuals based abroad. Terrorist financing can move through digital assets today and is better hidden than in the past.
The December draft recognizes some of this change. It reaches preparatory conduct, financing, transnational activity, and digital communications. It provides judicial authorization for interception and compelled decryption. These focus more on disruption than after-the-fact arrest and confession.
Custody still remains the main debating point of anti-terrorism legislation in the country. Counterterrorism investigations take time, and the complexity of these operations justify more investigative time. However, prolonged custody does not automatically lead to success against terrorism.
The PTA was fully operational when suicide bombers in 2019 killed more than 260 people. A parliamentary investigation and the presidential commission of inquiry found that officials had received specific warnings but failed to evaluate, share, and act on them. The state possessed extensive arrest and detention powers. What it lacked was institutional capacity to disrupt the attacks.
However, the 2025 December draft does not establish how intelligence agencies should share information, how competing warnings should be assessed, who is responsible for acting on them, or how intelligence should be converted into evidence that can survive trial. Those are matters of institutional design, resources and accountability as much as law.
One improvement over the 1979 law that the 2025 draft provides for is limiting the use of confessions made to the police as evidence. The question is whether the final bill creates conditions for financial, communications, and forensic evidence to replace confession-centered investigations, or merely adds safeguards around the old model.
The bill should therefore be judged by whether it is somewhat more liberal than the PTA. Once the Cabinet-approved text is gazetted, three questions will matter. Has the definition separated terrorist violence from protest, organized crime, and political advocacy? Can a court examine the basis for continued detention rather than simply record an executive decision? And does the law help institutions convert intelligence into timely disruption and prosecutable evidence?
Sri Lanka’s history shows why preventive powers are necessary. It also shows that locking people up for extended periods is not the same as prevention. A law designed to safeguard the state should strengthen the state’s ability to recognize and stop a credible threat.
The NPP government has an opportunity to move Sri Lanka away from a system that measures security through arrests and years spent in custody. The better test is whether the law helps the authorities disrupt credible threats and build cases that survive in court. A law that cannot turn intelligence into evidence will reproduce the central weakness of the PTA, regardless of how much power it gives the state.

TOI reporters visited govt schools across six Rajasthan districts after the row over CJP volunteers inspecting campuses. What they found, from Kota’s coaching hub to desert villages and tragedy-hit Piplodi, was a system in which children study under tin sheds, squeeze into unsafe rooms, and sometimes find their school locked.In Kota, a primary school with 78 students operates from municipal parking kiosks and tin sheds. Three teachers run the school on deputation, with no permanent teaching posts sanctioned. A PWD survey found 61 school buildings in the district ruined and hundreds of classrooms unsafe.Across Barmer, Jaisalmer and Balotra, some schools lack buildings, while transfers have left senior-secondary streams without teachers. List of Rajasthan districts TOI visited.

Days before this report, 27 students fell ill after eating their mid-day meal.A Public Works Department survey of Kota district’s 1,088 govt schools found 61 buildings entirely ruined and marked for demolition, plus two classrooms flagged as unsafe in each of 318 school buildings, and one classroom each in a further 98. Only 41 full buildings and 29 partial structures have been demolished so far.District collector Peeyush Samaria’s office has no record of any personal inspection visit to a govt school. Samaria remained unavailable for comment. Sanganer, Jaipur: The CM’s constituency
Bhajan Lal Sharma won the Sanganer assembly constituency in 2023
At Bojyawas Govt Primary School, there are toilets, but they have no water. The water tank has cracked and dense cobwebs, indicating it hasn’t been in use for some time. The school shares space with a sub-health centre, where fungus covers medicine boxes and water stains mark chairs and registers.A staff member said open defecation has become routine for her. She does her best by consciously holding off the urge to use a toilet. The school itself has 10 students in classes 1 to 5 under a single teacher.
Govt Secondary School, Kalyanpura, looks well-kept from the gate, till you learn that one of its two buildings has been shut as unsafe, leaving 404 students across classes 1–12 to squeeze into four rooms.The school runs two shifts, 7am–12 noon and 12:30–6pm, and some second-shift students sit under a tin shed outside because the classes can’t accommodate them. Washrooms don’t have regular water supply and are cleaned only twice a month, said a Class 12 student.With no security guard and a broken, low boundary wall, the campus has seen repeated thefts. As a result, each classroom door has three latches and three separate locks.At Govt Upper Primary Sanskrit School in Hasampur Basdi, 85 students from classes 1 to VIII are taught in four classrooms — one of which is assigned to a booth level officer for special intensive revision (SIR) work.
Teacher Rajendra Verma produced letters he has submitted seeking a playground, boundary fencing and a tubewell. The school has been running on tanker water for close to a year, he said.At Govt Primary School in Hasampura, there was no need to interview anyone about the school’s condition. The gate was locked at 9.30am on a weekday. Former ward councillor Ram Singh Choudhary said he has been writing to govt for three years about the school’s lack of facilities. Jaisalmer & Barmer: Studying under treesIn Rajasthan’s desert border districts, several schools have no building.In Ramsar panchayat, Barmer, Govt Upper Primary School Azad Nagar was sanctioned in the 2022–23 budget and began classes in March 2023. But its 37 students study in a hut built by villagers or under trees.“Whether it rains, there is a storm or it is extremely hot, we have to study under trees,” said a Class V student.Land for the school was allotted only in 2024, and construction funds await sanction.At the Govt Higher Secondary School in Majal village, Samdari block (Balotra district), students and parents locked the school gate after nine teachers were transferred out at once, leaving senior secondary arts, science and agriculture streams without lecturers.“When there are no lecturers in the school, how will we study? How can Grade-II teachers perform the duties of lecturers?” a student asked.The protest ended after education officials agreed to post three teachers on deputation.Assembly data, drawn from UDISE 2025-26 figures, shows both districts have building-less schools: 36 in Barmer and 25 in Jaisalmer. Jaisalmer also features among districts hit hardest by a separate supply failure — a shortfall in the milk powder needed for the state’s Pannadhay Bal Gopal Yojana. Jhalawar: After 7 deaths, wait on for a new buildingOn the morning of July 25, 2025, the roof of Govt Upper Primary School in Piplodi, a tribal village in Jhalawar, collapsed during class hours. Seven children died; 21 were injured.A year on, Piplodi has visibly changed — better roads, more power connections, regular health camps, rising enrolment — but the one thing it still lacks is a functioning school building.Classes at the school have run since last August out of the two-room house of Mor Singh, a 60-year-old farmer and shepherd who vacated his own home so children would not lose another year of school.A new school building — eight classrooms, an anganwadi centre and a kitchen — is under construction, originally due by July 24, 2026. It has since been delayed after villagers raised concerns about construction quality when work began last November. Officials demolished the substandard work and restarted.“Construction of the school is taking longer than expected as villagers raised concerns about the quality of construction,” said Jhalawar collector Ajay Singh, adding that surprise inspections are now held every few weeks and the building should be ready by October.
Among Rajasthan’s blocks, Jhalawar has the highest concentration of building-less govt schools. District-wide, 81 schools lack toilets.Assembly data show 611 govt schools statewide with no building of their own, including 10 girls’ schools, 2,047 schools with buildings that lack toilets, and 1,049 that lack drinking water. It’s not that govt doesn’t spend on educationRajasthan’s 2026–27 budget allocates Rs 64,205 crore to school and college education. Of this allocation, around 75% goes into staff salaries and only 10–15% goes infrastructure.The state employs the second-highest number of teachers in the country, at 7.93 lakh, second only to UP. Yet, it has 7,200 single-teacher govt schools serving over 1.5 lakh students. Around 1.5 lakh sanctioned teacher posts remain vacant.The state’s own infrastructure data lays out the scale of the problem: 3,768 school buildings, 83,783 classrooms and 16,765 toilets are classified as entirely dilapidated while another 2,19,902 classrooms and 29,753 toilets need repair.Over the past two years, govt says it has spent Rs 2,723 crore building 179 new school buildings and 7,945 new classrooms to replace dilapidated ones.With govt funds in scarce supply, state-run schools increasingly lean on voluntary and community money. Statewide, philanthropic donations for school development totalled Rs 138 crore in 2024 and Rs 140 crore in 2025.In Pali district, a donor-led ‘Aao Gaon Chalen’ campaign — connecting migrants and philanthropists to their native villages — has targeted raising Rs 300 crore for infrastructure work.“There are around 23,000 such teachers in the state who are posted in a school where they are not needed, and their posting should be in another school, but they have not accepted their new posting. For instance, in an English-medium school, a Hindi-medium teacher who was earlier posted does not accept their new posting after a transfer, and the Hindi medium school, where the teacher is needed, students are suffering in that school,” said Mahendra Pandey, chief general secretary of Rajasthan Primary and Secondary Teachers Association.
TOI Special Report from Rajasthan
Gen Z, Gen alpha protestsThe consequences have spilled onto the streets.In Sikar, Class 12 students protested dilapidated buildings that force school closures every time it rains, alongside a shortage of subject teachers.In Gangapur City (Sawai Madhopur), girls locked the gates of the Mahatma Gandhi English Medium School in Meena Badoda, Wazirpur, after the principal was pulled onto local-body election duty, compounding an existing teacher shortage.At Govt Senior Secondary School in Majal village in Balotra district, students locked the gates after nine teachers were transferred simultaneously.A Class XII student at Govt Higher Secondary School at Majal in Balotra said: “If we had to study without teachers, then we could have studied at home. What is the need to come to school? If a school is operational, teachers must be posted.”
TOI Ground Report
The infrastructure debate has become an open political fight.A civic campaign, ‘School Thik Karo’, backed by CJP, has sent volunteer teams to inspect schools across nine districts — Jaipur, Ajmer, Jodhpur, Udaipur, Dholpur, Bharatpur, Kota, Barmer and Hanumangarh — after receiving what it says are public requests.“It has been over a year since the school collapse tragedy in Jhalawar, and the education minister has still not shared a concrete plan on how over 80,000 classrooms in dilapidated conditions will be fixed. Students are being forced to study in unsafe buildings, risking their lives,” said CJP national spokesperson Ashutosh Ranka.One inspection, in Jaipur’s Bagru constituency, found a school that had been operating out of a buffalo shed for two and a half years after its own building was declared unsafe; it was shifted to a house only after drawing media attention.
The state education department has now issued an order requiring prior permission for any outsider to enter school premises, and barring photography, videography, interviews or livestreaming involving students without the principal’s consent.
Opposition leader Tikaram Jully called it an attempt to hide failures: “Instead of fixing schools, if you introduce ‘no entry’ measures just to hide your own failures, how can such accidents be prevented? A useless ‘double-engine’ govt,” Jully said.Additional reporting by Vimal Matta, Suparna Roy, Somdutt Trtpathi, Suntl Parmuwal & Shoeb Khan

U.S. Strikes Iran in First Military Action in a Month
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
03:05:16 UTC
12:05:16 KST

President Donald Trump vowed on Monday that the U.S. will strike Iran “hard” after the two countries exchanged their first publicly confirmed attacks in weeks.
Trump told Fox News’ Trey Yingst that “there will be a response” to strikes Iran launched against U.S. forces in Jordan overnight in retaliation for an American attack on an island in the Strait of Hormuz.
“We're going to hit them hard,” the President said, according to Yingst.
Trump’s threat comes after U.S. forces attacked two Iranian rocket launchers on Larak Island on Sunday, marking a resumption of military action after a roughly month-long pause.
CENTCOM spokesperson Capt. Tim Hawkins confirmed the strike in a statement to TIME, adding that Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) forces “were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines” into the strait.
Last week, U.S. forces finished clearing sea mines from the strait’s international shipping routes.
“U.S. forces are monitoring the area closely and remain prepared to protect the free flow of commerce through this essential waterway,” Hawkins added.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) issued a statement soon after the U.S. strikes that was carried by Iranian state news agency IRNA, saying that Iran would respond to the attacks on Larak Island “with punishment for the aggressor.”
The IRGC later said in a statement early Monday local time that it had launched ballistic missiles at a U.S. air base in Jordan and warned that “every shot will be met with more devastating responses,” IRNA reported. Jordan’s armed forces said they intercepted eight missiles that entered the country’s airspace early Monday morning.
In a statement, CENTCOM rebuffed the Revolutionary Guards’ claims, describing the Sunday attack as “limited, precise action against IRGC minelaying forces posing an imminent threat” to the strait.
A pause in attacks
Before the Sunday strikes, the last time the U.S. military confirmed targeting Iran was on July 29, announcing a “heavy wave of strikes” on dozens of IRGC targets in Iran, including command centers, missile and drone facilities, and coastal surveillance and defense sites.
On Aug. 1, President Donald Trump said that he agreed to “hold off” strikes in Iran at the request of the U.S.’s regional allies in the Middle East.
How the U.S.-Iran war began
The strikes mark the latest escalation in the war, which began on Feb. 28 when the U.S. and Israel launched a wave of attacks across Iran. Trump described the operation as a “massive and ongoing” campaign intended to eliminate what he called imminent threats from the Iranian regime and openly encouraged Iranians to overthrow their government.
The attacks came after U.S.-Iranian negotiations over Tehran’s nuclear program failed to produce an agreement and amid the Iranian government’s deadly crackdown on nationwide protests. Trump had accused Iran of rebuilding its nuclear capabilities following U.S. and Israeli strikes on three major Iranian nuclear sites in June 2025. Iran has consistently denied seeking a nuclear weapon.
Iran’s Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei was killed in the opening salvo of the Feb. 28 campaign. Iran retaliated by firing missiles at Israel, U.S. military bases and other sites across the Middle East, widening the conflict throughout the region.
The war also led Iran to militarize and largely close the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s most important energy transit routes, through which about a fifth of global oil production typically passed before the hostilities.
A U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports was lifted under a June agreement, but Trump reimposed it after that deal and its accompanying cease-fire fell apart.

China Focus: Centuries-old artifacts bear witness to vibrant Sino-Italian cultural exchanges
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
11:01:34 CST
12:01:34 KST

A visitor takes photos during an exhibition titled "Crown of Glory: 18th-Century Italian Court Treasures from the House of Savoy" at the Tianjin Museum in north China's Tianjin Municipality on July 2, 2026. (Xinhua)
TIANJIN, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- Chinese silk and decorative motifs found their way into the art of 18th-century European courts, while European tastes and designs came into contact with Chinese porcelain.
At an exhibition at the Tianjin Museum in the northern Chinese metropolis, more than 150 Italian artifacts offer a vivid glimpse into the rich cultural exchanges between China and Italy centuries ago.
Jointly presented by the Tianjin Museum, the Tianjin Digital Art Museum and the Turin City Museum of Ancient Art in Palazzo Madama, the exhibition, titled "Crown of Glory: 18th-Century Italian Court Treasures from the House of Savoy," ran from Feb. 10 to Aug. 31. The exhibition showcases centuries-old treasures from the House of Savoy, one of the most influential royal houses in Italy in the 17th and 18th centuries.
Rather than simply showcasing the splendor of the Italian royal court, the exhibition traces how Chinese art and craftsmanship influenced European tastes and how Chinese artisans, in turn, responded to European demand, providing a window into the cultural interaction between East and West.
A French court gown from the collection of Palazzo Madama is among the highlights at the exhibition.
According to Li Jun, deputy director of the artifacts research department at the Tianjin Museum and curator of the exhibition, the gown incorporates Chinese silk and embroidery techniques, offering evidence of the popularity of "chinoiserie" at the time. By the mid-18th century, the style had become a hallmark of European aristocrats and the wealthy bourgeoisie.
Another exhibit, a men's robe with decorative patterns, provides further evidence of the influence of Chinese craftsmanship.
According to scholars, the ivory-colored robe with floral patterns was made from precious Chinese fabric. The silk was produced using a combination of weaving, block printing and hand painting techniques.
Such oriental-style fabrics became highly fashionable in European society in the second half of the 18th century. They were used not only for luxury garments but also extensively in interior decoration, becoming an important carrier of the "chinoiserie" aesthetic.
In the 17th and 18th centuries, Chinese porcelain, silk, lacquerware and other goods featuring distinctive oriental aesthetics became increasingly popular in Europe. Travel accounts, images of exotic people and landscapes, and Chinese-inspired decorative motifs further shaped European perceptions of the Orient.
The 18th century also witnessed the Enlightenment in Europe, with thinkers challenging feudal autocracy and religious constraints.
The thoughts of Chinese philosophers emphasizing openness and rationality resonated with some Enlightenment ideas, said Yan Guodong, dean of the School of Foreign Languages at Nankai University and an expert in the history of cultural exchanges between China and foreign countries.
Against this backdrop, an unprecedented craze for Chinese-style art and design, known as "chinoiserie," swept across European society and courts, leaving a lasting imprint on Western art and aesthetics.
The influence of cultural exchanges is even more vivid in the exhibition's "East Meets West" section, where Chinese-style porcelain, round fans and bird-and-flower paintings evoke interactions between Chinese and European artistic traditions.
A Qianlong-period Guangcai porcelain plate with a Swedish coat of arms from the Tianjin Museum's collection is one example.
Li said the piece was commissioned by Count Carl Gustaf Tessin, a prominent European art collector of the 18th century.
"Its value goes far beyond an ordinary commercial transaction. It represents a profound cultural dialogue between East and West based on mutual aesthetic appreciation and romantic imagination," Li said.
Such exchanges were by no means one-way, as Chinese kilns also accepted bespoke orders from European aristocrats, producing armorial porcelain tailored to Rococo tastes, Li added.
Yan said European consumers regarded the patterns on Chinese porcelain, silk and lacquerware as representations of life in China, while Chinese artisans sought to cater to European tastes in the selection and design of porcelain motifs.
"These exchanges were not simply the movement of commodities, but also the interaction of aesthetics, craftsmanship and cultural imagination," Yan said.
The exhibition has so far attracted more than 24,000 visitors.
"I was amazed by the material culture and artistic achievements of the House of Savoy, and even more struck by how some of the pieces ingeniously incorporated traditional Chinese craftsmanship, vividly recreating the 'chinoiserie' craze in 18th-century Europe," said a visitor surnamed Wang in Tianjin.
The artifacts, he added, bear witness to cultural exchanges between China and Italy along the Maritime Silk Road.
For Giovanni Carlo Federico Villa, director of the Turin City Museum of Ancient Art in Palazzo Madama, the journey of these artifacts across mountains and seas to China tells a story that extends far beyond artistic beauty.
"These artifacts not only allow us to look back on exchanges between ancient civilizations, but also provide a historical reference for contemporary cultural cooperation between China and Italy, further strengthening the bonds between our peoples," Villa said.
Massimo Ambrosetti, Italian ambassador to China, said the exhibition reveals the profound influence of Chinese art on European "chinoiserie" aesthetics and the porcelain industry in the 18th century, demonstrating the mutual enrichment of Chinese and Italian cultures and arts.
He expressed hope that cultural exchanges between China and Italy will continue to deepen and deliver lasting benefits. ■
People visit an exhibition titled "Crown of Glory: 18th-Century Italian Court Treasures from the House of Savoy" at the Tianjin Museum in north China's Tianjin Municipality on July 2, 2026. (Xinhua)

Japan's July industrial output up 0.1 pct on month
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
11:01:02 CST
12:01:02 KST

TOKYO, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- Japan's industrial output in July edged up 0.1 percent from the previous month, as stronger semiconductor-related production was offset by weakness in transport equipment, government data showed Monday.
The uptick came on the heels of an upwardly revised 1.9 percent gain in June, according to a preliminary report released by the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry.
The seasonally adjusted index of production at factories and mines stood at 104.7 against the 2020 base of 100.
Ten of 15 industrial sectors covered in the report saw output increases in July, including production machinery, which was boosted by stronger exports of semiconductor manufacturing devices.
Transport equipment excluding motor vehicles was among the four sectors that declined, while electric machinery and information and communication electronics equipment held steady.
Based on a survey of manufacturers, the ministry expects output to climb 6.4 percent in August and contract 4.2 percent in September. ■

BEIJING, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- A fast-moving chain mudslide, triggered by a high-altitude glacier collapse in Nepal, struck Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal border in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region on Aug. 26, causing heavy casualties and leaving many missing.
Chinese rescuers immediately launched an all-out effort to reach the mudslide-hit port area and search for the missing. Here is what we know about the deadly mudslide and the latest rescue and relief progress in China:
-- Sixteen people have been confirmed dead and 546 others remain missing as of 6 p.m. Saturday, according to the regional government.
-- A total of 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries have been identified as unaccounted for. The figure was announced on Sunday morning at a press conference held by the information office of the regional government, following a joint search and cross-checking of information by foreign affairs, public security, culture and tourism, and emergency management authorities.
-- At the press conference, the regional government noted that the mudslide was triggered by an ice-rock avalanche originating from a high-mountain glacier in Nepal.
A glacier on Mount Langtang Lirung in Nepal fractured at an altitude of about 5,200 meters, triggering the ice-rock avalanche. The avalanche plunged rapidly to an altitude of around 4,000 meters, scouring the mountainside and developing into a massive debris flow, which surged about 22 kilometers before reaching Gyirong Port at an altitude of around 1,800 meters.
-- A total of 2,141 personnel have joined search and rescue operations, including personnel from the People's Liberation Army, the People's Armed Police Force, and China Anneng, a state-owned engineering and rescue enterprise. And 269 rescue vehicles and 3,922 sets of rescue equipment have also been dispatched to the front line.
-- The barrier lake above Gyirong Port has basically drained, forming a flowing state of the river channel, China's Ministry of Water Resources said Sunday, citing drone footage and panoramic images captured in the morning and reports from emergency response teams.
-- Communications have been restored at the core rescue site, as successful phone calls have been made with rescuers at the port via a newly-built base station on Sunday, according to the regional communications administration.
The first emergency base station adjacent to the border gate of Gyirong Port was put into operation at 1:30 p.m. on Sunday. Up to now, telecom operators in Xizang have restored one damaged base station and built eight new ones near the port.
-- On Sunday morning, the People's Liberation Army Xizang Military Command mobilized an epidemic prevention team to the disaster-hit area to carry out environmental disinfection, food and water quality testing, emergency vaccinations, and routine medical rounds for injuries and illnesses. This relief mission also included psychological support personnel, who will regularly provide psychological counseling for rescuers and the disaster-affected local residents.
-- China has provided emergency humanitarian assistance to Nepal, the China International Development Cooperation Agency said on Sunday.
At present, Chinese aid supplies have been delivered to Kathmandu, tunnel rescue experts have arrived at the disaster-stricken area in Nepal, and the Chinese side is simultaneously sharing important information such as images, satellite and hydrological data of the disaster area.
-- Gyirong County is expected to see more rainfall in the coming days, with significant nighttime precipitation, the National Meteorological Center said on Sunday. ■

Google has modified its Maps service to reflect a US government directive renaming Lake Ontario to "Lake America", highlighting escalating diplomatic and trade tensions between Washington and Ottawa.
"Since we update Google Maps to reflect name changes in official government sources ... people using Maps in the US will see 'Lake America'," Google said Saturday.
US President Donald Trump, who ordered the change, noted the adjustment on Truth Social, posting: "Google Maps changes Lake Ontario to 'Lake America' on US phones."
The company clarified that users in Canada will continue to see Lake Ontario, whilst those outside both countries will see both designations displayed as "Lake Ontario (Lake America)".
The update follows formal changes implemented by the US Geographic Names Information System, the federal agency tasked with standardising geographic names.
The adjustment stems from an executive order signed by Trump directing American government agencies to adopt the name across all official databases, with Trump stating the move takes immediate effect in response to recent bilateral friction.
Collapse of bilateral trade
In January 2025, shortly after returning to office, Trump similarly ordered the Gulf of Mexico renamed the "Gulf of America", prompting comparable regional display adjustments on Google Maps.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford rejected the measure, unveiling a new "Lake Ontario" sign on Saturday to reaffirm the waterway’s historical identity.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney also condemned the executive order, citing the Wendat, an Indigenous people of North America, as the origin of the historic name.
The dispute unfolds alongside an intensifying trade conflict.
Canada is scheduled to impose counter-tariffs ranging between 15 percent and 50 percent on $20 billion worth of US imports starting on September 8.
The retaliatory measures follow the collapse of bilateral trade talks and the subsequent US imposition of 50 percent tariffs on CAN$27.6 billion worth of Canadian products on August 22.

Philosopher’s Annual for 2025
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
02:41:07 UTC
11:41:07 KST

Philosopher’s Annual for 2025
The articles that made it into the latest edition of Philosophers Annual have been announced.
The list aims to “select the ten best articles published in philosophy each year—an attempt as simple to state as it is admittedly impossible to fulfill.”
This volume—the 45th—covers the literature from 2024.
The selections are:
Evan Behrle (Harvard), “Desert and Economic Interdependence” from the Journal of Philosophy.
Outside of philosophy, the idea that workers deserve to be paid according to their productive contributions is very popular. But political philosophers have given it relatively little attention. In this paper, I argue against the attempt to use this idea about desert and contribution to vindicate significant income inequality. I claim that reward according to contribution fails on its own terms when the following condition holds: the size of each worker’s contribution depends on what other workers only together do. When workers only together make another more productive, that is not reflected in the sum of their own contributions. Thus reward according to contribution recognizes individual accomplishments without recognizing their dependence on collectives, dependence that is, in complex economies, ubiquitous.
Sam Berstler (MIT), “The Structure of Open Secrets” from the Philosophical Review.
In conversation, we often do not acknowledge what we jointly know to be true. This article identifies a distinctive kind of non-acknowledgment norm, open secrecy norms, and analyzes how such norms constrain our speech. First, the author argues that open secrecy norms are structurally different from other everyday non-acknowledgment norms. Open secrecy norms iterate: when is an open secret, then there’s a norm not to acknowledge that , and this norm is itself an open secret. Then, the author argues that the non-acknowledgment at issue in open secrecy norms motivates a more complex understanding of discourse structure. When interlocutors are conforming to open secrecy norms, they rely on at least two disjoint common grounds, one of which has a privileged status. To understand why and how it is privileged, the author develops Erving Goffman’s notion of defining a social interaction. Finally, the author shows how strategic speakers can exploit the structure of open secrecy norms in order to both communicate about the open secret and shield themselves from retaliation for what they communicate.
Kyle Blumberg (Melbourne) and Ben Holguín (Johns Hopkins), “Fictional Reality” from the Philosophical Review.
This article defends a theory of fictional truth. According to this theory, there is a fact of the matter concerning the number of hairs on Sherlock Holmes’s head, and likewise for any other meaningful question one could ask about what’s true in a work of fiction. This article argues that a theory of this form is needed to account for the patterns in our judgments about attitude reports that embed fictional claims. It contrasts this view with one of the dominant approaches to fictional truth, which originates with David Lewis. Along the way it explores the relationship between fiction, counterfactuals, and vagueness.
Liam Kofi Bright (LSE), Nathan Gabriel (UC Merced), Cailin O’Connor (UC Irvine), and Olúfẹ́mi O. Táíwò (Georgetown), “On the Stability of Racial Capitalism” from Ergo.
What is the connection between capitalism and racial hierarchy? In line with the tradition known as ‘the theory of racial capitalism’ we show that the latter can functionally support the former. As a social construction, race has just those features which allow it to facilitate the sort of stable, inequitable distributions of resources that tend to emerge in capitalist systems. We support this claim using techniques from evolutionary game theory and cultural evolutionary theory, and end by discussing the normative political consequences of this relationship.
Colin Chamberlain (UCL), “How To Eat a Peach: Malebranche on the Function of the Passions” from Mind.
Nicolas Malebranche (1638-1715) holds that the senses, imagination, and passions serve the body’s needs. In this paper, I explain how the passions keep us alive by situating them in Malebranche’s account of ordinary bodily action. Malebranche holds a consent-based view of action. An agent translates her inclinations or motives into action only when she consents to them. The passions contribute to the preservation of life by helping the agent close the gap between inclination and action. The passions, according to Malebranche, are complex psychophysiological phenomena whose various elements—perceptions, shifts of attention, evaluations, bodily preparation, feelings, and so on—work together to elicit the agent’s consent.
Dai Heide (Simon Fraser), “The Transcendental Aesthetic and the Leibnizian Theory of Space” from the Journal of the History of Philosophy.
In considering Kant’s response to the Leibnizian theory of space in the Transcendental Aesthetic, scholars have overwhelmingly emphasized Kant’s response to Leibniz’s relationalism. They have largely missed the metaphysically realistic aspects of Leibniz’s theory with which Kant is primarily concerned. As such, scholars have failed to appreciate the threat Leibniz’s theory poses to Kant’s idealism, a point made publicly as early as 1786 by H. A. Pistorius. I argue that the Aesthetic does indeed contain a compelling argument against the Leibnizian theory of space. This argument crucially depends upon Kant’s claim that space is monistic: that the whole of space is prior to the parts of space and, as such, spatial representations are not decomposable.
Elselijn Kingma (KCL) and Fiona Woollard (Southampton), “Can You Do Harm to Your Fetus? Pregnancy, Barriers, and the Doing/Allowing Distinction” from Ethics.
When pregnant persons do not behave in the way deemed optimal for their fetus, they are often framed as doing harm. This framing acts as a justificatory bypass for defenses of widespread expectations of pregnant persons, allowing such defenses to avoid substantial questions about special obligations in pregnancy. Our main claim is that this justificatory bypass is unwarranted: in many cases either the pregnant person does not count as doing harm or substantive questions about special obligations cannot be avoided. Our secondary claim is that direct engagement with these substantive questions is unlikely to justify widespread expectations on pregnant people.
Alexander Meehan (Wisconsin) and Snow Zhang (UC Berkeley), “Bayes Is Back” from the Philosophical Review.
A core tenet of Bayesian epistemology is that Bayesian conditionalization is the rule of rational credal revision. But it has been pointed out in the recent literature that if learning can be nontransparent, then Bayesian conditionalization does not universally maximize expected accuracy. This result raises an explanatory challenge for any externalist Bayesian who does not want to give up on a connection between accuracy and epistemic rationality: Why is Bayesian conditionalization the rule of rational credal revision, despite the fact that it does not universally maximize expected accuracy? This article proposes an answer to this challenge. The article argues that an updating rule can be evaluated, not only on the basis of its expected accuracy in particular learning situations, but also on the basis of its total expected accuracy across different learning situations. The article proposes a notion of global evidential constancy, and shows that, out of all globally evidentially constant rules, Bayesian conditionalization has the highest total expected accuracy across all learning situations, including nontransparent ones. Bayes is back!
Paulina Sliwa (Vienna), “Changing Minds and Hearts” from Russ Shafer-Landau, ed., Oxford Studies in Metaethics, vol. 20.
Suppose you are uncertain about some moral question. Are you falling morally short, if you rely on moral advice? A popular line of thought is that the problem with relying on moral testimony is that it can change beliefs but not feelings. An agent who forms a moral judgment based on testimony will be emotionally alienated from the moral judgment they accept. They may come to believe—even know—that a given course of action is right or wrong. But they won’t feel it. The aim of this chapter is to challenge this diagnosis: that moral deference will leave the agent emotionally disconnected from the features that matter. It does so by examining the phenomenon of hermeneutical advice: this is moral testimony that aims at helping an agent to make sense of her moral situation. Hermeneutical advice, it is argued, has the power to change minds and hearts.
Quinn White (Harvard), “Love First” from Philosophy and Phenomenological Research.
How should we respond to the humanity of others? Should we care for others’ well-being? Respect them as autonomous agents? Largely neglected is an answer we can find in the religious traditions of Judaism, Christianity and Buddhism: we should love all. This paper argues that an ideal of love for all can be understood apart from its more typical religious contexts and moreover provides a unified and illuminating account of the the nature and grounds of morality. I defend a novel account of love for all that avoids serious worries about the incoherence or impossibility of loving everyone. Doing so requires countenancing a neglected form of love. Love admits as its object not just individual entities like people and groups; we can also bear a love for the Fs in general—for all the Joneses, all the philosophers, or even all the human beings. I go on to argue that while it is possible for ordinary agents like us to love all, we shouldn’t. Instead, we should approximate love for all. The minimal approximation of love for all is, surprisingly, respect; I derive the basic, structural features of deontological ethics (including anti-paternalism and anti-aggregation) from the ideal of loving all.
The editors of Philosopher’s Annual are Daniel J. Singer (University of Pennsylvania), Lila Graham, Lorenzo Manuali, Brett Thompson (University of Michigan). The executive editor is Patrick Grim (Center for the Study of Complex Systems, University of Michigan; Logic & Formal Semantics, Philosophy, Stony Brook).
The nominating editors this year were: Jc Beall, John T. Bengson, Brian Berkey, Ned Block, Ben Bradley, Liam Kofi Bright, Tyler Burge, Victor Caston, Andrew Chignell, Kathleen Creel, Roger Crisp, Cian Dorr, Elizabeth Edenberg, Adam Elga, Iskra Fileva, Branden Fitelson, Will Fleisher, Graeme Forbes, Aaron Garrett, Michael Glanzberg, Alexander Guerrero, Alan Hájek, Ned Hall, Gary Hatfield, Christopher Hitchcock, Des Hogan, Lily Hu, Simon Huttegger, Gabbrielle Johnson, Simon Keller, Zoë Johnson King, Niko Kolodny, Marc Lange, Harvey Lederman, Brian Leiter, Ernie Lepore, Neil Levy, Martin Lin, Ting-an Lin, Colin McLarty, Jeff McMahan, Lauritz Munch, Derk Pereboom, Duncan Pritchard, Theron Pummer, Greg Restall, Geoffrey Sayre-McCord, Anat Schechtman, Barry Schein, Ted Sider, Scott Soames, Roy Sorensen, Quayshawn Spencer, Katie Steele, Una Stojnić, Eric Swanson, Johan van Benthem, Mark van Roojen, Sergio Tenenbaum, Peter B. M. Vranas, Eric Watkins, Daniel Wodak, Gideon Yaffe, José Zalabardo, and Kevin Zollman.

====================================================================================================

Why South Asia’s Governments Must Build Disaster Institutions That Reflect the Region’s Borderless Hazards
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
02:37:00 UTC
11:37:00 KST

When part of a glacier collapsed above the Lhende Khola on August 26, the debris flow it triggered was initially mistaken by the U.S. Geological Survey’s automated network for a magnitude-4.4 earthquake. By August 30, the combined toll in Nepal and China’s Tibet had reached around 750 dead, with more than 3,000 missing, including nearly 900 hydropower workers feared trapped.
Nepal’s finance minister estimates rebuilding will cost $4-5 billion, nearly a tenth of the Nepali economy. The collapse occurred on the Nepali side, on Langtang Lirung, which lies wholly within Nepal, but the debris fell into the Lhende Khola-Donglin Tsangpo river system, which crosses the Nepal-China border. The flood surged through Nepal’s Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts, while rising downstream levels prompted precautionary evacuations in parts of India. The hazards crossed borders. The mechanisms for responding to them have remained largely national.
South Asia’s problem is not a shortage of frameworks to deal with natural disasters. After the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, SAARC’s 2005 Dhaka Declaration called for a permanent regional mechanism for disaster preparedness, relief and rehabilitation. A 2006 Comprehensive Framework promised shared early-warning and cross-border data exchange. A Rapid Response mechanism agreed after Pakistan’s 2010 floods entered into force only in 2016, and many provisions have struggled to acquire operational continuity. SAARC’s non-functioning has further hindered a regional response; the grouping has not held a summit since 2014. India, Bangladesh and BIMSTEC have developed bilateral and subregional mechanisms because SAARC has been non-functional for a decade. But even these working instruments remain disconnected.
Disaster cooperation has four parts: monitoring, data-sharing, warning and response. Monitoring tells us what is happening upstream; data-sharing determines who learns about it and how quickly; warning tells downstream governments and populations what to do; response determines whether teams and equipment can cross a border. South Asia has instruments for each, but lacks the chain connecting them.
The 2008 Kosi flood showed the cost of that missing chain. When the eastern Kosi embankment breached at Kushaha in Nepal, some 50,000 Nepalis and millions in Bihar in India were affected. A World Bank assessment recorded 3.3 million affected and nearly 500 deaths. Water scholar Ajaya Dixit identified a core institutional gap: the 1966 Kosi treaty did not establish a clearly defined bilateral operational channel for embankment monitoring and maintenance. That did not cause the breach, but left no fast mechanism to turn warning into downstream evacuation. In 2017, floods across India, Nepal and Bangladesh affected an estimated 41 million people, yet the response remained largely national.
The 2023 South Lhonak glacial lake outburst in Sikkim made the same point. Researchers had estimated a 42 percent probability of the lake bursting. It sent a 20-meter wave through the Teesta-III dam and 385 kilometers into Bangladesh. India’s forecasters alerted Bangladesh the same day, but the lake’s early-warning system was still being installed — a year late. This was initially a failure of domestic preparedness, not a cross-border cooperation failure.
But that domestic lapse does not stand apart from the region’s wider pattern. The weakness exists at every layer, from monitoring to data exchange, warning and response. Foreknowledge is not the missing ingredient.
The response to last week’s glacier collapse and flooding in the Tibet-Nepal region follows a familiar pattern. China’s Premier Li Qiang travelled to the affected Gyirong sector within a day, while India sent relief flights and medical teams within 48 hours. Kathmandu initially declined foreign teams, but later accepted limited foreign expertise for tunnel rescue, DNA testing and forensic work after international pressure. India has offered assistance for Nepal to take up as it sees fit. The aid is generous, but negotiated afresh rather than activated through a standing protocol.
Nepal’s consent matters, particularly for security-linked deployments, but the question is whether technical assistance can be pre-negotiated so tunnelling teams, DNA units and bridging equipment activate in hours rather than days.
India and Bangladesh’s Joint Rivers Commission offers a working model. Since 1972, it has shared water-level, discharge and rainfall data on major rivers, with the annual sharing window extended in 2022. Bangladeshi officials say it falls short of real-time forecasting on smaller rivers. The 1996 Ganges Water Sharing Treaty expires in December 2026; formal renewal talks have not begun, despite an Indian parliamentary panel urging action.
BIMSTEC offers experience that South Asia can draw on. India has hosted Disaster Management Exercises since 2017, including rounds in 2020, 2021 and 2025. Yet when a magnitude-7.7 earthquake struck Myanmar in March 2025, it did not produce a comparable regional deployment. Instead, India launched Operation Brahma, reaching the ground within a day. A BIMSTEC Centre of Excellence for Disaster Management was proposed weeks later. The bloc is rehearsing interoperability faster than it is institutionalizing it.
The most difficult test is managing cooperation with China. India and China have an Expert-Level Mechanism on trans-border rivers, established in 2006 for annual meetings and flood-season data exchange. But its continuity is fragile. The Sutlej hydrological-data MoU expired in November 2020 and the Brahmaputra MoU in June 2023. China suspended Brahmaputra data-sharing during the 2017 Doklam standoff, citing damage to hydrological stations.
When functioning, the Sutlej and Brahmaputra data-sharing arrangements transmitted water-level, discharge and rainfall data twice daily during the flood season. Such arrangements can also be affected by the wider state of bilateral relations, making continuity an institutional vulnerability. Days before the Lhende Khola collapse, India and China agreed to hold the next Expert-Level Mechanism meeting in September and discuss renewing the lapsed MoUs. China had also said a year earlier it would use the mechanism and share hydrological data during emergencies on humanitarian grounds.
But no comparable standing early-warning mechanism for Nepal-China glacial-lake and landslide hazards is publicly documented. Former Nepali Environment Minister Madhav Prasad Chaulagain recently said that Nepal received no timely warning from China before the August 26 disaster; a protocol agreed after a smaller 2025 glacier incident was not used. Those claims have not been independently established, but they reinforce the central question: whether existing channels can deliver actionable warnings before a cross-border hazard becomes a downstream disaster. China did directly warn Nepal about a new barrier-lake risk after the flood. The lesson is that mechanisms exist, but their continuity remains too dependent on the wider political relationship.
South Asia needs to make its existing cross-border mechanisms operational. Three steps are realistic: renew data-sharing agreements on fixed schedules rather than allowing them to lapse; pre-clear technical assistance so that specialized teams and equipment can move within hours; and jointly fund glacial-lake monitoring, starting where India and Nepal already cooperate while developing a separate track for China. The challenge is turning information into interoperable warnings that cross administrative and national borders. The region increasingly knows where the risks are. What it has not built is the chain that turns that knowledge into a warning someone downstream can act on, or into a response that can cross a border when minutes matter.
The ice and rock above the Lhende Khola did not stop at the border. The river carried its consequences through three countries. South Asia’s governments now have a choice: build disaster institutions that reflect the region’s borderless hazards, or keep discovering, every few years, that the next disaster arrived at a boundary for which there was no standing plan.

====================================================================================================

India Has a Complex Youth Unemployment Problem, And There Isn’t a Quick Fix
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-31
02:33:00 UTC
11:33:00 KST

India has been struggling with a multi-faceted employment problem, which is triggering deep frustration among its youth, especially those who are educated.
This frustration was on display recently, when tens of thousands of young women and men protested at New Delhi’s Jantar Mantar, demanding the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. While the immediate trigger for the protests was leaked question papers for medical entrance examinations, the underlying cause is frustration with an education system that doesn’t lead to meaningful employment.
The Indian economy is among the world’s fastest-growing large economies. Yet, it is producing an ever-increasing number of educated unemployed youth.
The problems are multifold. First, India is struggling to connect education and skills with available jobs. Second, its economy is not creating good-quality employment for a rapidly expanding and increasingly educated workforce. And third, poor government recruitment has rendered generic university degrees largely useless.
The warnings have been there for quite some time. A 2018 article by Indrajit Bairagya in the Economic and Political Weekly noted that the unemployment rate among the educated is not only higher than that among the uneducated, but it also increases with higher levels of education. Youth, both educated and uneducated, are more likely to be unemployed than older people. One reason is that the educated are unwilling to take low-grade informal jobs, while sufficient regular salaried jobs are also not available.
Developments over the last few years reveal a deeply worrying situation. A recent report titled “Reimagining Skilling for Viksit Bharat@2047,” published by NITI Aayog, the top policy advisor to the government of India, in August this year, said only 8.25 percent of graduates are employed in roles aligned with their qualifications. The remaining 91.75 percent are not working in roles that use the qualifications they acquired. They either acquired additional skills or are working below their skill level, the report said, blaming the poor education-to-job transition rate for India’s growing youth unemployment.
The report says that 80 percent of higher education students identify inadequate practical experience and industry exposure as a major problem. Degrees, diplomas and certificates do not consistently translate into employability when curricula remain disconnected from evolving workplace requirements. As a result, the unemployment rate among graduates stood at 13 percent, compared with the national unemployment rate of 3.2 percent; among women graduates, it was 20.4 percent.
The NITI report reveals that generic degrees don’t provide a direct pathway to employment. When a student with a graduate degree fails to land a job, she either turns to additional degrees or invests in coaching classes that she hopes will lead to a job. All these enhance the overall education costs for improving employability. The cost burden adds salt to the wounds of unemployment.
Some, including the NITI report, have suggested linking education to skills that will make youth more employable, but it cannot by itself create demand for their labor. India, therefore, also needs faster creation of productive, reasonably secure jobs capable of absorbing a large and increasingly educated workforce.
There is another problem—the informal sector is massive. Another paper published by NITI in March estimates that only 23 percent of India’s workforce are regular wage/salaried employees, while 19 percent are casual workers. The rest—about 58 percent—are self-employed/micro-entrepreneurs. Here, ‘self-employment’ often masks underemployment rather than genuine entrepreneurship.
Besides, the credibility of government data on unemployment has been called into question. A 2025 Reuters poll revealed that most of the independent economists who participated in the survey believed the Indian government’s unemployment data masks the severity of joblessness and underemployment. Official surveys use outdated definitions — counting anyone who works for as little as one hour per week as employed, they pointed out.
This means that India’s unemployment crisis is bigger than what it appears to be.
Economists have proposed various solutions. Raising concerns about the impact of automation and AI on future employment, development economist Santosh Mehrotra has called for a stronger manufacturing strategy. Former Reserve Bank of India chief Raghuram Rajan said India needed “structural economic pivots toward labor-intensive white-collar and specialized job creation.” Many have urged shifting focus away from purely capital-heavy incentives toward sectors like textiles, leather, and light engineering that can absorb the millions moving away from agriculture.
Such proposals would require policy reversals by the Narendra Modi government. Whether the government aims for such changes to earn the confidence of the youth remains to be seen.

Russia has the largest military presence and the most extensive military infrastructure in the Arctic and in recent years China has started to increase its activity in the mineral-rich area, mostly in partnership with Moscow.
Norway, a Russia's neighbour, this month expanded a recently created military brigade headquartered in the Arctic, the latest move by a NATO nation to boost its defence footprint in the wake of the Ukraine war which Russia started in 2022.
Moscow has previously dismissed allegations that it poses a threat to NATO. REUTERS

DUBAI – Iran is still seeking a negotiated solution to its conflict with the US, President Masoud Pezeshkian said on Aug 31, a day after the two countries resumed hostilities for the first time since late July, driving oil prices up more than 3.5 per cent.
Pezeshkian’s comments also came after US President Donald Trump posted an AI-generated video clip that he said showed Iran’s oil hub Kharg Island being destroyed.
There was no evidence of any such attack, and a US official said on Aug 31 that the military had not targeted Kharg Island in overnight strikes. An Iranian official dismissed Trump’s post as “laughable”.
US forces on Aug 30 struck two Iranian launchers on Iran’s Larak Island, some 660km east of Kharg, a US official said, prompting Iran to strike two US bases in Jordan, according to Iranian media.
Two people were killed, and others were injured in the attack on Larak Island, Iran’s IRNA news agency quoted the local governor as saying on Aug 31.
The return to hostilities followed weeks in which Trump’s administration has stepped up efforts to punish Tehran and its business partners with costly economic sanctions, shifting away from military options. Diplomacy remains in stalemate.
Pezeshkian, speaking to India’s Prime Minister Narendra Modi on the sidelines of a regional security meeting in Kyrgyzstan, accused the US of failing to fulfil its commitments under past agreements.
“Nevertheless, we are still trying to achieve an agreement and understanding, and we believe that continuing the war is in no one’s interest, neither ours, nor the region’s, nor humanity’s,” Iran’s semi-official Tasnim news agency quoted him as saying.
“We believe the solution to the existing issues is dialogue and cooperation and that every capacity must be used to prevent the spread of insecurity and conflict.”
‘Blown to smithereens’
Earlier, Trump had annoyed Iran by posting on his Truth Social platform the AI-generated video clip with the message: “Kharg Island being blown to smithereens!!! President DJT.”
Reuters confirmed that the video clip showing dramatic explosions was most likely synthetically generated, using software that detects AI-manipulated imagery.
The White House and the US Defense Department did not respond to Reuters requests for comment outside regular business hours.
Kharg handled 90 per cent of Iran’s oil exports before the US and Israeli launched attacks on Iran on Feb 28, sparking a war that would severely disrupt its energy trade and put huge pressure on the economy.
“Trump’s tweets are laughable, and conditions in Kharg are calm and appropriate,” said Hamid Bovard, chief executive of government-run National Iranian Oil, on Aug 31.
Oil operations had not stopped, and workers were busy repairing previous damage and modernising facilities, Bovard said in comments cited by Nournews, a semi-official outlet close to Iran’s top security body.
Iran vows to respond to any attacks
A US official said forces had attacked the Iranian launchers on Larak Island on Aug 30 after “Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps forces were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the Strait of Hormuz”.
Larak is a small island in the strait near the strategic Iranian port of Bandar Abbas. The Strait of Hormuz, which normally handles a fifth of global crude oil and liquefied natural gas shipments, has been effectively blocked since the start of the war.
In a statement, the US Central Command said it took “limited, precise” action against minelaying forces of Iran’s Revolutionary Guards that posed an “imminent threat” in the strait. It gave no details.
As well as attacking the US bases in Jordan, Iran’s army said it had also struck the Al Minhad airbase in the United Arab Emirates early on Aug 31. However, the UAE’s defence ministry dismissed that report as false.
The UAE Defence Ministry later said its air force engaged a drone that had come from Iran over its territorial waters. It provided no further details, including whether it was shot down.
The Jordan strikes targeted US bases used to launch and support the attack on Larak, Iran’s Foreign Ministry said.
The Revolutionary Guards used air defence missiles to shoot down a US drone that crashed in Gulf waters, the Mehr news agency said on Aug 31, citing a statement from the elite force.
A supertanker caught fire and was brought to a complete halt after being struck by two naval mines in the southern Strait of Hormuz, Iran state TV said, citing a Guards’ statement.
Piling economic pressure on Iran
Trump has yet to achieve the objectives he set out at the start of the war: dismantling Iran’s nuclear programme, curbing its ability to attack regional rivals and creating conditions for Iranians to overthrow their clerical rulers.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told Reuters on Aug 30 new secondary sanctions were likely to be unveiled weekly in the effort to pressure Iran, with an initial focus on banks.
The European Union said on Aug 31 it would continue to work with the US and others to maintain economic pressure on Iran.

Last week, Trump said all mines had been detonated or removed from the international waters of the strait and Iran had been warned that any vessel placing new mines would be destroyed.
Iran denied Trump’s assertion. REUTERS

SEOUL, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- South Korea's industrial output remained flat in July amid surging facility investment and sluggish private consumption, statistical ministry data showed Monday.
The seasonally-adjusted index of all industry production, which excludes the agriculture, livestock and fishery sectors, stood unchanged in July compared to the previous month, according to the Ministry of Data and Statistics.
After contracting for two consecutive months in April and May, industrial production rebounded 2.4 percent in June before stalling in July.
Production among manufacturers ticked up 0.2 percent month on month in July due to strong output of electronic components and primary metals that offset lower automotive production.
The average capacity utilization rate in the manufacturing industry added 0.2 percentage points to 74.9 percent in the cited month.
Output in the construction industry declined 1.1 percent, but production in the public administration sector jumped 10.4 percent.
Production in the services industry fell 1.3 percent in July from a month earlier, snapping a two-month growth streak amid prolonged high inflation and a severe summer heatwave.
The retail sales index, a key gauge of consumer spending, dwindled 2.4 percent in July, reversing an expansion of 2.7 percent in the previous month.
Durable goods sales dropped 7.7 percent on the back of lower demand for passenger cars, affected by the expiration of temporary consumption tax cuts.
Facility investment surged 7.5 percent, marking the second consecutive month of growth thanks to solid investment in transportation equipment and semiconductor manufacturing equipment.
Construction completion, which measures the actual value of construction work performed, retreated 1.1 percent in July on a monthly basis after rising 3.3 percent in May and 4.2 percent in June.
The cyclical variation factor for leading economic indicators, which gauges the outlook for future economic situations, rose 0.4 points to 104.2 in July compared to the previous month.
The reading for coincident economic indicators, which measures the current economic condition, went up 0.8 points to 101.2 last month. ■

Feature: Bobsleigh thrills bring summer visitors to Beijing 2022 venues

2026-08-31
10:13:23 CST
11:13:23 KST

by sportswriters Li Chunyu and Tian Chenxu
BEIJING, Aug. 31 (Xinhua) -- Can ordinary people experience the thrill of bobsleigh at speeds of up to 80 kilometers per hour? At China's National Sliding Center, a 2022 Winter Olympic venue in Beijing's northwestern Yanqing district, they can.
Even without an ice track in summer, visitors can experience the sport in wheeled bobsleighs that offer a ride similar to a roller coaster.
"While bobsleigh athletes can reach an average of 100 km/h in races, the recreational event for the public has been optimized to 80 km/h and runs almost all year round. On the iceless track, a professional helmsman like me rides along with the tourists to steer and ensure safety," said Wang Zhenlong, who also works as an ice maker at the National Sliding Center in winter.
With 14 curves over a total length of about 1,600 meters, the section of track designated for the public is relatively gentle. According to operators, around 50 visitors take part in the bobsleigh experience on weekdays, with the number rising to more than 200 on weekends and holidays during summer.
"Every curve is familiar to me. I joined the venue construction team back in 2018 and witnessed the great success of the Beijing 2022 Winter Olympics. Now, so many people are passionate about winter sports, gaining a deeper understanding of bobsleigh, skeleton and luge," Wang added.
One of the three competition zones for Beijing 2022, Yanqing is home to the National Sliding Center, the National Alpine Skiing Center and the Yanqing Olympic Village.
Higher up on Haituo Mountain, the National Alpine Skiing Center offers an alpine coaster winding along the mountain slopes, one of more than 20 summer activities available in the zone.
Sun Fei, who traveled from Baoding in Hebei Province, brought his 11-year-old son to try the alpine coaster.
"The mountain scenery is impressive. The higher altitude here makes it much cooler than downtown. We reserved rooms in the Olympic Village. It's really nice and convenient," Sun said.
Although the alpine coaster does not run on the ski courses used in winter, the facilities and cable cars at the National Alpine Skiing Center retain many elements from the Beijing Winter Olympics and Paralympics, including the Games' mascots, Bing Dwen Dwen and Shuey Rhon Rhon.
"Our snow season runs from late November each year to around March 15 of the following year. Operating Winter Olympic venues across all four seasons is a common challenge worldwide, particularly in summer," said Liu Xiyao, a manager of the Yanqing Olympic zone.
Taking advantage of Yanqing's natural environment and relatively cool climate, the Winter Olympic venues have developed a range of tourism activities. Visitors receive maps marking attractions and activities when they arrive to help them plan their routes.
Operators said the Yanqing Olympic zone has received 1.2 million visits since opening to the public on April 29, 2022, after the Games.
"Now, the Yanqing Olympic zone is not only home to venues for high-level domestic and international sliding and skiing competitions, but also a popular destination in addition to the well-known Badaling Great Wall in Yanqing," Liu said. ■
