The online privacy change that could give Australians more control over their data
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
23:20:03 UTC
08:20:03 KST

In brief
- The Australian eSafety Commissioner has recommended changes to how smart glasses operate.
- Further new protections will overhaul Australia's privacy laws related to social media, AI and smart glasses.
People's faces should automatically be blurred when being filmed by smart glasses as part of greater privacy measures, the online safety watchdog has urged.
In advice to industry, the eSafety Commissioner has called for extra protections to be put in place for smart glasses, or glasses with cameras attached to them.
The growing uptake of the technology, prompted by cheap versions of the products being sold in outlets such as Kmart, has increased concerns about privacy and people being filmed without their consent.
The commissioner said faces of people being filmed should be blurred by default if they have not given consent, with clearer indicators being given for when the glasses are recording video.
"Companies selling smart glasses must balance the benefits of the technology with the need to protect users and the public," the commissioner said.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"As smart glasses become more common, they may create new ways to perpetrate harms."
The eSafety Commissioner said the rapid evolution of the technology meant there was still a chance for extra safety features to be baked into the products before harms became more widespread.
"They may become increasingly interconnected with and create new ways to perpetrate different types of harms, such as image-based abuse, adult cyber abuse, cyberbullying of children, or the livestreaming of violent or other harmful content," the advice said.
"The harms linked to covert recording are not hypothetical. They are real and already occurring."
Among the concerns listed by the commissioner was how the glasses could be used by "pick-up artists" who use the glasses to film women without their knowledge.
"Most of the women do not realise they are being filmed. These posts often attract misogynistic comments, compounding the harm," the commissioner said.
"Used in this way, smart glasses can reinforce and normalise watching, recording and controlling women in public without their knowledge."
The commissioner has also called for livestreaming from the glasses to operate on a delay, as well as for recording to be disabled when the glasses are not being worn.
Attorney-General Michelle Rowland wrote to the privacy commission earlier this month to investigate whether extra regulations for smart glasses were needed.
The Greens have called for a 12 month ban on the importation of smart glasses.
Under changes the minor party will bring to parliament, the filming, storing or sharing of footage from the glasses without consent would be a breach of privacy laws.
Social media and deletion requests
Rowland is also set to outline further changes to privacy laws, including the right to erasure, on Monday.
The policy would mean social media users can ask tech companies to delete their personal information published online or held by the platforms.
The draft laws will not apply to media organisations publishing news articles.
Rowland said the privacy laws were needed to keep up with technology changes.
"The right to erasure will help put more control in the hands of Australians, allowing personal information to be destroyed from large digital platforms," she said.
"We must ensure appropriate safeguards are placed around technology and stop the erosion of our privacy protections."
The federal government will also roll out extra protections for identity documents online.
A service called IDLock will allow people to block or unblock the use of identity documents such as passports.
IDLock will be made available through the government's MyGov platform from 2027 after a small-scale trial in late 2026.
"Australians deserve to have control over how their personal identity information, such as their driver licence or passport, is used to verify their identity online," Rowland said.
"As data breaches, scams and cyber-enabled crime continue to evolve, Australia's approach must evolve with them."

Pacific forum set to open in Palau without several leaders

Pacific forum kicks off in Palau without several leaders
- At least five Pacific Island leaders are absent from the forum in Palau due to China-Taiwan tensions, with officials representing their countries instead.
- China disputes Taiwan's participation and issued a travel warning for Palau, while the US opposes China's attempts to pressure Palau through tourism.
- The forum focuses on economic development and regional unity, with security issues and oil supply disruptions also key topics but consensus on responses remains uncertain.
AI generated
WELLINGTON – At least five heads of government were absent from talks at the annual Pacific Island Forum that began on Aug 31, as China-Taiwan tensions weighed heavily over the meeting that was intended to demonstrate regional unity.
The prime ministers of Fiji, Vanuatu and Samoa and the Solomon Islands’ prime ministers and the president of Kiribati will not attend the summit in Palau, an archipelago of over 500 islands that has maintained diplomatic ties with Taiwan. The absent leaders are expected to be represented by ministers or senior officials.
China, which views democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory, has gradually whittled away the number of Pacific island countries with formal ties to Taipei, with only three remaining – Palau, Tuvalu and the Marshall Islands. It questioned Palau’s inclusion of Taiwan in the gathering, saying it had “no qualifications” to take part in the forum.
Taiwan Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung was invited for meetings and side events held alongside the forum. Taiwan is not a formal dialogue partner like China but instead is a development partner.
Beijing issued a travel advisory in July declaring Palau “unsafe” for tourists.
In response, the US embassy in the capital Koror said in a statement that it “opposes any attempts by China to weaponise tourism to coerce Palau”.
Dialogue partners including the US, China, Japan and Singapore will return to the forum after being excluded from the 2025 meeting in Honiara. US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau and China’s Special Envoy for Pacific Island Countries Affairs Qian Bo are among those expected to attend.
Solomon Islands’ Matthew Wale was due to attend but left Palau to face a no-confidence motion at home. He was elected prime minister in May, replacing a leadership that had deepened ties with Beijing and signed a security pact with China that alarmed the US and its allies. Kiribati said President Taneti Maamau was unable to travel because Parliament was sitting and flights were limited.
The meeting, hosted by Palau President Surangel Whipps Jr in Koror through Sept 4, is being held under the theme B.E.L.A.U. – Building Economies: Life. Action. Unity. “The theme reflects a simple but important conviction: that building stronger economies is not an end in itself,” Whipps said while opening a meeting of the Smaller Island States, the first gathering of leaders for the week.
“It must elevate the livelihoods of our people, create tangible and sustainable opportunities for our economies, and unite us in our ongoing efforts to deepen regionalism through integration.”
New Zealand Foreign Minister Winston Peters said Pacific countries wanted tangible outcomes. “We want more doing, less hui (meeting),” he told reporters on Aug 30, using the Maori word for meeting. He said oil supply disruptions were among the region’s most pressing concerns and foreshadowed an announcement on relief measures that could come soon.
Regional security is also expected to feature after a Pacific Island foreign ministers’ meeting in Suva earlier this month failed to agree on a collective response to a Chinese missile test in the Pacific. Peters said it was unclear whether leaders would reach a common position in Palau, adding that the time elapsed since the test raised questions about the value of a response now. REUTERS

Hong Kong WhatsApp hijacking scams surge 170% to nearly 2,000 cases
Police say victims lost HK$146 million in first seven months of 2026, with some suffering individual losses exceeding HK$10 million
WhatsApp account hijacking scams in Hong Kong surged by nearly 170 per cent to almost 2,000 cases in the first seven months of this year, with one victim losing as much as HK$12.2 million (US$1.55 million).
Police said the 1,993 cases logged from January to July represented a 169.7 per cent increase from the 739 cases recorded over the same period last year. The figure also surpassed the 1,669 cases recorded in all of 2025.
The cases over the first seven months resulted in losses of HK$146.3 million, down by 22.7 per cent from HK$189.2 million over the same period last year.
Despite the lower total loss, police warned that the threat was far from subsiding, noting that some victims lost between HK$1 million and more than HK$10 million.
“The rise in cases was related to the habits of our residents using these social media or instant messaging platforms,” said Superintendent Hui Yee-wai of the force’s cyber security and technology crime bureau.
“On the other hand, we have also seen that artificial intelligence is a factor. Every scam involved fake websites, while AI has made generating these fake websites significantly easier.”

Citi’s China-US corridor thrives as mainland firms hedge risks amid trade turbulence
Chinese firms lean on global banks to manage trade friction and expand supply chains, keeping corporate activity resilient, Citi says
Escalating US-China trade friction has failed to dampen corporate activity between the two economies, with Citi reporting steady revenue growth on its North America-China corridor as Chinese companies aggressively deploy risk-hedging strategies to protect their global market share.
Instead of retreating from the US market, mainland Chinese firms had leaned heavily on global institutions to navigate financial friction and complex supply chains, Citi’s Greater China executives said at a media briefing in Hong Kong.
“Our revenue has not decreased – there has been growth,” the bank’s China CEO Zhang Wenjie said, noting a 44 per cent year-on-year revenue surge across the bank’s China-US corridor in the first half of the year.
Geopolitical headwinds boosted demand for cross-border financial services, he said.
Because North America remained a vital market, Chinese enterprises increasingly turned to international banks to execute foreign exchange hedging, manage trade exposure and reconfigure capital flows, Zhang said.
The resilience comes as Chinese corporate expansion enters what Citi describes as a “Going Global 3.0” phase.

White House exodus poses new challenge for Trump at pivotal time

AI generated
WASHINGTON – US President Donald Trump is entering a critical stretch in his second term with a slew of resignations among his senior staff, forcing him to rely on an even smaller circle of aides.
Over the last month, Trump has lost his chief spokesperson, his top legal adviser, a key national security adviser and his liaison to Capitol Hill.
More senior officials are said to be weighing a potential exit over the next few months, according to people familiar with the matter.
While staff departures are typical before midterm elections, the departures of key aides such as White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt in August took some in the White House by surprise, according to a person familiar with the matter.
James Braid, White House director of legislative affairs and a long-time Trump aide, announced earlier in August his plans to quit in the coming weeks.
Braid’s announcement came a week after Leavitt – another of Trump’s most trusted advisers and fiercest defenders – said she would step down at the end of August.
Their successors have not been announced.
White House deputy national security adviser Andy Baker, who had been personally involved in negotiations with Iran, and White House counsel David Warrington have also departed and were replaced by existing administration officials.
The senior staff exodus comes at an already tumultuous time for Trump, who is struggling with foreign and domestic challenges – including some of his own making.
Republicans are facing the prospect of losing their congressional majorities in the November midterm elections, a result that could open his administration to subpoenas and investigations under a Democratic-led Congress.
As he enters the last two years of his final term, Trump faces historically low approval ratings, a shaky economy and an unpopular war in Iran that has roiled global energy markets.
He is engaged in a fresh trade war with Canada and has lashed out at South Korea, another long-time US ally.
The string of departures threatens to create a vacuum in Trump’s inner circle and finding replacements will not be easy.
“If your vetting process the first go-round mandates that you have to claim that the 2020 election was stolen, then the pool of candidates was probably already small and getting smaller now,” said Marc Short, who served in the first Trump administration.
The administration has expressed little outward concern over the outflow of aides.
White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said: “This movement is bigger than any one staff member, and the President’s mission to make America greater than ever before will continue unabated.”
Still, the loss of some of Trump’s closest advisers has left the White House without a clear succession plan in key offices.
Braid, whose job was to press congressional Republicans on the President’s legislative agenda, has lost much of his staff over the last six months, according to a person familiar with the matter.
Though Leavitt plans to remain in Trump’s orbit, her absence in the communications office deprives the President of one of his most effective messengers to sell his domestic and foreign policies to sceptical voters.
Trump, however, is in no rush to replace Leavitt, according to a person familiar with the matter.
In the meantime, the White House is weighing a plan to again rotate Cabinet officials through the briefing room as they did while she was on maternity leave earlier in 2026, the person said.
Lisa Camooso Miller, a former Republican National Committee communications director, said: “This also is, without question, the hardest time to hire into an administration.
“The real question is, who’s going to fill these roles? Will they be the right people, and will they be people the President listens to? It’s not so much about the vacancies, but who’s willing to go into the second two years of an administration that largely will face headwinds with a change in Congress.”
Strategy boost ahead of midterms
The administration has announced some key moves to boost its political operation and strategy ahead of the midterms.
In April, Trump announced that deputy chief of staff James Blair would temporarily leave the White House to lead the President’s political operation.
Earlier this summer, the White House brought back veteran advisers Jason Miller and Johnny DeStefano to focus on midterm messaging, Bloomberg previously reported.
Trump also tapped his Cabinet secretary, Will Scharf, to replace Warrington as White House counsel, partly in preparation for the onslaught of congressional investigations should Democrats take control of the House, according to a White House official.
Scharf was part of Trump’s legal team during his four years out of office and was one of the President’s lawyers in the election obstruction case.
Several other aides have left in recent months.
Trump’s pardons attorney and staunch ally Ed Martin has announced his departure from the Justice Department.
Abigail Jackson, a deputy White House spokeswoman, stepped down in July to take a job in the private sector.
Emily Underwood, who worked under White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, left earlier in August to join a venture capital firm, according to a person familiar with her decision.
Caleb Orr, a top adviser to Secretary of State Marco Rubio, is expected to replace her.
The remaining team members will have their work cut out for them.
In addition to resolving conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine, some within the party are pushing the White House for fresh economic plans, including further tax cuts to expand the President’s signature tax and spending law.
The administration is expected to unveil economic-focused policy proposals in the coming weeks, according to a person familiar with the matter.
Trump has also told aides that he wants to travel more frequently to stump for House and Senate candidates in the home stretch of the midterm campaign, the person said.
Cabinet members have been travelling ahead of the midterms, and there has been internal competition among them to do so, the person said.
Short said: “I think it’s clear that the No. 1 issue continues to be affordability and people feeling insecure in the current economy.
“There also has to be: Here’s what our candidates clearly laid out. And I’m less confident that American voters understand that right now.” BLOOMBERG

AI generated
CARACAS – Venezuela’s ousted President Nicolás Maduro resurfaced in a series of pictures posted on Aug 30 on social media, just days after acting President Delcy Rodríguez inked a sweeping energy agreement with the United States.
Photos, dated June 25, show a smiling Maduro dressed in a grey tracksuit and white sneakers while flashing two peace signs with his hands.
Aside from court sketches depicting him thinner and with grayer hair, these are the first images of the former leader since the early January raid that whisked him and his wife, Cilia Flores, out of Caracas to face federal charges in the US.
Maduro is still in US custody.
The photo drop follows Aug 28’s blockbuster announcement that Washington and Caracas forged a bilateral oil pact that Rodríguez has said will last 25 years.
The accord targets 17 strategic oilfields – including assets in the Orinoco Belt and Lake Maracaibo – with the goal of ramping up production past 1.5 million barrels per day.
While President Donald Trump touted the agreement as securing US majority control over more than 65 billion barrels of proven reserves, Rodríguez defended the pact as a sovereign mechanism projected to net the Venezuelan state roughly US$209 billion (S$266.45 billion).
The realignment triggered an immediate domestic backlash.
Rodríguez is facing intense crossfire from hardliners both within the ruling socialist party and an opposition wary of the sweeping terms, making her political tightrope increasingly precarious.
Following the January raid, Caracas and provincial cities bristled with billboards of the presidential couple as well as murals demanding their release.
Today, those billboards have been replaced by imagery thanking emergency responders.
Only a scattering of “#FreeMaduro” and “#FreeCilia” graffiti remains, jostling for space alongside slogans declaring “Trump out” and “Vote or street,” a reference to either voting or protesting in a sign of a fractured society.
Officials rarely mention Maduro, and state television has halted broadcasts of his archival speeches and his signature animated likeness.
Rodríguez now dominates state programming, complete with her own newly debuted cartoon character.
Meanwhile, a Venezuelan government team in US-backed talks on political guarantees ahead of potential elections with an opposition faction has yet to raise the couple’s release as a condition for concessions, according to a person with direct knowledge of the talks. BLOOMBERG

One dead, more than a dozen unaccounted for after Grand Canyon flash flood
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
22:34:46 UTC
07:34:46 KST

-    Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
The National Park Service recovered the body of a 46-year-old man after a significant flash flood in the Grand Canyon on Saturday.
The man’s identity has not yet been released, and the agency said Sunday night it was still searching for about 15 other people. Earlier Sunday, the park service had asked for the public’s help finding as many as 20 people. The body was recovered near Crystal Rapids along the Colorado River, and the Coconino County medical examiner’s office is on site as the search for more hikers continues, according to the park service.
“If you know of hikers or backpackers who were in the Bright Angel Creek corridor on August 29, or if you had a campground reservation in the affected area, please contact the NPS Investigative Services Branch,” the agency wrote in a news release and social media posts on Sunday afternoon.
This includes people who may have been traveling along the North Kaibab Trail from the trailhead to Phantom Ranch, staying at Bright Angel Campground or traveling or staying in the area known as “the Box” north of Phantom Ranch, officials said.
The park service said the flash flood happened around 2:30 p.m. Saturday and resulted in “significant impacts” to infrastructure throughout Bright Angel Canyon. Nearly all footbridges were destroyed, eliminating hiker access to the creek. The flooding widened the creek bed and created what appeared to be a new river rapid.
Dozens of people were evacuated as the flooding swept large boulders, metal structures and other debris into the Colorado River, which runs through the Grand Canyon, the National Park Service said. Flooding also knocked out the sole water pipeline that serves tourists and residents at the national park, officials said late Sunday.
Sixty-two people were evacuated from the area Sunday morning, and additional evacuations were underway from Cottonwood Campground, Phantom Ranch and other nearby sites.
Evacuees have been transported to the Maswik Lodge Cafeteria on the South Rim, where the American Red Cross is coordinating assistance.
Phantom Ranch, Bright Angel Campground, the Phantom Ranch Canteen and cabins, and the entire North Kaibab Trail from the North Kaibab Trailhead to Phantom Ranch are closed until further notice, the park service said.
The Black Bridge and Silver Bridge crossing the Colorado River are also closed until further notice, with no estimated reopening date.
Parth Desai was hiking through a narrow passage in Bright Angel Canyon with a group of fellow physicians and a park ranger when the downpour started.
“We saw the creek flood, waterfalls coming up out of nowhere, boulders, mud, landslides happening everywhere,” said the hiker, who was later rescued by helicopter.
A flash flood watch remains in effect in the Grand Canyon area through Monday evening, with more showers and thunderstorms in the forecast, according to the National Weather Service.
“Flash flooding will be possible in creeks, normally dry washes, swimming holes, and over recently burned areas,” the agency warned. “Raging killer currents will be possible in side canyons and narrow slot canyons. Low-water crossings may be flooded.”
Anyone with information is asked to contact the National Park Service Investigative Services Branch Tip Line at (888) 653-0009 or nps_isb@nps.gov.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Lake Ontario now called ‘Lake America’ on Google Maps for US users after Trump order
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
22:34:36 UTC
07:34:36 KST

Google Maps changes Lake Ontario to ‘Lake America’ for US users after Trump order
Canadian users continue to see the original name as the tech giant rolls out location-based labelling
Google has updated its maps application to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America” for users in the United States, reflecting a recent order by US President Donald Trump that changed the name of the lake, the global technology giant said.
The Google Maps update comes days after Trump’s order amid an escalating trade war with Canada that has led both countries to impose billions of dollars in added tariffs on each other’s goods. It echoes what Google did in 2025 when Trump issued an order to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America.
Google said in a blog post on Saturday that the decision was based on its practice of using names assigned by the US Geographic Names Information System, also known as GNIS.
“People using Maps in the US will see ‘Lake America’, those in Canada will continue to see ‘Lake Ontario’, and those outside of the US and Canada will see both names,” Google said in a brief statement. “These updates follow our long-standing policy for bodies of water with names that vary from country to country, and are starting to roll out now.”
Trump’s decision on Thursday to rename the lake was met with mockery and indifference in both Canada and the United States. On Saturday, Ontario Premier Doug Ford responded to Trump’s order with a billboard-sized message on the Canadian shore: “Lake Ontario. Now and forever”.
The White House, the office of Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Ford’s office did not immediately comment on Sunday on Google’s decision.

France’s ex-PM Edouard Philippe calls for new party to counter far-right
- Edouard Philippe calls for a new party or alliance to unite centre and right voters to block far-right Marine Le Pen and build a parliamentary majority after next year's election.
- Philippe emphasises shared values like rule of law, European integration, and a market economy to prevent France drifting towards far-left or far-right extremes.
- Centrist Gabriel Attal challenges Philippe's approach, claiming no clear favourite exists and urging focus on winning the presidential election before forming coalitions.
AI generated
TOURCOING, France - French presidential hopeful Edouard Philippe said on Aug 31 he wanted to bring together the centre and the right and called for the creation of a new political party, as moderates seek to prevent far-right leader Marine Le Pen from coming to power.
Seeking to energise his supporters in the northern town of Tourcoing, Philippe, the centre-right former prime minister, said he wanted to create a new party or an alliance of parties ahead of parliamentary elections expected to follow next spring’s presidential vote.
With less than eight months until the April-May presidential election, Le Pen, 58, is the front-runner in the polls.
“It is about building the governing pact, or the new party, or the new confederation of parties, that will enable all those who want to unite their efforts in the service of the country to govern together,” said the leader of the Horizons party.
“This will involve fielding a single candidate in each constituency,” Philippe, 55, said, adding such candidates would run “under a common banner” in order to build a parliamentary majority following the election.
While Philippe remains the best-positioned candidate on the right, recent surveys indicate that Jean-Luc Melenchon, the divisive leader of hard-left France Unbowed (LFI), could emerge as Le Pen’s most likely run-off opponent, raising some doubts over Philippe’s ability to secure a place in the second round.
Observers say that a crowded field of candidates from the centre, centre left, centre right and right risks fragmenting the moderate vote in the first round.
On Aug 30, Philippe stepped up his push for a “political realignment”, while offering few details of his programme.
“We must build a coalition of those who share the values to which we are fundamentally attached,” he said, referring to respect for the rule of law, commitment to European integration, and support for a market economy.
“Everyone who shares these simple ideas must unite to ensure that France does not drift either toward LFI’s so-called ‘new France’ or toward Madame Le Pen’s nationalist, identity-based brand of populism.”
Particular concern has mounted over growing competition between Philippe and 37-year-old Gabriel Attal, once France’s youngest, openly gay prime minister, as both men hope to secure the backing of the centrist camp.
Speaking in the north-eastern town of Chalons-en-Champagne, Attal sought to highlight differences with Philippe, arguing that his rival in the race was campaigning “with the ideas from 20 years ago”.
Attal, who campaigned throughout the summer, claimed that he was now polling at roughly the same level as Philippe.
“There is no natural candidate or clear favourite in this election,” the leader of the centrist Renaissance party argued.
At the botanical garden of Tourcoing, France’s influential justice minister Gerald Darmanin, who in August pledged not to stand himself and endorsed Philippe, lavished him with praise before a crowd of hundreds of supporters.
Darmanin argued that Philippe was not only “the only person who can win” the presidential election, but also “the only person who can secure a parliamentary majority”.
Responding to Philippe’s proposal, Attal said that “the cart should not be put before the horse”.
“First, you have to win the presidential election,” he said. AFP

More than 20 people may be missing after Grand Canyon flash flood

Grand Canyon flash flood leaves one dead, around 15 missing
- About 15 people may be missing after a flash flood hit Bright Angel Canyon and Phantom Ranch in Grand Canyon National Park on Aug 29.
- The National Park Service has evacuated 62 people and is working with Arizona authorities to rescue and account for missing individuals.
- More heavy rain and thunderstorms are expected through Aug 31, raising risks of further flash floods, debris flows, and dangerous trail conditions.
AI generated
LOS ANGELES – At least one person was killed and around 15 others are missing after a flash flood at the Grand Canyon, one of the most popular tourist sites in the US, the National Park Service said in a statement on Aug 30.
The floods hit the Bright Angel Canyon and Phantom Ranch area on Aug 29, forcing dozens of people to evacuate and damaging the sole water pipeline serving the park.
The body of a 46-year-old man was recovered on the evening of Aug 30 near Crystal Rapids along the Colorado River in northern Arizona, the park service said.
Video footage taken by hikers showed a torrent of muddy water rushing by trails and under footbridges as well as logs and other debris floating down swollen rivers, accompanied by a rumbling roar.
The park service said it was working with Arizona authorities to evacuate people and account for missing individuals.
As at the morning of Aug 30, 62 people had been evacuated, with others scheduled for later, it said.
It said around 15 people were thought to be missing, revising an earlier figure of more than 20.
Water pipeline damaged
The flooding damaged the Transcanyon Waterline, a key water pipeline into Grand Canyon National Park, the park service said, announcing water restrictions in its most visited area and a ban on wood and charcoal fires.
The 20km pipeline runs from the Roaring Springs source on the North Rim to the South Rim, providing drinking water and fire suppression, according to the park’s website.
The flooding also resulted in “significant impacts to infrastructure,” destroying footbridges and blocking hikers from crossing Bright Angel Creek, the park service said.
Overnight accommodations were to be closed from Aug 31, it added.
“These measures are crucial for ensuring the safety and sustainability of water resources,” the park service said.
The flash flood, which began about 2.30pm on Aug 29, was caused by rain on the Kaibab Plateau, it said.
More thunderstorms and heavy rainfall were possible through Monday, possibly leading to “additional flash flooding, debris flows, rockfall and changing trail and river conditions,” the park service warned.
Flash floods are common in Northern Arizona because the arid, sparsely vegetated environments found in the area have little capacity to absorb rain, the park’s website said, urging visitors to be especially cautious from July to mid-September.
The Grand Canyon – considered one of the greatest wonders of the natural world – is the result of the Colorado River eating away at layers of red sandstone and other rock for millions of years, leaving a chasm up to 29km wide and more than 1.6km deep.
In 2025, almost five million people visited the site. AFP

Bitter pill for EU as Iceland shuts door on entry talks
- Iceland voted 52.8% against restarting EU membership talks, disappointing Brussels and halting hopes of a new EU success story.
- EU leaders respect Iceland's decision but acknowledge it signals waning attraction and trust in the EU.
- Eurosceptics celebrated the vote, while EU officials stressed ongoing cooperation on security and Arctic issues despite the setback.
AI generated
BRUSSELS – The European Union put a brave face on Aug 30 on Iceland’s vote against restarting membership talks, but the outcome was a bitter pill to swallow – robbing Brussels of a hoped-for success story while delighting its eurosceptic critics.
European Council chief Antonio Costa told Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir after the referendum results came in that the 27-nation bloc “fully respects the democratic choice” of Iceland’s voters.
The North Atlantic island is already closely linked to the EU as a member of the European Economic Area (EEA) and the free-movement Schengen zone, and both leaders vowed to “continue to strengthen the relationship”.
But there was no disguising the dismay in wider Brussels circles. “The message is clear: The EU doesn’t inspire people any more,” summed up Green EU lawmaker Saskia Bricmont.
Fellow Member of European Parliament Sandro Gozi, a centrist, called it “a warning Europe should take seriously”. He said the bloc’s “power of attraction” should not “be taken for granted”, and that it must “keep earning trust” by cutting bureaucracy and boosting accountability.
The EU last expanded in 2013 by admitting Croatia, and while the bloc has revived talk of enlargement as a strategic priority since the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022, there has been little to celebrate since then.
Recent years have seen halting progress among candidates in the western Balkans, with Montenegro and Albania closest in line to join, and the opening of a vast and thorny accession process with Ukraine.
Brussels took care not to be seen as meddling in Iceland’s weekend vote – but it made little secret of its eagerness to welcome the wealthy, strategically located island to the EU fold.
For many European capitals Iceland looked like a model candidate, and Brussels had indicated it could give ground on sensitive issues such as fishing rights to smooth its path into the bloc. That appears to have fallen on deaf ears among Iceland’s nearly 400,000 people, who voted 52.8 per cent to 47.2 per cent not to resume entry talks suspended 13 years ago, burying the question for the foreseeable future.
Eurosceptic glee
Eurosceptics seized gleefully on the result, with French far-right leader Marine Le Pen saying it showed the appeal of a Europe of “free, sovereign nations” – over a path of closer integration.
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage congratulated Icelanders on “voting to keep their independence”.
At the hard-right end of the European Parliament, the ECR group said the fact Iceland voted “no” in spite of an “uncertain” international security environment “should give Brussels pause”.
The group’s co-chairman Nicola Procaccini said Brussels should ask itself hard questions about why “a prosperous, democratic and outward-looking European country” chose not to renew entry talks.
Geopolitics loomed large over the referendum, with US President Donald Trump’s threats to take control of Greenland resonating in neighbouring Iceland, a NATO-dependent country.
But the debate ultimately focused on bread-and-butter issues such as fishing and Iceland’s volatile currency.
Iceland’s vote marks a setback for the EU’s broader push to bolster its presence in the strategic Arctic region – which EU chief Ursula von der Leyen will underscore by visiting Greenland in September.
Lawmaker Kathleen Van Brempt of the Socialists and Democrats called Arctic cooperation with Iceland on security matters “more important than ever” – vowing that work would “continue, openly and respectfully”.
Echoing that message, her fellow socialist Andreas Schieder underscored that Iceland “is and remains part of the European family”.
“Now it is a matter of jointly withstanding the geopolitical pressure,” he said. AFP

Constitutional norm for jurist as SC judge unmet: Justice Bhuyan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
22:14:19 UTC
07:14:19 KST

SC judge says Article 124(3) provision for appointing distinguished jurists as apex court judges remains unused for 76 years.
NEW DELHI: Justice Ujjal Bhuyan, a Supreme Court judge, Sunday said though Article 124(3) permitted appointment of ‘distinguished jurists’ as judges of the apex court, it was regrettable that this provision had remained one of our Constitution’s unused mandates.“No jurist has been appointed so far to SC though Constitution has completed more than 76 years,” he said, adding that either Centre earlier or the collegium thereafter was not convinced about the depth in Indian academia or had not seriously explored Article 124(3) so far.Addressing the convocation of LLM students at National Law University, Delhi, Justice Bhuyan said, “No legal academic has yet been appointed as a judge of SC, despite there being brilliant minds who could have made a substantial contribution had they become part of the bench.”Addressing the ‘lack of practical experience’ argument against elevation of jurists as judges, he said, “SC is not only the highest adjudicatory body but it is the moral, legal and constitutional conscience-keeper of the nation. It is above technicalities.”
The objective behind appointing ‘distinguished jurists’ as SC judges is to diversify as they “can be a great value addition to the bench”, he said, adding, “By his or her scholarship, he or she can make a visible contribution to the decision-making process at the top level.
Participation of renowned legal academia and scholars would have a defining impact on the judicial functioning of Supreme Court.”He said academics were routinely appointed as judges to constitutional courts in US, UK, Canada and Kenya. In America, they could practise as long as it did not interfere with academic sessions, but this practice was opposed here by rule 49 of Bar Council of India, he said.In US, Felix Frankfurter became the first jurist to be an SC judge, picked by Theodore Roosevelt in 1939. Thereafter, several from legal academia have been appointed as US supreme court judges, many of whom had teaching experience prior to this role.

Sonam Wangchuk says CJP organisers may have political ambitions, but that's acceptable if platform remains non-party.
NEW DELHI: Climate activist Sonam Wangchuk has said Abhijit Dipke and his fellow organisers of the Cockroach Janta Party movement appear to have political ambitions, but there is nothing objectionable in this as long as the student platform retains its non-party character.Wangchuk, in a Prakhar Gupta Xperience podcast, said Dipke and the others had not disclosed any plans to him and his view was based on his own assessment. “Political ambition is very normal,” he said. “Past political connections I don’t care about, present and future political aspirations are not a problem.”
“They are not such saints that they want absolutely nothing and are doing all this entirely selflessly,” he said, referring to the possibility that the organisers had personal or political aspirations.Assessing their suitability for leadership, Wangchuk described the organisers as “well meaning”, “quite skilled” and “above average”.“Well meaning but unskilled” could create difficulties, while “very skilled but ill meaning” would pose a much greater danger, he said.
Asked whether they could become corrupt, Wangchuk said he had seen no such indications. “People go through changes, and I hope they won’t,” he said.
Wangchuk said the organisers could join an existing party or launch a new one later, but must not turn the CJP platform into their political vehicle. He said he had advised them to preserve it as a “neutral, apolitical pressure group”, arguing that this would help retain the trust of supporters who saw it as a students’ movement rather than an organisation aligned with BJP, Congress or AAP.Wangchuk acknowledged that his own standards sometimes led him to expect public figures to have no political ambition. That, he said, could be unrealistic because the organisers were ordinary people entitled to pursue political careers. Beginning such a career by championing an education-related cause could, in fact, be positive.He also expressed hope that participation in the movement would help them emerge as more mature and grounded politicians. “I am actually happy about that,” Wangchuk said of their taking up public issues.

Details

ASEAN and Japan’s Updated Free and Open Indo-Pacific Initiative
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
21:55:00 UTC
06:55:00 KST

A decade has passed since Japan proposed the Free and Open Indo-Pacific (FOIP) initiative. The “Updated FOIP,” announced in May 2026, carries on the original philosophy while adding a new focus on AI and data infrastructure, supply chains for energy and critical goods, public-private sector market co-creation, and security cooperation. It marks a shift from philosophy to building regional resilience in practice.
Asian growth has benefited from interdependence, but that same interdependence has created vulnerabilities. Disruptions to navigation in the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in the Red Sea ripple outward to affect Japan and ASEAN through energy prices, ocean freight, insurance premiums, and component supplies. Economic security is not merely about preparing for great-power competition; it is about protecting the shared foundation of sea lanes, energy, resources, and digital infrastructure from threats including armed conflict, disasters, cyberattacks, and economic coercion.
Japan is a U.S. ally, yet it is not pressing ASEAN to choose between Washington and Beijing. Japan’s role is to strengthen each country’s capacity to make its own decisions and expand the alternatives available to it in times of crisis. Japanese companies have invested in ASEAN for decades, building factories and logistics networks and developing technology and human resources. Japan and ASEAN share the same supply networks and maritime routes, making ASEAN’s resilience inseparable from Japan’s own.
If the FOIP and the ASEAN Outlook on the Indo-Pacific (AOIP) are pursued independently, AOIP priorities risk going underimplemented, while the FOIP risks being seen as little more than a vehicle for Japanese interests. The AOIP defines ASEAN priorities; the FOIP links funding, technology, and enterprise to drive implementation. This allows ASEAN to choose the cooperation projects itself and ensure that they are implemented in line with regional needs.
Concrete cooperation could take three forms. The first is joint preservation of maritime routes. The Strait of Hormuz, the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, and the Malacca and Singapore Straits constitute a single maritime logistics network. Japan, ASEAN, China, and South Korea, despite their different political positions, share a common interest in safe and stable navigation. What this requires, however, is not “joint defense” by extra-regional powers, but navigation safety, anti-piracy, search and rescue, and accident and disaster response that respect the sovereignty and initiative of coastal states.
The model here is the Malacca Strait patrols conducted by the coastal states of Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand. Japan has bolstered navigational safety through hydrographic surveying, navigation aids, maritime security information-sharing, and training. Such coastal-state-led, user-state-supported mechanisms can be extended to port and submarine cable protection, information-sharing on alternative routes, and rescue cooperation, with user countries including China participating as well.
The second is critical minerals supply chains. In 2026, Japan successfully conducted a test extraction of rare earth mud from 6,000 meters depth in its Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) around Minamitorishima Island. Though still at the demonstration stage, it marks a step toward supply diversification. Japan should advance collaboration with ASEAN on separation and purification, environmental monitoring, processing, magnet and motor production, and waste-product recovery. Linking future Minamitorishima output with ASEAN mineral and processing capabilities would reduce excessive dependence on single sources.
Third is energy mutual aid. In 2025, ASEAN renewed the ASEAN Petroleum Security Agreement (APSA), which governs cooperation on emergency oil supply. Similar arrangements will also be needed for natural gas disruptions. Japan and ASEAN should consider joint stockpiling of crude oil and petroleum products, shared use of regional storage, emergency mutual accommodation, and LNG-vessel scheduling adjustments. Crisis response can be accelerated by integrating Japan’s stockpiling system with ASEAN’s emergency mechanisms.
The moment is right to expand cooperation with countries such as Australia, South Korea, India, and the EU, building outward from the Japan-ASEAN relationship. But this does not require creating an entirely new bloc. Maritime routes should involve user countries like China, critical minerals should draw in reliable supply-chain partners, and energy should engage both consumer countries and oil- and gas-producing states. A functional approach to open collaboration is realistic: membership varies by issue, with no single grouping required for all.
There is no need to build from scratch. In addition to the ASEAN-Japan Comprehensive Strategic Partnership and ASEAN Plus 3, the supply-chain agreement of the Indo-Pacific Economic Framework for Prosperity (IPEF), in which seven ASEAN countries participate, can serve the FOIP as well. The agreement enables signatories to share risks of critical-mineral supply disruptions, develop alternative sourcing, and coordinate emergency response procedures, with lessons that can inform broader ASEAN-wide cooperation under the AOIP.
What the Indo-Pacific needs is not exclusive blocs but a system of collective stability across sea lanes, resources, and energy. The updated FOIP can take root only by working in tandem with the AOIP and broadening ASEAN options. What Japan and ASEAN should aim for is “collective self-reliance”: the resilience to withstand pressure from any major power or supply disruptions from outside the region.

Cantonal Police Commander Michael Leupold told reporters that authorities are pursuing three hypotheses: a terrorist attack, a rampage, or a criminal act such as a settling of accounts in an as-yet-unknown milieu. No motive has been prioritized, and investigators are examining all possibilities.
Ballistic evidence shows shots were fired from two different locations at the scene. Police recovered shell casings of two calibers: pistol ammunition and casings from a long weapon, such as an assault rifle. A "significant number of shots" were reportedly discharged.
A large-scale nationwide manhunt is underway. Police believe the perpetrators have fled the Aarau area and do not currently pose an immediate threat. The operation has mobilized all available Aargau police forces, with support from other cantons, the special unit Argus, the cantonal disaster response element (KKE), and a Swiss Army Super Puma helicopter. German police are also participating in the search as part of routine cross-border cooperation.
As of Sunday evening, police had no concrete leads on the identity or number of the perpetrators, and they ruled out any renewed threat from the shooter(s). ■

Reusable rocket milestone opens a door for Hong Kong’s space ambitions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
21:30:05 UTC
06:30:05 KST

Reusable rocket milestone opens a door for Hong Kong’s space ambitions
Flurry of commercial activity offers opportunities for Hong Kong’s financial markets, research universities and the Northern Metropolis
On the morning of August 19, LandSpace’s Zhuque-3 Y2 rocket lifted off from the Dongfeng Commercial Space Innovation Test Area. After deploying its second stage and payload into orbit, the rocket’s first stage touched down softly at a recovery site in Gansu province using deployable landing legs.
It was China’s first successful land-based recovery of an orbital-class rocket booster that had just completed an orbital mission – a feat previously achieved only by SpaceX.
The benchmark for reusable rockets remains SpaceX’s Falcon 9, which pioneered vertical landing after launches of this kind and has conducted hundreds of recoveries. Through first-stage reuse, Falcon 9 has driven its launch price down to about US$2,700 per kg (US$1,225 per lb) – a reduction of 85 per cent from an average of US$18,500 in the pre-reusable era. In contrast, China’s commercial launch prices hover at between US$8,000 and US$14,000 per kg, depending on rocket type and mission profile.
The Zhuque-3 is explicitly designed to close that gap. Standing 66 metres tall with a lift-off mass of roughly 570 tonnes, its first stage is powered by nine methane-liquid oxygen engines. Its stainless-steel structure – a deliberate departure from Falcon 9’s aluminium alloy – offers better heat resistance at a lower manufacturing cost. The booster is designed to be reused at least 20 times.

====================================================================================================

The Reason Japan Cannot Commit to Dialogue with North Korea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
21:24:00 UTC
06:24:00 KST

Only two Japan-North Korea summit meetings have ever been held, both between Japanese Prime Minister Junichiro Koizumi and former North Korean leader Kim Jong Il, in September 2002 and May 2004. Since then, an inter-Korean summit was held in October 2007, followed by three more in 2018. U.S.-North Korea summits were held in June 2018, February 2019, and June 2019. Yet Japan and North Korea have not met at the summit level in over two decades.
What makes summit dialogue uniquely difficult for Japan is the abduction issue. From the 1970s through the 1980s, North Korean agents abducted a large number of Japanese citizens. The abduction of Megumi Yokota, a middle school student at the time, especially shocked Japanese society, and resolving the abduction issue has been declared a “high-priority issue” by every successive administration.
Japanese sanctions on North Korea are the heaviest in the world, yet they have not led to the return of a single abductee to Japan since the five abductees came home in October 2002. Japanese public opinion nonetheless persistently calls for heavier sanctions, driven by anger and distrust. This is despite the fact that it was dialogue, not sanctions, that secured Koizumi’s signal achievement: an apology from North Korean leader Kim Jong Il and the return of five abductees and their family members.
The issue is serious and complex. Even if North Korea were to allow Japanese nationals to return, claiming that “new abduction victims have been identified,” that would not produce unqualified satisfaction on the Japanese side. Distrust toward a country that has long insisted “the abductions have been resolved” would only deepen; and even if ten people were to return, the Japanese public would suspect there may be still more abductees. Japan has struggled for years with the question of what would constitute a “resolution” of the abduction issue, but it proved an impossible task given that human lives were at stake.
The key figure who made Koizumi’s historic visit to North Korea possible was Tanaka Hitoshi, the then Director-General of the Asian and Oceanian Affairs Bureau of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. He conducted nearly thirty secret meetings with the North Korean agent known as “Mr. X,” in China and other third countries. The meetings were so secret that even Shinzo Abe, then Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary, was not made aware of them.
After Kim Jong Il admitted to and apologized for the abductions and the five abductees were returned to Japan, public anger fell not only on North Korea but also on Tanaka. Not all abductees had returned, and it emerged that Tanaka had accepted a North Korean suggestion for a “temporary return” of roughly two weeks rather than permanent residency for the five abductees.
Tanaka likewise attracted Abe’s ire. Having taken a strong personal interest in the abduction issue, Abe could not forgive Tanaka for advancing negotiations without informing him. Tanaka was ultimately summoned to Diet deliberations, where he broke down in tears under withering criticism of how the negotiations had been handled. Despite having acted on the prime minister’s instructions, Tanaka received no defense from Koizumi, perhaps because public opinion was too hostile. Koizumi’s diplomacy toward North Korea deserves a more positive assessment than it has received, and it is regrettable that this episode cast such a long shadow. Tanaka was so thoroughly pilloried by Japanese conservatives as a “traitor” that this once-promising diplomatic ace never became vice-minister for foreign affairs or ambassador to the United States.
The affair had lasting consequences. It taught subsequent administrations that even if they were to seriously pursue North Korea diplomacy, public support would be hard to secure given widespread skepticism toward dialogue, and that even partial success, short of a “full resolution” of the abduction issue, would expose them to harsh criticism regardless.
Having witnessed the keelhauling of Tanaka, even the most talented Foreign Ministry officials will not actively pursue North Korea diplomacy. Japanese civil servants are divided from the moment of hiring into elite “career” and specialized “non-career” tracks, with the hierarchy between the two tracks never reversed. Career diplomats rotate postings every two to three years and are guaranteed advancement if they handle North Korea safely without taking risks. The perverse result is that the most capable diplomats are the least likely to actively pursue dialogue with Pyongyang.
This structural problem must be addressed before Japan can make progress on any of its outstanding issues with North Korea. Ultimately, overcoming the problem requires strong political leadership from the prime minister.

Israeli curriculum to replace Palestinian program in all East Jerusalem schools
For the first time since Israel annexed East Jerusalem in 1967, all newly opened grades in public schools in the Palestinian-majority area will use the Israeli curriculum when the school year begins Tuesday.
After East Jerusalem was annexed from Jordan, the education system in the Palestinian areas of the city remained part of the West Bank education system and taught the Jordanian curriculum, which was later replaced by the Palestinian curriculum.
This year – after a long process that began at the initiative of parents, followed by Israeli government pressure on school principals in the city – all new first grade and seventh grade classes opening in the state education system in East Jerusalem will use the Israeli curriculum.
More than 45,000 students of a total of roughly 120,000 Palestinian students in East Jerusalem (38 percent) will study the Israeli curriculum in the coming year. Until about 15 years ago, the percentage was in the single digits. Until even about six years ago, fewer than 13,000 students were taught using the Israeli curriculum.

The Israel Police said two armed suspects rammed a police car in the central West Bank, lightly injuring a police officer and a soldier before fleeing down Highway 60, a key north-south road transversing the West Bank.
Police said the officer and soldier spotted a vehicle that pulled over on the side of the road with two armed men standing beside it. According to the police, the suspects noticed the two men getting in their vehicle and fleeing toward the Palestinian village of al-Ram, north of Jerusalem.
The officer and soldier fired at the car's wheels in an attempt to make it stop, police said, adding that the men continued driving, causing a collision on the road.
Police said the Israeli military placed al-Ram on lockdown, sweeping the Palestinian Authority's Area B for the two suspects. Police added that they are looking into all possible motives, adding that security officials believe a "serious incident has been averted."
Security increased around Israel's elections chief
Israeli authorities have increased security around Central Elections Committee chairman, Justice Noam Sohlberg.
Israeli strikes kill five people in Gaza, medics say
Israeli airstrikes killed at least five Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, health officials said.
Medics said two people were killed and several others wounded when one strike hit a crowd near the municipal public park in Gaza City, an area packed with displaced families.
Later on Monday, another Israeli airstrike hit a vehicle in the Tel Al-Hawa neighbourhood in western Gaza City, killing at least three people, medics added.
The Israeli military said the two attacks targeted Hamas militants, without giving further information.
Police arrest two pharmacists at IDF intelligence base, suspect drug theft
The Israel Police arrested two pharmacists employed at the IDF's Glilot intelligence base on suspicion of stealing tens of thousands of medications, including prescription drugs, and selling them on the black market, police and the Israeli military said.
The IDF and the Israel Police said the arrests followed an undercover investigation, adding that the suspects were taken in for questioning on suspicion of theft by an authorized person and aggravated fraud.
Police are expected to request that the Tel Aviv Magistrate's Court extend their detention. According to the statement, other suspects, including soldiers, are being investigated by the Military Police Criminal Investigation Division, with the military prosecution overseeing the investigation.

A Historic Villa in Yangon Gets an Upgrade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
21:21:00 UTC
06:21:00 KST

The lounge room of the teak villa has a seated figure of the Bogyoke (General) absorbed in a book. A dining table is set with his favorite meal of steamed yellow peas with naan. An upstairs bedroom has a crib-style cot for his two-year-old daughter, Suu Kyi.
Objects displayed at the Bogyoke Aung San Museum in Yangon offer a snapshot of General Aung San’s domestic routine shortly before tragedy ripped the family apart.
On July 19, 1947, the de facto leader of British Burma was assassinated by gunmen a few months before the nation gained independence. Several cabinet members were also killed in the attack orchestrated by a political rival. A government official on the scene reportedly lamented, “Burma is finished.”
The current military-aligned government appears keen to highlight conservation efforts at Bogyoke’s official residence despite its strained relationship with his daughter and former pro-democracy leader Aung San Suu Kyi.
The European-style villa, with its distinctive turret, received an official seal of approval in the form of a bronze plaque in July, marking the house as a heritage building. The tourism ministry hopes the spruced-up Aung San museum, along with 6,000 other historic structures earmarked for conservation, will attract visitors from neighboring countries. International arrivals to Myanmar dipped below 1 million in 2025 compared to a record 4.7 million in 2015.
Min Aung Hlaing, Myanmar’s president and former army chief, visited the house a year ago and inspected the vintage Wolseley car parked in a teak garage near the entrance. He urged officials to plan for the “long-term preservation” of the vehicle. Aung San traveled to Shan State in the British-made car to finalize the Panglong Agreement, the 1947 treaty that led to the creation of the Union of Burma.
“It took us about a year to complete the reconditioning,” automobile researcher Moe Myint Win told the state-run Global New Light of Myanmar. With newly installed pistons, “it may even be drivable,” he added.
While the Tourism Ministry was busy drawing up conservation plans for Aung San’s residence, other symbols of the general’s legacy were disappearing.
Radio Free Asia and domestic media outlets reported that the government had removed several bronze statues of Aung San in recent months. A portrait at the front gate of Aung San Suu Kyi’s lakeside villa in Yangon was also taken down in June. President Min Aung Hlaing’s spokesperson issued a statement asserting that only “disproportionate or incorrectly shaped” statues had been removed to preserve the dignity of a “pivotal historical figure.”
Aung San’s statues have been “canceled” on both ends of the political spectrum. The installation of a golden image in Kayah (Karenni) State triggered protests by local activists in 2019 and was seen as an attempt to paper over “suppression of the past.” The Panglong Agreement granting autonomy to ethnic minority states had fallen by the wayside 60 years earlier as the government gravitated towards centralized control. The general’s political heirs “failed to keep Aung San’s promises of federalism,” observed a scholar-activist who writes about Rakhine State.
In the last decade, ethnic armies replaced political parties as the main drivers for autonomy “after the issue of federalism was forcefully put on ice by successive military governments,” wrote a political commentator from Shan State. Under the 1947 Constitution, Shan State was given the option to secede ten years after independence. Following a military coup in 1962, however, the constitution (which Aung San helped draft) was abolished, and certain states lost the legal right to leave the union.
The Yangon residence is a less controversial piece of Aung San’s legacy. Next July, the museum will mark the 80th anniversary of his assassination, commemorated annually as Martyrs Day. Students, monks, historians and a few international tourists will visit the renovated rooms, a crop patch, and the ornamental pond where one of his sons died in a drowning accident in 1953.
Aung San Suu Kyi last visited the villa in 2017. She was released from prison in April but remains under house arrest.

For Indonesia’s Digital Banks, It’s All About Who You Know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
21:11:00 UTC
06:11:00 KST

Indonesia has been one of the most supportive countries in Southeast Asia when it comes to the rise of digital banking. In 2016, the Jenius banking app was launched by Bank BTPN (later acquired by SMBC). It was one of Indonesia’s first large-scale digital banking apps, and grew very quickly. This coincided with a tech sector boom the government was keen to support, and financial services authority OJK quickly passed a regulation in 2018 allowing more commercial banks to provide digital banking services. This was followed by a 2021 regulation governing the launch of fully digital banks, which are standalone digital platforms rather than an offshoot of existing commercial banks.
Full digital banks perform the same functions as conventional banks – take deposits, make loans – but do so mainly through digital platforms. Because they do not need to maintain large networks of physical branches, they can theoretically operate with less overhead. Another potential advantage is that because most services are online, digital banks can offer a level of convenience and access that conventional banks can’t. This should allow them to scale faster and reach a wider customer base, including those who have never had an account at a traditional brick-and-mortar bank.
In recent years Indonesia has seen a proliferation of new, fully digital banks. The typical playbook is that a large tech company with deep pockets buys a small, existing regional bank and converts it to a fully digital outfit, then pumps it with capital and rapidly grows. Events, even in just a few short years, have moved very fast and made a few things clear.
One is that the sector is now starting to consolidate around three leading firms: Bank Jago, Superbank and Seabank. Two of the very earliest entrants, Bank Neo Commerce and Allo Bank, have stagnated somewhat which suggests that with pure digital banking, at least in Indonesia, the first-mover advantage is not necessarily decisive. More important, as we shall see, is who is backing your digital bank.
Among the emerging digital-bank players, Bank Neo Commerce was the largest by 2020 with IDR 5.4 trillion in assets, including IDR 3.7 trillion in loans. Neo Commerce Bank’s largest shareholder is Akulaku, one of the early digital wallet and fintech companies to breakout in Southeast Asia. Other digital banks launched around that time include Bank Jago, backed by Go-Jek and Singaporean sovereign wealth fund GIC; Seabank Indonesia, which is part of Sea the parent company of e-commerce giant Shopee; and Allo Bank, backed by Indonesian e-commerce company Bukalapak and a major local conglomerate.
Together, these four digital banks had combined assets of $780 million in 2020 (using an exchange rate of 17,500 IDR to 1 USD). One year later their combined assets leapt to $2.2 billion as they began leveraging existing networks of e-commerce and fintech customers to take deposits and make loans.
They were soon joined by Superbank, which is backed by an international consortium, including GXS Bank (owned by Singapore’s Singtel and ride-hailing giant Grab), South Korea’s KakaoBank and Indonesian technology and media conglomerate Emtek. Emtek owns Indonesia’s largest home-grown streaming platform, among many other assets.
The sector has experienced rapid growth, with totals assets of these five digital banks reaching $8.8 billion as of June 2026 including $5.5 billion in loans. Although all five banks reached profitably in 2025, the explosive growth has been increasingly driven by just the top three: Bank Jago, Sea, and Superbank. As of June 2026, Neobank’s assets were lower than in 2023, while Allo Bank also seems to be slowing.
By contrast, between 2023 and June 2026 assets rose 88 percent at Sea, 95 percent at Jago and 386 percent at Superbank. Sea has the biggest platform with $3 billion in assets, and Jago following with $2.3 billion. Amongst the three leading digital banks, loans and deposits are steadily growing, as are profits.
In a way, this shouldn’t be too surprising when we consider who the major shareholders are in these firms. Sea, Jago and Superbank are backed by some of the largest consumer-facing companies and investors in the region, with very large existing networks of e-commerce, media and telecom customers they can tap to onboard new digital banking customers. Allo and Neo Commerce Bank, meanwhile, are tied to firms like Akulaku and Bukalapak, which don’t dominate the consumer landscape in the same way.
The sector has grown rapidly in a very short period of time, and there are surely going to be new and surprising developments in the years ahead. But one thing is becoming increasingly clear: in Indonesia’s crowded digital banking race the size of your network and who is backing you may matter more than how quickly you can bring your app or product to market.

Right to question not defiance, every dissent not a threat: SC judge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
21:10:44 UTC
06:10:44 KST

'In a democracy, the right to question is not an act of defiance.': Justice Bhuyan
NEW DELHI: In a constitutional democracy like India, govt must listen to citizens, give space for dissent, and have institutions that are accountable to society and do not treat every dissent as a threat, Supreme Court judge Ujjal Bhuyan said on Sunday."In a democracy, the right to question is not an act of defiance. It is an essential expression of citizenship, liberty and constitutional responsibility," Justice Bhuyan said at a convocation ceremony at National Law University, Delhi."If we want a democratic society that respects liberty and difference, that culture has to begin somewhere. It can only begin in our universities. A university... should be one of the first places where the habit of thinking freely begins," he said.A university should be a space where an idea is not accepted merely because it is familiar and where students do not hesitate to ask difficult questions simply because the answer may be uncomfortable,” Justice Bhuyan said.He said India’s Constitution guarantees free speech, thinking and believing differently. “Intolerance begins to undermine that framework when disagreement or dissent is no longer treated as a legitimate difference of opinion but as something that must be silenced, rejected or punished.
The ability to live with disagreement is not merely a social virtue. It is the very essence of a liberal constitutional democracy.”Justice Bhuyan said maturity of a democracy is reflected not merely in how it treated opinions that are popular, having the majoritarian mandate, but also in how it responds to opinions that are difficult, unpopular or inconvenient. “The freedom to express an opinion, to disagree with the prevailing view and to participate in public life would be meaningful only when there is space for dissent,” he added.
He quoted Justice O Chinnappa Reddy’s 1986 judgment in Bijoe Emmanuel case, in which the judge had said, “Our tradition teaches tolerance; our philosophy preaches tolerance; our constitution practises tolerance; let us not dilute it.”He pointed out that tolerance under our Constitution does not ask us to surrender our individuality. “It recognises that a free society would contain different opinions, beliefs and ways of looking at the world,” he said.

For every 100 laundered, only 1 recovered by authorities: CJI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
20:57:29 UTC
05:57:29 KST

Economic crimes move faster than treaties; global cooperation key to recovery: CJI Surya Kant
NEW DELHI: Chief Justice of India Surya Kant said for every Rs 100 laundered, authorities and law enforcement agencies recovered only Re 1, mainly because of the ingenuity of economic offenders, and lack of global cooperation on extraditing fugitives.Money laundered globally in a year was more than enough to buy every single person on earth a modest laptop, CJI said at the 43rd International Symposium on Economic Crime in Cambridge Saturday. "...For every hundred parts of that wealth, ninety-nine are simply referred to in speeches and reports, while only one part is ever actually put right."CJI Surya Kant quoted ancient Indian statesman Kautilya’s Arthashastra, which had recorded that it was impossible for an official to handle the king’s revenue and take nothing from it, and provided for an antidote through audits, cross-verification and confiscation of ill-gotten gain.Referring to India’s layered legislations against economic crimes and its balancing by judicial interventions, the CJI said though India had signed extradition and mutual legal assistance treaties with foreign jurisdictions, “the property we actually recover remains, frankly, underwhelming”.
The CJI said that illicit wealth and economic crimes moved faster than the pace of ratification of treaties and, hence, no jurisdiction, however well resourced or determined, could pursue them alone, despite the existence of provisions for non-conviction based forfeitures, unexplained wealth orders, beneficial ownership registers and financial intelligence sharing.
“None of these tools is missing from our shelves. What is missing, and what each jurisdiction owes the other, is the willingness to use them together rather than one at a time: a forfeiture order in one country acted upon promptly by a registry in another, an intelligence tip followed through to an actual freeze rather than left to gather dust,” he further added.India had initiated processes for extraditions of Vijay Mallya with the UK authorities in 2017 and Nirav Modi with the US in 2018.None of them has fructified in extradition of the two, accused of misappropriating huge sums and fleeing the country.

Diabetes impacts men, women differently: Study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
20:40:49 UTC
05:40:49 KST

Study finds type 2 diabetes complications differ by gender: men face higher heart and kidney risks, women more likely to develop mental health conditions.
NEW DELHI: For men, type 2 diabetes more often sets the stage for heart and kidney disease; for women, the greater threat appears to be mental health problems, a new study tracking nearly 29,000 patients has found.The study, published in PLOS Medicine, followed 28,720 people newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes between 2010 and 2020 using linked primary and secondary healthcare records in the UK. Researchers used a multi-state analysis to track the order and timing of hypertension, cardiovascular disease, end-stage renal disease and mental health conditions over a median follow-up of 6.8 years. Women were more likely than men to be diagnosed with a mental health condition.Women were more likely than men to be diagnosed with a mental health condition, including anxiety, depression or somatoform disorders, after developing diabetes. Such conditions were recorded in 8.1% of women compared with 5.3% of men.Men, meanwhile, were more likely to develop cardiovascular disease or end-stage renal disease, with 8.4% following this trajectory compared with 5.3% of women.
Mental health risks are higher for women with diabetes as compared to men
Senior endocrinologist Prof Ravinder Goswami of All India Institutes of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) said diabetes can affect men and women differently.
Men may develop diabetes at a younger age, while women with diabetes lose the natural protection against heart disease that is usually seen before menopause. The study also found that women with diabetes may have a higher risk of problems related to memory, thinking and mental health.However, he cautioned that these problems may not be caused by diabetes alone, as cognitive and neuropsychiatric problems are generally more common in women. He said doctors should, therefore, watch for these issues while managing diabetes.Hypertension was the most common complication after type-2 diabetes across all age groups and in both sexes. It affected 21.1% of men and 20.2% of women. Men also experienced most complications earlier than women, while women generally had a later onset of events.The study linked diabetes, mental health and mortality, finding that people who developed a mental health condition after diabetes died earlier. Among those with the same disease trajectory, men died on average nine years younger than women.Despite this, women had higher average healthcare utilisation and long-term prescribing than men. The researchers said the lower healthcare use among men in the high-risk mental health trajectory could point to gaps in engagement with healthcare services.
The findings point to the need for sex-specific diabetes care, including routine mental health screening, particularly for younger women, and earlier cardiovascular and kidney monitoring for men.The researchers further added that tracking the sequence and timing of complications could help identify patients at higher risk and enable earlier intervention. However, as an observational study, the findings cannot establish cause and effect, and differences in mental health diagnoses may partly reflect healthcare-seeking behaviour.
Anuja Jaiswal is a Senior Assistant Editor at The Times of India, with an impressive 18-year career in narrative journalism. She specializes in health and heritage reporting, expertly simplifying complex health information to make it engaging and understandable for readers. Her deep dives into heritage topics are well-researched, resulting in captivating narratives that resonate with her audience. Over the years, she has worked in Chandigarh, Chhattisgarh and West UP, gaining diverse on-ground experience that shapes her storytelling.
